en: The Collection of Treatises by Ratnakīrti
// Proof of the Omniscient One //
Homage to Tārā! Disrespect toward her leads to rebirth in hell, while devotion grants all that is desired.
He who is the unimpeded sole kinsman of the world is known here as the omniscient and stainless one.

For here, Kumārila—even though he does not desire one who knows all things without exception—acknowledges that one who knows only *dharma* is indeed sufficient; yet, while maintaining that the Veda is to be accepted only when such knowledge of *dharma* is established, he recites:
"But the negation of the knowledge of *dharma* alone is what is relevant here;
for who can prevent a person from knowing everything else?"

Thus, although this Teacher also desires a world as vast as space, graced by the dust from the feet of every omniscient being, he nevertheless speaks while internally reflecting that the repelling of all the doctrines of the wicked— headed by the mass of unauthoritative, dull-witted Vedic words— is achieved through the elucidation of the Lotus-like Person who knows the truth of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with its attendants, and who has become the crest-jewel of the three worlds.
He who makes known the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means thereto,
is accepted as a valid authority (pramāṇa), but not one who knows everything.
And so forth.
Therefore, let us first establish that he is simply omniscient regarding what is required;
eventually, however, we shall also dispel the desire for him to be omniscient regarding everything.
Be at ease.
Whatever mental quality is accompanied by practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-term is capable of becoming vividly manifest;
for example, the form of a young woman to a lustful man.
These mental qualities regarding the objects of the Four Noble Truths are likewise accompanied by the aforementioned practice; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In this regard, there is no possibility of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*) either by way of its locus (*āśraya*) or by way of its nature (*hetu*).

This is because the fact that the aspects of the Four Noble Truths, when firmly established through conceptualization, possess the mere quality of being mental states, is something to be personally realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedya*).
Nor is the qualification of the reason—characterized by practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-term—anything that cannot be conceived.

For it is thus: this cultivation of the aspects of the Four Noble Truths, undertaken as an ascent of resolve (*saṃkalpa*), has been begun in order to remove the excessive suffering that is the very nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
What, then, is this so-called "incredulity" (*asaṃbhāvanā*) regarding it?

(2) because it is impossible for that which is to be cultivated to be mounted upon conceptual construction; (3) because of a lack of desire [for it]; and (4) because there is no ascertainment of its nature as something to be abandoned.
(5) because that which is to be abandoned is eternal;
(6) because it is causeless;
(7) because its cause is eternal.

(8) due to the lack of thorough knowledge regarding the object of negation and its cause; (9) due to the absence of a sublater thereof; (10) due to the lack of thorough knowledge regarding the sublater.
(11) because the mind is of the nature of defects,
(12) because its qualities are fixed, and (13) because there is no other existence.
Or [the fault might arise] from the re-emergence of a fault that had been destroyed; thus there are thirteen alternatives.
In this regard, the first position is not tenable;

for that which is to be cultivated—the nature of the four noble truths consisting of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted along with their attendants—is accessible to individual self-awareness once it has been mounted upon conceptual construction.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for it is established by the experience of all people that even the mere abandonment of suffering is desired.
Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because the nature of the self within saṃsāra is perceived as being of the very essence of suffering.
If it is asked, "How is it that this has the nature of suffering? [the answer follows].
In brief,
it has been directly stated that hell is of the very nature of suffering, as are the forms of hungry ghosts and animals; even the happiness found here among mortals is everywhere consumed by misery.
And when the gods' provisions for their journey—merit—have come to an end, alas, those very same enjoyments emit a conflagration of fierce flames. Thus it is said.
Nor is it the fourth [alternative],
because suffering, which consists of the five present aggregates, is observed to arise.
Nor is it the fifth [alternative],
because suffering occurs only occasionally.
Nor is the sixth [alternative] tenable;
for the occasional nature of an effect is pervaded by having an impermanent cause.
Nor is there a seventh [cause].

This is because it is certain that the effect characterized by the five aggregates of cyclic existence cannot otherwise arise from a cause characterized by the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), which is accompanied by suffering, cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the activity of the faculties (*pravṛtti-śakti*), and karma.

First there is the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*); following that, the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*); from the production of both of these arise passion (*rāga*) and so forth; and from the mind afflicted by those two arises the fire of hatred (*dveṣa*).
From that, there remains affliction; from that, through the proliferation of emerging karma, there spreads a most dreadful saṃsāra, devoid of refuge.
Therefore, craving and cognitive distortion are determined— by means of their effects as causes— to be preceded by the view of self and to be the producers of the aggregates within cyclic existence.
Furthermore, that the view of a self is ignorance should be understood from the refutation of the self itself;
for even in its absence, the existence of future lives and so forth was established without contradiction during the discussion on momentary destruction.
Nor is there an eighth [alternative], because the vision of selflessness— which serves as the antidote to ignorance in the form of the view of a self— is possible. (Nibandh 3)
Nor is it the ninth,
because the vision of selflessness, which is denoted by the word "path," has been ascertained through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The tenth [alternative] is also impossible,
because at the stage of having faults, the mind depends upon conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*).
For that which has a certain intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not depend upon conditioning factors when it is established in that very nature.

Just as gold, having had its impurities removed, remains in a state of inexhaustibility, so too the mind—while in the state of ignorance—depends upon formative forces (*saṃskāra*). This is an "observation of the contradictory of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Since independence from formative forces is the pervader of that which is to be negated—the mind's nature of being free from defects—the dependence [on them] is its opposite; thus, the mind's character of being composed of defects is undermined.
The eleventh [position] is also untenable,
because we observe that when there is an excellence of specific mental formations (*saṃskāra*), there is a corresponding excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Nor is there a twelfth [moment], because the next world is established [thereby]. For it is thus:
whatever mind exists, that very mind links itself to another moment of mind.
Just like the present mind;
and since the mind exists at the time of death, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] by means of the final mind of an Arhat.
The existence of future birth is established because [the self] is known through scripture alone,
or because it gives rise to another mind free from afflictions,
or because the reason is qualified by the condition "when afflictions exist."
Thus, whatever is a mind is preceded by another mind, just like the present mind;
and since the mind exists at the moment of birth, it follows by implication that this is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*), thereby establishing the existence of a past life.
Nor is there a thirteenth [alternative],
because the vision of selflessness— which is the opposite of the vision of a self that is the cause of faults— is free from affliction and accords with reality.
And because it possesses intrinsic nature and exists at all times,
this reason is not unestablished even with respect to its qualification.
If it is argued that such practice is not seen in anyone at all, we reply:
let it not be seen;
however, its possibility cannot be denied.
Furthermore, since the current activity of people remains unimpeded, nothing further can be inferred;
for this very reason, this is called an inference based on probability (saṃbhāvanānumāna).
Nor is this reason contradictory,
because it is present in the similar class (sapakṣa), namely in the form of a beloved woman;
nor is it inconclusive.

When the causal relationship between the quality of a mind accompanied by practice and a vivid manifestation is established through perception and non-perception by means of a complete induction— just as in the case of a pot and a potter— the pervasion is established because the probans, namely "being a quality of a mind accompanied by practice," possesses the capacity to produce a vivid manifestation.

For instance, in the locus of pervasion—the form of a young woman present before one afflicted by desire—there is first the non-perception of the vivid appearance due to the quality of the mind resulting from diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term practice;
subsequently, there is the experience of the practice, which is the experience of the vivid appearance.

Thus, the causal relationship established through the three types of perception and non-perception is applicable here between the mental aspect and the practice accompanied by the vivid manifestation; this constitutes a pervasion that encompasses all cases.
Therefore, even the charge of inconclusiveness is impossible; thus, the reason is faultless.
Now, how can there be any hope for establishing an omniscient being through inference?

Since that being is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), the logical mark (*liṅga*) connected with it cannot be ascertained. Furthermore, in proving the existence of an omniscient being, every reason (*hetu*) inevitably falls into one of three types of fallacy.
For if the subject (*dharmin*) is omniscient, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*);
if it is not omniscient, it is contradictory (*viruddha*);
and even if it possesses both natures, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Moreover, since the perception of an effect as clearly manifest arises from the cause of repeated practice, it is inconclusive that causes must necessarily possess their effects.
If, on the other hand, it is the capacity for becoming clearly manifest that is being inferred,
that too is called a "power" (śakti).
And that [non-apprehension] is either immediate to the effect or separated from it;
therein, the former is apprehended through the effect itself.
Furthermore, for one who has already apprehended the effect, there is no utility whatsoever in that [non-apprehension].
But the second [type of reason] would not establish the ascertainment of the effect with certainty.
Furthermore, the determination of fitness is not possible without the cognition of the effect;
nor does the proponent of the proof fulfill his purpose by establishing mere fitness alone,
because the dispute regarding the effect— namely, the knowledge of the omniscient one— remains as it was.
Granted that the proof of clarity [of cognition] is established;
nevertheless, what is the occasion for one who has begun a proof in the dispute over omniscience to attempt to prove the clarity of the mind?

Furthermore, in the case of a well-known inference, since both the subject (*dharmin*), such as the ground, and the two properties (*dharma*), such as the potter and the jar, are perceived, the causal relationship can indeed be apprehended.

In the present case, however, because the subject— the form of a young woman existing within the continuum of one afflicted by desire— and its two properties— proximity to that [object] and clarity through repeated practice—
are themselves imperceptible, how can there be an apprehension of the causal relationship?

And just as you say to the Naiyāyika that by perception it is not established that every effect in general is pervaded by a person, but rather that only a specific kind of effect, such as a jar, [is so pervaded], in the same way, it is quite clear that it is not established that every form in general is preceded by practice,
but rather only a specific general form, such as that of a young woman.
Furthermore, clarity is not the result of repeated practice,
because it is observed even in dreams despite the absence of such practice.

Furthermore, if the state of omniscience for one who knows all things consists in the thorough knowledge of the four noble truths, then the state of omniscience would also apply to one who knows only a few objects such as a jar; this would be a commendable form of purity! Moreover, someone possessing knowledge is sought out for the sake of practicing what they have taught.
By those who, fearing deception, act upon the instructions of the ignorant.
Thus it is said by you yourselves;
yet one who possesses all-knowledge cannot be apprehended through the determination of specific attributes,
nor is there any utility in establishing his mere existence.
Because it is not a constituent part of the process of engagement, everything [you have asserted] is inconsistent.

To this it is replied: We do not admit that the logical reason functions directly toward the proposition of the existence of an omniscient being, as in the case of the existence of fire dependent on a mountain.

Rather, it is for the purpose of excluding the impossibility (*ayogavyavaccheda*) of the probandum—namely, clarity of manifestation—with respect to the subject whose nature consists of the aspects of the four noble truths, just as one excludes the impossibility of mere fire with respect to a mountain.
The quality of appearing vividly, however, is indeed observed in the example of the form of a beloved woman and so forth;
and that [quality], like the fire on the mountain, establishes—
by the force of its presence as a property of the subject— that the four truths have a real locus, which we declare to be omniscience.
As it has been said:

"By the power of such practice, that very state which is all-knowing—manifesting as the ten peaks of the perfectly clear stage, and possessing the qualities characterized by what is to be abandoned, what is to be adopted, and their respective limbs—is our [goal]. Thus.

In this case, the subject (*dharmin*) is the entirety [of the mind] characterized by the aspects of the four noble truths accompanied by cultivation; the reason (*hetu*) is merely the state of being a mental quality distinguished by cultivation; and the probandum (*sādhya*) is the fitness for the manifestation [of the result].
This is just as, when there is doubt regarding whether a mountain possesses fire or lacks fire, the subject is the mountain itself as it is cognized through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Likewise, here too, in the dispute concerning omniscience and non-omniscience, the subject (*dharmin*) is the nature of the four noble truths as personally realized within oneself.

Therefore, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the probandum—the state of appearing clearly—is established in the example, there is indeed the ascertainment of the logical mark (*liṅga*) connected to that [probandum].
Even when there is doubt regarding the probandum, because the subject—the nature of the four noble truths—is established, there is no occasion for the three types of fallacies.
Furthermore, the claim that the cognition of an effect from its cause is inconclusive due to the establishment of "capacity" (yogyatā) is refuted by our own non-acceptance [of that premise].
Moreover, it is precisely "with an interval" (sāntara) that capacity is established.
And even if this [capacity] does not necessarily imply the existence of the effect, [it remains valid].
Furthermore, the impossibility of its [the effect's] arising necessarily implies its non-existence.
Thus, even when there is doubt regarding a future effect, the suitability of the cause is indeed ascertained;
for one proceeds toward rice and the like based on the ascertainment of their suitability, even though the future fruit is not yet certain.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even fragments of stone and the like could serve as the material cause [of a cognition].

If it is argued that the capacity of something belonging to that same class—such as clay placed in a bowl—is observed, then here too it is the same: the suitability for making the form of a beloved woman manifest through a process of cultivation belonging to that same class has been observed.
Thus, the proponent of the proof has achieved his purpose merely by establishing the capacity [of the cause];
for he has demolished those who deny the existence of an omniscient cause,
and has established the possibility of the effect throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the engagement of those seeking liberation;
for even the proponent intends to establish only that [liberation].
Therefore, objections such as "What occasion is there for establishing manifest existence when debating the existence of an omniscient being? also find no footing.
Because by the term "omniscient" (sarvajña) what is intended is the capacity for the manifestation [of knowledge],
the perception of cause and effect is indeed possible in this way.

For instance, the observation of the agitated body and speech accompanying the continuous practice of a lover is itself the observation of the form of that lover and of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) thereof.
The non-perception of the body and speech as they truly are is precisely the non-perception of cultivation.
Likewise, the perception of a distinguished body and speech accompanied by a continuous stream of vivid appearances is the perception of vivid appearances.

The non-perception of the body and speech as they actually abide is precisely the non-perception of vivid appearances; thus, even in the present case, the causal relationship is indeed understood through direct perception and non-perception.

Furthermore, this established rule regarding the perception of a clear manifestation— arising from the repeated practice of the form of a young woman who is but a part of that [composite body]— must necessarily be accepted by those engaged in worldly convention when perceiving the speech or body of one afflicted by desire in such a state.

Otherwise, since visual perception— which grasps only a single part of the form of a pot, a location, or the like, which consist of a collection of atoms of color, taste, smell, and touch, as well as consciousness and its objects— would not establish the whole, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all conventional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, since external objects such as jars and women can belong to vastly different classes due to their inherent potencies (*śakti*), it is illogical to infer an intelligent agent from one class of object when one has grasped a pervasion based on another class.

However, mental constructs (*saṃkalpārūḍha*)—such as the forms of water, fire, or a young woman—even when superimposed as external, possess a single common nature insofar as they consist solely of consciousness. Therefore, let there be a pervasion with clarity based on the mere form accompanied by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Nor is there a deviation from clarity in dreams;

for even when there is an illusion of identity between the effects of two causes—namely, those characterized by cultivation and those established by nature—their difference in genus must necessarily be admitted.
Indeed, it is observed that the genus of clarity, whether accomplished or being accomplished, is interrupted by the interruption of sleep without depending on contrary cultivation.
However, that which arises through cultivation does not occur without the practice of the counteragent, even for one who is awake; as they say,
"Clarity in a dream is likewise [dependent on such practice]," yet nevertheless, there is no identity between these two.
The equality of the genus is understood as being just like the wall;

one [aspect] is subject to destruction and cessation, while the other is suppressed by efforts, yet it becomes clear again through the power of contrary cultivation, just as in the case of the distinction between cruelty. Thus it is said.
As for what was said— that one would become omniscient even through the knowledge of a few things such as a jar— even in that case,
if fear were abandoned upon knowing everything relevant to the jar and so forth,
what fault would there be? He too would attain omniscience.
Longing for liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, we shall once again resort to him who knows the means thereto, in order to remain upon the path he has proclaimed.
Thus the reply is to be understood.
Likewise, for those who disagree regarding mere existence, only existence itself has been established;

however, when there is a desire to know the specific details, the omniscience belongs only to the Blessed One, the Sugata, who maintains the doctrine of momentariness and selflessness as proven by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, this objection raised by Bhaṭṭa is also refuted:
"If Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not?
Or, if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them?"
Therefore, according to the system of the King of Sages, valid cognition manifests both immeasurable scope and compassion through the aforementioned sequence;
whereas in other systems, both of these are discarded. Thus, he alone who propounds the doctrine of selflessness is the sole refuge.

Thus, the establishment of this specific distinction is also faultless; yet those whose minds are agitated do not comprehend this entire matter as being free from confusion. Even though this proof is irreproachable, those whose intellects have been scorched by the fire of fallacious reasoning (durnīti) declare once again:

"The conventional designation of non-existence for an omniscient being is logical because of the existence of subverting evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa), or else it is because of the absence of establishing evidence (prasādhaka-pramāṇa)."

In this regard, it is investigated: what, then, is the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) for this Blessed One—is it perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), verbal testimony (śabda), or something else? Such are the alternatives.
First of all, it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For perception, when operating upon a bare location and so forth, negates only that object which is suitable for its own operation there;
it does not negate the mere existence of an object.
Furthermore, there is no possibility for the operation of direct perception with respect to the Omniscient One,
because He is remote by nature.
This might be so: we do not say that perception, while operating, establishes non-existence;
rather, it is [perception] when it ceases [to operate].
For instance, when perception ceases with respect to a given object, that object is non-existent,
as in the case of a rabbit’s horn and the like;
whereas when perception operates with respect to an object, that object is existent, as in the case of a jar and the like.
And since there is an absence of perception regarding an omniscient being,
who can prevent his non-existence as well?
It is said: what is the meaning of the statement that "perception, while ceasing, establishes non-existence"?
Does the establishment of non-existence arise from the very cessation of perception, or from perception accompanied by its cessation?
Or [the argument might be] "from the cessation of perception.

The first position is not tenable; for even when an object exists, since the cessation of perception is observed, it is not established that this cessation is necessarily concomitant with the non-existence of the object.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it is impossible for anything to coexist with intrinsic nature;
otherwise, its cessation would be impossible.
Nor is it the third [alternative];
for, since the establishment of non-existence occurs from a ceased perception, it follows that it is from a non-existent perception.
And the status of being a cause is not possible for that which is non-existent.
Because that [non-perception] is characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity,
it is not logical to claim that "it does not exist" and yet there is a cognition of it.
Therefore, perception cannot, for its part, serve as a sublater of the omniscient being.
Nor is it inference;
for that is of three kinds by virtue of being produced from a threefold mark (*liṅga*).
Among these, since the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*) are means of proving an affirmation (*vidhi*), [inference does not apply here].
When negation is the probandum, there is no opportunity [for such a proof];

nor is the non-perception of the perceptible, its specific varieties such as the non-perception of the effect and so forth, or the non-perception of the capable—as intended by the opponent—a valid means of knowledge here.
This is because omniscience, being remote in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakṛṣṭa*), is imperceptible.
But surely, the negation of omniscience is established simply through the non-perception of its cause;
for that cause must be either sensory cognition, mental cognition, or that which arises from the power of cultivation— and even that which arises from the power of cultivation must be visual, or...
Or is it mental? These are the alternatives.
In that regard, visual consciousness cannot grasp all objects, because its domain consists of specific, determined objects.
In other places and at other times, there is likewise a fixed determination;
otherwise, there would follow the consequence that the relationship between cause and effect would be non-existent,
as well as the consequence that the plurality of sense faculties would be purposeless.
And so says the *Kārikā*:
"He who imagines that an omniscient being exists by means of the cognition of a single sense-faculty surely perceives all tastes and other objects with his eye."
"By whatever kinds of means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) people of this world perceive objects of such-and-such a kind at present, so it was also in other times."
And therefore, the formal argument (prayoga) should be stated as follows:
The Buddha-eye does not have the past and so forth as its object,
because it is a visual faculty (cakṣus).
Like the eye of a person below [in the hells],
or like one who has no eyes at all.
Because it has as its object the past and so forth,
like sound;
all of this should also be understood to apply to the auditory faculty and the others.
The excellence of the eye and other senses is not observed to transcend their own respective objects;
even where an excellence is observed in a verse, it does so because it does not overstep its own object.
There would be [cognition] regarding distant or subtle objects and so forth, but not regarding color-form (rūpa), because of the functioning of the auditory faculty [in that regard].
And the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* states:
"An excellence in a person is observed through the perception of sounds that are distant or subtle when they reach the ear; it is not [observed] from the perception of visible forms and so forth."

Furthermore, even by means of the eye, the perception of subtle forms located at a distance is achieved through the attainment of excellence; however, there is no such seeing of sound and other objects.
Nor should this be said:

"Even if indeed each individual sense organ or its corresponding cognition does not grasp everything, nevertheless, through the five sense organs or their cognitions—each operating upon its own respective object and having attained excellence—all will be grasped.
For it is observed that even a single [organ or cognition] does not grasp its own object in its entirety.

Furthermore, because it does not apprehend supersensuous objects such as the minds of others, neither the sense organ nor the sensory consciousness can grasp everything; thus, the first position is not tenable.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for although that mental [cognition] has all objects as its domain, it nevertheless lacks an independent operation in the apprehension of objects,
because the mind possesses no independence with respect to external things.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth, since the mind exists in them as well. Furthermore, if [the mind] were dependent [on the senses], its objects would be limited to those things already grasped by sensory cognition; consequently, there could be no discernment by the mind of such objects as the past, the future, the distant, the subtle, the concealed, or the minds of others, which are beyond the range of sensory perception.
If it is not attained, how can there be omniscience?
Nor is it the case that what is born of the power of cultivation grasps all objects; this is the third position.
For if that which is born of the power of cultivation were also dependent on the sense faculties, then it would be the fourth position, and in that case, it would be inconsistent.
Because it is established that both the sense faculty and its corresponding cognition have a restricted object as their domain.
Now, the fifth position is that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) produced in such a way through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*) apprehends all objects;

however, since the term "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is etymologically derived from its literal meaning, and because that [mental consciousness], even when supported by the power of cultivation, is not born of the sense organs (*anakṣaja*), it must be demonstrated that it lacks the quality of being a direct realization of the object.
Furthermore, excellence is observed only without overstepping the boundaries of its own specific object.
But it is not by way of having all things as its object. How, then, could there be cognition of the entire range of objects and so forth through that [perception] alone?
For it is never observed that anyone, even through practice, attains the vision of supersensuous objects.

Bṛhaṭṭīkā: Even those men who are seen to possess excellence through their wisdom, intelligence, and strength, do not perceive supersensible objects, because their superiority consists only of very slight degrees of difference.
Even a wise man, though capable of perceiving subtle matters,
does not surpass others without transcending his own kind.
Whatever occurs within the direct perception of one situated in a single room,
his capacity would apply only to that very place, and certainly not to another room.
And as for those objects separated by great distances— by lands, mountains, and oceans,
or by other continents and regions— who here on earth could perceive them while remaining right here?
In this context, "year" refers to a specific period of time.
Thus, a great excellence is observed in the investigations of one's own scripture;
however, knowledge of other scriptures is not established by that alone.
Having understood that the science of grammar is far removed from the discernment of correct and incorrect words,
one's intellect is not drawn toward determining the lunar mansions, lunar days, and planetary conjunctions.
Even an eminent astronomer, regarding the eclipses of the moon and sun and so forth,
is not capable of knowing the grammatical correctness of words such as "ādi" (and so on).
Likewise, even one possessing superior knowledge of the Vedas, histories, and so forth,
is not capable of directly perceiving heaven, the deities, or *apūrva*.
One who can leap through the air a distance of ten cubits is not able to travel a single league even with hundreds of practices;
therefore, even those who have reached an extreme distance through superior knowledges [cannot go further].
Only something slightly beyond [the senses] can be known, but not that which is entirely beyond the senses.
Thus it is said.
In the *Pratyakṣasūtra*, however, the author of the *Kāśikā*, having raised an objection based on another's view, says: "That is not so,
because mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has as its object that which has already been cognized."
Furthermore, the arising of cognition cannot occur without a cause,
because all things that possess an origin must have a cause.
If it is argued that [the object] is manifested by means of another source of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply:]...
What is the use of cultivation? For that [result] is established from that very [source]. Moreover, what is its means of valid cognition?

Inference cannot [establish] dharma and adharma, because, since they have not been previously apprehended, it is impossible to perceive a logical mark (liṅga) that is pervaded by them. Even from the presumption (arthāpatti) based on the diversity of the world, one can only infer that "there exists some cause"; however, no specific [nature of that cause] is established.
Furthermore, there can be no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose object is not specified by its particular characteristics;
for even in the treatises on yoga (*yogaśāstra*), it is precisely these specific characteristics that are taught as the objects of meditation (*dhyeya*).
"The Self is the Lord who is to be meditated upon, who dwells in the heart like a lamp."

[This is] by such [statements as these]. If, then, it is understood from scripture (āgama), it will be cultivated; but if it is from a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), then since it is already understood from that very [means], [what would be the point of cultivation]?
What is the use of cultivation?
For an object is investigated for the sake of its abandonment or acquisition,
and those two are already established from that [investigation] itself.
Thus, meditation is useless;
for even one who is compassionate would merely explain the scriptures of the Dharma to his disciples,
rather than undergoing the various stages of meditative cultivation.
Now, one who, because scriptures abound in contradictions, doubts whether scripture is a valid means of knowledge or not, seeks to know this through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
That is not so;
for even by that means, it remains unestablished.
Even knowledge fully accomplished through the power of meditative cultivation has an object that is not to be relied upon,
because it manifests even that which is unreal as if it were a directly perceived object.
For it has been said by those very [masters]:
Therefore, whether it be real or unreal,
whatever is intensely meditated upon results, upon the completion of that meditation, in the form of a clear manifestation of the tree of conceptual construction.
Moreover, that which arises from the power of cultivation is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*),
because it apprehends what has already been apprehended;
for whatever has already been apprehended is precisely what is made an object of cultivation through meditative development.
Even by a slight measure, meditation does not take what is excessive as its object;
for it is precisely memory—arising from the proficiency of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced through the practice of yoga—that is designated as "meditation" (*bhāvanā*).
And it is already established that this [meditation] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no evidence that a direct perceptual cognition (*sākṣātkārijñāna*) arises at a time subsequent to that [scriptural knowledge];
for we never observe the direct perception of an object in the absence of sense-object contact.
Thus, yogis do not possess a cognition in which dharma and adharma appear as immediate (*aparokṣa*).
Because of the absence of sense-faculty contact, as is the case with people like us.
Vācaspati, however, says in the *Kaṇikā*:
"We do not deny that cultivation (*bhāvanā*) which ranges within the domain of what is heard [from scripture] and inferred is the cause of clear cognition.
However, only that class of objects which has been previously apprehended becomes the object of clear realization."
The excellence of the cultivation of form can never lead to the clarity of the consciousness of the object of taste.
Is it not the case that we do not assert that cultivation is the cause for the clarity of other objects?
Rather, we maintain that it is solely the cause for the clarity of the objects of scripture and inference.

And its object is the selflessness of all things; thus, the intensification of that cultivation, by making manifest the selflessness of all things, brings about the manifestation of all things, because that [manifestation of selflessness] is impossible without the manifestation of all things—this has been said.
It is true that this has been said, but it is incorrect.
For indeed, things that are devoid of self, though they are distinct entities existing in the ultimate sense, do not fall within the scope of scripture or inference.
For these two [means of knowledge] cannot take as their object the ultimately real particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which consists merely in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Nor can meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) have that [particular characteristic] as its object.

If it is argued that although the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not directly apprehended by that [conceptual cognition], it is nonetheless its object because it is determined by it; and since meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has that [particular] as its source, it too has that as its object, and thus the excellence of that cultivation is the cause for the clarity of that [particular];
[we reply: no, because even that which is determined by it lacks ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*).
For instance, both that which is apprehended by inference and that which is determined are exclusions of others (*anyāpoha*), not real entities (*vastu*).
Because if it were to penetrate the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression would be impossible.
Let it not be that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of those two; rather,
it will be the object of the mind that arises at the culmination of the excellence of cultivation produced by them, which possesses a clear appearance.

Just as for one afflicted by passion, the direct perception of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a beloved woman arises from the intensity of meditation on mental constructs (*vikalpa*) of her; so [I pray]:

O you who captivate with jar-like breasts as firm as an elephant’s frontal globes, whose eyes are as tremulous as those of a young deer, whose creeper-like body is as pure as a *campaka* petal, and who are a lake of loveliness—grant me an embrace, O most beloved of women, at the base of your lovely sprout-like arms that cling closely to my limbs!
True;
this experience is possible, yet its validity regarding the object is not possible,
because that which does not arise from that object and is not of the nature of that object cannot be subject to a rule of non-deviation from it.
Furthermore, there is no identity between the object and consciousness because the object exceeds [the nature of] consciousness;
and even if it did not exceed it, there would still be no identity because one consciousness differs from another,
since it is impossible for a single consciousness to experience another consciousness.

Furthermore, if one accepts that consciousness has a single intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would follow that one must practice the meditation on that eternal, unitary, and non-dual Brahman; thus, the acceptance of the practice of momentariness and selflessness (*kṣaṇikanairātmya*) would be rendered null and void.
Therefore, [the inference] is not non-deviant because of identity with that [consciousness], nor is it so because of being its effect.
This is indeed the effect of the intensification of cultivation (bhāvanā), not the effect of the object itself.

If it were argued that this is its effect through a causal chain, as in the case of inference— for instance, from the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of fire arises the specific characteristic of smoke— then [the following applies]:

First there is the experience of smoke, then the conceptualization of fire, and from that, inference arises; thus, through this succession, it leads to the attainment of fire because of its connection with it, and [it leads] to fire which performs burning and cooking.

In the same way, this [cognition] also—which arises at the culmination of the intensification of the cultivation produced by inference—is, through a succession originating from the object, [a means of valid cognition].

"Because of the rule of its non-deviation from that [object], it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) therein. If one asks: "Is it then the case that for one who has established fire through inference and then cultivates [the meditation], that highly vivid cognition (*mati-viśada-vijñāna*) whose object is fire is the valid means of knowledge?"—if one says "yes," then it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that when one ascends the mountain slope, the cognition of fire produced by sensory contact must necessarily coincide with the vivid cognition resulting from the predominance of cultivation (*bhāvanādhipatya*).
Furthermore, contradiction is frequently encountered;

and since deviation is possible even when there is a connection with the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), that very characteristic is sublated. Thus, even a cognition that appears clear is invalid, as it is overcome by doubt—much like a mere intuitive flash (*prātibha*).
Therefore, the fact that the cultivation of that [object] has a real object (*bhūtārtha*) is not the cause for the validity of the clear cognition arising from it.
Because of this deviation,

it follows that the Tathāgata’s direct realization of all things as being without self is like the realization of a wealth of riches by a beggar, brought about by a succession of desires for obtaining the root-cause of acquiring a vessel of barley-meal.

If it is argued that consciousness, which exists within a mental continuum refined by the cultivation of all objective entities, possesses the status of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mere object, and that there is thus a rule of non-deviation because [consciousness] arises from that [object], we say: no. For the status of an object as an object-condition with respect to consciousness is pervaded by its dependence upon the sense-faculties (*indriya*).

And that [cognition], being excluded from this [object] by the perception of its own contrary (*svaviruddhopalabdhi*), also negates the object's status as an objective support-condition (*ālambanapratyayatā*).
Indeed, a specific kind of fuel, though it is the cause of smoke, does not produce smoke even with a thousand refinements if fire is absent.
Furthermore, if [the object] were the basis for that [cognition], it would follow that all inference based on causes would be destroyed.

Moreover, since it is observed that a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward a real object possesses the capacity to produce a clear cognition even without depending on the external object—as in the case of one afflicted by desire and so forth—it follows that even when directed toward a real object, it is capable independently of it. Thus, it is impossible to establish that the object functions as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Moreover, it is logical that only those moments which are its immediate predecessors—being unseparated from it—are its object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Thus, only these are its objects of apprehension, and not those further back in time; nor are those simultaneous with it or those yet to come. Therefore, there is no cognition of all objects.

Now, since living beings belonging to the three realms who are currently being perceived have as their nature an appropriation (*upādāna*) and that which is appropriated (*upādeya*)— namely, the collection of past and future aggregates (*skandha*) acquired through the transition of other births—
the perception of them, by virtue of its identity with what is being perceived, takes as its object even the past and the future through those qualifiers.
Nor does it follow that the perception of people such as ourselves must likewise be of that same nature.

Because it is obscured by stains such as passion (*rāga*), the Blessed One’s consciousness—which has completely rubbed away the stains of all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśopakleśa*)—is unobstructed and shines forth everywhere; it should take as its objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) the entire range of objects in all their aspects.

And because it is somehow connected with everything, both directly and indirectly, it should likewise take as its object the very nature of all things, distinguished by their specific qualities, even when scattered across space and time.
And since this [omniscience] does not occur without the grasping of everything, its unobstructed cognition regarding all objects is established;
yet that is untenable,
because it cannot withstand critical analysis.

For instance, is this nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), which is distinguished above all others, real or not? If it is real, then it cannot possibly be one and the same across all object-conditions.
Because it is logically impossible for a single entity to subsist in multiple locations;
and if [the object] were manifold,
then all things would be both objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) and the ultimate reality (tattva).
And thus, since there is no connection [between the universal and its particulars], the apprehension of that [universal] does not entail the apprehension of everything.
However, it is well said that non-conceptual [cognition], by virtue of being superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is perceived everywhere as having all things as its object.

Non-conceptual [cognition] has as its domain only its own objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); yet, by generating a determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding an objective support characterized by all things, it is [figuratively] said to have all things as its object.
Therefore, although it is non-conceptual, its operation follows upon ascertainment, and thus it has all things as its object.
As it is said:
"Those of great intelligence ascertain all aspects from the very moment of perception."
If this is argued, then from what does this power of the experience that takes only a few things as its object arise, such that there is a determination of all things?
If it is argued that it is due to the removal of obscurations such as passion (*rāga*),
then one would perceive things exactly as they are.
Furthermore, it is not the case that this [scripture] lacks purpose;
otherwise, its skill in the manifestation of conceptual constructions would be untenable.
For while it is easy for afflictions and the like to obscure reality, they do not constitute an obstacle to the manifestation of conceptual constructions.
Therefore, because it arises merely from the intensity of meditative cultivation,
and because there is no certainty regarding its non-deviation from the object,
even though it appears clearly, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) and is not direct perception (*apratyakṣa*), as it is overcome by doubt; this is the correct conclusion.

(Nibandha 13) Furthermore, as for the claim that the manifestation of real objects is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of cognition, while the apprehension of unreal objects is adventitious (*āgantuka*),
and that in the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*), it must therefore be the manifestation of real objects alone—
That is incorrect;

for it would entail the validity of a vivid cognition whose object is fire that has been inferred and subsequently manifested. Since such a cognition is observed to be sublated in some instances, its lack of validity here is the same as elsewhere, due to attachment to something else.
Therefore, if it is here being proven that cultivation is the cause of a clear manifestation of consciousness by virtue of its connection with the three qualifications,
then this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Let it be that the Tathāgata possesses such a consciousness.
However, this cognition of it is not a direct perception, because it lacks validity;
and thus, due to the reason (*hetu*) not being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharman*), the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
This is because a subject whose properties are already established lacks the status of being an object of inference (*anumeya*), as its specific characteristics are no longer objects of inquiry.
Now, if it is argued that the fact of meditation being the cause of direct perceptual cognition is unestablished for the opponent and is therefore being proven,
then in that case the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because it is pervaded by the opposite of what is to be proven;
for even meditation possessing the three qualifications generates a cognition that is both vivid and non-erroneous.
Furthermore, because the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyahīnatva*).
And when [the cognition] lacks validity despite being produced by the cultivation of the true object (*bhūtārtha-bhāvanā*), on account of its not having that true object as its content,
then as for what is said:
The intrinsic nature of reality, which is free from affliction,
cannot be subverted by its opposites even through effortful mental activity, because the intellect has a natural bias toward that [reality].
Thus [it is argued]. That is untenable;
for even if cognition were to have real objects as its content, there would be no sublation by opposing views that possess real objects, because [cognition] would be partial toward them.
However, this [view of self], having become habitual though it has unreal objects, is subject to sublation—just like the view of a self and what belongs to a self.
Therefore, there is merely an increase of the counteragent,
but an absolute increase is not possible—
that [increase] by which the faults would be eradicated root and branch so that they would never arise again.
For this very reason, even though its basis is unstable and it does not require renewed effort, its ultimate finality is not possible; for,
like the views of "self" and "mine," there is the possibility of a contrary cognition arising,
and that possibility exists because [the view] has an unreal object.
However, perception whose objects are those of what has been heard or inferred is simply impossible;
for those two involve the apprehension of an imperceptible form,
whereas perception is the opposite of that.

Furthermore, because it conforms to both real and unreal objects residing therein, its status as a valid means of knowledge regarding its own object is untenable when compared to the knowledge derived from scripture or inference.

Thus it is established: that cognition which arises at the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of a real object is not a means of valid cognition with respect to its object, because it is not direct perception.
Whatever is not a means of valid cognition with respect to its object is not direct perception;
for example, the cognition of a woman in one afflicted by lust.
And that [cognition] is a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
This is because, while possessing extreme clarity, it is born from the excellence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-prakarṣa*).
Whatever cognition possesses extreme clarity and is born from the excellence of meditative cultivation is a valid means of knowledge.
*Nibandha* 14):
"Just as there is a clear cognition of fire that has been inferred and subsequently manifested.
Being produced from the same cause is pervaded by having the same form.
As it has been said:
"Entities that possess the nature of X or the nature of non-X are produced from causes that possess the nature of X or the nature of non-X.
Therefore, the absence of its validity also excludes [the possibility] of being produced from a similar cause.

Nor is this [cognition] distinguished from the clarity of fire inferred and meditated upon—which is not in contact with the senses—by being produced at the ultimate limit of the intensification of meditation on the true nature of reality, nor from the clarity regarding all things as being devoid of self.
Furthermore, the absence of obscurations such as passion (*rāga*) is not the distinguishing factor;
for these are not, like a woolen blanket or similar objects, physical obscurers of consciousness.

However, because the mind is drawn toward that [object] and overwhelmed by thirst for various distinct objects and so forth, one is unable to cultivate it; thus, the application of that [cultivation] is useful only for the sake of generating respect for cultivation (*bhāvanādara*).

Furthermore, here too, there is the application of the cultivation of fire in one whose body is sluggish due to dullness produced by the weight of the cold; therefore, the establishment of the pervasion (*pratibandha*) is not invalidated by a difference in the cause.

Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) on account of the various natures of odor, taste, color, and touch—which arise from the same inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), namely a single atom of earth, and which have as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) the conjunction with a single fire dependent upon the same heat.
Due to the diversity of capacities, even though the earth-atom is a single entity, there exists that diversity [of capacity];
and this is known from the observation of the diversity of effects.
Furthermore, that [diversity] is eternal, being eternally inherent [in the atom].
And it is clear that the effect, the composite whole consisting of earth, arises through the process of the causal capacity;
however, we shall explain the remainder at the time of commenting on the text.
Let this suffice for now.
Trilocana, however, states in the *Nyāyaprakīrṇaka*:
"In this context, there are indeed four noble truths known as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The direct realization of the intrinsic nature of these truths is the perception of the yogi (*yogipratyakṣa*)."

In that context, suffering consists of the five aggregates of clinging as the result; it is to be understood in its essential nature. Those same aggregates, when functioning as causes, constitute the origin.
And that [defilement] is to be abandoned;
the cessation of the mind in the state free from afflictions is to be realized.
The path is a specific state of consciousness characterized by aspects such as selflessness (*nairātmya*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), which serves as the cause for attaining that state;
furthermore, it must be cultivated—this is the doctrine of the Sugata’s followers.
To this, it is replied: it has already been stated previously that the path is not purified by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, through the habituation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose object is unreal, there would arise a cognition of an untrue object that is not reliable.

Furthermore, the Śākyan, who professes a path purified by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), when questioned regarding a valid means of knowledge, would have to state that conceptual construction arises from a mark designated as a sentient being;
consequently, everything in the form shown by conceptual construction is unreal.
Because it is associated with words,

when that object is being cultivated, the conceptual nature— which consists of the apprehension of an objective sign associated with words— ceases once the conceptualizing subject, conditioned by cultivation, attains clarity.
When that [conceptual nature] is excluded, the apprehended object, which was also associated with words, is likewise excluded.
Therefore, it follows that even the non-conceptual cognition of a yogin is devoid of an object;
for that which is of the nature of an ultimate reality is not purified by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Or, if it is for the sake of purification, what is the use of meditative cultivation? For that which is to be cultivated is already directly known.
Moreover, when one thing associated with a word is being cultivated, another distinct form does not clearly arise [in its place].

For even one afflicted by grief whose sensory faculties have ceased their activity would, through the cultivation of the thought [of his son], face the contingency of the appearance of friends and others. If it is argued that when momentariness is superimposed as the object of cultivation, it is precisely that real momentariness which appears in the cognition of the yogi—this is not so; for if, despite the absence of identity between the real and the unreal, there were an appearance of the real even when the unreal is being cultivated, then [the distinction between them would collapse]. This is because difference consists in the absence of identity between what is true and what is false. If such a difference did not exist, then even while cultivating the false, there would be an appearance of the true. Thus, the argument fails.

In that case, even when practicing the meditation on the sons of a real person, because of the identity of the word, there would follow the appearance of the essential nature of some other [person] called "son" who is non-different from him due to that verbal similarity.

Therefore, since even non-conceptual [cognition] arising from the practice of an unreal object is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it lacks correspondence with reality, an omniscient being is not established.
Furthermore, practice (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated placement of a future object in the mind.

And that [meditative cultivation], when practiced with devotion for a long time and without interruption through celibacy and austerity, becomes a firm ground that is desired to produce the clarity of a conceptualization whose form was previously indistinct.
This cannot be established by one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness and selflessness;
for, in that case, a conceptualization that grasps an object of meditation, exactly as it has arisen, ceases without leaving any trace.
And when that [preceding cognition] has ceased, a condition that arises again and again is produced as something entirely new and unprecedented.

Thus, by this reasoning, even over the course of a thousand eons, because there is no distinction in the production of what is previously non-existent, the cultivation (*abhyāsa*) consisting of a formative predisposition (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [condition] does not arise.
By this, the production of a distinguished consciousness as cultivation is explained.
For if each preceding consciousness has ceased without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*), how could it produce a subsequent state that is distinct?
In every respect, only a form that persists can be conditioned by successive conditions;
however, that which does not persist is merely characterized by its own arising and perishing, and thus would remain undifferentiated.

Therefore, we see it as logical that for that very self which possesses the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from the cognition of the object to be cultivated— which arises upon returning [from distraction] and is opposed to the latent impressions of the cognition of emergence— it is precisely that [impression] which, even when intensified, becomes the cause of the cognition that directly realizes the object to be cultivated. Furthermore, practice is performed in order to abandon distraction and to establish the mind in one-pointed concentration.

Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇika-vāda*), there is no such thing as a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), because every mind is one-pointed (*ekāgra*) by virtue of being restricted to each respective object. For instance, if conceptual consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*) possesses an objective aspect (*sākāra*), it is necessarily one-pointed due to its restriction to its own appearance; how then could it be distracted?

Now, even if it is formless (*nirākāra*), that which is conceptualized remains distinct from the conceptualizing cognition; however, there is no single object of conceptualization common to all conceptual cognitions.
Therefore, even though consciousness is formless, it is indeed one-pointed (*ekāgra*) because its objective support (*ālambana*) is restricted.
It is not distracted;
for the proponents of momentariness, there exists in no way a single, stable mind that possesses multiple objects and which is intended to be made one-pointed.
Thus, because such practice is impossible within a stream of consciousness that lacks omniscience, a specific state of consciousness characterized as omniscient cannot be established.
The author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, however, says:
"If all cognitions were without an object (*nirālambana*) and consisted of mere consciousness (*saṃvedanamātra*), what would be the distinction between the cognition of a yogi and that of others?
If it is argued that the distinction lies in their being pure or impure,"
Let it be so for the sake of argument; nevertheless, it is illogical that [the cognition] has the four noble truths and so forth as its object.

For it is not tenable to say that the four noble truths and so forth have been directly realized by means of a cognition that knows only itself, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
(Commentary 16:
If it is argued that "it has that as its object because it possesses the form of that," then is the Sautrāntika doctrine now being accepted as true?
Even so, how can there be an object that is past or future?
For that which is non-existent possesses no form whatsoever.
And if the forms of what has been seen, heard, or inferred appear clearly through the power of cultivation, [how can they be said to be non-existent]?

And if that were so, yogic perception would be nothing but erroneous, because it appears in the form of something existing when it is actually non-existent, like a dream. [Objection: It is not erroneous because it is non-contradictory. [Response: No.
Even if inferential cognition is erroneous, it is accepted as being non-discrepant.
Now, if validity belongs even to that which is erroneous by virtue of its being non-discrepant,
nevertheless, the qualification of "non-erroneous" in the definition of perception would be contradicted.
Moreover, even non-contradictoriness is not tenable according to your position;
for it must consist either in the perception of an object that is actually reached,
or in the indication of an object that is the locus of purposeful activity.
For you, non-contradiction is intended to mean either the manifestation [of an object] or the successful accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
This is not possible in the case of knowledge of past objects and the like;
nor is it even tenable in the case of knowledge of present objects under the view that things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Therefore, the description of yogic perception by the followers of the Sugata is indeed untenable.
Moreover, this also ought to be said:
if knowledge born from the power of cultivation regarding objects is a vessel of confidence only when preceded by inference,
then let us for now set aside any hope for the efficacy of inference.

Even in the case of direct perception, after apprehending [an object] such as the eye or fire, there may arise at the culmination of the intensity of cultivation a more stable cognition bearing that same form— provided one has not reached the limit of engagement in contrary cultivation, or until the object has vanished or entered another state. Thus, even when the domain consists of an object brought forward by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be confidence in its correspondence?

Furthermore, when even a plowman might manifest [an object] through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by inferring it from its consumption as an offering, that would then not be yogic knowledge because it lacks an ultimate reality as its object; thus, it would follow that it is merely another form of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Moreover, is that yogic knowledge distinct from sensory cognition or non-distinct?

On the view that there is no difference [between types of cognition], there is no such thing as "yogic perception" distinct from sensory perception, since it is subsumed under sensory perception itself.
Nor can a distinction be established on the grounds that it arises in a mental continuum refined by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
for if that were the case, it would follow that one must establish yet another type of perception based on the refinement produced by elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like.
Furthermore, on the view that they are distinct, it would follow that meditative cultivation produces a cognition that directly perceives momentariness, while sensory cognition grasps stability;
thus, the proof [of the yogi’s perception] would be successful.
However, if even sensory cognition were to grasp instability at that very stage, then there would be no need for yogic cognition.
Furthermore, his realization of momentariness is not accidental;
for that realization arises from the clarity produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
and such cultivation does not pertain to sensory cognition.
Rather, it occurs in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

furthermore, if direct realization were attained even without that [mental consciousness], cultivation would be rendered useless. Thus, due to the absence of the necessary cause, there is an obstruction to omniscience.
To this it is replied:

as for that prattle regarding what the cause of the cognition of all objects might be— such as whether it be sensory perception and so forth— our very fifth position is that it is precisely mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), born from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābalaja*), which grasps all objects.
Therefore, the objections arising from alternative positions are refuted by our non-acceptance [of them]. Furthermore, as for the criticism stated against our accepted fifth position—
that the word "perception" (pratyakṣa) is meaningless— [it is likewise rejected].

Furthermore, the claim that even though [the cognition] relies on the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it lacks direct perception of the object because it is not born of the senses (*anindriyajātva*)—

that is inconsistent. For it has been established that, regarding the word *pratyakṣa*, dependence on the senses (*akṣāśritatva*) is the etymological basis (*vyutpattinimitta*), whereas the direct perception of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*) is the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

(Nibandha 17) Furthermore, there is no obstruction to the power of mental consciousness— which relies on the force of meditative cultivation— to directly perceive an object, even though it does not depend on the sense organs.
For just as the visual faculty functions to produce its own cognition by depending on an object situated in a suitable location without exceeding its own capacity,

so too the mental faculty, accompanied by the cultivation of the object that serves as the antidote to all ignorance, will function to produce its own cognition upon reaching an object situated in a suitable location.
Because the quality of acting without reaching [the object] (aprāpyakāritā) is common to both,
and because the possession of an object (arthavattā) is also accepted at that time for the mind;
however, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) does not possess such power.
Since the mind (*manas*), like the eyes and ears, would likewise produce cognition only by encountering an object situated in a suitable location according to its own specific spatial limits—
due to the absence of the particular cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that uproots all ignorance— there is no over-extension [of its range].
In that state, however, just as with the ears and eyes, the mind is also capable of cognizing only when the object is situated at a certain distance.
Only this much is said:

to whatever extent an auxiliary object capable of imparting its own form can be apprehended by that [cognition], to that extent it becomes the object of that [cognition] in a manner distinct from other people, appearing as something momentary.
Therefore, since the form of the object is not in reality produced by mere mental cultivation, there is not even the slightest suspicion of non-correspondence.

Furthermore, through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), a certain extraordinary power has been instilled in his mental continuum—much like a special collyrium applied to the eye—by virtue of which he possesses a perception that is not shared by other persons.
Therefore, even though mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not born of the senses (*anakṣaja*), its direct realization of the object is possible.
[Objection: But is it not the case that the mind lacks independence regarding external objects?

Otherwise, it would follow that there are no blind or deaf persons and so forth. And it has been stated: "Yogins do not possess direct perceptual knowledge (*aparokṣapratibhāsa*) of dharma and adharma, because of the absence of sensory contact (*indriyasannikarṣa*), just like ourselves."
Moreover, the status of an object as an objective condition (*ālambanapratyayatva*) is pervaded by its dependence upon the sense faculties.
This [dependence], being excluded from the object by the perception of its own contrary (*svaviruddhopalabdhi*), also excludes its status as an objective condition.
Indeed, a specific kind of fuel, though it is the cause of smoke, does not produce smoke even with a thousand refinements if fire is absent.
If that were the case, it would follow that all inference based on the cause-effect relationship would be destroyed.

And if you argue that no one has ever been seen to possess the vision of supersensible objects or omniscience through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), we reply: by the word "mind" (*manas*), we intend nothing other than cognition not born of the senses (*an-akṣaja-vijñāna*).
Nor does it follow that this [state] would entail the absence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth;
for the blind and others lack that specific auxiliary condition characterized by the cultivation of the reality that serves as the antidote to all ignorance.

As for the argument that "it is due to the absence of sense-object contact," since this is based merely on the requirement of direct perception of an object, the non-perception of the cause is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.
Furthermore, with respect to the direct realization of the object by one such as myself, this would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

If it is argued that [the reason] is not inconclusive because we observe that the mere quality of directly perceiving an object depends upon the sense faculties— this being the case for one who is devoid of qualifiers such as "ourselves" and so forth— then, by the same logic, since the mere quality of directly perceiving an object is observed to depend upon light just as it depends upon the sense faculties, owls and other such creatures would not be able to see in the dark. If you reply that light is not a universal pervader because its absence is observed in certain cases [of visual perception], then [the same applies to the sense faculties].
In that case, due to the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), even the sense organ would lack pervasiveness (*avyāpakatva*).
If it is argued that "the suspicion is destroyed by pervasion (*vyāpti*)," then because the suspicion is possible, pervasion itself is impossible.
For if pervasion were established from the very beginning,
then no deviation would ever be observed.
Therefore, the observation of deviation occurs precisely because of a laxity in pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And when there is such laxity in pervasion, who can prevent even a doubt that arises from logical necessity?
If it is argued that because owls and other such creatures belong to a different species, they may possess direct perception of objects even in the absence of light; [we reply: ...

In that case, for the Blessed One as well— who has dispelled the adversary of beginningless ignorance by means of the great wind of the final limit of the excellence of meditation on the true nature of reality—

there indeed exists a marvelous and unique character (*vaijātya*) compared to living beings fallen into the pit of *saṃsāra*. Therefore, it is logical that his direct perception of objects occurs without the aid of the sense organs, arising immediately from the antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) consisting of the excellence of meditation on the antidote to ignorance, and from the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

Therefore, the non-perception of the cause [adduced] by the author of the *Kāśikā* and the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) [adduced] by Vācaspati are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because their negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.
That the state of having a doubtful negative concomitance constitutes a logical flaw has been established in our critique of [Udayana’s] proof for God.

Therefore, since for those such as ourselves—whose [cognitions] arise from common karma—the direct perception of objects is pervaded by dependence on the sense organs, this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Furthermore, there is no damage to well-known inferences, because there is no contradiction in grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and the like through perception and non-perception, given that "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

However, with respect merely to the direct perception of objects that are not within the range of worldly beings, the reason is characterized by a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*).
Because it is impossible to grasp a pervasion (vyāpti) with respect to an invisible object through either perception or non-perception,
and because a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the contrary is impossible; furthermore,
neither the capacity for perceiving supersensible objects nor omniscience can be negated merely on the basis of non-perception.
Since negation is impossible on the basis of the non-perception of the imperceptible,
if it is argued that its negation occurs through the non-perception of its cause,
then the absence of a cause is itself not established by mere non-observation; thus, the refutation remains in force.
As for what was stated by the author of the Kāśikā:
"If that which is already understood through another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is then cultivated, what is the use of cultivation?"
"Because that [object] is established from that very [source]"—
this too is inconsistent,
for inference is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since the destruction of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) does not occur without direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), even for one’s own sake, meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is logical once the reality of the nature of the Four Noble Truths has been ascertained.

Moreover, when there exists a mental continuum that realizes reality, others—recognizing that "this is capable of being realized"—will proceed toward its realization immediately after their own ascertainment;

and they will follow the means for achieving heaven taught by that [realizer] through the cultivation of the object (*arthabhāvanā*). Thus, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, characterized by heaven and liberation (*apavarga*), meditative cultivation is fruitful.
Otherwise, the word of one who has not transcended the world and has not directly realized reality would be utterly untrustworthy; thus, what talk could there be of benefiting others?

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And whatever that means of valid cognition may be" and ending with "Therefore, whether it be real or unreal," which states that inference does not apply to dharma and adharma—what is intended by the terms *dharma* and *adharma* therein?

If momentariness and selflessness are the reality of things, then even if that [reality] is not ascertained through direct perception, the apprehension of pervasion occurs by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding its opposite; this has been established on the occasion of proving momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Alternatively, if what is intended is that things possess the capacity to bring about [results] such as heaven and so forth, [then...]

In that case, even if the thorough knowledge of those objects is not established, there is no loss for us, because the state of being omniscient is established simply through the thorough knowledge of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa along with their accompaniments. As they have said: "Of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted," and so forth.
Furthermore, as for the claim that what arises from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended—
therein, "what has been apprehended" refers to that which was apprehended by either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*),
since there is no other means of knowledge.
To begin with, direct perception does not exist for anyone of limited vision regarding [properties] such as momentariness.

And even though an inference has determined the reality of an object as qualified by the exclusion of one [particular feature], the direct perception that directly realizes the reality of the object in its entirety does not grasp what has already been grasped.
Because inference does not touch upon the actual reality of the object (*vastutattva*).
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "nor at a subsequent time" and so forth has already been refuted in the section concerning the critique of the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).
