As for what Vācaspati said, starting with "It is true," and so on—repeatedly raising further and further objections—he asks: "If that [subsequent cognition] is preceded by inference, then why establish the fire by means of inference? and so forth, regarding that which arises from the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanābalaja*).
Therefore, the fact that meditation has a real object (*bhūtārthatva*) is not the cause for the validity of the clear cognition arising from it,
because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This [objection] is incorrect.

For instance, regarding this clear cognition of fire produced through the power of cultivation preceded by inference concerning fire: is it produced from the fire itself, or from the mere cultivation of such [an inferential] state?
If the first position is held, then what was said—that "contradiction is frequently observed"—is poorly stated.
For even if there were the possibility of error in that which arises directly from an object, it would follow that one must abandon the hand [of authority] over all other forms of perception as well.

In the second case, however, although error is frequently observed in that which arises solely from the intensity of cultivation and does not arise from an object, to claim that there is likewise the possibility of error in the yogic perception— which arises directly from both cultivation and the object— is a most gross delusion.

If it is argued: "But if yogic cognition arises even without the sense-faculty through the cultivation of an object, then let a non-erroneous cognition of fire arise on a mountain through the cultivation of fire;
yet, contradiction is frequently observed"—we say: no.
Since there would be no contradiction if [the cognition] were produced directly from fire,
the mere production [of such a cognition] is simply difficult to achieve.

For we do not claim that the mental faculty, accompanied by the cultivation of an object perceived through a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), generates a cognition that grasps the intrinsic nature of that object.
Rather, it is accompanied by the cultivation of the reality of all things, characterized by momentariness and selflessness, which serves as the antidote to ignorance characterized by false views.
Furthermore, "fire-ness" is not the reality of all things;
rather, it is precisely momentariness and selflessness, as has been established through the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Furthermore, this clear cognition regarding the object of fire—which is neither inferred nor meditated upon—is indeed merely imagined by one's own fancy;
it has no possibility of occurrence in the world.
For no one who is not insane would meditate upon something that serves no purpose.
And the purpose [of the action] is merely the burning and so forth, even for one whose body is sluggish from the weight of the cold;
and that is accomplished by approaching that place through fire inferred [by the smoke].
If one does not approach, the cultivation [of the intention] would be in vain.

But as for the claim that "when [the object] is imagined beforehand, it flashes forth, and in relation to that object there is an error, like that of a crawling infant," this is laughable; it is as unbearable to the virtuous as the belch of an old jackal bloated by eating the putrid cow-flesh of one who has perished through bad policy.

Furthermore, what was subsequently argued—that because of the apprehension [of the object], its status as an objective support (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is pervaded by dependence upon the sense faculty—[is also flawed].
That has already been answered previously.

Furthermore, the objection beginning with "likewise, of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)"—namely, that it is impossible to ascertain that an object (*artha*) serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)—is also irrelevant.

For even in the case of the visual faculty, its capacity to produce clear erroneous cognitions regarding things such as double moons or floating hairs is observed even in the absence of an external object; thus, it is capable of acting alone, even when accompanied by an object.

Therefore, since even the status of objects such as jars as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) would be impossible to establish, sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*) itself would be undermined. Furthermore, the entire passage beginning with "Moreover, it is only those [very things] that are logically fit to be objective conditions" and ending with "it is not a restriction on the construction of conceptualization" is redundant;
for we do not accept such a [position] in the present context.
For this very reason— that is, because it arises merely from the intensification of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā),
because it lacks the necessity of non-deviation from the object,
and because, despite its vivid appearance, it is beset by doubt— [it is not a valid cognition].
To conclude that it is both immeasurable and imperceptible is likewise contemptible,
because all the reasons [adduced] are unestablished;
for [the knowledge] born from the power of cultivation arises even from an object, just like sensory perception.
That the manifestation of the true object is the very nature of the intellect is pleasing even to us;
furthermore, it is established in general that meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause of cognition characterized by vivid appearance.

Moreover, when that cultivation culminates in the objects of the Four Noble Truths as established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its status as the cause of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) is also established by implication.

Therefore, even though the appearance of a beloved woman is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) and is not a direct perception (*apratyakṣa*), because the general property to be proven—namely, "having a vivid appearance" (*sphuṭābhatva*)—is possible therein, the logical reason (*hetu*) is not contradictory (*viruddha*).
Nor is the example devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnyatā*).
Furthermore, the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadṛṣṭi*) is not subject to sublation (*saṃbhavadbādhā*).
Because [the object] arises from the meaning, there is an absence of non-existence of that meaning.
Furthermore, it is also incorrect to say that perception cannot have as its object what is heard or inferred;
for the objects of scripture (āgama) and inference (anumāna) are twofold: the apprehended (grāhya) and the determined (adhyavaseya).
In that context, the apprehended object is its own internal form (*svākāra*), whereas the determined object consists of the ultimate particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the real entity.
And since this [particular] is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), it becomes the object of inference when the causal conditions for inference are present.
Furthermore, when the causal complex for perception is present, it is indeed observed that [the object] becomes an object of perception in a gradual sequence.
Thus, the conclusion beginning with "that is established" is also utterly confused.
Moreover, the first reason, "because it is not a means of valid cognition," is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because that which arises from the power of cultivation (bhāvanābala) also arises even from an object,
since the capacity for valid cognition is possible,
just like sensory perception (indriyapratyakṣa).
The second [reason], "because it arises from the power of cultivation" (bhāvanābalaja), is inconclusive because its negative concomitance is doubtful.
Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the example—"the clear cognition whose object is fire as cultivated through inference"—is also impossible.
Or, even if it were granted, the fact that the cognition of a yogi shares the same cause as that [example] remains unproven.

For that [knowledge] arises merely from the cultivation of things perceived through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, yogic knowledge arises from the cultivation of the reality of all things, which has as its object the antidote to ignorance. Thus, this person of dull intellect—who has fallen into a precipice—fails to comprehend even this great distinction and should therefore be disregarded. As for what was stated in the *Nyāyaprakīrṇa*, namely that the path is not purified by valid cognition: [The text continues: "If one asks how it is known that the path is not purified by valid cognition, it is because the Blessed One taught that the path is not purified by valid cognition when he said: 'O monks, there are four kinds of persons who have entered the stream of the Dharma (*dhamma-sota-ppaṭipanna*). What are the four? They are: the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry; the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Once-returning; the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Non-returning; and the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Arhatship. Now, if the path were purified by valid cognition, then since the fruit of Stream-entry is established by the three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) and the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), and since the remaining fruits are established by the nine supramundane paths and fruits (*navānupubbavihārasamāpatti*), the Blessed One would have taught that the path is purified by valid cognition. What are the four? They are: the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry... [as above] ...the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Arhatship. Now, if the path were purified by valid cognition, then since the fruit of Stream-entry is established by the three knowledges and the six direct knowledges, and since the remaining fruits are established by the nine supramundane paths and fruits, the Blessed One would have taught that the path is purified by valid cognition. But since he did not teach that the path is purified by valid cognition, it is therefore known that the path is not purified by valid cognition. What are the four? They are: the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry... [as above]
That has already been refuted by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it.
Furthermore, regarding the statement beginning with "And as for... up to "it follows that the knowledge of the yogin would be objectless" (*nirviṣaya*): what is this so-called "objectlessness"?
Does it mean being formless (*nirākāratā*) upon the cessation of the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or...

[The cognition] would either have a form dissimilar to the form of the object, or, even if it had that same form, it would not touch upon that actual entity. First of all, the first position is not tenable.
The first [position] is untenable because it is impossible for cognition to be formless.
Nor is the second [position] tenable,
because in the meditative cultivation of a beloved woman and the like, one perceives precisely that form with clarity.
Nor is it the third [alternative], because apart from contact with the aspect presented by the object, no other contact with the object is possible. And so it has been said:
"By means of the object, it connects this [cognition] with that," and so forth.
Because of the determination of those two as one, activity and cessation occur toward the external object itself.

Furthermore, the manifestation of the conventional [object]—that which is intended to be external—is ultimately nothing but the arising of a clear moment that is the material cause of conceptual construction.
To that extent alone is there the conventional usage that "that object has been directly perceived by him," even when [the cognition] arises from the object alone;
otherwise, because of deviation, there would be a lack of validity.
Furthermore, even a form presented by conceptual construction is not a non-entity, because it has the nature of cognition;
for if it lacked that nature, its manifestation would be impossible.
And the cultivation of that [cognition] is itself the cultivation of the object.
The manifestation of that [internal cognition] alone is the manifestation of the external; for it is impossible for there to be an external contact in any other way.
By this, everything from "that which is ultimately real" up to "the non-establishment of an omniscient being" has been refuted.
Furthermore, the refutation stated from the words "And as for that which is perceived... up to "...we see that this is not logical" is also inconsistent.

For there is no cause whatsoever—other than a touch by the goddess Caṇḍī—for determining the rule that another cognition arises exactly like the first cognition which apprehended the object and ceased without leaving a trace.
If it is argued that this is because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), we reply: surely momentariness is contradicted by permanence, not by the arising of something dissimilar.

For if that preceding [moment], despite its cessation without any persistence (*niranvaya-nirodha*), were to initiate a subsequent similar moment, then—by virtue of being endowed with a capacity residing in its own cause, which is to be inferred from the production of the effect—it would have to be distinguished by at least some slight degree of particularity (*viśeṣaleśa*).
In that case, there is no inconsistency whatsoever;
for indeed, you do not harbor such an aversion toward the momentariness of an entity as you do [toward its continuity].
Therefore, there is no contradiction between momentariness and the production of a subsequent moment distinguished by excellence; thus, repeated practice is not purposeless.
Furthermore, that which was stated— beginning with "whatever this may be" and so forth— that the mind is undistracted when [the object] is momentary,
is also incorrect; for it is averse to such realities as selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Because the entire face is distracted,
whereas one who realizes reality through the power of meditative cultivation is concentrated;
nevertheless, because of the attainment of the realization of reality, the grasping of the form of the subject is possible.

There is also a distracted mind even at the conventional level, because the engagement in the practice of the path is obstructed by the thought, "The destruction of my own faults will surely come about. This is because,

although from the perspective of ultimate truth there is no attainment and so forth, it is precisely the conceptualization of those things— conditioned by beginningless ignorance— that functions as the motivator in all cases.
Therefore, it is precisely through the cultivation of the truth of the path that the omniscient one is established.
Furthermore, even for Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, the critique from the perspective of the Yogācāra is irrelevant,
because his method of proof proceeds solely by accepting external objects.
As for what was said— namely, "Even so, how can there be an object that is past or future?
For that which is non-existent has no form whatsoever"—
this is the result of failing to penetrate the context.
For this is based on the context of the omniscience that is actually required— namely, the cultivation of the realization that all things are momentary and selfless—
and not with respect to an omniscience of everything.
Therefore, even the past and future, though not being perceived, do not constitute a contradiction.
For the cessation of suffering is established by that alone;
and for the sake of others, there is the introduction to the teaching based on [the principles of] momentariness and so forth.
Nor is there a relinquishment by the hand of every omniscient being;

for, upon attaining the direct realization of the four noble truths, one whose internal organ is free from obscuration— due to an excellence of compassion and a dedication to the welfare of others in all its aspects— will, through a mind in which zeal has long been rooted and which ranges over the entire field of experience, achieve the mastery of such specific means.
When one practices [this], even in the absence of the actual production of those [objects], by the sovereign power of the deity— as in the case of a true dream—
there arises a cognition that is clearer, which conforms to the specific location, time, and form of every object down to its subtlest atomic constituents; at that time,
there is no lack of correspondence caused by the deviation of the object.

Because only objects themselves appear [to consciousness], the establishment of what is cognized occurs through both arising and similarity; however, this is from the perspective of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
For yogins, however, the principle is that apprehension occurs through similarity alone.
Or rather, that Vārtika is intended for those of impure intellect.
"This reflection on the grasped and the grasper is the inconceivable domain of yogins.
Thus, even though the future and the past do not produce [the cognition], their manifestation in the knowledge of a yogin is uncontradicted.
Now, if there is a manifestation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the future and the past, [then...]

It would necessarily be only the present state. Alternatively, if it is argued that cognition itself, being present by its own nature, possesses that form and is thus invariably without an external object,
that too is not the case.

Since even when an object is not present, cognition arises through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that conforms to its place, time, and form, how could it be without an objective support (*anālambana*)?

This is because there is a determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) of it as being such [as it appears], and thus one attains that very object as qualified by the time determined, just like in a true dream.
Insofar as that [object] was seen as connected with a time such as autumn, its verbal description is not sublated;
however, it was not seen by him as connected with that [other] time, so even if it is perceived in that way [later], there is no fault.
However, because mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) manifests as reality (*tattvataḥ*), the consequence that it must be present is not tenable.

Likewise, even in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), there is no impairment whatsoever for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to conventional practice (*vyavahārika*), owing to the capacity for the superimposition of unity; this has been elaborated upon in the treatise (*śāstra*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement beginning with "it is also appropriate to say this," which addresses the mention of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—whether [the cognition] is preceded by inference (*anumāna*) born from the force of mental cultivation (*bhāvanābalaja*) or preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*)—[this is as follows]:
This is also refuted by the admission that [cognition] born from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) arises directly even from that object.

Just as a cognition of two moons and so forth, though produced by the sense faculties, lacks validity because it does not arise from the object, whereas a cognition arising from both the object and the sense faculties possesses validity; likewise, that which is preceded by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) yet produced from mere cultivation lacks validity.
However, the validity of that which has arisen from both meditative cultivation and the object [itself] is established.
If it is argued: "If the cognition of the yogin arises from the object, there is no purpose in depending on its being preceded by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)."

For if one does not ascertain that all things existing in every direction and at every time, in their mere generality— setting aside distinctions of place, time, and substance— are momentary and devoid of self, there would be no engagement in the cultivation [of this insight], which requires great effort and extends throughout a human lifespan.
Nor does a plowman, having inferred the consumption of sacrificial offerings, manifest it clearly such that it would follow that this is a separate kind of perception.
This is because its impossibility has been demonstrated through [the reasons of] incapacity and futility.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that the cognition of a yogin is either non-different or different from sensory cognition—
regarding that, first, in the case of the first position, there is no defect in the object itself.
Because such a distinguished person is established, there is no refutation of the systematic arrangement [of the path].

This is because that specific state—which transcends the world, possesses extraordinary excellence, and consists of the supreme human goal—is presented as something to be accomplished; it is distinguished from the sensory cognition common to ordinary people for the purpose of demonstrating the specific means of its attainment.
Because of this explanation,

and precisely because it lacks the status of having the supreme human goal as its object, even knowledge born from the refinement of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like does not constitute a separate type of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, even on the view that there is a distinction [between the two cognitions], there is no possibility of the aforementioned criticism based on the manifestation of stability versus its opposite.
Even by sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*), which grasps an object in its entirety, only that aspect which is currently manifesting is apprehended.

For previously, determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) was difficult to obtain; however, now, in the mental continuum where ignorance has been crushed by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābalanirdalitāvidye cittasantāne*), even that [determinative cognition] is produced by sensory perception—this is the distinction.
If it is argued that for a yogin who perceives through both mental consciousness and sensory cognition, there would be the undesirable consequence of two forms appearing,
this is true;
however, the form of the true cognition is not spatially distinct from the object, because otherwise one or the other would necessarily be an error.
Therefore, who is capable of determining by what manner of movement those two incomparable forms pervade [all things]?
As it is said:
"The movement of yogins is inconceivable."
In every respect, however, it is established that there is no impairment of the knowledge of the yogin.
Thus, even from the non-perception of a cause, the non-existence of omniscience is not proven.
Now, even if there is indeed no sublation of the inference favored by you, [the following remains to be considered...]
Nevertheless, there is indeed a subverting inference;
for it can be stated as follows: "The Sugata is not omniscient."
Because it is knowable, because it is cognizable, because it exists,
and because it is a person.
Because of being a speaker,
because of possessing sense organs and so forth;
like a man on the street.

And so it is said in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*: "Who indeed would postulate that [self] against whom reasons characterized by being knowable, being an object of cognition, being a real entity, being existent, and so forth, are powerless to strike?"

Who indeed would postulate that [person] whose existence is not contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition, and for whom [qualities such as] being an object of knowledge are capable of precluding his non-existence?
To this it is replied: Are these properties, such as being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and so forth, directly contradictory with omniscience, or indirectly?
For a negation is not possible when there is no contradiction.
And that direct contradiction must be characterized either by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*), or...
It is like existence and non-existence; or it is characterized by non-coexistence,
like fire and snow.
The first position is not tenable;
for contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion exists only between two things where the determination of one is inseparable from the exclusion of the other.
And knowability and the like do not exist through the exclusion of omniscience.
What then?
[It is established] by the exclusion of being unknowable and so forth;
likewise, omniscience is [established] by the exclusion of non-omniscience.
But it is not by way of excluding knowability;
nor is there a second type of contradiction.
For contradiction characterized by non-coexistence exists only between two things where, while one is present with its causes unimpaired, the other ceases to exist due to the proximity of the first.

Furthermore, omniscience has never been observed to have functioned previously with its causes intact, such that it could later be understood to cease upon the existence of knowability and other such properties.
If that were the case, there would merely be a negation of [omniscience] in certain places and so forth, rather than a total abolition.
Nor is there a contradiction by way of a causal chain.
For that [existence], being the opposite of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the omniscience to be negated,
is the opposite of its cause (*kāraṇa*), and is the opposite of its effect (*kārya*).
Because it is the effect of what is contradictory to the essential nature, because it is the effect of what is contradictory to the pervader,
and because it is the effect of what is contradictory to the cause.
Because it is an effect contrary to the effect [of the probandum],
because it is pervaded by what is contrary to the essential nature [of the probandum],
and because it is pervaded by what is contrary to the pervader [of the probandum].
It would have to be because it is pervaded by something contradictory to the cause, or because it is pervaded by something contradictory to the effect;
in that case, [it follows] from the non-existence of omniscience.

Since pervading causes and their effects are unestablished, and because there is no absence of an effect that is pervaded by what is contradictory to them, properties such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) are not contradictory to omniscience even indirectly.

[Objection: But surely the state of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*) is indeed contradictory [to omniscience], because the state of being a speaker is the effect of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is contradictory to non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*) regarding all objects.
[Response: This is not correct.
Since conceptual and non-conceptual [cognitions] do not function simultaneously, there is no contradiction in the omniscience of one who possesses conceptualization.
If it is asked, "What then is the distinction between this [omniscient being] and an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)? it is said in reply:
Just as a magician, determining that the consciousness whose object is a magically created horse or the like is devoid of a real object and is thus non-erroneous,
is superior to others,
so too the Blessed One, even when pure mundane conceptualization is present before him, is neither erroneous nor equal to ordinary beings.
Consequently, since there is no contradiction between non-conceptual omniscient cognition and conceptualization, the state of being a speaker is indeed not incompatible with omniscience.
By this, the following argument of the author of the *Kāśikā* is also refuted:
"If it is argued that [the Buddha] will teach after emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), we say no;
for the verbal cognition of one who has emerged from absorption is a deluded speech and would therefore be invalid (*apramāṇa*)."
Furthermore, as it was stated in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*:
"And when one teaches something as a single [doctrine], like an ordinary speaker, that would be the song of one who knows only a portion; it would not be the speech of an omniscient being."
That too has been refuted;

for even when instruction is given by means of conceptual thought (vikalpa) by bringing some single object to mind, everything is understood through non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpa), precisely because those words were spoken by the Omniscient One.
Furthermore, as it is stated in the *Kārikā*:
"By the mere presence of that Person, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), teachings issue forth at will even from walls and other such objects."
Indeed, such statements as these are appropriate for one who possesses faith;
however, because [the teaching] appears to have issued from walls and other such sources, we have no confidence in the teachings.
Could these have been composed by the Buddha, or were they uttered by certain wicked beings,
such as piśācas and others, who are invisible, for the purpose of deceiving?
In the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* as well, it is said:
"When he is established in that meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*), remaining like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), teachings issue forth at will even from walls and other such objects."
Through them, human beings come to know all matters they wish to understand,
and they swiftly attain their respective benefits as appropriate.
Such declarations as these are fitting for one who possesses faith;
but we, being without faith, seek logical arguments.
Furthermore, those [sounds] emerging from walls and such would not be taught by a reliable authority,
nor would there be confidence in them, as one would wonder, "By whom were these uttered?"
Could these have been proclaimed by the Buddha, or were they taught by those deceiving brahmins who play with echoes from afar?
Or perhaps they were fabricated by unseen minor spirits and the like;
therefore, those who consider themselves wise should place no trust in them.
This too is refuted by the very fact that it is not accepted;
for it is accepted that he is a teacher precisely through the manifestation of pure worldly conceptualization.
Alternatively, just as a wheel continues to spin by the force of its prior momentum even when the activity of pushing with a staff has ceased,

so too, while the Blessed One remains with the entire web of conceptual constructions completely subsided, if there were a teaching that flows continuously and effortlessly due to the force of his prior vows, what contradiction would there be?
One should not ask how speech can proceed in the absence of a desire to speak.
Because even in the absence of that [intention], we observe distinct utterances from one who is asleep;
for there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between mere speech and the desire to speak.

Therefore, just as for one suddenly awakened by an enemy through the infliction of a blow or the like, there is an immediate and corresponding course of action such as drawing a weapon, [so too is it with the sleeper].
Likewise, it is not contradictory that all the arts belong even to the Omniscient One;
as the Alaṅkāra says:
"They proceed without hesitation by the mere presence of the Enemy."
How much more so, then, the preliminary steps for its refutation, which were fashioned out of anger!
Furthermore, as for the claim that it is not appropriate for the wise to have confidence in this [scripture] due to the suspicion that it was composed by Piśācas and the like—
that is inconsistent, because it presents base matters such as nonsensical chatter, violence, and so forth.
For beings such as playful piśācas and the like, no function exists within those [senses].
That [scripture] is held to be in agreement with the two means of valid cognition regarding its entire subject matter,
such that not even the slightest sublation by those two means of valid cognition is observed.
Just as [the teaching] regarding that which is entirely beyond perception is not contradicted by what precedes or follows it, so too,
through the arising of qualities such as compassion, it serves as an impetus for all persons.
It proclaims the antidote to the entire mass of latent tendencies and shatters the door-panels of the gateway to the city of Nirvāṇa.
If that [teaching] were the word of playful Rākṣasas,
let them alone be the perfectly awakened ones (saṃbuddhas), for they abide in all those characteristics.
There is no dispute regarding the name,
nor does the cessation of the name entail the cessation of the underlying entity;
on the contrary, it is more reasonable to conceive that the Veda itself was composed by playful beings such as piśācas.

By whom [these] practices involving the consumption of cow-flesh and so forth, as well as sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*) and other unrighteous conducts (*asatya-samudācāra*), were proclaimed;
and by whom the worldly renown was established that the three authors of the Veda are sages, buffoons, and night-stalkers (*niśācara*).
Thus, enough with this excessive persistence.
Is it not the case that omniscience is held to be pervaded by the state of being free from passion and so forth,
while the possession of passion and so forth— which is its opposite—
is the cause of speech?

If it is argued that this statement—which is the effect of something incompatible with the pervader—establishes the absence of an omniscient being because it is indirectly contradictory [to omniscience], we say: no.
This is because the causal relationship between passion and the like (*rāgādi*) and speech is not established.
For instance, a particular kind of speech is the effect of passion and the like; [but such a relationship is not proven here].
That which is produced by passion alone,
or which is a mere word—
of these, the first position is not tenable.

Because it is impossible to find a means of determining such a statement, [one might argue]: "The act of revealing indecent sexual conduct is its effect. This is not so, because the underlying intention is difficult to discern.
The intention that "even one who is dispassionate acts as if impassioned, and even one who is impassioned acts as if dispassionate" is difficult to comprehend.
Consequently, because of this confusion in specific conventional usage, it is not tenable to infer passion with absolute certainty from such behavior.
Nor is mere speech the effect of passion and the like;

for even those in whom passion and so forth are not manifest are observed uttering mere words when performing the praise of their chosen deity, or when conversing with mothers, other relatives, teachers, and elders.
And it is not the case that whatever occurs in the absence of something is said to be its effect.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
If it is argued that the capacity for passion and so forth is the cause of speech, since speech is not observed in a piece of stone or similar objects in the absence of such capacity, we say: no.
For the cause of speech is indeed the desire to speak, which possesses the quality of being an instrument;
it ceases in the case of a piece of stone and the like precisely because of the absence of that [desire],
not because of the absence of the capacity for passion and so forth.

If it were established that speech does not arise because of the absence of the capacity for passion and so forth—even when all other causes, such as the qualities of the cause and so on, are present—then its status as a cause would be proven.
However, in the case of a piece of stone or the like, there is no desire to speak;
how then can it be a cause of words?
In that case, let desire simply be the wish to speak; since this is accepted, nothing would be contradicted,
as there is no dispute regarding the name.

Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), they say that passion (*rāga*) is the mind’s attachment to objects associated with outflows (*sāśrava*), which is projected by the view of a permanent self, pleasure, and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya*).
If it is argued that even the intention to speak is not appropriate for one who has accomplished all perfections,
this is no fault, because such an intention exists for the sake of others (*parārtha*).

If it is asked: "Since there is an absence of attachment to objects in one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), how can there be activity even for the sake of others? We say: No, because activity occurs through compassion (*karuṇā*) even in the absence of attachment.
If it is argued that this [compassion] itself is passion (*rāga*):
There is no fault, because it is desired [as such].
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of passion (*rāga*) has already been explained.
If it is argued that even for a compassionate one, an undertaking that is fruitless is not appropriate, we say: no.
This is trivial, because the fruit is characterized by being desired, and [in this case] the welfare of others alone constitutes the fruit. (Nibandh 27)
[Objection: But how can compassion arise in that state for the Blessed One who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*)?
For it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that compassion originates from the conceptualization of suffering;
therefore, since the cause is absent, how can the effect arise? [Response: This is not so.

Just as even when the potter has ceased his activity, the persistence of the jar and so forth occurs solely through its own continuum, so too, even in the absence of the conceptual thought that initiates it, the engagement of objectless compassion cannot be prevented by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
As the Teachers have said:

Even when brought about by the imposition of existence, it attains hardness through the power of cultivation; likewise, even in its state of laxity, there is just as intense an effort for the destruction of suffering.
However, while there is a determination of cause regarding the arising of the fruit, there is none regarding its continued persistence.
Therefore, homage to him who, even while the vision of suffering has ceased, continues to radiate loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
By this, the following objection is also refuted, which was stated in the *Kārikā*: "If he were established as being free from passion and the like, and devoid of activity,
then the teaching would necessarily have been composed by another, in the absence of his own discernment."
Now, one might object: "Granted that being a speaker is not incompatible with omniscience, yet possessing a body, sense faculties, intellect, and so forth, is indeed incompatible.
This is because the body and its constituents have as their cause passion and the like, which are contrary to passionlessness—the pervader of omniscience.
Therefore, since we perceive the cause of what is incompatible with the pervader of the property to be negated (omniscience), there is an absence of an omniscient being."
It is said:

although the body and so forth are causes, these alone—merely as auxiliary conditions and lacking the appropriating cause characterized by the adherence to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*)—do not produce attachment and the like. Therefore, the body and so forth are non-probative regarding the absence of an omniscient being.

Consequently, because [the reasons such as] "being an object of knowledge" (*jñeyatva*) lack causal capacity, the non-existence of an omniscient being cannot be established even through the inferences imagined by others.
Nor does that which is imagined by one's own conceptualization, such as verbal testimony (*śābda*) and so forth, constitute a sublation of the Blessed One.

For although it is a coarse objection that if these were valid they would necessarily be included within inference (*anumāna*), and if they were not included they would simply lack validity; [nevertheless, they do not sublate him].
Nevertheless, even while conceding its authority, we say this:
first of all, for you, any human statement is simply not authoritative;
nor is any Vedic statement found that establishes the non-omniscience of all persons.
On the contrary, in another Vedic branch known as the *Nimitta*, the omniscient one is established even more clearly; for instance,
by such passages as "He knows the universe, yet there is no knower of Him," the omniscient one is established in the Veda.
Nor is its non-existence established through analogy (*upamāna*).

For it is an established principle that analogy perceives similarity—either as an attribute of the cow or the like present before one, or as an attribute of the cow and so forth—by means of the similarity with the gavaya or the like currently being perceived.
However, the mental states occurring within the continuum of an omniscient being have not been experienced by any [ordinary] omniscient person such that they could be made objects of memory.
Because it is impossible for there to be knowledge of another's mind.
As for what was further stated by Kumārila:
Having observed that all men of the present day are non-omniscient,
one determines that all remaining [men] are likewise non-omniscient by means of an analogy based on their similarity to them.
That too is incorrect,
because there is no certainty regarding the non-omniscience of all contemporary persons;
and if such certainty were possible, it would entail the undesirable consequence of admitting one's own omniscience.

Nor is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) a subverting factor; for presumptive testimony is defined as the postulation of an unperceived object on the grounds that a perceived or heard object would otherwise be inexplicable. And there is no perceived or heard object regarding all men that would be inexplicable without [the existence of] non-omniscience, such that it could be postulated through presumptive testimony.
Now, it may be argued that the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is indeed established by means of valid cognition;
yet that [beginninglessness] cannot be known by an omniscient being,
because if there were non-existence beyond the limit of his knowledge, it would follow that its beginninglessness is destroyed.

If it is argued that this [reasoning], being otherwise inexplicable, establishes the beginninglessness of all things and the non-existence of an omniscient being, we reply: first of all, this is not a fault with respect to an omniscient being who is merely "functionally relevant" (*upayukta*).
For even if his beginninglessness is unknown, his status as a functionally relevant omniscient being remains unimpaired.
Even when the non-existence of an omniscient being is to be proven, this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is incapable [of doing so].

For instance, just as the beginninglessness of saṃsāra implies that the existence of preceding entities has no starting point, so too the knowledge of an omniscient being would have an unbounded range due to its pervading the existence of each preceding entity. Thus [the argument fails].
Since even a single unknown object would remain unestablished,
the fact that beginninglessness is logically consistent even if an omniscient being exists does not entail the non-existence of such a being;
therefore, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) also does not subvert the existence of an omniscient one.
Furthermore, the omniscient one is not sublated by the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*).
Non-existence as a means of knowledge is held to be the cessation of the five [other] means of knowledge.
In this context, "cessation" is intended merely as the non-arising of a means of knowledge, understood through a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
Alternatively, by way of exclusion (paryudāsa), it is another entity;
and that other entity may be either insentient in nature or of the nature of cognition;
and even cognition may be mere cognition.
Or is it the cognition of an object associated with that single cognition? These are the alternatives.
Among them, first of all, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of mere negation is not tenable;
for that, being devoid of all causal capacity, is nothing at all.

And how could that which is nothing at all determine an object of cognition, or produce a consciousness having it as its object, or even be itself cognized? All this is merely the dancing of darkness. As it has been said:
For non-existence (abhāva) is neither the cognition of anything nor the cause of cognition;
furthermore, how could there even be a cognition of it?
Nor, under the view that it is a distinct entity, is it logically consistent for the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva) to be insentient in nature.
Because it is impossible for that [non-existence] to delimit its own object of cognition,
since delimitation is a property of cognition;
nor is non-existence of the nature of mere cognition.
Otherwise, it would follow that even things remote in terms of space, time, or intrinsic nature would be non-existent,
because from that perspective, everything is merely consciousness. Or, if you accept that its nature consists in being associated with a single cognition, [then...]

Then, there is no injury [to our position] because of the expectation that non-existence is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is precisely a particular kind of perception that is designated by the name "non-existence as a means of valid cognition," and because we ourselves have accepted that very thing as the means of proof called "non-perception of the perceptible" (*dṛśyānupalambha*).
Furthermore, it has already been explained that the non-perception of the perceptible is incapable of proving the non-existence of the Blessed One (*Nibandh* 29).
Moreover, what exactly is this "absence of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*) intended by you?

There is the cessation of the measure of one's own class of beings, and then the cessation of the measure of all classes of living beings. Among these, the cessation of the measure of one's own class of beings is inconclusive (*vyabhicāriṇī*),
because even when that [measure] has ceased, an object that is obstructed cannot be denied.
However, the cessation of another's means of valid cognition is unestablished for one who is not omniscient;
as it has been said:
"The non-perception by all is doubtful, while one's own non-perception is inconclusive."
"Because of the existence of dūrvā grass and other things within the caves of the Vindhya mountains, even though they are not perceived. Thus [it is said].
Thus, it is established that the negation of an omniscient being cannot be achieved even by means of the pramāṇa of non-existence.
But even so, there exists no means of proof for this [omniscient being] either, for the sake of establishing its existence as a reality.
For instance, since an omniscient being is beyond the senses, our own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) cannot be a means of proving him;
and just as he is not perceived by us, he likewise cannot be perceived by those of our kind, because it is a fixed rule that his nature is imperceptible.
Nor is the conceptualization that "this did not exist at another time" tenable;
for while it can be refuted by this inference— "because it is a time, just like the present time"—
it cannot be established in the same way.
However, others postulate an omniscient being, or the lack of human authorship in the Veda;
since these are postulated as being on equal footing, this [following] must be carefully considered.

"A omniscient being is not seen by us and others at present; nor is it possible to conceive that such a one existed in the past, just as [the existence of] a refuter [is impossible]. Thus [it is said].
Nor is the existence of an omniscient being established through inference, because there is no ascertainment of a logical mark (liṅga) invariably concomitant with it.

Furthermore, in proving the existence of an omniscient being, every reason (hetu) fails to transcend the three types of fallacy: being unestablished (asiddha), contradictory (viruddha), and inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For instance, when the omniscient being is made the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*) is not established as a property (*dharma*) of that subject;
because that very subject is unestablished due to its being the probandum (*sādhya*).
Or, if it were established, there would follow the consequence of futility (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*).
If the subject (dharmin) is not omniscient, the proof of an omniscient being is not established;
for the reason (hetu) would be contradictory (*viruddha*), since it would prove the opposite of omniscience. Nor can a property that is both omniscient and non-omniscient serve as the reason.
Because that [reason] is inconclusive;
therefore, the existence of an omniscient being is not established even through inference. (Kārikā)
"And no single part has been perceived which could serve as a mark (liṅga) to lead to an inference."
Nor is it accessible through scripture (*āgama*).
For scripture is of two kinds: human (*pauruṣeya*) and eternal (*nitya*).
Among these, even a human scripture—whether composed by him [the Buddha] or otherwise—is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [subject].
Or [it might be] composed by another person;
in that case, it would not belong to him [the Buddha],
because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence.
For the authority of scripture depends upon its being spoken by an omniscient being;
and since its authority is established, the existence of an omniscient being is proven from it.
However, that which is composed by another person is not even accepted as authoritative; therefore, for this reason as well, there is no proof of an omniscient being.

Furthermore, if an omniscient being is established through a statement composed by an omniscient being, what wrong has one’s own statement done that this [omniscient being] should not be understood from it as well? Nor is the omniscient being cognizable through an eternal scripture (*nityāgama*).
This is because there exists no eternal scripture (*nityāgama*) that establishes an omniscient being.
Furthermore, any statement in the Upaniṣads and other texts that purports to establish an omniscient being must be understood as having another meaning.
Moreover, an eternal sentence cannot be the means for establishing the omniscience of a non-eternal being.
Because it would follow that [the scripture] lacks an object;
furthermore, if an eternal scripture is accepted,
what is the use of postulating an omniscient being?
Only an eternal scripture will be the authority regarding Dharma;
nor can an omniscient being be established by means of scripture, because of their mutual dependence.
How can the authority of that which was composed by another person be understood?
Furthermore, no such eternal scripture can be found here;
if one were seen, it would be a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), and its primary meaning would thus be non-eternal.
And once the eternity of the scripture is established, the postulation of that [creator] is futile;
for from that [scripture] alone men will understand dharma.
(Bṛhaṭṭīkā)
Furthermore, there is no eternal scriptural injunction that establishes an omniscient being;
thus, forty-seven verses beginning with these words set forth this point in detail.
Therefore, even from the standpoint of scripture, the existence of an omniscient being is not established.
Nor is it to be apprehended by the means of valid cognition known as analogy (*upamāna*).
For analogy functions invariably through the perception of similarity and has as its object an entity not present to the senses,
such as the recollection of a cow by means of perceiving a *gavaya*.
And there is no one at all who is equal to the Omniscient One; for if we were now to see anyone at all who resembles the Omniscient One, [we would know it].
Therefore, we should know the Omniscient One by means of analogy.

Nor is the existence of an omniscient being established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). The definition of presumptive testimony is the postulation of an unperceived object on the grounds that a perceived or heard fact would otherwise be inexplicable. However, in this case, there exists no entity cognized by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which, being inexplicable without an omniscient being, could lead us to its actual existence.
Therefore, even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) does not establish an omniscient being;
nor is its establishment possible through the means of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*), which consists in the absence of the five [other] means of valid cognition,
because this [means] establishes only the non-existence of a real entity.
On the contrary, it has been demonstrated that this very [argument] establishes its non-existence.

Furthermore, as for the Buddhist proof for the existence of an omniscient being—which was raised and refuted in sixty-one verses within the *Kārikā* and the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*—that too is loathsome; however, it is not written here for fear of excessive length.
*Nibandha* 31:
For indeed, these are the proofs asserted by the followers of the Sugata (*saugata*) for the purpose of establishing an omniscient being;
it is true that "an omniscient being exists."
Because he has spoken all things, because he is the teacher of the Dharma,
and because there is a long-standing and firm tradition that the Buddha is omniscient.

This is because he first thoroughly understood the various types of minds and mental factors of the entire assembly of disciples, and because he taught the reality of the totality of all categories of phenomena.
Therefore, it is established that there is no direct perceiver of supersensible objects; rather, his perception occurs solely through the medium of eternal scripture.
Thus, since no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists in any way to establish an omniscient being, the Buddhists' conventional usage of the term "omniscient" is untenable.
To this it is replied: If [the object] were not established by means other than inference, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Nor is it unestablished that [it is known] even through inference, because inference was explained previously.

The entire series of refutations beginning with "because there is no certainty regarding the mark (*liṅga*) connected to that" has also been countered; thus, for now, an omniscient being who illuminates the three worlds is established.
This proof applies even to the position that everyone is omniscient:
whatever speech is determined to be in conformity with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether directly or through a lineage...
It is preceded by a cognition that directly realizes its object,
as in the statement, "Fire is a burner.
Furthermore, this statement is consistent with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and expresses a determined object.
"All the conditioned factors of the Omniscient One are momentary" is, in terms of its meaning, a logical reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).
There is no lack of proof for this,
because this statement possesses a true referent, as it establishes the momentary destruction of all entities.
Nor is there contradiction, because [the reason] exists in the similar class (sapakṣa);
nor is it inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Even though speech in general may be preceded by doubt or error, speech whose object is determined by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is—either directly or indirectly—preceded by a cognition that directly perceives that object;
otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be invariably in accord with a pramāṇa.

And this formal argument (prayoga) of the Commentator for establishing that all [beings] are omniscient has been elaborated by the scholar Jitāri; therefore, it should be understood in detail from that very source. Disregarding the prowess of opposing disputants who are like door-keepers, this Omniscient One—the sole eye of the world—has arisen through the maturity of valid cognition; such is the power manifested herein.
This is a summary by me, Ratnakīrti, who fears prolixity; it concerns our teacher, the mountain of the lineage of the earth where the Perfectly Awakened One abides.
May the entire world, through this auspicious [act], attain joy according to its desire; and may Ratimanmatha and Mañjuvajra, at the conclusion, grant their feet as the bestower of true fruit.
May I become Mañjuvajra, Mañjughoṣa, and Mañjuvāk; may I be Mañjuśrī, the foremost of the Mañjus, Kumāra, and the bearer of the Victor’s burden.
The Proof of the Omniscient One is completed. (Nibandha 32) // 2 //
Refutation of the Proof of a Creator God (Īśvara)

Oṃ, homage to Tārā! Having drawn forth a small portion from the ocean of my guru’s speech— which, by being the repository of jewels of well-spoken verses, has surpassed the ocean of jewels and the like— I write this in order to remember it.
This style is a treasury of nectar for the virtuous,
a flame of poison for the hostile, and for the one who knows only a little, it is nothing at all.

Here, these Naiyāyikas and others maintain that there exists a particular person who is skilled in [knowing] the essential nature, material cause, instruments, recipient, purpose, and distribution of the subject of dispute, such as the earth and so forth, and who is distinguished by qualities such as omniscience.
As they say:
"There is one, all-pervading, omniscient, the locus of a single intellect, eternal, known as Īśvara."
"The Creator of the world is accepted as the authority; he is to be sought after by those who desire heaven and liberation. Thus [it is said].
When asked how that [conclusion] is established, they state this proof:
"That which is the subject of dispute has an intelligent cause,
because it is an effect."
Whatever is an effect has an intelligent cause,
just like a jar;
and this [world] is an effect.
Therefore, [the world] has an intelligent cause.
It is impossible to demonstrate that a reason (hetu) establishes an imperceptible object among those reasons that are merely fallacious (hetvābhāsa), which have been experienced.
And there are five types of fallacious reasons, as it has been said:

The [fallacious reasons] are: the deviating (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the equal to the point at issue (*prakaraṇasama*), the equal to the probandum (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*).
Among these, this reason is certainly not "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*);
for that which is called "equal to the probandum" is defined as being unestablished (*asiddha*).
When briefly analyzed, that [unestablished reason] is established as being of two kinds:
either it is unestablished because its locus (*āśraya*) is unestablished, as in "The sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus";
or, even though the locus exists, it is unestablished because its connection [with the probandum] is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
*Nibandha* 33: For example, "Sound is impermanent because it possesses parts.

There is no lack of proof for the reason (*hetu*) under discussion through these two modes, because the probans (*sādhana*), namely "being an effect," is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in a subject (*dharmin*) such as a tree, which has been ascertained by valid cognition.

Furthermore, in the case of a subject such as a mountain that has existed for a long time, its state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is to be understood by means of the reason of having parts (*sāvayavatva*). For example: "The subject under dispute is an effect, because it possesses parts."
Whatever possesses parts is an effect,
just like a garment; and this [subject] is likewise.

Therefore, it is an effect. Now, one might object: by the reason of having parts (*sāvayavatva*), only substances (*dravya*) are established as effects, but not the qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth that are inherent (*samaveta*) in them.
If it is argued that this is because there is no connection with constituent parts (*avayava*) in their case, that is true;
however, their status as effects must be understood through another reason, namely, by virtue of their possessing qualities and so forth that are themselves effects. For instance:

Qualities and so forth, which possess birth and inhere in that which is either eternal or otherwise as the subject of dispute, [are non-eternal], because they are effects such as qualities. Whatever is an effect such as a quality, all of that is likewise [non-eternal].
Just as the form and other qualities of a jar and so forth [are produced],
so too are these;
therefore, they possess birth.
Furthermore, "being an effect" (kāryatva) should not be understood as inherence in its own cause or as a specific universal (sāmānyaviśeṣa),
for if it were so understood, the reason would be partially unestablished (bhāgāsiddha) because it does not pervade [the category of] destruction (pradhvaṃsa).
However, it is merely that its nature is dependent upon a cause;
and since this is apprehended by direct perception even in the case of destruction and so forth—just as in the case of sound and other phenomena—this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*).

For instance, that which exists only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is indeed called "contradictory" (*viruddha*), because it proves something contrary to the probandum (*sādhya*) due to being pervaded by the opposite of the probandum;
for example, "Sound is eternal, because it is produced.
But this [reason] is not like that.
Because its existence is observed in the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as jars and the like, which have well-known makers; [one might object]:

"But if 'being preceded by an intelligent agent' is what is to be proven, it is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana), for even our opponents accept that the entire class of effects is born of karma."
And because karma consists of volition,
or has volition as its cause;
and the world has that [volition] as its cause.
But when "being preceded by an omniscient being" is the property to be proven (sādhya), pervasion (vyāpti) is not perceived even in a dream;
moreover, the example (dṛṣṭānta) lacks the property to be proven,
because potters and the like are not omniscient.

Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed in jars and the like to be pervaded specifically by having a non-omniscient being as its antecedent.
Nor is it correct to say that the mere state of having an intelligent being as its antecedent is the object of the proof,
while the specific quality of having an omniscient being as its antecedent— which is not itself the object of that proof— is nevertheless established from it.
For instance, if this particularity is not the object of the proof, how can it be established by it?
Or, if it is established, how can it not be its object?
And if it is its object, why would it not be touched by the fault of lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*)? If this is asked:

It is said: even though the pervasion (*vyāpti*) pertains to the universal (*sāmānya*) alone, inference regarding a particular (*viśeṣa*) indeed occurs, because the universal—which already contains the particular within it—is inferred with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) by virtue of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all inference. For instance, even the inference of fire does not have the universal alone as its object.
Because that [fire] has already been established;
nor can it have as its object a mountain qualified by that [fire], since the universal *vahnitva* (fire-ness) cannot function as its qualifier due to the absence of any relation with it.
Otherwise, just as individual cows such as Śābaleya possess the inherence (*samavāya*) of cowness (*gotva*), the mountain would also result in being fire due to the inherence of *vahnitva*.
If it is argued that there indeed exists the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) between the mountain and fire, then,
since this [inference] cannot be established without first apprehending the specific fire conjoined with the mountain, that specific fire would likewise not be subject to inference.
And thus, the fault of lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would follow.

This same principle should be observed even in the case of the inference of the sense faculties (*indriya*), just as there is the establishment of a specific instrument characterized as a sense faculty.
For even in that case, no action is ever perceived that has a sense faculty as its instrument.
Indeed, actions such as cutting are not accomplished by means of the sense faculties,
because axes and the like are not sense faculties;
nor is it possible for an action characterized by the discernment of form and so forth to have axes and the like as its instruments.

Therefore, just as the generality of being an action (*kriyātva-sāmānya*), though pervaded by dependence on a mere instrument (*karaṇamātra*), results in the establishment of a specific instrument characterized as a sense organ (*indriya-lakṣaṇa-karaṇa-viśeṣa*) by virtue of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), so too here, although the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by a mere agent who knows the material cause, the instruments, the recipient, and the purpose, nevertheless, by virtue of its presence in the subject regarding the disputed objects, there is the establishment of a general agent who knows the material cause and so forth, with its specific nature being implied.

Otherwise, even the universal (sāmānya), which is intended to be all-pervasive, could not be established, because it would be untenable for that [universal] to be either devoid of particulars or incapable of possessing particulars.

Furthermore, since a non-omniscient being— one lacking the knowledge of distinctions such as the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth— cannot possibly be a controller, the distinction consisting of omniscience necessarily follows by implication.

If it is argued that pervasion by non-omniscience, embodiedness, and so forth is likewise unavoidable—just as it is by being the agent of the super-knowledge of grasping (upādāna) and the rest—since the absence of any observed deviation is the same in both cases; we reply:
no, because neither omniscience nor non-omniscience, nor embodiedness nor disembodiedness, is of any utility in the production of an effect.
For omniscience does not establish the capacity of creators [to produce specific things],
because it would follow that pots and the like could not be produced by non-omniscient potters and others;
nor does non-omniscience [establish such capacity], because it would follow that armlets and the like could also be produced by potters and others.
Likewise, the state of being embodied is not useful for the production of an effect, because it would follow that bracelets and other such items could be produced from a potter alone;
nor is the state of being unembodied [useful], because it would follow that pots and the like could not be produced from a potter.
Therefore, being preceded by a person who possesses knowledge of the material cause and so forth is the only pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the property of being an effect.
And that very [property] is what is expressed by the term "having an intelligent person as its antecedent.

Therefore, although the mere state of having an intelligent antecedent is the object of the pervasion (vyāpti), nevertheless, the specific quality of omniscience is obtained through the force of the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā); thus, the inference has a specific [quality] as its object, and the aforementioned fault does not follow.

Because, due to the variation in properties between the subject (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the objection characterized by "exaggeration" (*utkarṣa*) and "diminution" (*apakarṣa*) applies universally to all inferences; therefore, it serves as a reason for rejecting the validity of inference in general.

By this, that which was stated in the *Kaṇikā*—namely, that if potters and others possess knowledge of only a few instruments and so forth, they do not possess knowledge of all instruments and so forth—is [refuted].
In that case, by that very same illustration, even Īśvara would possess knowledge only of those instruments and so forth;
if there is knowledge only of those, omniscience is not established. For, such being the case, he would be a knower of only a few things.
Nor does the Lord possess even that limited knowledge [of his own actions] like a child or the like;
for it is observed that children, madmen, and others act here and there without intention, even though they lack full awareness of the purpose of their own actions. (Nibandh 35)
And since there is no restrictive reason why potters and the like should not be examples, nor why hair and the like should be, that [objection] is refuted.

For if God possesses knowledge of even a few supersensible instruments and so forth, it is unavoidable that he must possess knowledge of all such instruments, since the cause for that knowledge is the same in every case.
And the cause for that knowledge is nothing other than their existence, because worldly means of proximity, such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), are impossible in his case.
And when there is no difference in the cause, there is no difference in the effect;
otherwise, even a limited knowledge of supersensible things would not be possible.
For just as a potter and others are not non-omniscient regarding objects within the range of their common perceptual equipment, so too is Īśvara regarding supersensible instruments and the like.
Because there is no difference in their capacity.
Furthermore, it is not logical to deny knowledge of a few specific instruments by using the examples of children, the insane, and so forth;
for that would entail the absurd consequence of denying even mere intelligence by means of the example of a seed.

Therefore, just as there is no statement of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) on account of seeds and the like— since it is possible for them to possess knowledge of their respective materials and so forth—
likewise, this applies to children, the insane, and others as well. Thus, it is logical that potters and the like alone serve as the examples,
because the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)— namely, being an effect of an intellect possessing knowledge of the material cause and so forth— are well-established in those cases.

Likewise, regarding the claim that God’s desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and effort (*prayatna*) are eternal just like His knowledge: as for what was stated— that if these two are eternal, what is the use of God’s knowledge which serves to employ desire and effort,
since those two are already eternal?
"Because it does not depend on its own production," and so forth—
this too is without substance,
because it is impossible for there to be agency without [the agent] being known.

For knowledge, in cases where desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) and effort (*prayatna*) are non-eternal, indicates the instruments and so forth by presenting them; however, in cases where those two are eternal, it is fruitful even while indicating the instruments and so forth.
Therefore, although desire-to-act and effort are eternal, the Lord’s knowledge is fruitful, even if it is not directly instrumental in the production of an effect.

For this very reason, such talk as "how can this particularity, which cannot withstand critical inquiry, be subsumed under the subject of the thesis even by the force of the property's presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatā)? is mere idle chatter;
for as long as the knowledge of God remains uncontradicted, the specific quality of omniscience is unavoidable.
As it has been stated: "The activity of discerning persons is pervaded by [the presence of] a purpose."
Furthermore, we do not perceive any purpose for a wise Lord in the creation of the world,
since there is nothing further to be attained by one who has already attained all that is to be attained.
Moreover, even that [purpose] would be flawed.
Because his intention is difficult to comprehend,
because the absence of a purpose is not established,
and because there is no perception of a pervader.
Because of the state of doubt;
for the mental activity of a mere human being is indeed diverse, let alone that of the Creator of the universe,
since it is even conceivable that He— who has attained all that is to be attained— might still engage in acting for the sake of others out of compassion.
Furthermore, his engagement in the creation of hells and so forth does not impair his compassion;

on the contrary, like a father’s act of lancing a son’s boil, it leads to a manifestation of even greater compassion, because by inflicting a small amount of pain he removes a vast and terrible suffering.
Since his activity is established as being both necessary and stable, just as in the case of discerning persons, the inference of a purpose is indeed logically required.

And as for this which has been stated: "If indeed there were a single creator of all effects, then, because it would be impossible for one who is ignorant to produce [them], he would have to be omniscient. On the other hand, if each individual effect is produced by a separate agent, then whoever produces a particular thing knows only the causes of that thing, and is not omniscient."

To this it is replied: [The existence of] a single agent is established because there is no distinction in the effect as a logical mark (*liṅga*), just as the oneness of existence is known from the non-distinction in the cognition "it exists.

Since a plurality of things inferred from some logical mark must itself be inferable from another logical mark, a further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would have to be stated to establish that plurality.
Just as the diversity [of pleasure and so forth] is asserted by those who establish the diversity of the self,
there is no other means of valid cognition here for apprehending a multiplicity of agents.
But if there were unity [of the creator], no other means of proof would need to be sought;

for in the absence of a single creator, there would be the non-production of effects simultaneously by many who possess conflicting minds, due to their independence, mutual opposition, and lack of understanding of each other's intentions conducive to the task.
Alternatively, there would be the undesirable consequence that even what has been produced might be destroyed or otherwise disrupted.
Once unity is established, the proof of omniscience is not contradictory;
nor is there a lack of knowledge on the part of the Lord due to the absence of causes for knowing the merit and demerit inherent in all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*),
because the knowledge, volition, and effort inherent in those [souls] are eternal.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between cognition and its eternity.
Nor is it logical that the intellect of God (īśvara-buddhi) should likewise be non-eternal simply because cognition is observed to be non-eternal in various instances;
for if that were so, it would follow that even color and other qualities—which are non-eternal yet observed in various places and inherent in atoms of water and so forth—must also be non-eternal.
It is indeed logical that this [soul] should also be the substratum for the merit and demerit inherent in another person,
because of the existence of the relation of inherence-in-what-is-conjoined-to-what-is-conjoined (saṃyuktasaṃyogisamavāya).
For atoms are indeed conjoined with God.
And by these [qualities], the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas),
as well as the merit and demerit inherent in them, are manifested.
Thus, having extracted the essence of the refutation of the Lord (Īśvara) by Vācaspati as it appeared in the *Kaṇikā*, we have set it aside.
Furthermore, other arguments—which are mostly mere chaff and swallowed up by their own unacknowledged and established tenets—have not been written here for fear of excessive length.
Therefore, since the very specific characteristic intended, namely omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), is indeed established, this reason is not one that contradicts the specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*).
Nor is it established by means of actions; thus it is settled.
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
for if it were, it would have to be either an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, such as "earth is eternal because it possesses odor"; or...
Or it may be inconclusive because it cannot be applied, as in: "Everything is eternal, because it is knowable";
or it may be common [to both sides], as in: "Sound is eternal," [because it is audible].
Regarding the phrase "because of the absence of tangibility":
therein, first of all, the first two positions are not tenable, because they are refuted by the observation of their presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Nor is the last [alternative] tenable, because the exclusion of the probans from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), such as space and so forth— where the cessation of an agent has been established— is indeed perceived. If it is argued that the world, not observing grass and other things arising without human activity, does not even apprehend the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever is an effect is preceded by a person," [we reply:]...
If that were the case, then even the established status of valid inference would be reduced to a mere handful of water [i.e.,

destroyed]. For even in that instance, at the very moment of perceiving the pervasion (*vyāpti*), when one observes smoke in a place extremely difficult to access and infested with tigers and the like— without the operation of fire— or observes a jar previously established there without the operation of a person, the world [would have to conclude] that smoke alone is preceded by fire.
Or, it could be argued that one simply does not apprehend the pervasion— that every jar is preceded by a person.
If it is then argued that there is no rejection [of the inference] because fire and the person are remote in terms of space and time;

If that is so, then since a person is by nature remote even from grass and such things, there would be no rejection [of their agency] either; thus everything is the same, except for one's dogmatic attachment.
First of all, the fact that grass and such are preceded by human activity is not perceived.
And let that [precedence] not be perceived because the person is invisible or non-existent.
What is the use of this investigation?
If it is argued that, in every case, not perceiving any effect to be preceded by a unique person, no conscious being understands the pervasion of "mere effect" by "person," [we reply:
if that were so, then the fact that smoke is preceded by fire alone would likewise not be perceived.
Furthermore, a pot has as its antecedent a person who made it;
and whether that [person] is not perceived because of being spatially remote from the fire, or because of being non-existent, or because of being temporally remote, or because of being non-existent—
what is the use of investigating this?

Even the claim that no conscious person could ever perceive the non-pervasion of smoke by fire alone, or of a jar by a person alone— without having previously observed smoke in every case to be preceded by the activity of fire, or a jar to be preceded by a person— does not cause one's face to turn away in embarrassment.
So what is the use of this futile rejoinder that denies well-established inference?
