It might be argued as follows: the certainty of non-deviation [of the reason from the probandum] does not arise merely from its observation in similar instances (sapakṣa) and its non-observation in dissimilar instances (asapakṣa), because there is no rule of non-deviation for that which does not possess the nature of the probandum or does not originate from it. Thus, this property of being an effect (kāryatva) is not a valid proof, as its exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is doubtful.

To this it is replied: there is no doubt regarding the exclusion [of the reason] from the counter-example (vipakṣa), because the causal relationship—which is established through the means of perception and non-perception—is proven, just as in the case of smoke and fire;
however, the proof of its arising is for a specific effect alone, not for the generality of effects.

If it is argued that, for example, there is no certainty regarding the production by fire and so forth of "thingness" (vastutva) and the like which reside in smoke and such [phenomena], we say: no, because there is no distinguishing cause.

For perception and non-perception, which are accepted as the means of proving causal origination, are without distinction; thus, just as with a specific effect, the dependence of a general effect upon a substrate of awakening is established.

For just as an effect such as a cloth is seen to possess a material cause (*upādāna*), so too another effect, even if its material cause is unobserved, is established as possessing a material cause because it is an effect; likewise, that very same effect such as a cloth, though its agent (*kartṛ*) is unobserved, is determined to possess an agent because it is an effect, since the agent, like the material cause, exhibits positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the effect.
And because the conventional designations of cause and effect are everywhere based solely upon that [the apprehension of the object],
just as it is impossible to suspect that an effect could exist without a material cause—
since the production of any mere effect is established through a mere material cause— likewise, one should not suspect that an effect could exist without an agent.
Because there is no distinction [in the argument], since the production of any effect whatsoever is established from any agent whatsoever.
Granted, one might say something;
nevertheless, the inference of an intelligent agent does not arise from the mere fact of being an effect, but rather from a specific kind of effect alone.
If it is argued: "From the perception of which [a thing], even one who perceives no activity would form the notion that it has been produced;

and it is not logical for the establishment of a probandum to occur through a mere similarity of words, without following the underlying reality, because it would follow as a consequence that speech and other such things possess horns simply by virtue of being denotable by the word 'cow'."
This very point is superior, unsurpassed, and worthy of respect,
because it establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*) based solely on the generality of the effect (*kāryasāmānya*). Furthermore, what indeed is this "cognition of having been produced" (*kṛtabuddhi*)?
Is the determination of authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*) the conclusion that [the text] depends upon the operation of another, or is it the certainty that "this was produced by a person"?
If it is the first position, how is it that this [dependence] does not exist in the case of the earth and so forth?

Since the nature of being an effect—defined as the acquisition of its own essence through the operation of causes—is no different in the case of the earth and so forth than it is in the case of a jar and other such objects, [the inference fails].

If, on the other hand, you maintain that the certainty of being human-made (*pauruṣeyatva*) consists in the cognition of something as "made," then it must be stated: for whom does such a cognition of being "made" not exist?
Is it for one who knows the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the reason "because of being an effect," or rather for one who is the opposite of that?
It is not the first position,
because for one who knows the inseparable connection, the non-comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) is impossible.

Now, it might be argued that because the cognition of the probandum does not arise for that which is contrary to it, the inference of an intelligent agent is rejected on the grounds that the property of being produced by an intelligent cause is absent in the case of the earth, mountains, trees, and so forth.
But if this were so, all inference would be abolished; for no reason whatsoever could be a means of knowledge for one who has not grasped its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Therefore, being the cause of a cognition produced by effort is not a distinguishing feature.
Or, even if there were some indeterminate nature as a distinguishing feature, what would it matter?
For the pervasion is understood simply from the effect in general, just as it is from smoke in general.
Nor is the product of clay on the same footing as the reason "being an effect," because the latter is seen to deviate from its own probandum— the visible potter— in hundreds of instances;
whereas "being an effect" is invariably concomitant with a mere intelligent agent, whether visible or invisible, and thus this [reason] is not inconclusive.
Nor is it a "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) reason,
because it lacks a counter-position;
for there exists no other property that could establish a counter-argument against it.

For example, in the case of the argument "Sound is eternal because, while being a real entity, its eternal properties are not perceived," there exists a counter-argument based on a different property: "Sound is non-eternal because, while being a real entity, its non-eternal properties are not perceived. And this [latter] should not be stated as a sublation (*bādhaka*).
"The world is not created by a Lord,
because it possesses substantial reality," and so forth;
for there is no contradiction here, since the state of being created by a Lord is itself a form of substantial reality.
Thus, the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) [reason] is also [not a fallacy],
nor is it "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because that [status] belongs to one whose subject matter is sublated by perception, inference, or scripture,
whereas this [reason] is not in contradiction with them.
Among these, that which contradicts perception is:
"The composite whole of light is not hot, because it is produced.
That which contradicts inference is:
"Atoms have parts because they possess form";
this contradicts scripture. "A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being."
In this regard, this [reason] is not first of all contradicted by perception, because the opposite of the probandum is not an object of perception;
nor is it contradicted by inference.
Because its object is not sublated by an inference that apprehends the locus (*dharmī*),
nor is it contradicted by scripture, since [scripture] does not establish the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*).
If it is argued that this is because there is no definitive determination [of reality], or because the scriptures of the Sugata and others provide a contrary determination,
we say no; for those scriptures lack authority, as they are observed to be inconsistent with such matters as momentariness.
Nor should the Vedic scripture be suspected of being a sublater [of this position],
because in passages such as "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads," it is precisely the Creator who is established therein.

Furthermore, because there would be a lack of validity [in the scripture] were it not preceded by such a superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*), this reason [of the opponent] is not one whose time has passed [i.e., it is not irrelevant].

Thus, when the confusion regarding fallacious reasons has been removed, from this proof, an intelligent author who possesses knowledge of the materials and so forth is established as the intended agent.
It is settled that he alone is our Lord, the Blessed One (*Bhagavān*).
*Nibandha* 39:
Furthermore, for the sake of establishing this [Self], Śaṅkara intends this proof:

This world—whose production depends upon that which is the substratum of consciousness; which is other than what is produced by beings such as ourselves; and which consists of desire, pleasure, atoms, substrata, priority and posteriority, inferable universals, inherence, ultimate particularities, dimension inherent in the same object as those [particularities], unity, separateness, gravity, viscidity, color and taste not belonging to earth, touch, non-terrestrial fluidity, immaterial conjunction, mutual non-existence, and non-origination—is [the Self].
Because it has insentient matter as its material cause;
whatever is thus is so, just like a jar.
And so it is with this:
"Therefore, this too is likewise. This is its meaning.

"World" (*jagat*) is the subject (*dharmin*). "Arising dependent upon the locus of awakening" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). By means of the qualification of the subject, beginning with "desire" (*abhilāṣa*) and ending with "the formless which is non-arising," the class of eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*) is excluded.
By this qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaṇa*), namely "other than that produced by ourselves and others," there is the exclusion of jars and other things whose makers are well-known.
Furthermore, "desire" (*abhilāṣa*), "pleasure" (*prīti*), and "the atomic form" (*paramāṇumūrti*):
the substratum (*ādhāra*) of these is space (*ākāśa*), the self (*ātman*), and the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Space and time are to be inferred from the notions of "priority" and "posteriority.
However, categories such as generality (sāmānya) and the rest are to be accepted just as they are commonly established. Thus Narasiṃha has said:

The collection of objects of cognition, whose birth is dependent upon a substratum of consciousness and which is delimited by birth, is experienced as having a positive existence preceded by a person who is the subject of no dispute between both parties regarding the self as delimited by birth;
because they possess the quality of being produced.
Whatever is connected with the means of proof as stated is a substratum for the property to be proven as expressed;
for example, a garment.
And this [subject] is likewise.
Therefore, this too is likewise;
its meaning is as follows:
the collection of objects of cognition is the subject (*dharmin*).
The thesis to be proven (*sādhya*) is that [the self] has an origination dependent upon a substratum for consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"A self delimited by non-origination" is the qualification of the subject (*dharmin*).
By this, the class of eternal entities such as space (*ākāśa*) is excluded.
By the phrase "a negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) whose subject is a person not disputed by either proponent," there is also the exclusion of jars and the like which have well-known makers.
"Experiencing existence" (*bhāvānubhāvī*) refers to the nature of a real entity (*vastu*);
by this, the exclusion of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) and so forth is achieved.
The statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"whatever is connected with the stated means of proof"—means that which has the nature of a subject (*dharmin*) is possessed of the stated means of proof.
Trilocana, however, states this formulation as a negative inference (*vyatirekin*): "Every effect is caused by something possessing awakening."
Because it possesses the nature of arising.
It is observed that whatever is eternal, such as space and so forth, lacks such arising—just as the unawakened [self] is seen to be causeless.
Furthermore, that which possesses the nature of arising is the subject of our proposition, excluding what is produced by ourselves and others.
*Nibandha* 40):
Therefore, [the world] has a cause just like consciousness.
Furthermore, regarding the proof of the dyad and the Lord (*īśvara*), Trilocana himself said:
The duality under dispute depends, for its own production, upon a cognition whose object is each of the two individual entities,
because it is a number consisting of duality; whatever is duality is such [as this].
Just as there are two substances,
so too is this duality residing in the dyad;
therefore, it is so.
And he whose intellect is required in this matter is the Blessed Lord Īśvara.
And thus Vācaspati provides the proof:
"The bodies, trees, mountains, oceans, and so forth, which are the subjects of dispute, have a creator who is cognizant of their material causes and other factors,
because they are effects."
Whatever is an effect is produced by an agent who possesses knowledge of its material cause and so forth,
as in the case of a palace and the like; likewise, the body and other such things under dispute are effects.
Therefore, it is so;
for, having remained thus again and again, it possesses the nature of proceeding and it possesses a structural arrangement.
The reasons such as "because of being capable of purposeful action" (arthakriyākāritva) and so forth are to be understood according to the stated sequence of the five members [of a syllogism].
This is merely the vacillation of a dull-witted mind, which blinds the world; it is not fitting for the wise to overlook it, and thus something is said in response.

Here, indeed, the pervasion (vyāpti)—which encompasses all instances—between the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana), namely between "intelligent agency" and "merely being an effect," must necessarily be grasped.
Otherwise, the relationship between the signifier and the signified would be impossible.
And when that [invariable concomitance] is apprehended, is it to be grasped by the force of a subverting cognition that excludes the opposite, as in the case of mere cause and effect;
or rather, is it to be understood through specific perception and non-perception—which are inclined toward grasping specific positive and negative concomitances—as in the case of fire and smoke?

Furthermore, there are four possible alternatives: must it be understood through repeated observation and non-observation of the similar and dissimilar instances according to its own established state;
or must it be known through a single observation and non-observation of the similar and dissimilar instances?
First of all, the initial position is not tenable.

Because there is no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the general property of being an effect (*kāryatvasāmānya*) as a probans when its opposite—the absence of an intelligent agent—is the probandum.
Now, it might be argued that the absence of a subverting proof is unestablished;

for instance, just as this state of being an effect is held to be pervaded by an intelligent agent, so too is it pervaded by the necessity of place, time, and intrinsic nature (*deśakālasvabhāvaniyatatva*).
It has been observed that [the production of effects] is pervaded by both the presence of occasional causes and by being the effect of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Furthermore,
that restriction of place and so forth— whether it be the presence of occasional causes or the causal complex— is established as being preceded by an intelligent agent.

If, on the other hand, insentient things that are not presided over by consciousness were to produce an effect, then they would produce it wherever they happen to be situated; thus, an effect characterized by necessity regarding place, time, and intrinsic nature would not be observed.
If you argue that an effect is not produced by causes individually, but rather arises from the conjunction of causes, [we ask]:
from what does the very conjunction of those causes arise?
If it is argued that this occurs due to a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) whose maturation is occasional, [we reply]:
how indeed could this insentient entity bring about causes in their proper order?
For surely those [causes] do not remain situated anywhere [by themselves].

(Nibandha 41) Without the effort of a potter, the staff and other implements come together with one another solely by the power of a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force); or, once brought together, they are capable of producing the effect. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established between the restriction of place, time, and nature, the occasional presence of causes, and the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Since these pervading factors would cease to exist in the absence of an intelligent agent, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is thus excluded, is pervaded by having an intelligent agent as its antecedent. Therefore, three types of non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) are presented to establish this necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
And thus, it is not possible to conceive that an effect exists without a cause simply because an intelligent agent is excluded,
for that would entail the consequence of there being no restriction regarding place, time, or intrinsic nature.
Nor should it be suspected that the effect arises from something other than an intelligent agent.
Because it would follow that there is no production even once;
nor is it conceivable that this [effect] arises from something other than this [cause],
for if the cause were indeterminate, it would follow that there is no cause at all.

Likewise, if it were produced by a non-conscious entity in the absence of an intelligent agent, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that activity would never cease; thus, these four over-extended consequences (atiprasaṅga), which serve as subverting arguments against the contrary view, establish the pervasion (vyāpti). Therefore, just as the state of being preceded by a cause is unavoidable for an effect, so too is its being preceded by an intelligent agent unavoidable—if this is your argument.

To this it is replied: this royal dream would indeed be established if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) were proven—that the restriction of place, time, and nature, the occasional presence of causes, and the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) are preceded by an intelligent agent—but this alone is difficult to achieve.
For even in the absence of an intelligent agent, [these phenomena] arise from the presence of their own inherent causes.

Since things produced by a specific cause characterized as a causal complex— which, though insentient, possesses restricted power with respect to place, time, and capacity— are logically consistent as effects of a causal complex that brings about necessity regarding place, time, and intrinsic nature through the presence of causes at particular times,
the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is inconclusive (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
If it is asked, "In the absence of an intelligent being, how can there even be a conjunction [of causes]?"—

that too arises solely from a specific insentient causal complex as previously described, which is not presided over by a conscious agent. Since that [complex] also arises from such [a complex], and since a restriction regarding place and so forth is possible through an infinite succession of insentient causal complexes, there is no necessity for dependence upon an intelligent being.

If it is argued that since the restriction of place, time, and nature, as well as the occasional presence of causes and the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of jars and the like are seen to be preceded by an intelligent agent, other instances of such restrictions of place, time, and nature must likewise be so; then,
since jars and other effects are also frequently observed to be preceded by an intelligent agent, let every effect be of that same nature.
What is the use of this obsession with presenting the non-perception of a pervader?

Even though it has been observed many times that jars and the like are preceded by an intelligent agent, if one does not reach a certainty that every instance of a mere effect is likewise [preceded by an intelligent agent], then what follows?
Since this same [objection] applies equally to the restrictions regarding place and so forth, how can doubt be dispelled even in this case?
If it is argued that, in that case, perception alone must be the grasper of pervasion (vyāpti) in all instances,
then the establishment of the grasp of pervasion cannot be achieved through the force of a valid cognition that sublates the contrary (viparyayabādhakapramāṇa).
Furthermore, it will be explained during the discussion of the second alternative that perception is incapable in that regard.

Thus, once the relationship of cause and effect is established, if the possibility arises that smoke might arise without a cause, or arise from something other [than fire], or even arise from yet another [cause], then the absence of restriction regarding place and so forth, the abandonment of the [already] postulated cause, and the consequence of [postulating] a different cause all follow logically.
In the present case, however, the causal relationship between "intelligent agent" and "mere effect" has not yet been established;
nor can it be established.
Furthermore, regarding the agency of an insentient entity, [the possibility of] action—[is not possible].
(Nibandha 42) The consequence of non-cessation is relevant;

for it is not the case that whatever is insentient is always endowed with causal capacity, since even that possesses a capacity constrained by its own successive chain of causes. Thus, when there is the possibility of a succession of specific insentient causes—
It is not necessarily a refutation of an intelligent agent; rather, this is merely the outcry of one distressed by the collapse of his own position, and there is not even a scent of logic here.

Thus, the three types of non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) adduced for the sake of proving pervasion are "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*), and the fourfold absurdity (*atiprasaṅga*) is likewise irrelevant because the pervasion between "being an effect" and "having an intelligent cause" is unestablished.
Therefore, the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.
Regarding this, Vācaspati said:
"The state of having a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva) is not indeed a fault of the reason (hetudoṣa).
Therefore, how could it be excluded?"

For indeed, a reason that is observed in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) would not establish the intended [thesis], just like "knowability" (prameyatva) and so forth. But how could a reason—which, despite being sought with great effort, is not perceived in the dissimilar instances—not establish the probandum?
Those who do not see a restrictive factor must necessarily entertain doubt.

Thus, when given such an opening, the demoness of doubt— having gained free rein by transgressing the boundaries of worldly convention— is nowhere absent; consequently, no one would ever engage in any activity,
since every object whatsoever can be seen as a locus for suspicion,
and for discerning people, the apprehension of harm is a necessary factor for desisting from action.
Since death is observed even at the end of consuming wholesome food and drink,
one who maintains the worldly course according to authoritative tradition should entertain doubt based on what is actually seen,
but not regarding what is unseen.
For doubt depends upon the recollection of specific qualities; it does not arise from a lack of recollection.
Nor does recollection occur regarding that which has not been previously experienced.
As it was stated by the author of the Mīmāṃsā-vārttika in the *Adhyuṣṭasahasrikā*:
"An apprehension is not without a basis.
Likewise, in that same *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*:
"For he who, out of delusion, might imagine an invalidating cognition even though it has not arisen..."
He who is skeptical regarding all worldly transactions shall go to ruin. Thus it is said.
This is mere idle talk.

For the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of a reason is not established merely by its non-observation, even when sought with great effort, in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). To explain: the statement "the reason is not perceived in the counter-example" expresses only the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that would perceive it.
Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the effect of the object of cognition (*prameya*),
according to the principle that "that which is not a cause is not an object";
and yet, the cessation of the cause is not observed upon the cessation of the effect.
For fire is perceived even when devoid of smoke;
however, if the existence of the object of cognition were pervaded by the existence of the means of valid cognition, then this [argument] would be correct.

This pervasion alone is impossible, because it would entail that everyone is all-seeing. Therefore, the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be achieved by mere non-perception. As it has been said:—
Nibandha 43):
"Non-perception by everyone is doubtful, while non-perception by oneself is inconclusive;
for even though [grass] such as *dūrvā* is not perceived in the hollows of the Vindhya mountains, it nonetheless exists there."
Because it is not perceived by a person who is still subject to all opposing factors.
As for what was said— that because the demoness of doubt has found a foothold, there is nowhere [for action] that is not "non-existent," and thus no action would ever occur— that is inconsistent;
for even doubt regarding an object is a factor for the activity of discerning persons, and thus activity is indeed not precluded.
If it is argued that doubt regarding harm can be raised in every case—
leading to non-engagement because death is observed even from the consumption of pleasant food and drink—
this is difficult to ascertain.
For instance, "doubt regarding the goal" (*arthasaṃdeha*) or "doubt regarding the non-goal" (*anarthasaṃdeha*) is not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Rather, it is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyapadalopī samāsa*), like *śākapārthiva* ("vegetable-king"), meaning "a doubt directed toward the goal" (*arthonmukhaḥ saṃdehaḥ*) and "a doubt directed toward the non-goal" (*anarthonmukhaḥ saṃdehaḥ*).

This being the case, there is indeed doubt regarding the purpose of pleasant food, drink, and so forth; for we observe that things of that same kind— such as those intended for sight, nourishment, and the like— are produced millions of times within the continuums of both oneself and others, while misfortunes such as death are observed only occasionally and in certain instances.
The opposite of this should be understood as doubt regarding what is not beneficial (*anarthasaṃśaya*).

Therefore, due to such doubt concerning the object—even from the standpoint of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—the engagement of discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) in various matters is indeed unavoidable.
As for this statement— that what is spoken according to one's perception is to be doubted even if it has not been seen before, because doubt depends upon the recollection of specific features,

and so forth— that is incoherent. For, due to the absence of both proving and subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), doubt arises everywhere by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*) from the nature of other entities.
Furthermore, this doubt depends precisely upon the recollection of specific characteristics;
for it is by means of the presence or absence of those characteristics that something must be designated as belonging to that class or not belonging to that class.
Otherwise, the formulation of definitions would be purposeless.

This being the case, since— according to your own view— the properties of knowability (*prameyatva*), "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), being an effect (*kāryatva*), and so forth, are of the same class by virtue of the common characteristic of lacking a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) defined as either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), it is precisely the observation of the deviation of knowability that gives rise to doubt; thus, this doubt is raised exactly in accordance with what is observed.
As for the citation of Kumārila as a witness, it certainly does not exceed the popular proverb that "a cat is the witness in a pot of curd"— so what more need be said here?

Thus, since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason is not established merely by its non-observation in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the fault of the reason known as "doubtful exclusion from the counter-example" (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*) is indeed unavoidable.
For this very reason, what has been stated—that the presentation of this [fault] constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "failing to point out a fault"—is itself flawed.
On the contrary, while this valid refutation of the reason ought to be addressed, this [other party] claims it is not a fault in the reason and therefore need not be addressed.

By asserting that "the pointing out of what is not a fault" (*adoṣodbhāvana*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "objectioning against one who does not deserve it" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), this poor fellow is himself defeated by the very point of defeat defined as "objectioning against one who does not deserve it" according to his own doctrine; thus, he deserves our compassion.
Therefore, since there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to subvert the contrary [position], the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) remains unestablished.
The reason characterized as "being an effect" is inconclusive, because its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) is doubtful.

Now, the second position is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained through specific perception and non-perception—which are inclined toward grasping a specific positive and negative concomitance—just as in the case of fire and smoke.
To this it is replied:
Is the pervasion grasped with respect to a mere intelligent agent (*buddhimat-mātra*) whose limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is a visible body?

Or is it by means of that which is distinct from the limiting adjunct of the visible body, yet common to both the visible and the invisible? These are the two alternatives. If the first position is held:

In that case, since the state of being an effect is observed in things such as branches even when they arise without an object of proof (*sādhya*) of that nature, the reason is "inconclusive by being common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), just like "knowability" (*prameyatva*).
[Objection: But trees and the like have been made the subject (*pakṣa*);
how can there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of them?
For there are three kinds of categories of entities:
those whose agent is doubtful, such as trees and the like;
and those whose agent is well-known, such as pots and the like.

Just as space and so forth are without an agent, one takes up the pervasion (vyāpti) through perception and non-perception in the case of things like jars, which have well-established agents; then, having applied the property of being an effect to things like trees, which are subjects of doubt, an intelligent agent is inferred.
Furthermore, this [inference] cannot possibly be a case of deviation (vyabhicāra).
As for what was said— that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of the probandum itself—
this is incorrect;
for that which is the very object of deviation cannot possibly be the subject (pakṣa).

Because of the principle that "when there is doubt, one speaks of the reason; what is excluded [from the domain of the reason] is not a locus for the reason," and because the subject of deviation—the mere intelligent agent characterized by a visible body—is refuted in the case of the production of grass and such by the non-perception of a visible [agent], it follows that only mountains and the like are suitable to be made the subject (*pakṣa*) as having a doubtful agent. Therefore, one should not accept a fourth category of entities, namely that trees and the like have non-intelligent agents.

Now, for the sake of establishing the threefold collection of states (*bhāva*) through the wonder of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the second alternative is as follows: it is understood that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by a mere intelligent being (*buddhimat-mātra*)—who is not rejected by perception and who is common to both the visible and the invisible—with respect to a tree trunk and so forth. In that case, since a mere intelligent being is merely possible with respect to a tree trunk and so forth, we do not assert that there is a "common inconclusiveness" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntikatā*).

Rather, we maintain that the reason has a doubtful exclusion (sandigdhavyāvṛttikatva) because, at the time of grasping the pervasion, the probandum—being merely an intelligent agent (buddhimatmātra)—is invisible as it is common to both the visible and the invisible; thus, since its absence cannot be established by the non-perception of the visible, the pervasion does not exist.

For instance, when the absence of the jar prior to the activity of the potter is to be understood, at that time the absence of the jar cannot be understood as being caused by the absence of the probandum.

For just as at the time of the production of a tree and so forth, because a mere intelligent agent is invisible and thus impossible to negate, there is a possibility of its existence; likewise, even in the case of a jar and the like, at the time of ascertaining the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because a mere intelligent agent is invisible, there is a possibility of its existence. Consequently, since the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) necessitated by the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) remains unestablished, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not exist. Therefore, how is it that the reason is not one whose negative concomitance is doubtful?
As it has been said: "One should not suspect that an effect could exist without a material cause;
likewise, one should not suspect that an effect could exist without an agent.
In that regard as well, you have been utterly deluded by whom, such that you claim it need not be stated that an effect could both exist and be without a material cause?

For if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) were grasped here through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), then how could it be established that every effect is preceded by its material cause? Furthermore, you have not proposed any other method for grasping pervasion;

for it is impossible to infer the pervasion between the mere material cause and the mere effect—which are common to both the visible and the invisible—by means of perception and non-perception whose objects are restricted to the visible alone.
However, the consequence of undermining one’s own position has no place at this juncture when we are investigating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Alternatively, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established here by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary.
For instance, just as an effect such as a sprout is pervaded by having a restricted place, time, and nature, so too is it pervaded by being a rice seed (*śālitva*) and so forth.
[Commentary on Verse 45: It is observed that [the property of being an effect] is pervaded by a specific genus (*jātibheda*).

Therefore, since the opposite side (*vipakṣa*), which lacks a material cause, is excluded from the pervading factor—the specific genus such as "being a rice plant" (*śālitva*)—the property of being an effect, upon its own cessation, comes to rest in having a material cause; thus, it is established as being pervaded by that [having a material cause].
Furthermore, it is not tenable that a specific genus such as "rice-ness" (*śālitva*) could be produced even without a material cause (*upādāna*);

for if an effect of a certain genus or its opposite were to arise from a single, uniform cause that is itself devoid of a material cause, it would follow that the differentiation of effects is causeless. As it has been said:
"Entities possessing this or that form are born from causes possessing this or that form."

Otherwise, since sprouts and the like would arise from earth and other factors even without an *upādāna* (material cause), those seeking sprouts would not pursue seeds. Therefore, it is a logical principle that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" by "having a material cause" is established through the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary, just as it is established by "having a cause in general. However, there is no such subverting proof against the contrary to establish a pervasion between "mere being an effect" and "mere being an agent."
Since the three types of non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) and the four types of absurd consequences (*atiprasaṅga*) previously mentioned have already been refuted,

an opponent who raises the doubt that "something might be an effect yet not preceded by an intelligent agent" cannot be prevented [from doing so] without resorting to such measures as trampling his feet.

Now, one might object: "If the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the universals of cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception only when they are both perceptible—just as it is for the perceptible universals of fire and smoke—then the inference of another's mind would be undermined.

This is because it is impossible to grasp the pervasion through direct perception by means of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is common to both one's own and another's continuum and is thus both perceptible and imperceptible, since such a subject is distinct from the perceptible object. This objection should not be raised. For, while external objects exist, even though pure consciousness—which is common to one's own and another's continuum—is imperceptible in its own nature, it nonetheless exists in an inseparable state due to its connection with the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīpratibandha*) as the perceptible body.
Therefore, just as a perception whose object is a jar— though it functions with respect to only one part of its form— nonetheless presents the whole aggregate because of its non-deviation,

so too the very perception that grasps the body, occurring inseparably from the body, apprehends pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as the pervader of trembling and other such qualities; this consciousness is common to both one's own and others' mental continua.

Thus, in this way, the establishment of an object—whether it be of a perceptible nature or existing as inseparable from the perceptible—and the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) occur through ordinary, sharp perception;

however, this does not apply to pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is imperceptible and devoid of such perceptibility. Therefore, inference regarding another mental stream (santānāntara) is appropriate.

Consequently, if the apprehension of pervasion is achieved through perception and non-perception, then the logical rule is that it must be by means of the perceptible [subject] for the sake of the perceptible [object].
Thus, this is the summary of the meaning:

if an imperceptible creator is postulated to prevent the occurrence of "being an effect" in the heterologue (vipakṣa), how can pervasion (vyāpti) be established when it is deprived of the proof of negative concomitance (vyatireka)?

If, on the other hand, with the intention of establishing a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), one resorts to an agent who is observable, then even when that [agent] is excluded, grass and so forth would clearly remain as a momentary instance in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Therefore, pervasion is not established even by means of perception and non-perception.
But surely, since the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is cognized through repeated observation and non-observation, our third position alone is correct;
it is simply that this connection should not be understood as being characterized by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*),
but rather as being intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).
That very [self] is perceived through seeing and not-seeing; and Vācaspati has stated this same point as follows: (Nibandh 46)

We maintain that the probative force of "being an effect" (kāryatva) does not arise from its observation in similar instances (sapakṣa) and non-observation in dissimilar instances (asapakṣa), but rather from the power of an intrinsic connection (svābhāvikapratibandha).

However, since that very connection is apprehended through observation in similar instances and non-observation in dissimilar instances according to the sequence to be described, it is also appropriate to introduce those [observations].
Therefore, it is logical that only that for which this intrinsic connection is established as necessary is the prover (gamaka) and the proven (gamya), while the other related factor is the correlate.
For instance, the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), but not that of fire and the like with smoke and the like;
for those [fires] are perceived even without smoke and the like.
However, when they undergo contact with moist fuel (*ārdrendhana*), then they become connected with smoke and the like.
Therefore, the relationship between fire and the like with their fuel and so forth is produced by adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) and is not intrinsic; consequently, it is not necessary.
However, the relationship between smoke and the like with fire and the like is intrinsic, because no such adventitious condition for them is perceived.
Because deviation is not observed in any instance,
and because it is illogical to postulate something that is not being perceived;

nor is it reasonable to claim that an unperceived *upādhi*— which, due to its unobservability, is suspected precisely because of the absence of any proving or subverting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*)— can obstruct the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of the relationship.

As was stated previously in the passage beginning with "this demoness of doubt," therefore, by diligently searching for a limiting condition (upādhi) and failing to perceive one, we understand that it does not exist and thus determine that [the relation] is intrinsic (svābhāvika).

It might be argued as follows: if an intrinsic relationship were to exist between one thing and another without a cause, then everything would be related to everything else; and in that case, everything would be cognized from everything.

Now, if one thing is the effect of another despite being distinct from it, why does everything not arise from everything? For there is no difference in their distinctness. Consequently, that same logical over-extension (atiprasaṅga) remains.
If it is argued that intrinsic natures (svabhāva) are not subject to questioning, [we reply:]...
Therefore, even though there is no difference in their being other than one another, only some things are causes and only some things are effects.

But is this not the same as the objection regarding the nature of things (*svabhāvānanuyoga*), since it applies equally to those that are neither effect nor cause if there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*)? Consequently, this [objection] is also trivial.
If it is asked, "What is the means of valid cognition that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this relationship?
it is replied: "It is indeed well-established that pervasion between two general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) is to be understood through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*)."

The meaning of this has been explained by the author of the *Kāśikā* as follows: "In the final perception, aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by numerous previous observations, the nature of smoke as being invariably concomitant with fire appears in the mind— just as the true nature of a gem appears to an expert examiner, or as the true nature of words appears to one refined by the study of grammatical tradition."
[This is] like the status of being a Brahmin [which depends on] the recollection of the relationship with one's mother and father, and so forth.
For it is not the case that because all this does not appear at first glance, it therefore becomes otherwise even when it appears later.
Trilocana, however, has explained this matter as follows: through repeated observation, aided by repeated observation, the mind grasps the relation of those things belonging to that same class.
Therefore, smoke does not deviate from fire;
for were it to deviate from it, it would transcend a relation that is free from any limiting condition (*upādhi*).

The means of valid cognition that removes the suspicion of a counter-example to the reason is precisely perception known as non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which is the cause for determining the absence of any limiting condition (*upādhi*) that meets the criteria for perceptibility.
From this, the natural connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is established. Thus, his own position is established here as well.
In *Nibandha* 47,

Vācaspati also stated this: "It is logical that it is the sense organ itself— assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation— that grasps the natural relationship (*svābhāvikasaṃbandha*) between smoke and so forth with fire and so forth, just like the discernment of the true nature of a high-quality gem."

To this it is replied: If there were a difference [between the two], then the claim that "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) constitutes another, intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is merely a verbal flourish;
indeed, when scrutinized, it is not found to exist.
For instance, the relation of smoke and the like with fire and the like is intrinsic, because no limiting condition (*upādhi*) for it is perceived.
"You yourself have stated its definition as 'because no deviation is observed anywhere.
But this is unestablished;
for by the word 'condition' (upādhi), something other than itself that must be depended upon must be denoted."
Nor is it certain that an external object must be perceptible,
because even that which is imperceptible— being remote in terms of place, time, or intrinsic nature—
is possible; and consequently, there might be a limiting condition (upādhi) even for the relation between smoke and fire.
And since it is not observed, how can it be said that it does not exist simply because it is not seen—given that the establishment of an intrinsic connection depends upon such observation?
Now, if it were the case that something else must be depended upon as the internal relation, one might ask:
"How is there a necessary restriction such that 'smoke' implies the existence of fire? But surely this very point is what is being investigated.

If the production of smoke from fire is not accepted, then even if it is observed a thousand times, how can one be certain that fire necessarily occurs wherever there is smoke? Might it not be that at some point, depending on another factor—an adventitious condition (*upādhi*)—there would be smoke without fire?
What, then, is the definitive cause [of certainty] in this matter? It is the non-perception of such a condition.
As for the statement that "deviation is not observed in some cases," that has already been refuted;
for it is possible that an unobservable condition (*upādhi*) exists,
and because deviation cannot be ruled out even when it is not directly perceived due to the deficiency of other causes of cognition.

For this very reason, even in the absence of a sublater (bādhaka) for those two, doubt certainly arises due to the absence of both a proving and a subverting means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Furthermore, it does not turn away merely by your distressed outcry;
nor, by this much, is there a transgression of the worldly conduct of those who follow authoritative tradition.

For it is precisely by those who accept the authority of valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) that doubt, which is established by logic in the absence of either proving or disproving evidence, is prescribed.
Nor does this entail the consequence of total inaction,
since activity is justified both through the means of valid knowledge and through doubt regarding the object.
Furthermore, doubt regarding the absence of purpose cannot be maintained in all cases,
because in some instances one observes a clear orientation toward a purpose.

Just as the fact that, despite the lack of distinction in their being "other," only some things are causes and only some things are effects is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that cannot be questioned,

so too this non-questioning of intrinsic nature applies equally to those things that are not related as cause and effect when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*). Thus, Vācaspati’s employment of a "counter-argument" (*prativandī*) merely to confound the simple folk reveals an extreme lack of subtlety.

For instance, although there is no difference in their being real entities (*vastutva*), just as it is appropriate that fire burns while space does not— since this fact is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thus no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occurs—

likewise, even though there is no difference in their being distinct, the claim that only a specific thing is the cause of a specific effect and only a specific thing is its effect is also free from the charge of over-extension.
This is precisely because, given their distinction, the causal relationship characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is established by valid cognition.
Furthermore, there is no object denoted by the term "essential relation" (svābhāvikasaṃbandha) that is established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
because its definition has been shown to be unestablished.
Nor should it be argued that one must not state an objection regarding an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) when the subject of the thesis (pratijñā) itself is unestablished.
Because it would follow that everyone would be a victor everywhere merely by asserting a form [of their own] for everything; as the author of the *Alaṅkāra* said:
"Having established whatever one considers to be one's own position, one is rendered speechless there by the opponent."
It should be stated thus: "by the intrinsic natures of things";
in that case, everyone would be victorious in the end.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "intrinsic relation" (*svābhāvika-sambandha*)?
Are there three positions: that it is produced from itself, produced from its own cause, or uncaused?
First of all, it cannot be the first position.
Because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself;

however, in the second case, the very production of that [effect] is accepted as the relation through another formulation, so there is no dispute at all. Furthermore, if it were causeless, there would follow the consequence of an absence of restriction regarding place, time, and intrinsic nature; therefore, an inherent relation is untenable.

By this, it should be understood that the following statement is merely an expression of a personal whim: "We do not say that the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is a means of cognition through its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and absence in dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*), but rather by the force of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasaṃbandha*); however, that very [connection] is apprehended through the presence in similar instances and absence in dissimilar instances according to the sequence to be described."
For it has been stated that the definition of an essential (svābhāvika) relation is its necessity independent of any limiting condition (upādhi).

Since such necessity is unestablished by the reasoning already mentioned, it is impossible to state with any sense of compassion that this necessity flashes forth in the final cognition—whether that be the mind (manas) or the intellect (cetas)—assisted by the mental impressions (saṃskāra) produced by repeated observation.
Furthermore, as for the two examples cited—"like the essence of sound" and "like Brahminhood"—both of these are unestablished for us; therefore, it is improper to employ them as examples.
It is indeed reasonable that the true nature of the various types of noble gems becomes manifest;
for, through a succession of instructions, even one such as Māṇikyavatta has ascertained their characteristics—such as the light appearing in the form of a rainbow—with great difficulty.
However, you have not ascertained through any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) the characteristic of an intrinsic relation (svābhāvikasambandha), even though it was fabricated by your own cheek.
This argument—that by means of which such a state of affairs might also apply to this [other case]—is trivial.
Furthermore, let us grant for the moment that this intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) exists despite its unascertained nature;
even so, its apprehension through perception and non-perception (*darśanādarśana*) is extremely difficult to achieve.
For instance, if the necessity of smoke with respect to fire were to be grasped by a final cognition aided by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by numerous previous perceptions, [then...]

In that case, the fact that being earthen is necessarily concomitant with being scratchable by iron must be apprehended by the final cognition, aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation and non-observation among similar and dissimilar instances; thus, let the proof of being scratchable by iron also follow from being earthen.

Now, it is not the case that being earthen (pārthivatva) is necessarily concomitant with being scratchable by iron (lohalekhyatvaniyatatva), because an instance of deviation is observed in the case of a diamond (vajra).
Therefore, how can there be a grasping of such necessity through perception?
If that were so, then smoke would likewise not be necessarily concomitant with fire.
Since the absence of deviation is impossible to demonstrate, the objection—"How then can a restriction be grasped by the final moment of consciousness?"—is equally applicable.
If it is argued that there is no deviation because no deviation is observed, [we reply: the same applies here.
Now, what is the meaning of "non-deviation" [being established] because deviation is not observed?
Does non-deviation follow from the non-observation of deviation, or from the absence of deviation?
In the first case, let there be deviation or not; to claim that there is no deviation simply because no deviation is observed is the height of expertise!
Now, as for the second case:
from what is the absence of deviation known?
If it is argued that [the non-existence of the object] is due to its not being perceived, then is this merely a lack of perception, or is it the non-perception of something perceptible?
The first case is incapable [of proving non-existence].
For it cannot be asserted that there is no deviation even when [the cause] is not observed, just as in the case of the deviation of a Brāhmaṇī who has been lost for a long time;
[this applies] even when there is no direct observation.
Even in the case of Nibandha 49, deviation is observed due to the intervention of a very long period of time;
and the second [alternative] is impossible,
because deviation is observed whenever and wherever the conditions for observing deviation exist through some [means].

But in the absence of the causal complex for perception (*darśanasāmagrī*), due to the deficiency of other conditions or because [the object] exists at another place or time, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) since everything lacks the attainment of the characteristics of perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*).
Therefore, even though deviation exists, there is a non-perception of that deviation because of the absence of the causal complex for its perception.

Alternatively, if there is no deviation [of smoke from fire] by virtue of its being produced from that [fire], then there is no perception of deviation; thus, in both cases, let there be an absence of the perception of deviation.

However, as for the observation and non-observation described by you as the basis for establishing non-deviation, since these are subject to deviation in the case of "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) and so forth, they cannot serve as a basis for non-deviation even in the case of smoke. Consequently, it follows that even smoke would not be a ground for confidence according to your own view.
In our view, however, once the causal relation between two things has been established in a single instance through perception and non-perception, there can be no possibility of doubting deviation;
for in the absence of such [causal relation], one might overstep the state of being possessed of a cause.
By logical necessity, there is no occasion for the demon of doubt;
thus, in this way, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established even through repeated observation and non-observation.

If that is so, let the fourth position alone be accepted: that the certainty of pervasion arises from observing [the reason] once in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and once in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*).
For instance, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of "being an effect" with "having an intelligent agent as its antecedent" is observed in the case of a jar and the like;
and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of "being an effect" upon the absence of an intelligent cause is observed in the case of space and the like.
Therefore, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through the single instance of both positive and negative concomitance being proven, how can there be any inconclusiveness?
To this it is replied:

If a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between being an effect and having an intelligent cause were established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in a single locus, then it would be logical that the absence of an intelligent cause in space and so forth entails the absence of being an effect.

However, as has just been explained, that necessary connection—whether consisting of identity (*tādātmya*), causality (*tadutpatti*), intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*), or otherwise—is not established, due to the absence of any proof (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*).

Consequently, there would also be the exclusion of intelligence from space and so forth, yet there is no exclusion of the property of being an effect; thus, because its exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is doubtful, the property of being an effect is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Now, in our view, space is eternal, whereas in your view, it is non-existent.

If it is asked, "How then is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of 'being an effect' doubtful in this case? it is replied: For the negative concomitance is not merely the exclusion of being an effect from space (*ākāśa*).
However, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the absence of the probans necessitated by the absence of the probandum;
and that [absence] cannot be apprehended in the case of space (*ākāśa*).
For just as there is an exclusion of an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇa*) therein, so too is there an exclusion of cause in general.
Of what absence, then, would the absence of the effect be understood as being conditioned, by which the negative concomitance (vyatireka) could be established?
Surely this is true:

just as there is an absence of an intelligent cause in space, so too there is an absence of cause in general; thus, it cannot be determined that the state of being an effect (kāryatva) follows the exclusion of an intelligent cause.

Nevertheless, because the concomitance of the state of being an effect with an intelligent [cause] is observed in the case of jars and the like, the absence of the state of being an effect in space is understood to be necessitated by the absence of an intelligent [cause].
If it is asked, "In that case, how is the negative concomitance (vyatireka) unestablished?"—
well, in the case of a jar and so forth as well, it is not the mere presence of "being an effect" that constitutes positive concomitance (anvaya);
rather, it is the presence of the probans (sādhana) being necessitated by the presence of the probandum (sādhya).
And that [property] cannot be apprehended in the jar;

for just as the existence of an intelligent agent is present there, so too is the existence of mats, walls, and the like. Therefore, who could know this: does the state of being an effect exist because of the existence of an intelligent agent, or does it exist because of the existence of mats, walls, and the like?

Therefore, in this context, one must follow specific perception and non-perception which are inclined toward grasping a qualified positive and negative concomitance; for it is only when the cause and effect are both perceptible that positive and negative concomitances are established through the proof of their production from that [cause].
Furthermore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) even in a dream, the fourth position is also refuted.

Thus, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between "intelligent agency" and "mere product" remains unestablished, the hope that a specific omniscient person—who is cognizant of the material cause and so forth—could be proven by the logic of an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established incidentally) is merely a vain hope.

As for the example shown—that the specific instrument characterized as the eye is established through the force of the presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) regarding the generality of action—that too is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*).
For in that case, the eye-faculty is merely a name given to another cause established through the fact that the cognition of form would otherwise be impossible;
this is because no specific characteristic of the eye distinct from its being the producer of the cognition of form has been established.
Now, if it is argued that the very state of being the producer of the cognition of form is what constitutes "eyeness":
Let it be; what is the fault?
This very point is stated by us as another reason:
likewise, if you also apply the name "particular person" (puruṣaviśeṣa) to that which is merely the substratum of the generality of intelligence, [then there is no disagreement].
In that case, we have no disagreement. Rather,

we dispute the point that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), specific qualities such as omniscience are established upon a common substratum of intelligence— just as the specific qualities of the eye and so forth are established—
because both the example and the subject of the example lack the capacity to prove such a distinction.
Thus, this is the summary of the meaning:
if the visible is the probandum, there is indeed deviation; if it is not visible, there is no establishment of deviation.
Alternatively, because it is common to both sides, or due to doubt regarding the counter-example, the probandum is therefore not established.
Thus, the argument for an Īśvara is cast away like water poured from cupped hands.
Now the nature of the probans (*sādhana*) is being examined.

As for this mere effect—common to Meru, Mandara, the earth, pots, cloths, and so forth—which has been presented as the probans: as long as its conformity to the presence and absence of an intelligent agent is not ascertained in even a single instance, its capacity to prove [the conclusion] is untenable.
And that cannot be apprehended even in a dream;
for instance, while the potter is at work, let the effect characterized as a jar indeed be perceived arising from the lump of clay.
However, prior to the activity, it is not possible to apprehend the absence of the mere effect—just as there is no jar—[prior to the activity].

Because even in the absence of a potter, effects characterized by drying, breaking, and so forth are observed in a lump of clay; and because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to claim that whatever is observed to be invariably concomitant with something else must be its effect.
If it is argued that even the mere effects such as drying and breaking of the lump of clay are included in the subject (pakṣa), just like [the case of] grass and other things—

Let the absence of the effect as a whole be established even in a single instance where there is an absence of an intelligent agent; for, once pervasion is proven, one could infer an intelligent cause from the drying up and breaking [of things] just as one does from grass and the like.

(Nibandhana 51) Furthermore, the example based on the dissimilarity with space and so forth has already been refuted, because in that case it is possible for there to be a prior cause consisting merely of a non-intelligent factor, just as there might be a prior cause consisting of an intelligent factor, since it is not understood what causes the absence of "being an effect" [in such cases].

By this, that which was stated—namely, that because no deviation is observed, we do not perceive any specific characteristic in jars and the like, distinct from their "coming into being after not having been," upon which basis we could establish their being preceded by an agent—that too is refuted.

For even in the absence of a potter and others, effects such as drying or breaking are observed in clay lumps and the like; thus, since the definition of an effect as "coming into being after not having been" lacks a negative concomitance (vyatireka), there is an absence of pervasion (vyāpti).

Now, if it is argued: "If the pervasion of mere 'being an effect' with 'having an intelligent agent' is not grasped through perception because of the absence of negative instances (vyatireka), then how do you yourself determine the pervasion of 'being produced' with 'impermanence'?
We reply: "By the force of a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) consisting in the contradiction of the opposite, characterized by independence."
And that [reason] establishes the exclusion of "being produced" from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) only for that which is excluded from what does not possess its nature;
furthermore, it has already been demonstrated that you are unable to state a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) that sublates the contrary.
Therefore, this mere quality of being an effect is inconclusive (anaikāntika), because its exclusion from the dissimilar class is doubtful.
By this, that mockery of the Naiyāyikas' objections and rebuttals is addressed:
"In this context, there are indeed two kinds of 'being an effect':
the mere fact of being an effect [and the specific nature of the effect]."
And [the reason] is qualified.
In that case, because the first [reason] lacks a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
because the qualified [reason] is impossible in things such as mountains, it is unestablished (*asiddha*).
That is incorrect,
because the logical connection is established solely on the basis of being an effect.
As for what was said regarding "distinct causality," it must be explained what that is like. Now,

whatever effect is observed to be preceded by [the existence of] a person, by virtue of its conformity to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with that person— [that is the distinct causality].

That which, upon being seen, gives rise to the cognition that "it has been made" even for one who does not observe the act of making, and which is found in all palaces and the like while being excluded from mountains and so forth, is called a "distinct effect.
This is not tenable,
because the [possible] alternatives are untenable.
And thus Śaṅkara said: "Does one who has formed a cognition [of pervasion] have the cognition of the probandum (sādhya) or the cognition of the means of proof (sādhana)?
If it is the cognition of the probandum, that indeed occurs for one who has grasped the pervasion."
Now, for one who has not grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*),
is that [pervasion] seen to exist elsewhere as well? Or is it the cognition of the means of proof (*sādhana*)?
In that case, there would be a contradiction with one's own tenets,
because one accepts that every entity is produced.

Vācaspati, however, says here: "May your honor examine this more precisely: is the distinction the conformity to positive and negative concomitance with an intelligent agent, or is it the observation of that [concomitance] which is said to be absent in mountains and the like?
If it is the former alternative,"
This [existence] is indeed accepted by those who maintain that bodies, worlds, and so forth have an intelligent cause;
for no one other than a shameless person would claim that a cause does not conform to the presence or absence of its effect.
Now, if it is argued that this is merely "seeing" (darśana), that is the final alternative.
In that case, the notion that something has been produced cannot arise for one who perceives only non-action.
For it is only that very jar which was seen by him to follow the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent that is considered an effect, and not one found in the marketplace.

If it is argued that because one thing of a certain class is seen to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of another, then even something whose concomitance is not observed must likewise belong to that same class; then, alas, since objects such as jars, which possess an origin, are seen to follow the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent, other things like the body and the world—which likewise possess an origin—cannot be denied [to be of the same class] by the mere fact that they are different from a jar. Thus, whatever possesses an origin is preceded by an intelligent agent, just like a jar.
If that were so, would not palaces and the like fail to have that [clay] as their cause?
For they do not belong to the same class as a jar.

Now, whatever kind of thing is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance [of a cause] is of that same kind, even if its positive and negative concomitance is not observed, and it must have that as its cause.
Why then is a class of effects such as palaces not seen to have an intelligent cause, such that the world and the body, which possess an origin, would not likewise [have an intelligent cause]?
Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever in being of that same class.
Vittoka, however, says: "Let there be some particularity whose nature is not determined;
but what is intended by this proponent of a particularity?
Is it that the generality of being an effect (kāryatva-sāmānya) is unestablished?"

Now, [is it] with respect to a specific effect? Or with respect to an effect in general that there is a deviation from an intelligent agent? Or is it merely a dissimilarity between the probandum and the example?
What follows from this? If it is argued that the general property of being an effect is unestablished, that is not so;
for even in the case of the earth and other such things, the fact of being produced by the operation of a cause is established for both parties.
Now, if it is argued that the specific effect residing in jars and the like is unestablished in the subject (*pakṣāsiddhi*),
then there is no flaw here, because the specific [effect] was not intended as the reason (*hetu*).
This is so provided that what is intended to be demonstrated is the deviation of the general category of "effect" from its creator.
It cannot be [established] because it is not observed in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because grass and the like have been included within the subject (*pakṣa*),
and because mere suspicion is in every way prohibited.

It has been established that for the Naiyāyikas there is the "fallacy of pointing out what is not to be pointed out" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*) due to the doubtful nature of the negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*), while for the Buddhists the non-mentioning of a fault constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Nevertheless, the subverting proofs (*bādhakapramāṇa*) have indeed been stated.
Therefore, because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established, there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in all cases.
Now, as for the pointing out of dissimilarity between the thesis and the example,
that is not [valid],
because such a dissimilarity is easily found everywhere.

If the probandum were not established merely because of the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between the subject and the example, then even the very discourse of inference would now cease; for even between a bower and a kitchen, some sort of dissimilarity can always be found despite both possessing smoke. Thus, this [objection] is entirely trivial. This, then, is the summary of the point here: [The opponent might argue: "But surely, the probandum is not established by mere dissimilarity, for there is no such rule that the probandum must be established solely through similarity (*sādharmya*). Rather, it is established when the reason (*hetu*) is present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). To this we reply: No, for the reason is not established as being absent from the dissimilar class merely by its non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) there. For non-perception is twofold: that which consists in the perception of something else, and that which consists in the absence of all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Among these, the first does not prove the absence of the reason, since it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). As for the second, it is impossible to establish the absence of all means of knowledge regarding an object that is remote in space, time, or nature, or that is subtle. Therefore, the reason remains doubtful with respect to the dissimilar class. Consequently, the reason is not established as being absent from the dissimilar class merely through non-perception. Thus, the probandum is not established by mere dissimilarity. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the reason is not established as being present in the similar class merely through perception, because that too is inconclusive. For instance, although the quality of being a product (*kṛtakatva*) is perceived in a pot, which is similar to sound in being impermanent, it is not established as being present in all things similar to sound, such as lightning and so forth. Therefore, the reason is not established as being present in the similar class merely through perception. Hence, the probandum is not established by mere similarity either. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the probandum is not established by the combination of both similarity and dissimilarity, because that would involve a contradiction. For if the reason is present in the similar class, it cannot be absent from the dissimilar class; and if it is absent from the dissimilar class, it cannot be present in the similar class. Therefore, the two do not combine. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the probandum is not established by the negation of both similarity and dissimilarity, because that would result in the absence of any means of proof (*sādhana*). As for the mere state of being an effect (*kāryatvamātra*), since its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established by the aforementioned sequence, it is our accepted position that what is observed in mountains and the like leads to the inference of a Person (*puruṣa*); thus, the non-establishment of our intended probandum (*sādhya*) is perfectly logical. So why should we concern ourselves with further [objections]? This was stated even while conceding the point regarding "specificity of the effect" (*viśiṣṭakāryatva*). However, since it has been demonstrated at length once again that such specificity does not exist, all of that [objection] is likewise entirely unworthy of consideration.

For, since the pervasion of "merely being an effect" by [the probandum] is unestablished according to the sequence already stated, its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) is unavoidable. Furthermore, as for that specific kind of "being an effect" which was refuted through various alternatives, our own position does not accept it; therefore, the effort expended in that refutation results in nothing but exhaustion. Indeed, we do not maintain that "being an effect" is of two kinds.
One [universal] accompanies all effects, while the other is excluded from mountains and the like, following after jars, cloths, palaces, and so forth; however,
the effect is of many different kinds.

In that regard, even if a cloth indeed shares a commonality with palaces and the like through properties such as being a real entity, possessing a specific configuration, and being an effect, nevertheless, conventional perception does not apprehend those properties as being preceded by an intelligent agent,
because properties such as being an effect do not invariably follow the presence of an intelligent agent.
How then can there be an inference of an intelligent agent based on seeing that palaces, mountains, and the like possess the property of being effects?

Rather, it has been stated that the pervasion by an intelligent agent is established through perception only for that class of effects—such as a jar—for which the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the absence of such an agent is established.
Therefore, in another place or at another time, the inference of an intelligent agent is possible only from things belonging to the same class as a jar.

But when even a thing of the same class as a palace is separately determined in one instance to have an intelligent cause, then the existence of an intelligent agent is established from anything of that class as well.

Thus, by means of the cycle of effects—such as various types of water-jars, ladles, carts, cloth, and armlets—which are each separately determined to be preceded by an intelligent agent, the inference of an intelligent creator is faultless.
With this very point in mind, it was stated by the venerable Teacher:
Whatever arrangement and so forth is established as following the presence or absence of a presiding agent, that which is inferred from it must be endowed with those same characteristics.

Thus, although jars, cloths, mountains, and so forth share a commonality through properties such as being effects (*kāryatva*) or being real entities (*vastutva*), it is shown that the perception which grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*) for worldly people proceeds by taking into account internal distinctions of genus (*jāti*), such as jar-ness, cloth-ness, or mountain-ness.
Therefore, with respect to the cognition of a person proficient in conventional usage, [the rule applies] "from the sight of which [a person], even without seeing an action... [and so on].

It has been stated that one becomes "one whose intellect is formed" (*kṛtabuddhi*), but this is not said with reference to a person whose intellect is dependent upon the treatises (*śāstra*). For instance, in the case of a person who lacks the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the treatises but is proficient in worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*), such as a temple attendant (*devakulika*), [the term applies].
