For one who has ascertained that [the city] was preceded by a conscious agent and has entered the forest from the city, upon seeing both a mountain and a temple, even though he perceives no activity in either of those two, he forms the cognition that it was made in the case of the temple, but not in the case of the mountain. Therefore, although these two— the temple and the mountain— belong to the same genus by virtue of being effects and so forth, the presence or absence of the cognition that they were made cannot occur without establishing a distinction between them based on their respective sub-genuses, namely "temple-ness" and "mountain-ness."
They are capable of remaining [in their respective places].

Furthermore, once a distinction between types is established, pervasion is grasped as belonging to the type of divine temples, not to the type of mountains, nor is pervasion established for the type of palaces; therefore, there is no inference of an intelligent agent from that.
But when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended separately even for a palace, then let there be an inference of an intelligent agent from that which belongs to that same class.

However, the pervasion is not apprehended even in a dream for that which belongs to the class of mountains and the like; for although things such as pleasure-mountains differ from [ordinary] mountains in name only, their essential natures (*svarūpa*) are absolutely distinct from them.
And as for what was asked: "What is this notion of being 'made' (*kṛtabuddhi*), etc.?"—[the answer follows].
In this regard, we say that it is indeed the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*) itself.

As for what was stated here: "If the cognition of the probandum occurs for one who has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), then even for one who has not grasped the pervasion, is such a cognition seen to occur elsewhere as well?"

To this it is replied: we have no disagreement regarding the point that inference occurs for one who has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), but not for one who has not grasped it. We simply maintain that, in this particular case, it is impossible for one to have grasped the pervasion.

Because, according to the stated sequence, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished— since there is no certainty regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" by empirical perception (*vyāvahārika-pratyakṣa*)— the existence and non-existence of this cognition were stated solely from the perspective of an empirical person (*vyāvahārika-puruṣa*) for the purpose of establishing a distinction between intermediate classes (*avāntara-jāti-bheda*). Furthermore, the purpose for the distinction between these classes has already been explained previously.

As for what was stated here by Vācaspati, who considers himself clever: "Is any class of effects, such as palaces and the like, not seen to have an intelligent cause, such that the body, the world, and so forth—which possess the property of being produced—would not be likewise?
Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever in their belonging to that same class. That is inconsistent.
For instance, let it be granted that palaces, mountains, and so forth share a commonality with [the subject] by virtue of being effects (*kāryatva*) and the like;
nevertheless, this [commonality] cannot be apprehended through empirical perception as being pervaded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*).

This is because, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is impossible to demonstrate in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of mere effecthood that is necessitated by the absence of an intelligent agent.
Nibandha 54:
Thus, this is the summary of the meaning:
because mere "being an effect" lacks negative concomitance (avyatireka), it is non-pervasive (avyāpta) and therefore not a probans.
However, we ourselves do not even accept a mere "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*) that is common to intermediate objects such as pots and palaces.

Rather, the established order of inference is maintained by taking into account various specific universals (*jāti*) such as "pot-ness" and "cloth-ness," and this has been established beyond reproach.
Now, the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) is being examined.

If it is argued that when a proponent has presented a proof (*sādhana*), setting aside the presentation of its refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) and instead engaging in a conceptualization of the nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvarūpavikalpana*) constitutes, in the Nyāya system, a "reproach for what is not to be reproached" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), whereas in the Buddhist system it constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "failing to point out a fault" (*adoṣodbhāvana*); we reply that this is merely the prattle of a fool.

For instance, as long as the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established, how can there be a determination of the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) that follow from it?
And since that is unestablished, it has been stated that defects such as "unestablishedness" (*asiddhatā*) and virtues such as "presence in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) cannot be determined.
Therefore, the opponent should not remain silent, claiming that now there is no discussion of the defects or virtues of the reason (*hetu*).

Therefore, this definition of the probandum (sādhya) is intended solely to point out a fault in the reason; thus, it is the proponent himself who is defeated by the ground of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "accusing one who is not to be accused" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*) according to his own system. What is the point of this insistence?
Is this "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) the means of proof by which the world's being preceded by a mere intelligent agent is established?
Or rather, its being preceded by an intelligent agent characterized by qualities such as oneness, omnipresence, omniscience, and eternity?
In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
In the second case, however, because there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
[Objection: But even when pervasion is cognized in a general sense, the establishment of a particular [conclusion] occurs by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Just as the exclusion of non-connection with mountains and so forth is established for fire;
otherwise, there would be the destruction of all inference.
For one who hates inference speaks thus:
In this mire of the refutation of inference, the elephants that are the disputants are submerged:
there is a lack of positive concomitance (anugama) with respect to the particular, while with respect to the universal, it is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).
To this it is replied: indeed, a specific feature is established by the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), but not every [feature].
That specific feature is established without which the probans residing in the subject would be untenable.
Just as the specific qualities of fire, such as its location on a mountain and so forth, do not include its beautiful mass of five-colored flames;

nor is it the case that the fact that mountains and trees are effects cannot be accounted for without a creator possessing unity, omnipresence, omniscience, and so on, since these qualities are observed in other [causes] as well. Therefore...

There is no fault in merely distinguishing between the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*); however, there is a fault when [the latter] exceeds what is intended, because it fails to establish the desired [conclusion] and lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
If it is thus established that the agent is one who knows the own-nature, the material cause, the instruments, the recipient, and the purpose; and here,
the "own-nature" is the dyad (dvyaṇuka) which is the effect,
while the "material cause" is the fourfold class of atoms.
The instrument (*upakaraṇa*) consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) inherent in all knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
The recipient (*sampradāna*) consists of those knowers of the field toward whom this Blessed One directs himself through his own actions.
[Commentary on Verse 55: The purpose for the *kṣetrajñas* is the experience of pleasure and pain.
Since the intelligent [Self] is thus the probandum (*sādhya*), how can there be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)?
Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
Because, by the example of the potter, it is possible for there to be knowledge of the material cause and so forth;

and thus Vācaspati provides the proof: "The body, mountains, oceans, and so forth, which are the subjects under dispute, have as their agent a maker who possesses knowledge of the material cause and so forth, because they are effects."
Whatever is an effect is produced by an agent who possesses knowledge of its material cause and so forth,
as in the case of a palace and the like; and likewise are the body and other such things under dispute.
"Therefore, it is so.

Thus, having established by this proof merely that there is an agent who is cognizant of the material cause and so forth, Vācaspati himself spoke again in order to prove that [agent's] omniscience: "Let it be granted for now that there is a proof of a mere agent cognizant of the material cause and so forth;

however, by means of the inference known as *vyatirekin* (the method of difference), which functions through elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), the specific qualities [of that agent] are established. For instance:"
The creator of the body, the world, and so forth, is not one who possesses non-eternal and non-omniscient cognition;
for it would follow that such a creator would lack knowledge of those materials and other factors [of creation],
whereas one such as we does not possess knowledge of those materials and so forth.
And this [Lord] is one who possesses direct knowledge (*abhijña*) of their respective material causes and so forth;
therefore, it is "thus.

Indeed, no one other than such a Lord is capable of knowing the immeasurable distinctions among atoms nor the distinctions among the latencies of karma (*karmāśaya*) inherent in the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*).
To this it is replied: Regarding all those dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) that exist as effects with distinct places, times, and natures—does a single intelligent being act upon them all, or many?

Or rather, are there distinct intelligent beings acting upon each individual dyad, who are ignorant of one another's activities and who know only the respective material causes and so forth pertaining to their own specific objects, and who possess distinct places, times, and natures?
There are three positions. First of all, it is not the first position,
because the oneness of a creator for all dyads— which differ in terms of place, time, and intrinsic nature— is unestablished.
Furthermore, the argument presented for establishing oneness—namely, "because there is no distinction in the mark consisting of the effect" (*kāryaliṅgāviśeṣāt*) and so forth—is inconsistent.
For even when there is no distinction in the mark of smoke, the suspicion that fire might be manifold remains possible;
likewise, the reason "because there is no distinction in the mark 'existent'" (*saditi liṅgāviśeṣāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) for us with respect to the example.
Therefore, just as I must state a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish multiplicity, you too must state a proof to establish unity.
Now, if you think that unity is established due to the absence of a proof for multiplicity,
then why do you not likewise understand multiplicity itself due to the absence of a proof for unity?

As for what was also said— "In the case of unity, however, no other means of knowledge need be sought, because in the absence of a single agent, there would be a contradiction among many whose minds are [in conflict]," and so forth—
that too should be considered: if [the world] were produced by many, why would the effect not arise simultaneously?

*Nibandha* 56: What is intended is the non-arising of effects that exist in different places and times; or rather, the non-arising of a single great whole (*mahāvayavin*) in the form of the earth, a jar, and so forth.
In that regard, we do not perceive any contradiction to production when many [causes] act toward a single effect,
because there is no rule that many [causes] must necessarily be in disagreement with one another.
Because neither kind of contradiction— namely, mutual exclusion nor contradiction with manhood— is possible;
for manhood is indeed contradicted by non-manhood,
but not by mutual non-exclusion.

However, as for those [entities] that are differentiated by infinite distinctions of place, time, and intrinsic nature, the negation of multiple operations among them is all the more impossible; thus, the second position is also rejected.

Furthermore, the pervasion is not established by the observation of a single agent, because even multiple independent individuals—such as deer entering a village seeking their own respective purposes—are seen to perform a single action, such as killing.
If that [dual-atom] is also made the subject of the argument (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), then even for that which is intended to have been preceded by a single agent, let it be preceded by a self as its agent.
Thus, in this way, the oneness of the agent of all dual-atoms is not established.
And so it has been said:
If the existence of a single creator is not established, on what basis can omniscience be maintained?
For this very reason, the second position is also refuted;
for if even a single creator does not act upon all dyads (dvyaṇukas), it is all the more impossible for many to do so.

As for the third position, if it were the case, then even though one might possess expertise regarding the specific objects of their own respective activities, no single individual would be established as omniscient. Furthermore, knowledge does not grasp all objects merely by its existence, as is the case with the perception of a few supersensible things; for if it did, then due to that lack of distinction—just like the aforementioned atoms—there would be a non-differentiated grasping of everything, which would constitute omniscience.

For even if the perception of a few supersensible objects is established through inference, it is only by virtue of [the Lord's] connection with those causes that His status as their cause is ascertained;
since there is no ascertainment by means of any other way than the mere existence of knowledge, how can there be omniscience?
If it is asked: "But why would one who knows supersensible things such as atoms not possess omniscience?"
So then, what hope can there be for omniscience based merely on the perception of supersensible objects by those who are not all-seeing?

If you say, "It is exactly so," then alas! Even if such an omniscient being has been fashioned by your hand while you were bewildered by logic, it still remains for others who exist in boundless and distant places and times—

Because he is like one blind from birth regarding the material causes and other factors of dyads and so forth, and because he does not know the supreme goal of man, neither the common people nor authoritative persons accept his omniscience.
However, we do not harbor hostility toward those who merely perceive what is beyond the senses.

Furthermore, since the oneness of a creator is thus unestablished, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as a logical reason is also ineffective; for if a single creator of all things is not established, then the state of being cognizant of their respective materials and so forth remains unestablished.
Moreover, one who acts upon only a limited portion of things cannot be omniscient, as they would only be cognizant of the materials and so forth pertaining to that specific portion.
Even if there were multiple substrates, the general category of those possessing supernormal powers such as the knowledge of appropriation would still have its purpose fulfilled.

Thus, even if a mere person possessing the supernormal power of knowing appropriation and so forth were established, a specific person distinguished by qualities such as oneness and omniscience would not be established.
Furthermore, regarding a mere person, it has been stated that this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

If it is asked, "How can there be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) for those who desire that [the world] be preceded by a mere intelligent being (*buddhimān-mātra*), when the probandum is that it is preceded by an intelligent being who possesses knowledge of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth?
We reply: No, because the charge of *siddhasādhana* is leveled with respect to that [mere intelligent being].
We maintain that even if the specific [qualification] intended to exclude the unestablished (*asiddha*) is proven, the Naiyāyika’s own desired conclusion is still not established.
If it is argued that this results in the establishment of something undesirable for the Buddhist (Saugata), we say no;
for by means of establishing a probandum and a probans that one intends for oneself, the undesirable [consequence] for the opponent is also established.
Otherwise, even through such things as recollecting the grief for one's mother, that undesirable [consequence] would be established.
The summary of this [is as follows]:
In establishing [a thesis], there is the proof of what is desired by others, not the sublation of what is undesired by others; [this applies] to the mere effort of cognition.
When proving a specific desired [property], there is a lack of positive concomitance (ananvaya); a probans that tolerates doubt regarding the counter-example (vipakṣa) is a faulty means of proof.
The third chapter: The Investigation of the Probandum.
In this way, other reasons as well should be inferred and refuted according to their respective applications.
Thus, for the time being, the conventional designation of God as "existent" has been negated.

However, regarding the designation of Him as "non-existent," one should understand that the very proofs for existence and so forth—which establish the momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) characterized by being distinct from His [alleged] characteristics—are precisely what serve to refute Him.
May this light— producing understanding of the conceptual constructions regarding the agent, pervading and obstructing the darkness of delusion,
stainless and beautiful through its composition of jewels— remain for a long time unobstructed.
(Nibandha 58)
// 3 // Proof of Apoha (Exclusion) //
Homage to Tārā.
The meaning of a word is defined as *apoha*. Now, what indeed is this so-called *apoha*?
Is it that which is excluded from others?

Alternatively, based on the etymologies "that from which other things are excluded" or "that in which other things are excluded," what is intended is either the external object itself as distinguished from those of a different class,
or the form of the cognition.
Alternatively, there are three positions: that "exclusion" (apoha) means the act of excluding, or that it is merely the exclusion of others.
The first two positions are not tenable, because by the name "exclusion," it is precisely a positive entity (vidhi) that is intended to be expressed.
Even the last [alternative] is untenable,
because it is contradicted by common experience.
For instance, the verbal cognition "there is fire on the mountain" is observed to represent only a positive form.
The statement "it is not the case that it is not non-fire" merely indicates a simple negation;
furthermore, it is well known that where a matter is contradicted by direct perception, there is no room for any other means of proof.
Now, even if there is no conceptual construction (vikalpa) in the form "I cognize an absence," nevertheless, the very mention of the object that has ceased is itself the mention of the absence.
For a cognition of a qualified object is not possible without the inclusion of its qualifier.

Therefore, just as for others, the cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) is a conceptual cognition because the common form flashes forth—even in the absence of a conceptual construction such as "I cognize a universal"—so it is here.

If it is argued that the cognition of exclusion (nivṛtti-buddhi), projected by the cessation of [positive] conceptualization, extends the conventional usage of the apprehension of exclusion (apoha), then we reply:

if the establishment of a cognition of a universal is based on the manifestation of a common form in the manner of a positive entity (vidhi-rūpa), what has been gained for the establishment of a cognition of exclusion when the mind does not manifest the form of an absence?

If there were a manifestation of the form of exclusion (*nivṛtti*), even in the absence of a mental mode such as "therefore I cognize exclusion," who indeed could deny the established fact of the cognition of exclusion?

Otherwise, if one were to maintain that the conventional usage of its cognition occurs despite the absence of any appearance, then let it be that even when the mind has the form of a cow, there is a cognition of a horse.
Now, it might be argued that the cognition of exclusion is included as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Nevertheless, if the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) takes such a form as "that which is excluded from non-cow," then let there be an entry of that [exclusion] as a qualifier; however, the cognition is "cow.
And in that case, since the qualifier characterized by exclusion (*nivṛtti*), though existing, is not manifested therein, how can that cognition be established?
Now, if this thought occurs: "That which manifests in a positive form also possesses the exclusion of others (*parāpoha*); therefore, it is called the cognition of that [exclusion]."

Even then, the relation belongs only to the exclusion (*apoha*); it is the positive entity itself that appears directly. Moreover, in this way, it is unavoidable that even perception has exclusion as its object—especially in the case of conceptual construction, which delineates the exclusion of one thing while perceiving everything else as excluded.

Therefore, since conceptual cognition, like perception, apprehends a positive form (vidhyākāra), its object is exclusively a positive entity and not the exclusion of others (anyāpoha). How then can it be proclaimed that "exclusion" (apoha) is the meaning of words?
To this, it is replied:
by the term "exclusion," we do not intend a mere positive entity alone.

Nor is it merely the exclusion of others; rather, the meaning of words is a positive entity (vidhi) qualified by the exclusion of others (anyāpoha). Consequently, there is no room for the faults that arise from each of the individual positions.
As for the view of the proponents of affirmation (vidhivādins), that when a cow is perceived, its "not being of the nature of another" is subsequently determined through implication as apoha;
or the view of the proponents of negation (pratiṣedhavādins), that when the exclusion of others is perceived, the "excluded from others" is determined through implication— that is not tenable.

Even for a beginner, there is no observation of a sequential order [of cognition]; for no one, having first understood the positive injunction (*vidhi*), subsequently understands the exclusion (*apoha*) through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*),
nor does one, having understood the exclusion, understand that which is excluded from others.
Therefore, the cognition of a cow is said to be the cognition of that which is excluded from others.

Even though it has been stated that there is no explicit mention of the word "exclusion of others," it does not follow that the exclusion of others, which serves as a qualifier, is not cognized at all;
for the word "cow" is applied precisely to that which is excluded from non-cows.
Just as when the word "indīvara" (blue lotus) is applied to a blue lotus, the manifestation of blueness at that very moment upon the cognition of the blue lotus is unavoidable,

so too, when the word "go" (cow) is applied to that which excludes non-cows, the manifestation of the exclusion of non-cows (*agopoha*) is unavoidably simultaneous with the cognition of the cow, because it functions as its qualifier. Just as for perception, the apprehension of absence in the form of a simple negation (*prasajya-rūpa*) is nothing other than the capacity to produce a conceptual construction of absence, so too for affirmative conceptual constructions (*vidhi-vikalpa*), the apprehension of absence is designated as nothing other than the capacity to provide the corresponding practical application.
However, the apprehension of absence in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) is indistinguishable for both [parties], as it is simply the awareness of a determinate intrinsic nature.
Otherwise, if the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) were not grasped at the time of understanding the meaning from a word, how could there be activity by way of avoiding what is other?
Consequently, one commanded "Tie up the cow" might even tie up horses and the like.
As for what Vācaspati said— that individuals possessing a genus (jāti) are the domain of conceptualizations and words,

and that the form of those [individuals] which possess that [genus] is distinguished from what does not belong to that genus; and therefore, because of the cognition of that [form], one who is commanded "Bind the cow" does not bind horses and the like— that too is refuted by this very [argument].
If, even when a higher genus (*jāti*) is added, the nature of the individuals remains as it was— namely, excluded from what does not belong to that genus—
then how can there be an avoidance of that non-exclusion, given that they become the objects of words and conceptual cognitions precisely through that very nature?

Now, if the form of the individual (*vyakti*) is not excluded from what is of a different class, nor is it perceived as such, then this is merely the grace of the universal (*jāti*); how, therefore, can there be an understanding of it even through its meaning? This has already been explained. If, on the other hand, it is excluded from others solely by the power of the universal—let it be so, whether excluded from others by the power of the universal or by the power of its own causal series.
In either case, when there is a cognition of exclusion, there is indeed a cognition of exclusion.
Furthermore, in the process of establishing the convention for the word "cow" as that which is excluded from non-cows, there is no fault of mutual dependence.
Even if the convention were established with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*) or that which possesses it (*tadvat*), those same defects would still apply;
for by "universal" one does not mean a mere universal in the abstract, as that would entail the absurd consequence of applying the word "cow" even to a horse.
But it is "cowness" (gotva).
And by that much, the same fault remains; for even when a cow or the like is fully cognized, there is no full cognition of the universal "cowness."
Because the denotation of the word "cow" cannot be understood as long as the universal *gotva* (cowness) is not fully known,

there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) when the convention "this is a cow" is established with respect to that conceptual form (*vikalpabuddhyākāra*) which— though appearing as if common to all individuals— is externally projected based on the prior perception of a single individual.
Furthermore, once the application of the word "cow" is accepted, it is logical that the remaining [individuals] are also denoted by the word "non-cow."

Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and that which is excluded from others (*anyāpoḍha*), nor is there any impairment of their relationship as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*),
because there is no mutual exclusion between them and because their co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) exists.
It is like the absence of a jar on the ground;
for it is well known even among children that there is a contradiction with its own absence, not with the absence of another.
In the expression "This path leads to Śrughna," exclusion (apoha) is indeed understood as well.
In relation to other paths not under discussion, this very [path] is indeed Śrughna; and in relation to undesirable destinations that are the opposite of Śrughna, it is indeed Śrughna.
Because there is no interruption, as in the case of a forest path, it stands [as the goal] right away.
Since the exclusion [of alternatives] is easily established at every step—such as by excluding a caravan or a messenger—it is simply "the path."

Therefore, from a word whose nature is exclusion (apoha), there is the comprehension of that which has a positive form, just as from the word "puṇḍarīka" there is the comprehension of a lotus characterized by whiteness.
If it is argued that, in this case, it would be more appropriate to say that the meaning of a word is simply a positive injunction (vidhi), and why then is "exclusion" (apoha) proclaimed?
To this it has been said: by the term "exclusion," what is expressed is a positive injunction qualified by the exclusion of others.
In that case, when a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is being cognized, the cognition of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) occurs simultaneously as a qualifier.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to establish that perception (*pratyakṣa*) also has exclusion as its object;
for there is no dispute regarding its having a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, just as there is none regarding verbal cognition (*śābdapratyaya*).

By the word "positive injunction" (vidhi), two things are intended: the external object as excluded from what is not its own form according to conceptual determination (adhyavasāya), and the mental aspect (buddhyākāra) according to appearance (pratibhāsa).
Among these, the external object is established as the denotation of a word solely through conceptual determination.

It is not by way of the manifestation of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because— unlike direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)— there is no manifestation of a clearly evident specific characteristic determined by place, time, and state. As the treatise says:
"Because an object does not appear in the cognition of one whose eyes are not engaged by the word, just as it does not appear when the object is [directly] perceived.
If it is argued that there is a difference in the appearance of a single and identical object due to the differences in the means— namely, the nature of the sense faculty and the word— then:
Regarding this, it has also been said:
"In reality, the basis for the various cognitions is not distinct;
how then can that which is a single entity appear as having diverse forms?"
For two mutually contradictory forms, one clear and the other indistinct, cannot belong to a single entity,
such that one would appear in sensory cognition and the other in conceptual construction;
for if that were the case, it would follow that the entity itself is divided.
Nibandha 61): Indeed, there is no difference in reality other than a difference in essential nature;
nor is there any difference in essential nature other than a difference in appearance.
Otherwise, the three worlds would constitute a single reality.

If it is argued that, although there is a difference between clear and indistinct appearances for two persons situated at distant and near locations regarding the same tree, there is no difference in the tree itself—we say:
we do not claim that a difference in appearance is necessarily restricted to different objects; rather, we say it is necessarily restricted to the absence of having a single object.
Therefore, wherever there is a difference in appearance accompanied by a difference in causal efficiency and so forth, there is a difference in the real entity, as in the case of a jar;
elsewhere, however, because it necessarily excludes having a single object, a single appearance is erroneous.

By this, that which Vācaspati said— namely, "And there is no non-difference in cognition between verbal and perceptual [cognitions] when they have a real entity as their object, because the distinction between mediacy and immediacy is established through the difference in their causes"— is not tenable;
for it is impossible for a mediate cognition to have a real entity as its object.
However, the distinction of causes based on mediacy is fulfilled simply by the absence of the apprehension of objects within the range of the senses;
that is not so,
for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) manifests clearly in verbal cognition.

Furthermore, if a thing were expressed as having its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its essence, then because it would be apprehended in its entirety, affirmation and negation would be impossible;
for if it exists, the statement "it exists" is redundant,
and the statement "it does not exist" is contradictory.
But if non-existence were the case, "it does not exist" would be redundant,
and "it exists" would be ineffective; yet the employment of words such as "exists" and so forth does indeed occur.

Therefore, the fact that the appearance of a verbal cognition is common to both the existence and non-existence of an external object does not permit it to have that [external object] as its objective referent.

And as for what Vācaspati [said], having himself introduced the view that the individual possessing the universal (*jātimad-vyakti*) is the denotation of the word, he immediately thereafter stated: "Nor is it untenable that the universal, which is the meaning of a word, is common to both existence and non-existence;

for although it is eternal by its own nature, it becomes common to both existence and non-existence by virtue of being the substratum of many individuals scattered across space and time, and thus becomes fit for connection with 'is' and 'is not.
For the existence of a universal consists in its connection with a present individual."

Furthermore, the claim that there is no connection with past or future individuals is subject to doubt regarding its negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*); thus, it is either inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it is common to both existence and non-existence, or else it is "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*).
This has been already considered. Therefore, that [objection] is irrelevant.
To that extent, there is no damage to the present topic;
for by one who places the burden on the universal (jāti), the denotability of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is itself accepted.
Furthermore, in all cases, the existence and so forth of an object are considered solely in terms of its nature as a specific characteristic.
To claim that existence and so forth belong to the universal (jāti) only insofar as it is related to a particular (vyakti) such as one currently existing is a deception of children.
Likewise, there is a fault even in the view that the word denotes a particular possessing the universal.
For if the cognition of the particular is established, let the universal be cognized additionally, or let it not be; [it does not affect the fact].
But there is no liberation from the fault of perceiving an individual [as the object];
by this, that which is stated by the followers of Kumārila is refuted: namely, that because a thing possesses commonality (*sabhāgatva*), there is no fault of generality;
for "treeness" is understood from the word as something whose existence or non-existence has not yet been determined.
That it is connected with one of those two as understood through another word is also inconsistent;
for it is impossible for an eternal universal, when being apprehended, to be something whose existence or non-existence has not been determined.

As for this [objection]: "And it is not the case that the manner in which words convey their meaning is identical to that of perception, such that—as in the case of perception—there would be no dependence on words like 'exists' (*asti*) and so forth; for the means of valid cognition possess diverse powers. (Nibandha 62)
That too has been refuted by the critique of "distinct appearances" regarding the fact that sensory perception and verbal cognition grasp a single nature.
Furthermore, the diverse capacities of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are fully accounted for even by direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) and conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Therefore, if verbal cognition were to present the object of perception, its appearance would have to be exactly like that [perception].
And since they did not exist, it cannot be tolerated that there be a manifestation of them as objects.

If it is argued that, when the word "tree" indicates the aspect of treeness (*vṛkṣatva*), words such as "exists" (*asti*) are employed for the purpose of ascertaining the aspect of existence (*sattva*) and so forth;
[we reply: what scope is there for another word regarding a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is apprehended by perception as being partless?
Or rather, [what need is there for] the affirmation or negation of other properties through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
If it is argued that even in the case of perception, dependence on another means of knowledge is observed, let it be so;
for that [perception] is non-conceptual and thus lacks the nature of ascertainment regarding objects whose specific forms have not been previously familiarized.
But conceptual cognition, being itself of the nature of ascertainment, has no need for anything else in respect to that which it grasps.
Moreover, there is a dependence on other words and logical marks;
therefore, there is no apprehension of the actual nature of the thing-in-itself.

Now, since properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are distinct from one another and from the substratum (*dharmin*), even when the tree is cognized by way of a single property characterized by its genus, it is not cognized as possessing other properties; therefore, why should the cognition of other properties— such as being blue, moving, or very high— not depend upon distinct designations?
This is inconsistent,
because the partless particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) appears even in perception;
for the distinction between property and substratum (*dharmadharmin*), which is observable, is refuted by perception itself.
Otherwise, there would be the over-extension that everything would exist everywhere;
however, it has been established in the treatise that the conventional usage of "property" (*dharma*) and "property-bearer" (*dharmin*) is based on conceptual distinctions.
Or, let the distinction between property and property-bearer be even ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

Nevertheless, since relations such as inherence (*samavāya*) have been refuted, proximity must be accepted as being characterized solely by causal efficacy (*upakāra*). And in this way, just as through perception there is the apprehension of all the properties of a subject (*dharmī*) upon the apprehension of that subject via proximity with the sense-faculties,

so too, upon the apprehension of a subject through word and inferential mark— which are bound to the relationship between the signified and the signifier— there would result the apprehension of all its properties without exception.
Because mere proximity is without distinction.
And as for what Vācaspati said:
"When that [substance] qualified by one adjunct, such as existence (*sattva*), has been apprehended, there is no apprehension of it as qualified by another adjunct;
for it is the very nature of a substance that is qualified by adjuncts."
But neither the adjuncts nor the state of being qualified constitute its intrinsic nature;
that too is indeed subject to sublation.
For it is not the case that the apprehension of another adjunct is necessitated by non-difference.
For if one were to apprehend the benefactor only by presupposing a distinction [from the beneficiary], it would follow that the beneficiary must also be apprehended.
Nor is it appropriate to postulate a rule for the cognition of property and its locus based on their intrinsic nature alone— such as the case of fire and smoke being related as cause and effect—
because those two [property and locus] are likewise not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And the principle is that the description of an intrinsic nature applies only to that which is established by valid means of cognition.
Furthermore, the objection raised by Nyāyabhūṣaṇa— that the perception of the sun and other planets would entail the perception of the entire mass of objects dependent upon them—
is the result of failing to grasp his underlying intention.
For, in your own system, there is a distinction between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin).

And since proximity is defined solely as "being beneficial," when there is the apprehension of that which is beneficial, it follows that only that which occupies the same location and is of the nature of a property (*dharma*)—namely, that which is benefited—can be apprehended.

Therefore, how could it be logical to suggest the apprehension of something else, such as a substance occupying a different location that is benefited by the sun, or something whose deviation [from the rule] has been observed?

Consequently, if the essential nature of a thing were understood even through the medium of a single property, then because its entire self would be perceived, what room would there be for affirmation or negation by means of another word?
And yet it does exist.
Therefore, it is established that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not appear in words, conceptual constructions, or logical marks.
Nor does the universal appear in verbal cognition.

When one hears the words "cows are grazing on the far bank of the river," from such words as "cow" and so forth, there appear the dewlap, horns, tail, and other features, surrounded by the forms of the syllables; these appear as if condensed because there is no consideration of the differences between individuals of the same class.
Yet that [appearance] is not the universal itself.
Indeed, "cowness" (*gotva*) is said to be empty of color, shape, syllables, and form;

yet that very thing, consisting merely of the dewlap, horns, and so forth—which, though utterly distinct from every individual (*vyakti*), is unified with its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*). Since such an external object is not attained, this [notion] is nothing but an error, like the appearance of [illusory] hair.
Therefore, let this be a transformation (*vivarta*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) itself into that form due to the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
or let that form appear as something non-existent;
or let the individuals themselves appear otherwise by disregarding their own internal distinctions; or let it be called a "loss of memory" (*smṛtipramoṣa*) because of the intervention of experience.
In every respect, this cognition of a universal is indeed devoid of an object;
where, then, is there any talk of a universal?
Furthermore, as for the claim that the cognition of a universal would be causeless in the absence of a universal, that is incorrect.

Since the causal complex— which, assisted by the recollection of the perception of previous individual instances, produces a cognition of a distinct particular— generates a conceptual construction of a universal that lacks an objective referent;
therefore, in this way, the universal does not appear in verbal cognition,
nor does it appear in direct perception.
Nor is there establishment [of this] through inference,
because no connected logical mark (*liṅga*) is perceived given its invisibility.
Nor is there establishment of it like that of the sense-faculties from the effect of cognition, since only another occasional cause is established [thereby].

When one demonstrates the absence of the cognition of "cow" either within another individual cow or in the interval between them, then, since all individual cows such as the *śābaleya* and others would be absent, the resulting absence of the cognition of "cow" would be logically established; how could it imply a separate entity [as its cause]?
Furthermore, the individual cow exists solely because of "cowness" (*gotva*);
otherwise, even a horse would be an individual cow.
If it were so, then cowness would arise from the cow-individual alone; otherwise, even horseness would be cowness.
Therefore, it is only through a succession of causes that the cow-individual [arises]; as for cowness, let it exist or not.

Now, if the capacity to produce a cognition of a universal is non-different from a single individual entity, then another individual entity excluded from heterogeneous things would be incapable [of producing that cognition].
If, on the other hand, it is different, then that very thing is the universal itself.
If it is argued that there is dispute only regarding the name, [we reply:
that capacity is indeed non-different for each respective object.
For if one entity possesses a capable nature, what kind of fault does another entity incur by being likewise?
Just as for you, even a single universal (*jāti*) is the cause for producing a common designation,

and another [universal] is likewise [the cause] by its own nature alone, independent of other universals; so too for us, an individual (*vyakti*) is also the cause, being distinct by its own nature alone, independent of a universal.

As for what Trilocana says— that the inherence of general- particulars such as horse-ness, cow-ness, and so forth, in their own substrata, is the cause of the designation and cognition "the universal is a universal"—
if this is so, then let this very [inherence] be the cause of such designation and cognition even in the case of individuals; what is the point of the error of accepting [separate] universals?
Nor is inherence possible;
for the establishment of inherence depends on the cognition "it is here," and that cognition "it is here" arises from the perception of two things.
Since it is never observed in its own object, [inherence] is merely one's own conceptual construction; therefore, it is not a valid means of proof.

By this, his attempt to raise the objection— "How can this recurrence of cognition, which follows a recurring entity, occur among individuals that are absolutely distinct and which themselves follow the occurrence of cognitions whose objects are excluded?"—
is refuted; for there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of universals (*jāti*), which, though mutually distinct, are perceived as recurring through a recurring cognition.
Furthermore, as for the subverting argument he stated regarding the contrary case—

that the persistence of verbal designations and cognitions, occurring only in certain instances after having ceased elsewhere, must possess a cause, and that no other cause exists, and so forth; [this is refuted as follows].
That is not correct;

for it has already been established that the continuity of designation and cognition occurs even without a recurring [universal], because one must necessarily accept a specific nature that is excluded from what is not of that form (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta*). Therefore:
"When difference is equal, by whatever proximity a universal extends..."
Let that very [form] be the basis for the cognition of the word in some cases, and not elsewhere.
Furthermore, as for what has been stated here by the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*: "It is not the case that [the relationship] is thus:

let that very proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by which a staff, a string, and so forth extend to certain things but not others, be the basis for the linguistic usage of 'one possessing a staff' (*daṇḍin*) or 'one possessing a string' (*sūtrin*) in relation to persons, crystals, and so on;
what is the use of the staff, the string, and so forth?"
That is inconsistent;

for it is not denied that when a staff and a thread are in proximity to a person and a crystal respectively, they are perceived as the causes for the cognitions of "one with a staff" and "one with a thread.
However, a universal (sāmānya) is not seen even in a dream.

If this [universal] is to be postulated, then it would be better to postulate proximity itself as the cause of the cognition of a universal; for what is the point of a cumbersome postulation? This is said because [the opponent] has failed to understand the intended meaning. (Nibandh 65)
Now, this inference establishing [the existence of] birth (jāti) is stated:
whatever is a qualified cognition is invariably preceded by the apprehension of its qualifier,
just as the cognition of a man with a staff.
Furthermore, this specific cognition, "This is a cow," is a *kāryahetu* (effect-reason) by implication;
for in the example, the specific cognition is established as the effect of the experience of the qualifier. To this, the following objection is raised:

The probandum (sādhya) must be either that a specific cognition is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of a distinct qualifier, or that it is necessarily preceded by the mere experience of the qualifier.

In the first case, the thesis is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), which renders the application of the proof impossible; for in a perception that grasps a real entity, there is no appearance of both [the qualifier and the qualified] simultaneously.
Furthermore, the state of possessing a qualified cognition is an inconclusive general reason (*sāmānyahetu*),
because it is observed even in the absence of the apprehension of distinct qualifiers;
for example, "the pot possesses its own nature" (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*).
Or [the claim] that "cowness is a universal" (sāmānya).
However, in the second case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

This is because, just as in the case of "the pot possesses its own nature" (svarūpavān), the relationship between qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) is accepted based on a conceptualized distinction, such as "the individual possesses the universal cowness" (gotvajātimān piṇḍaḥ); furthermore, the cognition "this is a cow" is produced by an experience that excludes non-cows.
Thus, in this way, there is no establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Furthermore, there is well-known subverting evidence against the cycle of adjuncts such as universals, qualities, and actions: namely, either a sharp perception that apprehends only the individual (*vyakti*), or the non-perception of something perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*).
Thus, in this way, affirmation alone is the meaning of a word;
and that [meaning] is intended as either an external object or a mental form.
In that regard, neither affirmation nor negation applies to the mental form, whether in terms of ultimate reality or conventionally.
Because it is accessible through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), and because there is no conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*),
there are neither affirmation nor negation even of the external object in reality.
Because that [object] appears in verbal cognition,
for this very reason all phenomena are in reality inexpressible, since there is no determination of what appears.
Therefore, affirmation and negation pertain only to the external [object] in conventional reality.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of conventional discourse. Thus, in this way, neither the mental aspect (*ākāra*) nor the external object can be established as real through positive proof.
For it is only the external that exists conventionally; however, even conventionally, the mental aspect does not exist.

By this, Dharmottara’s claim—that there are both affirmation and negation of an externalized [object] that has been superimposed—is shown to be unworldly, contrary to scripture, and unworthy of a logician; it is thus cast aside.
Now, if in a non-determinate cognition (*avyavasāya*) the object to be determined (*adhyavaseya*) does not appear, then what is the meaning of saying "that has been determined"?
Even though there is no appearance [of the object], the meaning is that it has been made the object of activity.
If it is asked: "Since there is no distinction in the absence of appearance, how can activity be restricted to a specific object to the exclusion of other objects?", it is said in reply:
Although the entire universe is not grasped, nevertheless, because conceptualization is produced by a specific causal complex and thus possesses a restricted form,
its activity is restricted to water and so forth due to its restricted capacity,
just as smoke generates the cognition of a remote fire.
(Nibandha 66:
For entities have restricted objects and their natures are determined by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); they do not admit of questioning regarding a confusion of capacities.
Therefore, the determination of that [object] consists in the production of activity toward it due to its connection with a specific form (*ākāra*).

Nor do we say that activity occurs through superimposition based on similarity, which would provide an opening for criticism regarding the superimposition of an external object upon a mental form, or of a mental form upon an external object.

Rather, cognition itself, arising by the power of the maturation of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), extends its activity toward an external object even while not perceiving one; thus, it is indeed erroneous (*vipluta*).
Thus, it is established that the object qualified by the absence of others—that is, the object excluded from those of a different class—is the positive injunction (*vidhi*).
That very same thing is what is denoted by the term "exclusion" (*apoha*), and it is the meaning of words as well as the objective domain for engagement and withdrawal.
Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
Whatever is denotative has as its object only the thing-in-itself (vastumātra), which is determined as being excluded from what does not possess that nature;
for example, the statement "there is water in this well.
And since this form of words such as "cow" and so forth is denotative, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
This [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*);

for even though, according to the reasoning previously stated, there is no ultimately real relationship between the signified and the signifier, that which is produced by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) must necessarily be accepted by all those engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cessation of all worldly transaction.
Nor is it contradictory,
because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa);
nor is it inconclusive.

For thus, since others who do not accept that words have as their object merely the thing-in-itself (vastumātra) excluded from heterogeneous classes (vijātīyavyāvṛtta) as determined by conceptualization, must [accept] that the ultimate referent (*paramārthataḥ*) is either the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the qualifier (*upādhi*), or the connection with the qualifier (*upādhiyoga*), or that which possesses the qualifier (*sopādhi*), or perhaps the mental construction (*buddhi-kṛti*); for there is no other possible alternative.

And since denotative capacity is impossible if there is no object [of denotation], there can be no linguistic convention (*samaya*) regarding the first and the last [sounds] because of the loss of the power to produce the result; nor can it be in the middle [sounds] due to the absence of adjuncts (*upādhi*); therefore, it must be associated with all three together.

Thus, since there is no other object of expression, when the pervader—characterized by having an object—is excluded, expressiveness, which is excluded from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*), is pervaded by the state of having an external object as its determined referent;
thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.
[Composed by] the great scholar Ratnakīrti.
The Chapter on the Exclusion of Negation (*Tama-apoha-prakaraṇa*) is completed. (Nibandh 67) // 4 //
The Proof of Momentary Destruction (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi)
It consists of positive concomitance (anvaya).
Homage to Tārā.
The pervasion that consists of positive concomitance (anvaya), wherein the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is implied,
is here stated for the reason "existence" (sattva) in the case of a similar instance (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
Whatever exists is momentary,
just like a jar;
and these entities under dispute exist.
The capacity of a reason to establish an imperceptible object cannot be demonstrated without first eliminating the suspicion that it might be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
And fallacious reasons are of three types, distinguished as unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Among these, this reason is certainly not unestablished.
Even if it is true that in every philosophical system various definitions of existence have been stated—
such as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) or inherence in being (*sattāsamavāya*)— [the following applies].
Existence as intrinsic nature,
the state of being endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence,
and the state of being an object of valid cognition— that is, being within the scope of the means of knowledge that apprehend it.
Regarding the phrase "being the object of designation" and so forth:
nevertheless, what is the use of this irrelevant matter being determined at this very moment?
For we ourselves shall accept whatever existence of external objects is established as tenable when examined through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This very capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), which is well-known to all people, is indeed intended here by the word "existence" (*sattva*) and is employed as the probans (*sādhana*). Since this [capacity] is apprehended through means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth, with respect to those entities whose existence is established by perception and inference and which are made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is not even the possibility of [the reason] being unestablished (*asiddha*) either in its own nature or by way of its locus (*āśraya*).
Nor is there contradiction,
because [the reason] exists in the jar, which has been established as a similar instance (sapakṣa). But how can this [jar] be a similar instance?
In this case as well, [the argument] is like the previous position, because momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is not established;
for its momentary destruction is not established through direct perception,
since it is not ascertained as such.
Nor can it be established through inference from existence,
because that would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress due to the necessity of further supporting examples;
nor is there any other form of inference.

If it is argued that since momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established by that very [reasoning] even in the case of its occurrence, there is no need for the inference based on existence (*sattvānumāna*), we reply: There exists another independent inference, consisting of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), which is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing the momentary destruction of a jar.
To explain: a jar performs at least one purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) during the present moment.
[Nibandha 68] It performs [an action].
Would it perform that same purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) even in the past and future moments, or another?
Or else, there is no action whatsoever; thus there are three positions.
The first position here is not tenable, because it is impossible to perform what has already been performed.
Now, if the second [position] is accepted,
Therefore, let this be investigated here:
when a jar performs an effect belonging to the present moment, is it then capable or incapable of performing effects belonging to past and future moments as well?
If it is capable, then it should produce at that very same time the effects belonging to past and future moments, just like the effect belonging to the present moment.
Because it possesses causal capacity even then,
and because that which is capable cannot be delayed;
otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that even an effect existing in the present moment could not be produced.

Because there is no distinction in its capacity even between the prior and subsequent times, and because it is impossible for that which is capable to depend upon auxiliary causes; or, if it is incapable, [then it could never produce the effect].

In that case, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties— namely, being capable and incapable with respect to a single effect— the momentary destruction of the jar would become unavoidable.
Nor does the third position hold together,
precisely because the nature of being capable persists.
For when even a delay by a capable entity is intolerable, then non-performance is utterly ruled out;

otherwise, as it has been stated, there would be non-performance even of a present effect. Therefore, whenever something is fit for the conventional usage of "producing" something else, it must produce that thing at that time.
And not performing [the action], it does not become a subject for the conventional usage of "producing.
Thus, because the jar possesses a different nature at every moment—being capable or incapable with respect to a single effect—its status as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) remains unimpaired.
Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
Whatever is at whatever time capable of the conventional designation of "producing" that, at that time, necessarily produces it;
just as the final causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) produces its own effect.

Furthermore, this jar is fit for the conventional usage of producing effects belonging to past and future moments even at the time of performing an effect belonging to the present moment, and also at the time of transcending all activity; thus there is a *prasaṅga* based on an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Since the locus of this *prasaṅga-sādhana*—the state of being an object of the conventional usage of performing effects in the second and subsequent moments—is established in the subject (the jar) merely by virtue of the opponent's own admission during the time of performing the present effect and during the time of transcending all activity, its lack of proof (*asiddhi*) is certainly impossible.
Nor is there contradiction (*viruddhatā*), because its presence is possible in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) within the final causal complex (*antyakāraṇasāmagrī*).
[Objection: But is this not a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika-hetu*)?

If it is argued that [the reason] is observed even in a non-producer—such as a seed situated in a granary and so forth—which is a counter-example (vipakṣa), because the property of being the object of the conventional usage "capable" is seen there; we say no.
For the conventional usage "capable" is of two kinds: ultimate (pāramārthika) and figurative (aupacārika).
Of these, that which is ultimate—the state of being the object of the convention "producer" as necessitated by actual production—is what is employed here as the probans (sādhana).

Furthermore, since that [seed] residing in a granary or similar state is merely a cause of the cause and thus falls within the scope of figurative discourse regarding "production," its existence [as a producer] is impossible; how, then, could there be the fallacy of inconclusiveness due to commonality?
Nor is there any doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of this [reason].
Because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary [position].
For it is well-established through the experience of all people that this state of being the object of the conventional usage of "producing" is pervaded by having a restricted object;
nor is this [usage] without a cause.
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of any restriction regarding place, time, and intrinsic nature;
nor is any cause other than production perceived,
since we observe that [the effect] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of that [production].

And if the status of being an object of the conventional usage "production" were to occur even in the absence of actual production, then there would be no restriction, such that the usage of "production" would apply to everything everywhere;
yet this [usage] is observed to be restricted.

Therefore, since the pervader—namely, having a restricted scope—is absent in the counter-example (vipakṣa) where production is absent, the status of being an object of the conventional usage "production," which is thereby excluded, must rest solely upon actual production. Thus, because the pervasion is established, [the argument] is faultless.
This is the reason:
this jar does not produce an effect belonging to the past or future moments at the moment of performing its present function, nor when all activity has ceased;
therefore, it is not fit for the conventional designation of "producing."
This is because of the logical principle that every reductio ad absurdum must culminate in its opposite.
Here too, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Whatever does not produce something at a certain time is not capable of being conventionally designated as "capable" with respect to that thing at that time; just as, for example, *kodrava* grain, when not producing a rice sprout, is not capable of being so designated with respect to the rice sprout.

And this jar does not perform the effect belonging to past and future moments, either at the time of performing the effect existing in the present moment or at the time when all activity has ceased; thus, there is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which excludes [the possibility].

Here too, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because it is impossible for that which performs the effect existing in the present moment, or at the time when all activity has ceased, to also perform the effect existing in past and future moments.
Nor is there contradiction, because [the reason] exists in the similar class (sapakṣa);
nor is there inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā).

This is because, by the reasoning previously stated, the pervasion—possessing universal application—between being the object of a valid linguistic usage and being the producer [of cognition], both of which are positive (vidhi) in nature, has been established.
Furthermore, regarding what was stated here—
that whatever does not produce something at a certain time is not capable of it at that time— in this context, what is the meaning of "producing"?
Is it being a cause?
Is it the completeness of auxiliary causes conducive to the production of the effect? Or is it the non-deviation from the effect? Or is it the connection with the effect?
In this context, the very state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) is the meaning of "acting" (*karoti*).
Consequently, the faults that might arise from alternative positions are neutralized by the fact that those positions are not accepted.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assert here—on the grounds that "causality" and "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) are synonyms—that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*).

Since the probandum is the absence of being an object of the convention "capable," and since there is a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) between "causality" and "being an object of the convention 'capable'"— just as there is between "tree" and "śiṃśapā"— there is no occasion at all for such trivial chatter.
Thus, by the force of both the original reductio (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established in the example of a jar.
How then can it be said that there is no inference other than existence (*sattva*) that establishes momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) in the example?
Nor is the reason of existence thus rendered useless,
because momentary destruction is established in the example alone through both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its inversion (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*).

[Commentary on Verse 70: If it is argued, "But surely, by these two [arguments] alone, the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) may be established even in the case of the [opponent's] position," we reply:
"Let it be so; what is the fault?"

For that practitioner who is unwilling to set forth the argument for each individual object—that "whatever is at any time capable of the conventional usage of producing something, produces it at that time," and so on—the proof of momentary destruction follows from that very [general principle]. However, he who is afraid of the effort required to apply that logic to every single object indeed determines, by means of the logic applied to a single subject—that "whatever is at any time capable of the conventional usage of producing something, produces it at that time"—that existence (*sattva*) alone is pervaded by non-stability; and then, based on that very existence, [he establishes it] elsewhere.
Since one perceives momentariness,
how could one who is vigilant declare this [momentariness] to be futile?

Thus, for a jar that performs a single function, there arises— relative to its effects occurring in the second and subsequent moments— the superimposition of contradictory properties consisting of a capable and an incapable nature.

Since it is indeed a case of difference, the reason "existence" (sattva), when perceived in a jar which possesses the status of a similar instance (sapakṣa) due to its momentary destruction, is not contradictory (viruddha).
Nor is this [reason] inconclusive (anaikāntika),
because the pervasion (vyāpti) that includes all cases has been established precisely here in the example characterized by similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
If it is objected: "Surely the establishment of pervasion (vyāpti) results from the force of a valid cognition that sublates the contrary;
yet there is not even a mention of its presentation.
How, then, has pervasion been established?"
This is merely the play of a flickering intellect.

For it has been stated: at the time when a jar performs its function belonging to the present moment, if the capacity for performing functions belonging to past and future moments were also possible for that jar, then those [past and future] functions would have to be performed at that very same time.

And if they are not performed, then because of having natures that are respectively capable and incapable, there must be a difference from moment to moment; thus, that causal efficiency (arthakriyā-śakti) is necessarily pervaded by momentariness.
If it is asked, "In that case, let there be mere positive concomitance (anvaya); but how is the absolute exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) obtained? [The answer is:
Precisely from the establishment of pervasion (vyāpti).

If it is asked, "How can the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occur when there is doubt regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?", we say: no, for the establishment of pervasion is twofold.

One is in the form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), which is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*): namely, the necessary presence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in a subject (*dharmī*) that possesses the proving property (*sādhanadharma*).

And the negative form (*vyatireka-rūpa*) is the property of the action, which consists in the necessary absence of the probans when the probandum is absent. Furthermore, the cognition of either one of these two necessarily implies the cognition of the second; otherwise, one of them alone would remain unestablished.

Therefore, just as when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established as being necessarily restricted by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) in the case of the contrapositive, the doubt previously situated regarding the domain of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) subsequently vanishes, and thus no separate proof is stated for the sake of establishing that positive concomitance; so too, when the positive concomitance is established as being necessarily restricted by the force of the two reasons— the *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*tadviparyaya*).
Even if doubt regarding the domain of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) was previously present, it subsequently dissolves entirely;
nor is any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) required to establish that negative concomitance.
Consequently, there is an absolute negative concomitance of the probans (*sādhana*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*).
When the means of proof (*sādhana*) exists, there must necessarily be the concomitance (*anvaya*) of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*); thus, there is no difference in meaning.

Therefore, even without a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of positive concomitance is established by the force of the two reasons—namely, the reductio (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*).

Consequently, since the reason "existence" (*sattva*) lacks inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), the establishment of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) from this means of proof is beyond reproach.
[Objection] (Nibandha 71): But surely this proof is unestablished;
for an effect is not apprehended by means of the cognition of its cause.
Because that [cause] has already perished;
nor is it the case that the effect lacks a cause, for that [cause], though past, exists as a condition.
Furthermore, there is no apprehension of the past and the future by means of a cognition that apprehends only the present,
for that would lead to an over-extension;
nor is there a single synthesizing subject existing across the two times of the prior and the subsequent.

Because it would entail the consequence of the destruction of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Furthermore, for one who maintains the doctrine of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), the realization that the absence of a cause entails the absence of an effect is not even within the scope of their imagination.
But surely there is cognition at both the prior and subsequent times?

If it is argued that from those two [the senses and the mind] arises latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), and from that arises conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which determines cause and effect— that is incorrect;
for such a conceptual construction must either be a synthesis of what has been previously grasped or a superimposition of what does not possess that nature.
The first position is not tenable;
for in the absence of a single unifying subject, the grasping of what precedes and what follows would be impossible,
as there would be no latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for it would entail the consequence that even the cognition of water in a mirage would be valid.
Thus, since neither positive nor negative concomitance is established, existence characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) remains unproven.
Furthermore, this proof is unestablished (*asiddha*) even from another perspective.
For instance, the capacity of seeds and the like must be ascertained either through the cognition of the seed and so forth, or through their effect, such as the sprout.
And the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is established only upon the establishment of the reality of the thing itself (*vastutva*).
And its being a real entity [is established] from another effect;
the status of that other effect as an effect is established upon the proof of its being a real entity;
and that reality, in turn, [must come] from yet another distinct effect—thus there is an infinite regress.

Now, if, for fear of infinite regress, it is held that at the final limit no further effect is required, then by that very fact, the non-existence of all preceding [causes] would follow; thus, the causal efficiency of even a single thing is not established.

If it is argued: "But since 'being an effect' (kāryatva) and 'existence' (sattva) have distinct exclusions (vyāvṛtti), what harm is there if 'being an effect' is established even when 'existence' is not?"
That is inconsistent.

Even if there is a difference in the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and "existence" (*sattva*), how can "being an effect" be established when "existence" is not yet established?
For "being an effect" is indeed the state of coming into being after having not existed.
And existence (*bhāvanā*) is being (*sattā*);
and for the followers of the Sugata, being is nothing other than causal capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Consequently, when there is doubt regarding that capacity, it is impossible even to say "it exists."
How can the state of being an effect—defined as coming into existence after not having existed—be established?
Furthermore, even the property of being an effect, defined as depending on the operation of another, is not a characteristic of that which is non-existent;
for existence is itself the capacity [for causal efficiency].
And since that [reason] is doubtful, how can the state of being an effect be established?
If that is not established, the capacity of the former [cause] is not established; thus, the reason is "doubtfully unestablished" (sandigdhāsiddha).
Likewise, this [position] is also contradictory;
for if momentariness were true, it would first of all be impossible for that which is unborn or already ceased without continuity to initiate an effect.
Nor is there even such a moment for that which has already been produced as could be utilized for the sake of some effect.
Therefore, on the very position of momentariness, there is a contradiction because purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is untenable.
Alternatively, whatever is presented by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is entirely non-substantial (*avastu*).
Consequently, when momentariness—which is of the nature of a real entity—is to be proven, the inferential conceptual construction that presents a non-entity is contradictory.

Alternatively, if momentariness is to be proven of every cause whatsoever, there is a contradiction: for if it does not persist across different places and times, the relationship between the probandum and the probans cannot exist; and if it does persist, then a single non-momentary entity existing over various times would contradict momentariness. (Nibandh 72)
"This [reason] is also inconclusive, because there is no contradiction between existence and stability.
To this it is replied: as for what was said—that the capacity is not perceived—[we respond as follows].
