Is it then that nothing at all is perceived, or is this so only under the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)?

In the first case, because the entire cycle of causes— both those that produce and those that indicate— would be annihilated, it would follow as an absurd consequence that one could not even perform the mere movement of the face.

Otherwise, the very statement by which it is established that there is no capacity would itself arrive at the unimpeded capacity to establish that [very absence]. Therefore, for one who is engaged in the investigation of the reality of things with the desire for the supreme human goal, activity must necessarily be preceded by the acceptance of causal capacity. If that were not accepted, no one would engage in anything anywhere, and the world would become devoid of all activity.
Now, as for the second position:
there is, at least, the cognition of capacity;
and if that were not possible given momentariness, then it would be appropriate to state a contradiction.
The lamentation of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* author that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) is a wretched cry.
Furthermore, even if momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) exists, there is no contradiction in the cognition of causal capacity.

For instance, by means of the cognition apprehending the effect—which is the product (*upādeya*) of the cognition apprehending the cause and which contains within it the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that [prior cognition]—there is produced the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), namely: "when this exists, that exists."

Likewise, with respect to the cause, by means of the cognition apprehending the bare ground—which is the subsumed effect (upādeya) of that [prior] cognition—and with respect to the effect, by means of the cognition apprehending the bare ground which contains within it the latent impression (saṃskāra) deposited by that [prior cognition], the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is produced in the form: "in the absence of this, there is the absence of that.
As the Teachers have said:

A subsequent cognition, arising immediately after the single determination, brings about a reflective inquiry into the sequence; likewise, the cognition of exclusion from others, produced by the experience of the absence of that one [object], manifests the cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

This being the case, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is merely one that synthesizes what has been previously apprehended, because it synthesizes two successive perceptions that have apprehended [the object] as cause and effect.
As the *Alaṃkāra* states:

"If indeed a single perceiver does not possess the cognition of both the preceding and the succeeding [moments], then how could there be a cognition of the prior and the posterior when two perceivers exist? Thus [it is said].
Nor is the second [alternative] a variety of the unestablished (*asiddha*),
for it is the established position of the Buddhists that existence (*sattva*) is indeed causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*);
nor is this our undertaking begun only now for the sake of proving that.

However, where there is a real substratum (*dharmin*) such as a seed, which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and wherein causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) is also established by valid cognition, it is for that [substratum] that the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is intended.

Therefore, even if the capacity is doubted because the effect—such as a sprout—is not observed, the state of being a mere existent (*sanmātratva*), which is established by clear perception and excludes what is non-existent, cannot be denied.
Otherwise, if one does not admit the mere existence of the sprout and so forth, it would be impossible to formulate a definition of the characteristic [of existence] for each respective case.

Furthermore, it would follow that the conventional usage of "existence" (*sadvyavahāra*) would be absent everywhere. Therefore, even when there is doubt regarding the scriptural definition of existence, the fact of being an effect—such as a sprout—is perceived through the force of clear direct perception (*paṭupratyakṣa*) as having a real ontological status (*vastubhāva*); this establishes the causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the seed and so forth. Thus, there is no room for the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Nor is there any loss of causal capacity in the case of momentariness, such that there would be a contradiction;

for there is no contradiction between momentariness and causality characterized by necessary antecedence, since causal capacity is possible even for that which lasts for only a single moment. Thus, this first contradiction does not exist.
Nor is the second type of contradiction applicable;

for even if the own-form (*svākāra*)—whether it be a non-entity or an entity—is what is apprehended, validity is established in all cases only with respect to the object that is determined (*adhyavaseya*). Thus, since the momentariness of the very nature of the entity is proven, where is the contradiction?
If it is argued that both that which is grasped (*gṛhyate*) and that which is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) are merely exclusions of others (*anyanivṛtti*) and not real entities (*vastu*),
because if they were to penetrate the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the association with verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃsarga*) would be impossible— [we reply]: No,
for there is a lack of understanding regarding the essential nature of determination (*adhyavasāya*).

The determinative nature (*adhyavasāyitva*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists in its capacity to induce the activity of the mind and other faculties even with respect to an object that has not been grasped [by perception].
The state of being determined (*adhyavaseyatva*) consists in being made the object of such activity even though it does not appear [in the cognition].
And this state of being determined is logically possible only for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and not for anything else.
Because the activity of a seeker is directed toward that which is sought for the sake of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Thus, in such a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear at all.
Nor does the non-appearance of that [particular] entail the consequence of prompting activity everywhere without distinction.
Because it is produced from a specific causal complex,
because it possesses its own specific form,
and because it is endowed with a specific capacity.
Even when that which is excluded from what is not its own nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta*) is not explicitly perceived, activity is observed to be restricted [to specific causes],
just as a sprout arises only from a seed despite the non-existence of everything else;
for it is impossible to reject the observed relationship of cause and effect as being restricted.
However, the distinction is that validity exists when there is a connection with an external object,
whereas otherwise there is invalidity.
Likewise, the third position is also fruitless in its effort;

for even though a single entity existing at various times is impossible in reality, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans—which exist in all places and times and are excluded from what is not of their nature—is grasped by perception.
For the object of perception is twofold: the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*).

Let it be granted that the mere thing (*vastumātra*), which is excluded from everything that does not possess its own nature, cannot be the directly apprehended object (*grāhya-viṣaya*) of perception because it does not manifest [directly] to it.

However, when one part of it is grasped, it certainly becomes the determined object (*adhyavaseya-viṣaya*), because the perception generates a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that ascertains the pervasion between those two [the part and the whole].
This is just like the ascertainment of a continuum (*santāna*) upon the grasping of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Just as when there is the apprehension of mere form, there is the ascertainment of a jar consisting of color, taste, smell, and touch;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the abolition of all inference.

For instance, there are the following alternatives regarding the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*): is it between two universals (*sāmānya*), between two particulars (*viśeṣa*), between a particular characterized by a universal, or between a universal characterized by a particular?
The first alternative is not tenable, because the universal is subject to sublation; even if it were not subject to sublation, it would be imperceptible.
Even though it is perceptible, it cannot be an object of inference because it is not conducive to human goals;
nor can there be an inference of a particular from an inferred universal,
because— according to the reasoning to be stated later— it is impossible to apprehend the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between a universal and all particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because a particular (viśeṣa) lacks universal concomitance (ananugāmitva).
Regarding the final two alternatives, the particular must either be made the qualificand or the qualifier of the universal while it is perceived as having that universal as its common substratum;
or it must be unperceived, existing in another place or time;
or else every particular—consisting of both the perceived and the unperceived, existing in another place or time, and excluded from what is not of that nature [must be so].
The first position is not tenable because it lacks concomitance;
nor is the second, because it has never been observed.

Nor is it the third [alternative], because even when one particular instance is observed, the particulars existing in other places and times are not perceived. Or, if it is argued that all those particulars are indeed similar, [then...]

Because it is produced by a similar causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and because it performs a similar function, perception—which, through such proximity, grasps a single particular—generates a determination regarding the mere exclusion of what is not that form (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*). Thus, it establishes the mere particularity of the exclusion of what is not that form. This is just as perception, which grasps only the form dependent on a single causal complex, generates a determination regarding a jar and is thereby established as "grasping the jar."
Otherwise, even a jar and its continuum would not be established through perception, because there is no apprehension of them in their entirety;
for the apprehension of only one part is no different [from the case] of that which is excluded from what does not possess that nature.
If this is so, then let the apprehension of pervasion for every particular instance also occur through this very same sequence, just as there is the relation between qualifier and qualified.

Why, then, should one accept a single non-momentary entity existing at various times, such that the proof of momentariness would become contradictory? Thus, there is no contradiction regarding the consequence of differentiation.

Nor is this reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because, according to the sequence previously stated, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) form of pervasion is established in the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) by means of both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*) reasons. Now, if momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) were established in the example of the jar through the force of these two reasons— the *prasaṅga* and its contrapositive— then, since existence would be necessarily pervaded by momentariness, the charge of inconclusiveness [of the reason "existence"] would be refuted.
It is logical that [the pot] would act through inhalation;
however, this alone is impossible.
For even a capable pot will produce its effects sequentially by depending on sequential auxiliary causes.
And this should not be said:
"A capable entity acts by its own nature,
and since that nature exists at all times, it is not logical to depend on auxiliary factors which provide no assistance."
Even though it possesses its own nature as a causal factor (*kāraka*), how could it act if it lacks efficacy (*sāmarthya*)?
For efficacy is indeed the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*),
while the lack thereof is inefficacy.
Nor does the possessor of those two suffer any impairment through their appearance or disappearance, because it is distinct from them;
therefore, the object may indeed be capable.
And because it does not act, the reductio argument (prasaṅga-hetu) has a doubtful negative concomitance (sandigdhavyatireka).
To this it is replied: Let it be granted for now that capacity (*sāmarthya*) is simply the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārisākalya*).
Even so, that entity (*bhāva*) must first of all be an agent by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*).

And if its very same nature—which possesses the property of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyādharmā*) at the final moment—exists exactly as it was in the first moment, then it would necessarily act even then, and could not be prevented even by Brahmā.

Moreover, even that nature which possesses the property of non-delayed action cannot be said to be distinct from the entity when it has arisen in its entirety, because that would entail the consequence that the entity itself is not the agent.
Thus, as long as there is the conceptualization of other properties, for that long the entity remains indifferent [to its effect].

Therefore, if it is said that it produces by means of its own nature upon assuming a certain form, how could there ever be non-production if that nature existed even previously? Or, if the prior nature—which is opposed to immediate action—persists later on, how could the effect ever possibly come into being?
Now, if that [single cause] alone were the agent, this would indeed be logical;
however, it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces the effect.
Therefore, at a time when other auxiliary factors are absent, even a powerful [cause] does not bring about the production of the effect—what contradiction is there in this?

For an entity does not act by its own nature alone; rather, it acts precisely through its own nature when accompanied by auxiliary causes, since it is observed that the effect arises only from that [nature] when conjoined with auxiliaries.

Therefore, just like pervasion (*vyāpti*), the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must also be understood in one case as the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) and in the other case as the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
It is because there is such a consensus among worldly investigators as well.
To this it is replied: when [causes], being conjoined, perform an effect, let them possess "cooperation" characterized by the performance of a single purpose; who is there to deny that?
But from what source is it obtained that that effect must be produced *only* by those that are conjoined?

Because an entity possesses a single nature throughout its prior and posterior states, it would follow— irresistibly— that it must be restricted at all times to either always producing or never producing;
therefore, the claim that "the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, not a single [entity]," is beyond the reach of even the aspirations of those who maintain the doctrine of permanence.
If it is argued that "this is indeed seen," let it be seen; however,

the point of contention is whether the production of an effect arises from a pre-existing entity that has entered into the midst of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or rather from some other distinct entity that has arisen.

In that case, since [the cause] exists even previously, the effect would either arise at all times or never at all; thus, without resolving this contradiction, one merely repeats the probandum by closing one's eyes and saying, "Because we observe the production of the effect from that very [cause].
This does not deserve compassion.
Furthermore, oneness is not established through the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like.
This [argument] is refuted because even in cases such as hair and nails being cut and regrown, human effort is observed;
because it is impossible to demonstrate any difference in their characteristics; and because we have already extensively rejected the proof of permanence in the *Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa*.
Therefore, with respect to a direct causal relationship, there is an exclusion of connection with anything else (anyayogavyavaccheda) in both cases.

However, regarding pervasion (vyāpti), with respect to the cause alone—whether directly or indirectly—in the case of the cause as the pervader (vyāpaka), there is an exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda);
whereas in the case of the effect as the pervaded (vyāpya), there is an exclusion of connection with anything else.
Thus, when the pervader (*vyāpaka*) possesses that nature or does not possess it, there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*);
and when the pervaded (*vyāpya*) possesses that nature, there is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).
With respect to the form mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpārūḍharūpa*), there are these two kinds of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Now, if an entity possessing a single nature were observed at both prior and subsequent times as being pervaded by either productivity or non-productivity throughout, then this reductio ad absurdum would be applicable;
however, for the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*), there is no single [entity] across prior and subsequent times.
If it is argued that "something has been perceived," this is extremely crude. For the meaning of the statement "given that there is a single nature across prior and posterior times" is as follows:
If the very same nature of an entity that is a producer at a later time were to exist at an earlier time,
or if the very same nature that is a non-producer at an earlier time were to exist at a later time, then production or non-production would be perceived [simultaneously].
This being the case, since one is merely superimposing identity upon two established natures, it follows that either production or non-production is already established [and thus redundant].
But surely it is only the effect that requires an auxiliary cause,
not the cause of the production of the effect;
for capacity is of two kinds— innate and adventitious— and does not require another auxiliary.

If it is argued that even for a non-momentary entity, because its various auxiliary causes occur sequentially, it is possible for its various effects to arise sequentially, and thus it is impossible to establish that entities undergo change at every moment—
then we reply: let it be granted, for now, that capacity is twofold, consisting of the intrinsic and the adventitious.
Nevertheless, regarding that specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a thing which possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-dharmaka*) and must necessarily be admitted—
whether it exists prior [to the effect] or only afterwards— we do not understand what has been stated by this [opponent] concerning the refutation raised through such a dilemma.
Furthermore, the qualification that "auxiliaries are required only by way of the effect" is also useless.
For if the effect itself were independent in its own production, this would be logical;
however, this being the case, the postulation of the capacity of the totality of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-sākalya*) would be fruitless,
since the effect would arise only occasionally from that which is itself independent.
And this being the case, the existent causes are entirely incapable;
thus, the pure understanding is that this effect is non-existent and independent.
Now, if it is argued: "This is merely the fault of the effect, in that it sometimes does not arise even when the cause is capable," [we reply:]...
In that case, it is not its effect because of its independence; as the commentary states:
"If there were non-effectness even when the cause remains identical in all its states..."
In this way, the effect would be independent; if that were the case, it would not be an effect at all.

If it is argued that something is called an effect because it does not exist when that [cause] is absent— rather than merely because it exists when that is present— due to the predominance of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), we say: no.
For if the cause, by its very existence, were to produce its own effect, then there would be the cognition that "its non-existence is necessitated by the non-existence of that [cause].
If this were not the case, then just as an effect might not arise even when the cause is present due to its independence, [the same would apply here].
Likewise, even in the absence of that [cause], by whom could the suspicion that it does not exist arise solely out of its own independence? As the Bhāṣya says:
"If it does not exist even when that [cause] is present, how can there be non-existence when it is absent?"
"How can it be said that its non-existence is caused by the non-existence of that [other thing]?
Therefore, just as it necessarily does not exist when that is absent, it would likewise necessarily exist when that is present;
and since it does not so exist, it cannot admit of being the cause of itself."

As for what was stated [in *Nibandha* 77]: "At the time of producing the first effect, indeed, it possesses the nature of producing subsequent effects; therefore, it should produce all effects at that very first moment."
This is illogical due to self-contradiction, like saying, "My mother is barren.
For how could that which has the nature of producing a subsequent effect produce an effect at the outset? If it does not, then it does not have the nature of producing that effect.
For it is not the case that something whose nature is to produce blue also produces yellow and so forth.
To this it is replied: If an entity possesses a stable nature, how can it be established that this effect occurs only at a later time and not at an earlier time?
And in the absence of such [an effect], how can it be established that the cause also has the nature of producing an effect at a later time?
What can we do?
If you argue that its birth occurs only at a later time, let it be;
since that [birth] is impossible if [the entity] were stable, it must indicate instability.

If it is argued that even if [the cause] were stable, its very nature is such that it acts only at the subsequent moment, then all hope for valid cognition is destroyed; for in the case of "there is fire here because of smoke," one could equally say that its nature is such that there is smoke here now even though there is no fire.
Therefore, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); however, the intrinsic nature is not undermined by the apprehension of that intrinsic nature.
Consequently, if one were to assert that the effect exists in its first moment while accepting that the cause performs its function at a subsequent time, [it would lead to a contradiction].
There might be a contradiction with one's own words.

However, when the posteriority of the effect is logically untenable given the permanence of the cause, then the cause’s actual capacity to produce a subsequent effect is impossible; thus, this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum).
For it has been established that being the object of the conventional usage "producing" is pervaded by the act of producing itself.

Furthermore, the state of being the object of the conventional usage of "producing a subsequent effect" is established in the subject, the jar, at the very time it performs its first action, according to your own admission.
Therefore, since a subsequent effect—defined as being invariably concomitant with that [first action] alone—is impossible in the first moment, the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is formulated.

For indeed, even if one were to falsely attribute the status of being a producer of yellow to the cause of blue, there would be no *prasaṅga* of the actual occurrence of yellow; this is what is called a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
Thus, that which is capable is pervaded by the act of producing because it does not depend on auxiliary causes;
and that which is incapable is indeed distinct [from the capable], due to the imposition of the contradictory properties of incapacity and capacity.

Now, it may be granted that by the force of the reversal of the *prasaṅga*, there is the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by capacity and incapacity with respect to a single effect;
nevertheless, difference is not thereby established.

For instance, if a seed, while producing a sprout and so forth, were to produce soil and so forth by the very same nature (*svabhāva*) by which it produces the sprout and so forth, then it would follow that the soil and so forth must possess the nature of the sprout.

If, however, agency were due to a plurality of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), then because those natures are invariably characterized by mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), existence and non-existence—which are mutually contradictory—would occur in a single locus; thus, even a single seed would be divided.
The same applies to a lamp, which performs the exhaustion of oil, the burning of the wick, and so forth.
Likewise, a preceding form (*rūpa*) would also produce subsequent form, taste, smell, and so on, being conceptualized as possessing multiple intrinsic natures.

Furthermore, because those intrinsic natures do not deviate from their mutual non-existence, if they were to be conjoined despite being contradictory, then lamps and other such things would be divided;
yet they are not divided. (Nibandh 78)
Therefore, the superimposition of contradictory properties is not a differentiator.

Likewise, a seed possesses the property of being a producer with respect to a sprout, but the property of not being a producer with respect to a donkey and so forth; thus, being a producer and not being a producer are indeed contradictory properties.
Yet, despite their conjunction, there is no difference in the seed itself.

Thus, in this way, the superimposition of contradictory properties—such as being capable or incapable—which is observed in the case of the seed, the lamp, and form when they are opposed [to their effects], does not constitute a differentiator of jars and the like.
To this we reply:

let it be granted for now that seeds and the like possess a differentiation of multiple intrinsic natures (svabhāva) consisting of various properties (dharma), due to their capacity to produce multiple effects.
Nevertheless, what occasion is there for the superimposition of contradictory properties?
For when the mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*) of natures is invariable, it is "difference" (*bheda*) that finds its scope, not contradiction (*virodha*).

Contradiction, however, would exist between two things where the affirmation of one entails the negation of the other, and the negation of the other entails the affirmation of the first, by virtue of their existing as mutual exclusions within a single substratum (*dharmī*).
Therefore, in this case, it is logical that one intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is contradictory with its own absence, as in the case of existence and non-existence;
however, it is not contradictory with another intrinsic nature, as in the case of "pot-ness" and "substantiality.
Likewise, the capacity to produce a sprout and so forth is contradictory with the incapacity to produce that same thing, but not with the capacity to produce some other thing.

Furthermore, the operation of perception here establishes an entity as non-different even when it is superposed with various properties, just as it establishes that which performs a certain effect as distinct from that which does not perform that effect.
Therefore, if two natures— which, despite being non-deviant from mutual exclusion due to the absence of counter-correlativity— are not contradictory,

or if the capacity and incapacity toward a single effect are not contradictory because their objects differ, then what contradiction arises between two mutually exclusive properties, such as capacity and incapacity, which possess mutual counter-correlates?
Furthermore, if there is no contradiction between these two as well, then so-called "contradiction" is as good as consigned to the depths of the ocean.

Let it be, then, that the contradiction between capacity and incapacity exists only with respect to a single effect. However, just as capacity and incapacity are not contradictory due to a difference in location—such as having power toward that same effect in one place and a lack of power in another place—so too, they are not contradictory even due to a difference in the time of the effect within the very same locus, just as a crystal is previously inactive and yet that same [crystal] is subsequently active. If this is your argument:
It is said:
we do not assert that there is capacity and incapacity regarding a single effect based on a mere technical convention due to spatial difference when there is no contradiction;
rather, we do so because there is an absence of contradiction.
For the performance of an action in a particular place is indeed contradictory to the non-performance of that same action in that same place;
it is not, however, contradictory to the non-performance of that action in another place, nor to the performance of some other action.
If this is so, then the state of performing a function at that specific time is contradictory to the state of not performing that function at that specific time;
it is not, however, contradictory to not performing that function at another time, nor to performing some other function.
If you ask, "In that case, how can there be a contradiction even when there is a difference in time? [the answer follows].
It is said:
For contradiction between two properties residing in a single substratum is defined as the rule of non-coexistence, characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion.
And this [contradiction] may occur either through direct mutual opposition, like existence and non-existence, or...

Alternatively, because it is necessarily sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be like [the properties of] permanence or existence; thus, there is no difference in meaning.

Therefore, in this case, regarding a single subject (*dharmin*) which is the locus of performing that action at that time, there is a contradiction because its non-performance of that action at another time, or its performance of some other action, is necessarily sublated by another means of valid cognition.
For instance, in whatever subject the performance of that action at that time was perceived, in that very same [subject], it is not [perceived] at another time.
Nibandha 79: Neither the incapacity to produce that effect nor the capacity to produce another effect can be reconciled even by Brahman, such that there would be no contradiction between these two;

for, by means of the reasons resulting from the reversal of the aforementioned reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*), a difference in the substrata (*dharmibheda*) must necessarily be established in subsequent moments.
Nor is the identity [of the self] established by recognition,
because its human origin has been thoroughly uprooted;
for this very reason, even the "diamond" (vajra) argument has been cast into the belly of the thesis.
How can this wretched crystal serve as an example for establishing non-difference despite a difference in time?

Furthermore, it is not logical that there should be a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*) among effects produced at the same time even when they occupy different locations, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish such a difference.

Moreover, since non-difference is established by sensory perception—which eliminates any suspicion of error—there is no contradiction between capacity and incapacity even when there is a difference in time; nor can this [contradiction] be set aside merely on the basis of one's own dogmatic tenets.
Because neither convention nor valid means of knowledge apply [in that case].
Therefore, in all cases, the establishment of difference is simply the establishment of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*).
However, for one who is in disagreement, the conventional usage of "difference" is established on the basis of the superimposition of contradictory properties.
But even so, this existence (*sattva*) remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), either because it is over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) or because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

For just as this [existence] is excluded from the non-momentary when succession and simultaneity are excluded, so too is it excluded from the momentary when the two pervaders—dependence and independence, or unity and plurality—are excluded.

To explain: a moment of the seed, accompanied by the causal conditions for its approach such as Devadatta’s sprout-like hand, arises capable from that very same prior complex; thus, it is independent (*anapekṣa*) in producing its first excellence.

Furthermore, among the many series of seeds produced from the same granary, why does only one particular seed produce, through a succession, a moment of the seed that is conducive to the arising of a sprout, and not other moments of the seed belonging to different series? For prior to the advent of the auxiliary conditions, there is no mutual distinction whatsoever among those moments of the seed residing in either the same or different series.

Furthermore, prior to the condition of contact (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*), even those [moments] existing in that same continuum do not produce [the effect], because for them, the seed merely generates a seed-moment (*bījakṣaṇa*) that is conducive to the production of the sprout through a continuous succession.
Rather, it is only for a certain seed-moment, co-arising with the condition of contact, that there is the production of an initial excellence (*atiśaya*).
Well then, in the absence of that [auxiliary], even if it has arisen, it would simply not produce [the effect].

And thus, since deviation is possible for those [causes] taken alone, one must—even against one's will—accept that earth and the other factors produce the sprout or the initial excellence only when they are mutually dependent.
Therefore, independence is not possible for a momentary entity.

Nor is dependence logical, because between two moments occurring at the same time—like the left and right horns of a cow—the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary is impossible; thus, the first pervading absence [of the reason] is not unestablished.
Furthermore, if the final seed-moment, while producing the sprout and so forth without dependence, produces the sprout by that very same nature [by which it produces other things],...
In that case, since earth and the other elements would have the same cause as the sprout, they too would necessarily attain the nature of the sprout; therefore, their identity is not possible.
But surely it acts through a different form;
for instance, the seed functions as the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the sprout,
whereas it functions as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*) with respect to the earth and so forth.

If this is so, are the states of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) and being a material cause (*upādānatva*) one and the same reality or are they distinct? If they are one, how can it be a producer by means of a different form?
If they are distinct, however, are these two different from the seed or not different from it?
If there is difference, how can the seed be the producer, since the sprout and so forth arise from those two [the seed and the sprout] themselves?

Or, if there is non-difference, how is it that the seed does not possess multiplicity, given its identity with what is different; or else, these two would possess oneness, due to their identity with one another?
If it were argued that when earth and so forth are to be produced, their material cause (*upādāna*) is already a different form (*rūpāntara*) of the seed of earth and so forth—
then the seed would not be the producer of earth and so forth independently of them;
for if it were independent of them, it would be impossible for those [products] to be distinct from the sprout.
And you yourself have stated that things do not depend on those that provide no assistance.

Furthermore, since no assistance is possible for a momentary entity other than its production—and because that [moment] is indivisible—multiplicity also does not exist. Thus, the second pervader’s absence is likewise not unestablished.

Therefore, [the reason] is non-exclusive and inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), like "possessing odor. If one should think: "Even though they provide no assistance, auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are still to be depended upon because their presence and absence are followed by the presence and absence of the effect, and because they act together";

[we reply: "In this manner, even a non-momentary entity might depend upon sequential auxiliary causes—even those that provide no assistance—since its positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is replicated by the sequential effect."

Furthermore, since effects will be produced sequentially by virtue of sequential auxiliary causes, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished; thus, existence (*sattva*) is an inconclusive reason with a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*) for proving momentariness.
To this we reply:
on the basis of what meaning of "dependence" is it asserted that dependence and independence are excluded in the case of a momentary entity?

If it is asked, "What does it require from the auxiliary? then an assistance must be rendered to it by that auxiliary. Or else, it is the previously existing seed and so forth that, together with the auxiliary, performs the action in combination.

Or rather, the meaning of "requiring" (*apekṣā*) is merely the state of being conjoined, where the phrase "previously existing" implies that there is no requirement for anything other than this state of conjoined existence.
In this regard, since the first position is impossible, the momentary entity is indeed independent;
how then can there be the exclusion of both [possibilities]?
If it is independent, why does it not act even in the absence of the conditions for its approach?
If it were the case that [the self] acts,
then how could it act if it were itself impossible? Furthermore, whether it was thus or otherwise, there is no distinction whatsoever.
If it is argued that, given the possibility of such a nature, non-production [of the effect] implies a lack of independence regarding auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*),
this is irrelevant;
for even when there is similarity in color and configuration, the absence of an agent means that the nature [of the cause] is lacking [in that capacity].
Furthermore, this specific nature characterized by the capacity to produce an excellence not seen before is not possible in all seed-moments residing in either similar or dissimilar continua;
rather, it occurs only in certain seeds that are accompanied by the hands of the laborer.

[Objection: But surely, when all seeds have been harvested from a single field following the processes of ripening and reaping, and brought to be placed together in one granary, they are perceived as having entirely common characteristics.
If it is asked, "Whence comes this distinction of others arising from a single seed?", it is replied: Indeed,
in every effect, the cause is twofold— the perceived and the unperceived.
This is well-established among all those who maintain that "everything exists" (Sarvāstivādins).
Therefore, it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to perceive through direct perception the totality of conditions—both perceptible and imperceptible—that act as auxiliaries.

Consequently, due to a specific difference in the causal efficiency of the collection of causes, there may indeed arise such a distinction in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of certain seed-moments (*bījakṣaṇa*), by virtue of which only those very seed-moments [produce] either an initial excellence or a sprout through a continuous succession.
Nor would other seed-moments produce them.

[Objection: But as for those [moments] which, accompanied by the conditions of proximity (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*), are capable of producing the initial excellence characterized by the generation of a specific quality due to a particularity in the power of their own causes—how is it known that such a distinction necessarily exists there?
If you say, "We [conclude this] from the effect characterized by the initial excellence inferred from the arising of the sprout," then if it is argued,
"In that case, due to the non-perception of the cause, there will be its very absence," we reply: No.
Because the non-existence of a cause is not established merely by the non-perception of a collection of visible and invisible factors, the non-apprehension of the cause remains doubtful and unproven.
Therefore, the meaning is this:
for a momentary state possessing the quality of tactile contact, there is no difference from other moments of time that are distinct.
Between these two views—namely, that there is either a distinction [between the cause and the effect] or that there is not—the one whose power of cognition is superior shall be the victor.
In this regard, for one view, the absence of a [separate] cause is a factor in the production of the effect; for the other, it is the causal totality (*sāmagrī*).
However, the totality is in no way capable of being perceived, whereas the effect is indeed apprehended by means of valid cognition. Thus it is said.
Thus, since "dependence" does not mean "assistance," there is indeed no dependence on auxiliary factors for that which is momentary; therefore, neither [of the two] is excluded.
Now, if "dependence" (*apekṣā*) means acting in combination,

then if it requires the qualification "of that which was previously existing," the momentary [entity] would never act in such a way, and thus its independence (*anapekṣā*) remains unimpaired. On the other hand,

if one disregards the phrase "of that which was previously existing" and takes "dependence" to mean the act of producing only that which exists in a combined state, then there is indeed dependence, not independence.
And thus, since there is no exclusion of both [properties], the first non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Likewise, the exclusion of the two pervaders—unity and plurality—from the momentary is also unestablished.

This is because, although there is a conceptual distinction in its nature as being a material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth based on the differences in the exclusions of this or that [property], it produces multiple effects through a single essential nature (*svarūpa*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); therefore, there is an absence of the exclusion of both.

And as for the argument that if the seed were a producer by means of only a single nature, then the earth and other factors would necessarily share the nature of the sprout— otherwise, even if there were no difference in the cause, a difference in the effect would result in the absurdity of the effect being causeless— that is inconsistent;
for the identity of the cause and the diversity of the effect are established by clear sensory perception.

Because the pervasion between being produced by a single cause and being a single entity has been refuted, and because the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is inapplicable; furthermore, regarding the statement that "there is no difference in the effect when there is no difference in the cause," what is intended as the "cause" there is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself.

The meaning is that when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is of a homogeneous nature, its effect cannot be of a heterogeneous nature. It does not mean, however, that a single factor within the causal complex must not produce multiple effects;
for it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that multiple things can arise from a single cause.
Furthermore, it has already been largely established that identity is not proven by recognition even when there is a difference in time.

Nor is it observed anywhere that sensory perception apprehends two distinct objects— one occupying a different location and the other being resistant— as being one and the same, such that one might suspect identity even in those cases.
Alternatively, if one were to deny even clear perception when faced with doubt, it would follow that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are abolished.
Nor is there any doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "existence," because we do not accept that earth and other such substances possess the nature of a seed.
Since dependence upon that which provides no assistance has already been rejected, it is impossible for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) to be unestablished.
Thus, both of these non-perceptions of the pervader being unestablished, they do not exclude existence from momentariness; therefore, this is not an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason.

Moreover, an existent entity whose positive and negative concomitances with both the probandum and its opposite are unascertained is rightly considered "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*), like the property of possessing odor.

Furthermore, due to the non-perception of the pervader of the subject at hand, causal efficiency itself is entirely non-existent; for, having been excluded from both [the probandum and its opposite] by both disputants, it lacks a basis.
Therefore, how could this be an "uniquely inconclusive" reason? Enough with this insistence on mere prattle!

Thus, since it is impossible for that which is capable to undergo delay, being the object of the conventional usage "capable" is pervaded by production; therefore, given the existence of both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*), the reason is not inconclusive either.
Consequently, the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established. This is the conclusion.
Thus ends the establishment of momentary destruction through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the form of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
This work is by the great scholar Ratnakīrti. (Nibandha 83) 5.
The Proof of Momentary Destruction (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi)
// That which consists of exclusion //
Homage to Tārā.

In this context, it is stated that in a negative (vaidharmya) example, the pervasion consisting of negative concomitance (vyatireka), which implies positive concomitance (anvaya), is established for the reason of existence (sattva).
Whatever exists is momentary,
just like a jar; and these entities under dispute exist— this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

First of all, its non-establishment is not possible, because the probans— defined as the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva), which is intended by the term "existence"— is established by valid cognition within the subject (dharmin) that is itself cognized through the appropriate means of knowledge, namely perception or inference. Nor is there the fault of being contradictory (viruddha) or inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Because pervasion is established by a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) consisting in the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) in the case of the contrary:
that which possesses neither succession nor simultaneity lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*),
just like the horn of a rabbit.
Since neither succession nor simultaneity exist for that which is non-momentary, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
First of all, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*),
because it is impossible for succession or simultaneity to exist in a non-momentary subject (*dharmin*).

For instance, if that which has reached [the present] and that which has not yet reached it were one, there would be permanence. Yet, if such a thing were to possess succession or non-succession, there would necessarily be a difference even between two moments.
Since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, how could succession or non-succession possibly occur in a non-momentary entity?
If there is a difference between two moments, there is the possibility of succession or simultaneity.

For if there were no difference, since [the cause] would be potent in the very first moment, it would follow that it must produce even future effects; how then could there be room for a sequence in the production of other effects?
Nor can a non-momentary entity achieve its own stability by performing all its effects simultaneously.
Because it would possess efficacy even at another moment, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of it performing that same effect again;

therefore, "non-momentary" refers to the non-difference [of the entity] between earlier and later times. "The connection with succession and simultaneity" refers to the difference [of the entity] between earlier and later times.
Furthermore, between these two there is a contradiction characterized by their mutual exclusion.
Therefore, this reason— characterized by the absence of succession and simultaneity in a non-momentary subject— cannot be said to be unestablished (*asiddha*),
precisely because of the contradiction between being endowed with succession and simultaneity and being non-momentary.
Nor is it contradictory, because it exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa).
Nor is it inconclusive,
because the absence of succession and simultaneity is pervaded by the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).

For by that very means of valid cognition consisting of perception— which establishes that there are no other modes [of existence]— the pervasion of affirmative causal efficiency by the two affirmative modes of succession and simultaneity has been demonstrated.
Therefore, it must be admitted that by that very absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of succession and simultaneity has been established.

For there exists no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of establishing the pervasion of the absence of fire and so forth by the absence of smoke and so forth, apart from the means of valid cognition that establishes the pervasion of smoke and so forth by fire and so forth.

Consequently, since the principle that "whatever establishes the pervasion of two positive entities (*vidhi*) also establishes the pervasion of two absences (*abhāva*)" is inviolable, [the conclusion follows].

Since the absence of succession and non-succession is indeed pervaded by the absence of existence, the reason is not inconclusive; thus, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is faultless.

Therefore, as this [absence] excludes existence—which is pervaded by itself—from the non-momentary, it causes that existence to reside in the momentary. Consequently, the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) through the reason of existence is likewise faultless.
(Nibandh 85)

Now, one might object: how can the existence [of a probans] establish its necessary connection with its own probandum on the basis of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), since this [reason] too is vitiated by many defects?
For instance, this is certainly not a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) reason.

Because it is established by valid cognition in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), because it is not established merely by the opponent's admission, and because there is no reduction to the opposite [of what is intended].
If, on the other hand, it is independent,
then it is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*),
because a non-momentary locus is impossible.
Or [it may be] because it is not established [for the opponent].
For that which is established would have to be so either through perception, inference, or mere conceptualization (*vikalpamātra*).

In the first two positions, if there were the performance of a function characterized by one's own cognition—either directly or indirectly—the fundamental reason (*maulasādhāraṇahetu*) would be "unestablished" (*asiddha*), and the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalambha*) would be "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*).
Because, in the case of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), either succession or simultaneity must necessarily occur;
however, in the latter alternative, no cause whatsoever would be without a substratum,
since a subject established merely by conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) is easily found everywhere.
Furthermore, that conceptual cognition must either arise subsequent to perception,
or be born from a logical mark (liṅga),
or be produced by a mental impression (saṃskāra).
Whether it be of a doubtful nature or of no nature at all—
in either of these two initial cases, the existence of that which is non-momentary remains unimpeded.
How does the subverting argument apply?
In the third case, however, there is no negation of momentary existence at all times,
because in the absence of the mental impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by that [experience], its recollection would be impossible.
In the fourth [case], however, the defect of the reason is that its locus is doubtful.
And in the fifth, the non-existence of its object is not established by perception,
because according to your own view, a non-momentary self is never perceived at all.

Nor can its non-existence be established through inference, because no probans (liṅga) invariably concomitant with it is perceived; thus, first of all, the "unestablished locus" (āśrayāsiddhi) fallacy has been refuted. Likewise, the example (dṛṣṭānta) must also be rejected.
Furthermore, this reason (hetu) is also unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddha).
Even for a stable [entity], the performance of purposeful action (arthakriyā) through both successive and simultaneous means is possible by depending on successive or simultaneous auxiliary causes.
Furthermore, there is no consequence of the faults mentioned regarding the positions of succession and simultaneity.
For instance, it is not contradictory that a stable entity produces effects successively by depending on successive auxiliary causes.
And thus, this is Śaṅkara’s concise intention:
for capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed the completeness of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-sākalya*),
and incapacity (*asāmarthya*) is their deficiency (*vaikalya*).
Furthermore, there is no impairment whatsoever of that which possesses those two [properties] due to their appearance and disappearance,
because it is distinct from them.
Therefore, how can there be the undesirable consequence of producing an effect without depending on auxiliary causes?
This is also the condensed meaning of Trilocana:
for it is only the effect that depends upon auxiliary causes,
not the cause of the production of the effect.

Since there are two kinds of capacity—innate and adventitious—as well as other auxiliary factors, it follows that even for a non-momentary entity, a plurality of successive effects can be accounted for through a plurality of successive auxiliaries; therefore, it is impossible to establish that entities undergo change at every moment.
Thus speaks Nyāyabhūṣaṇa as well.
If it is argued that at the time of producing the first effect, [the cause] possesses the nature of producing subsequent effects,
and therefore it should produce all effects at that very first moment—
this is untenable because it involves a contradiction of one's own words, like saying, "My mother is barren."
For how could that which has the nature of producing a subsequent effect produce that effect at the beginning? (If it were to do so...)
In that case, it does not have the nature of performing that specific effect;
for that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth.
Vācaspati also recites this:

But surely this non-momentary entity produces its effect by means of its own nature; and since that nature of it exists at the second moment just as it does at the third and subsequent moments, it should produce the effect then as well. Or, if it does not produce it then, it would not produce it at the third and subsequent moments either.
Because it remains in that same state;
or, if it does not remain in that state, that itself constitutes its momentariness.
To this it is replied: It is true that a cause produces an effect by its own nature, but not by that [nature] alone;
for we observe that the production of an effect occurs only from that [cause] when accompanied by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).
Therefore, just like pervasion (*vyāpti*), the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) also exists in a single locus through the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).

It should be understood as an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); for it is precisely thus that there is consensus among both worldly people and investigators. Therefore, there is no occasion for the faults mentioned regarding the position that [the causes] produce their effects sequentially.
Nor is there any room for the faults mentioned regarding the position of simultaneity in the case of non-momentary entities.

For those specific substances that have produced an effect possess an activity capable of producing that determined effect; even while those substances continue to exist after the effect has been accomplished, the causal complex (sāmagrī) becomes deficient because its purpose has been fulfilled.

How, then, could that which has already been produced produce [anything]? For the staff and other such instruments are not by their very nature agents, such that they would perform an action starting from the moment of production; rather, they become so only when infused with activity (*vyāpāra*).
And it is not by virtue of this much of their own nature that they are not agents;
rather, they are agents because they enter into activity for the sake of fulfilling their own nature as causal factors.

Furthermore, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*), because it would follow that there is an absence of both succession and simultaneity, yet no absence of existence.
For the absence of any other mode besides succession and simultaneity is not established, since a negation of specific alternatives implies the admission of the remaining possibility.
Furthermore, if another mode [of existence] were perceptible, its absolute negation would not be established;

if it were imperceptible, there could be no certainty regarding the non-existence of remote things. Thus, the pervasion of causal efficacy by either succession or simultaneity is not proven. Consequently, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) remains one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

Furthermore, since the totality of auxiliary conditions—consisting of both visible and invisible factors—is entirely beyond perception, existence (sattva), which is pervaded by that [succession and simultaneity], is likewise imperceptible; thus, the necessary connection (pratibandha) is not established through perception. Nor is it established through inference.
"Because there is an absence of a mark (liṅga) connected to that.
Furthermore, it is a most excellent saying that the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva) is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity;
if it is pervaded by succession, how could it be by simultaneity?
If, then, it does not occur through non-succession, it cannot occur through succession.
By asserting that [the object] is pervaded by both succession and non-succession, one actually demonstrates the very absence of pervasion;
for it is not the case that smoke is pervaded by both the presence and absence of fire.
Therefore, the pervasion is inconclusive.
Furthermore, does this subverting argument prove the non-existence of non-momentary things, or rather the exclusion of existence from non-momentary things?
Now, regarding the necessary connection between existence and momentariness:
the first alternative is not tenable, because according to the sequence already stated, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for the meaning of the term "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*) is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) accompanied by the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
If that [absence] were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then existence (*sattva*) would be its cause, and thus [existence as a reason] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).
If that [non-perception] is further analyzed, then it must be refuted by analyzing it into five ways according to the sequence previously stated.
For this very reason, even the third alternative is not tenable.
Because if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established, the relationship [of pervasion] is not established.
Furthermore, unlike the case of the bare ground, a non-momentary subject (*dharmin*) is not perceived here.

Moreover, when there is a non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) cannot be subsumed under it without the apprehension of some perceptible object.
Furthermore, if it were a property of non-existence, there would be the fallacies of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) and mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*);

if it were a property of existence, there would be the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddhatva*); and if it were a property of both, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). Thus, it does not escape these three classes of logical defects.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "in the case of non-momentariness, there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to [the impossibility of] succession or simultaneity":
one who seeks to establish that contradiction must also understand the contradictory term itself,
because the establishment of a contradiction is inseparable from the cognition of that [contradictory term].

Just as in the case of cold and fire, or of dependence and permanence; furthermore, a non-momentary counter-correlate (pratiyogin) that is perceived must be real, because it is an object of cognition, for that which does not produce [cognition] cannot be an object of knowledge.
If it is argued that the establishment of contradiction is achieved through non-momentariness established by conventional consensus (*saṃvṛti*), [we reply:
even that which is established by convention must be either real (*vāstavam*) or conceptual (*kālpānikam*).
If it were real, how could it be non-existent?
And how is there a contradiction with the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? For that which performs causal efficiency is said to be real;
otherwise, it would be merely conceptual (*kālpnika*).
In that case, is the contradiction real or conceptual?
It is certainly not real.
Because it is a contradiction between two imagined [entities], like the contradiction between a barren woman’s son [and something else].
Now, if even the contradiction is merely conceptual, then the exclusion of existence is not ultimate; thus, momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is as good as consigned to the waters of oblivion.

This very series of objections was summarized by our teachers: "The eternal does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition; therefore, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), one's own experience is undermined, and even the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is discarded."
And emptiness is established by means of a dyad; nor is non-existence [established] as existence.
Just as the establishment of contradiction with the eternal is not possible through the non-existent, so it is also for succession and the like. Thus.

To this it is replied: here, even with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), the conventional usage of subject (*dharmin*) and property (*dharma*) is observed, as for example: "cowness in a cow," "whiteness in a cloth," or "motion in a horse," and so forth.

The conventional usage of subject (*dharmin*) and property (*dharma*) is observed even in the case of non-entities (*avastu*), such as: "the absence of sharpness in a hare's horn," "the absence of speakerhood in the son of a barren woman," and "the absence of fragrance in a sky-lotus" (Nibandh 88), and so forth.
In that regard, regarding the claim that there is no subjecthood in a non-entity: does this mean that subjecthood is absent by virtue of being a property of a real entity (*vastu*)?
Or is it by means of a property that does not exist?
In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established;
in the second case, however, there is a contradiction with one's own words.
As the teachers have said:
"Regarding any dharma that is not established by means of cognition in a non-entity, is there here any conventional practice of negation or affirmation, or not?
If it exists somewhere, how can there not be so many refutations? If it does not exist at all, then there is the establishment of a contradiction with one's own words."

The meaning is that, since the pervading property— the necessity of first accepting the subjecthood (*dharmitva*) of a non-entity— is absent, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the refutation based on the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) could not be put forward.

For by the very statement by which the subjecthood of a non-entity is denied, one has simultaneously accepted subjecthood through that very property, namely, the absence of subjecthood in a non-entity.
But that it is being negated— this is clearly the handiwork of the Lord;
for, by the statement that "a non-entity lacks the status of a subject," is the absence of subject-status being predicated of the non-entity itself, or of something else?
Or "not anywhere at all"— these are the three positions.

In the first position, there is no negation of the subject-status (*dharmitva*) of a non-entity, because the property (*dharma*) consisting in the absence of subject-status is precisely enjoined therein.

In the second case, what has occurred regarding a non-entity (*avastu*), other than the prescription of its lack of being a subject (*dharmin*)? As for the third position, it is indeed futile because it lacks a basis; thus, how can there be a negation of a non-entity’s status as a subject?

Therefore, just as the presentation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is pervaded by the prior acceptance of an object of cognition (*prameya*), [so too is the negation of a subject pervaded by the prior acceptance of a non-entity].

The presentation of a denoting word is pervaded by the prior acceptance of a denoted object; likewise, the presentation of the statement that "a non-entity lacks the status of being a subject" (dharmin) is pervaded by the prior acceptance of the non-entity's status as a subject. Otherwise, the presentation of that statement would be purposeless.

Therefore, if the presentation of the statement is the pervaded property (vyāpyadharma), then the acceptance of the non-entity's status as a subject is also the unavoidable pervading property (vyāpakadharma).

If, on the other hand, it is not a pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*), then the presentation of even the statement of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is impossible; thus, silence is forcibly imposed here. How, then, is the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana-pratirodha*) not established? As the Master said: "For one who does not speak is not able to enlighten another, nor is one who speaks able to avoid this fault"—thus one enters into a great dilemma.
If you argue that silence alone is appropriate for those with aesthetic sensitivity when the subject under discussion is a non-entity (*avastu*),
oh, what great cleverness!

Having yourself leaped about as best you could during the discussion of a non-entity, you now wish to escape by the technical term that "silence alone is logically attained" once one has been defeated.
Furthermore, a discussion concerning a non-entity cannot be prevented merely by royal punishment or by unwanted consequences such as the trampling of one's feet;

for even in this case, when the presence of succession and simultaneity is the probans and the absence of existence is the probandum, who can deny that a momentary entity—whether its nature is doubtful as to being a real thing or indeed a non-entity—is the subject (*dharmin*)?
(Nibandh 89)
For dharma is seen to be of three kinds:
some is restricted to a real entity, such as blue and so forth;
some is not restricted to a real entity, such as the absence of all designations.

There may be something common to both, such as mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-mātra*). In that case, it is logical to negate the status of a subject (*dharmin*) belonging to a non-entity by means of a property belonging to an entity;
however, it is not [logical] by means of a property belonging to a non-entity.

Whether by means of a property of a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*), since it would follow that one’s own statement could not be presented [as a reason], the status of being the subject (*dharmin*) remains unimpeded even when there is doubt regarding the non-existence of the non-momentary; thus, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is not "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*). Nor is it correct to say that the reason is "unestablished in its locus" because the non-momentary is not cognized. Therefore, what was stated is logical.
For without that cognition, its conventional usage would be impossible.
However, this cognition, which serves as a factor in conventional usage, is not of a single form with respect to both real and unreal entities.
For the cognition of a real entity arises either directly or through a causal chain from the objective power (*sāmarthya*) of the entity itself.
Just as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon direct perception [are cognitions of real objects],
whereas for that which is not a real entity, because it lacks causal efficacy, cognition is merely conceptual construction;
for the cognition of a real entity arises through the power of the object itself, just like direct perception.
Through a traditional succession, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon it and inference (*anumāna*) are [also based on it].

However, for that which is not a real entity (*avastu*), there can be no cognition produced by the power of a real entity (*vastubala*), because that would entail the loss of its status as a non-entity due to its acting as a causal factor.
Therefore, the cognition of a non-entity is merely conceptual construction alone.
For non-existence (abhāva) is not something that possesses a physical form such that it must be directly perceived; rather, it is to be dealt with through conventional usage (vyavahāra).
And that conventional usage is indeed established even by conceptual construction (vikalpa);
otherwise, the conventionally well-known worldly discourse regarding non-entities would not exist.

And since it is accepted [by the opponent] that this follows from the negation of its being the substratum (dharmin), even one who does not desire it must admit that the non-momentary is established merely through conceptual construction (vikalpamātra). Therefore, this reason should not be called "unestablished in its substratum" (āśrayāsiddha) on the grounds of being unperceived.

Consequently, as for what was said—that when the non-momentary is established merely through conceptual construction, no reason is without a substratum because such a substratum is easily found everywhere—that is inconsistent.

Even though a subject (*dharmin*) established merely through conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) may exist in all cases, it cannot function as a subject by virtue of being a real property (*vastudharma*).
This is because, with respect to a reason that must be a real property, there is the possibility of a reason being "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*).
For example, the proof presented for the purpose of establishing the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the self: "because its qualities are perceived everywhere."
Furthermore, this conceptual construction (vikalpa) prior to the presentation of the reason has a doubtful objective basis;
however, once the reason has been established, we say it is without an objective basis.
Moreover, the so-called "fallacy of a doubtful locus" (sandigdhāśrayatva) is not a defect of the reason here.
Let this be for now;

for even a doubtful non-entity, established by mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), can be proven to possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*) with respect to its own non-substantial properties (*avastudharma*).
This is because a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) whose locus is doubtful is defined only with respect to reasons that are properties of real entities (*vastudharma*).

Just as here [one infers] "there is a peacock in this bower because of its cry," the non-existence of the object of a conceptualization that lacks a real basis has been established precisely through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
In the same way, it should be understood that even for a simile such as a sky-lotus, its status as a subject (*dharmin*) and its cognition occur through mere conceptualization alone.

Therefore, since the subjecthood (*dharmitva*) of a real entity (*vastu*) in relation to the properties of that very entity cannot be denied— given that it is apprehended through mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*)— this reason is not "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Nor is there any deficiency in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*),
nor is this [reason] unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).

Because in a non-momentary subject (*dharmī*), neither succession (*krama*) nor simultaneity (*akrama*)— its two pervaders (*vyāpaka*)— are possible. For instance, if it possessed the capacity to produce effects occurring in the second and subsequent moments during its first moment, then it would have to produce the effects of the second and subsequent moments just like the effect produced in the first moment.
Because it is impossible for that which is capable to be delayed;
for if at that time the capacity characterized by the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) is absent, then there exists the incapacity characterized by their deficiency.

If it is argued that an entity does not act by its own nature alone, but acts precisely through its own nature when accompanied by auxiliary causes— since it is observed that the effect arises only from such a [causal complex]—
then, at the time when these [causes] are conjoined and produce the effect, let them possess the status of auxiliarity characterized by the performance of a single purpose.

Who is the preventer? For how can it be established that the effect must be produced by the cause alone? Because a thing possesses a single nature at both earlier and later times, it would be impossible to avoid the undesirable consequence that it must be restricted to either always producing or never producing.

Therefore, it is not even within the realm of the imagination of those who maintain the existence of permanent entities that a single thing is a producer; rather, it is the totality [of conditions] (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer.
If you argue, "What can we do? It is simply observed to be so," [we reply:]...

Let it be seen: however, the point of contention is this—whether the production of an effect arises from the very same entity that previously existed and subsequently entered into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or rather from a different momentary state produced by that specific complex. In this regard, if the cause were already present, the effect would either be produced at all times or never at all; thus, without resolving this contradiction, one who merely asserts the probandum—that the effect arises from that very [cause]—deserves compassion.
Furthermore, identity is not established through recognition alone.
Because its human effort is crushed in cases such as hair that has been cut and grown back again, or the stalk of a plantain tree;
and furthermore, the refutation of recognition (pratyabhijñā) has been set forth by us in detail in the *Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa*, so it should be understood from that very source.
[Objection: But surely it is only the effect that depends upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
But it is not the cause for the production of the effect.

If it is argued: "Because capacity is of two kinds—innate and adventitious—and since there is another auxiliary factor, even for that which is non-momentary, there can be a variety of successive effects due to the variety of successive auxiliaries."
Let it be granted, then, that capacity is twofold by way of the distinction between innate and adventitious;
nevertheless, that specific individual characteristic (*vastusvalakṣaṇa*) must necessarily be admitted as possessing the property of causal efficiency (*kriyādharman*) immediately.
If, therefore, it [possesses this property] even previously, [then...]
If it were so even before, there would be the consequence of the effect existing [then as well];
if, on the other hand, it occurs only later, then the entity is not stable.
Nor is it logical to say that an effect depends upon auxiliary causes, because [the effect] does not exist;
and if a cause, despite being present, does not produce its own effect, [it would follow that it is not a cause].
In that case, it would not be that very cause of that effect, because of its independence.
And as for what was said— that how could that which has the nature of producing a subsequent effect produce an effect at the beginning?
If it were to perform that action, then it would not have the nature of performing that specific effect;
for something whose nature is to produce blue does not also produce yellow and so forth— thus, [the opponent's position] is inconsistent.
If an entity possesses a stable nature, how can it be that this [nature] exists only at a later time and not at an earlier time?
