And since that [earlier existence] is absent, how can it be said that the cause also possesses the nature of a later effect?
If you say, "What can we do? Its birth occurs only at a later time," [we reply: ...
If it is argued that since [the capacity] is untenable in the case of stability, it must indicate instability;
or if it is argued that even in the case of stability, this very nature belongs to it, namely that it produces the effect only at the subsequent moment—[we reply: no.
Since it is impossible to accept an intrinsic nature that is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a non-momentary entity cannot first of all produce effects sequentially;

nor is the production of effects non-sequentially possible, because if its causal nature were still present in the second moment, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it producing the effect once again.

If it is argued that once the effect has been produced, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is deficient because its operation upon that object no longer exists, and thus it cannot produce what has already been produced—this is not so.

For it was established previously that whether a causal complex is possible or impossible, as long as the essential nature of the action and the factors of action (*kāraka*) is present, their capacity to produce is unavoidable.
Indeed, the very fact that the effect has already been produced makes it impossible to produce again; this impossibility itself indicates that the cause is no longer capable.
Therefore, this absence of the capacity to produce effects either successively or simultaneously is not unestablished in the case of what is non-momentary.

Nor is there the possibility of any other mode besides succession and simultaneity, such that—due to the reason being unencompassed by those two—the reason would have a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*).
For if one were to suspect another mode, since that too must be either visible or invisible, even if those two modes are refuted, it would follow that one could not trust one's own position either.
Therefore, for two things established through mutual exclusion, no other mode is possible;
for neither a real entity nor a non-entity that does not enter into the nature [of the former] can possess that intrinsic nature,
since any other mode would likewise fail to enter into the nature of succession.

Likewise, although the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), the pervasion of existence—which is itself perceptible—by means of succession and simultaneity is established through perception alone by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), [namely] that which is perceptible only when accompanied by a perceptible auxiliary. Thus, causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by succession and simultaneity; since these two, succession and simultaneity, are established as mutually exclusive, causal efficacy cannot exist elsewhere apart from these two modes.
The meaning is "not gone.
For this very reason, when these two cease, [the stream] ceases.
Regarding Trilocana’s three alternatives, the refutation of the first has been set aside by avoiding the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
The second is also irrelevant,
because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is apprehended through conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).
For non-existence (abhāva) is not something possessing a physical form that must be directly realized;
rather, it is to be dealt with through conceptual construction (vikalpa) alone.
Indeed, for non-existence, there is no way of apprehension other than through conceptual construction, nor is there any non-apprehension whatsoever.
In either case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the loss of that conventional usage.

Thus, the understanding of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) and the absence of the reason (*hetu-vyatireka*) occurs precisely through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the third criticism as well is irrelevant.
Because the pervasion of existence by momentariness remains unimpeded through a faultless non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*),

it is established that this non-perception of the pervader proves the non-existence of the non-momentary, the exclusion of existence from that [non-momentary], and the pervasion of existence by momentariness, since its nature consists of a single functional operation.

Now, if "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) refers merely to non-perception in general, then it cannot produce a cognition of the probandum because it is a non-entity. Nor can "perception of something else" be called "non-perception of the pervader," since there is no perception of any other thing in the manner that one perceives a bare ground or the like. If this is argued, it is incorrect.
Because non-apprehension elsewhere is established precisely as the apprehension of the locus (*dharmin*) itself;

for instance, in the case [of the inference] "there is no *śiṃśapā* here because there is no tree," the apprehension of the locus—the bare spot—in relation to the tree is the non-apprehension of the tree, and the apprehension of the locus—the bare spot—precisely in relation to the *śiṃśapā* is the apprehension of the absence of the *śiṃśapā*. Thus, the operation culminates in a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
[Nibandha 92] This is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

Likewise, with respect to a permanent subject (*dharmin*) determined by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), there is the non-perception of successive or simultaneous causal activity simply through the apprehension of the [subject] in isolation.

Furthermore, since the mere perception [of the subject] with respect to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is itself the perception of its connection to purposeful action, this [non-perception] is not distinct from another type of non-perception of the pervader.

Furthermore, with respect to determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is the conventional usage of establishing the absence of the pervaded due to the absence of the pervader in an external, non-momentary entity.

It should be understood that determination possesses the power to induce activity even toward an ungrasped object, owing to its connection with a specific form acquired through the force of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
And such a determination has been established in our *Citrādvaitasiddhi*.
And that non-contradictory conventional usage cannot be avoided;
for by this sequence as well, the very same point is established: "that which is empty of the pervader is empty of the pervaded."
And this principle applies just as it does when the subject (*dharmin*) is a real entity, so too when it is not a real entity; what difference is there?
For in this case, that which is associated with a single cognition is merely conceptualized.

Just as a horn was perceived on the head of a deer because it is associated with that [deer] in a single cognition, so too on the head of a hare, a horn is negated precisely through the possibility of its being associated with it in a single cognition.

Likewise, in the case of blue and so forth, where the status of being permanent or impermanent is not yet established, succession and simultaneity are observed to be associated with a single cognition along with their own substratum;

if they were to apply to a permanent entity, they would have to be apprehended by the cognition grasping that permanence together with the permanent substratum itself. It is on the basis of this possibility that [succession and simultaneity] are refuted precisely by way of their association with a single cognition.
But how is it that succession and non-succession do not manifest in this eternal cognition, given that we conceptualize the eternal as being precisely encompassed by succession and non-succession?
For this very reason, there is the application of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), since such an argument would be useless without the imposition of the opposite.
Furthermore, eternality consists in having a single nature even at different times.
Succession and non-succession exist as distinct forms within two moments;

therefore, since eternity and the capacity for successive and non-successive effects are characterized by mutual exclusion, their contradiction is unavoidable. How, then, can succession and non-succession be subsumed within the eternal? And because they are not so subsumed, [the object] is apprehended through the conceptualization of pure eternity.
How can there be a conceptual representation through the superimposition of succession and simultaneity, which have been set aside?

Consequently, even when the counter-correlate is conceived as eternal—and thus attains the characteristic of being associated with a single cognition—the non-perception of succession and simultaneity (which are the opposites of eternity) is simply the non-perception of that which is eternally perceived;
and for that very reason, there is the non-perception of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*).
Therefore, because it consists in the perception of a subject that is distinct from the pervader, it has no distinction from other non-perceptions of the pervader.
If it is argued that this [subject] is not a non-entity because the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is based upon an entity that serves as its substratum (*dharmin*),
then what is this so-called "being based upon an entity"?
Does it mean being derived from an entity even through a mediated succession?

Now, [the definition of a reason] consists in its being a cause for conventional usage with respect to an object in some particular form, or its being dependent upon a real entity as the subject (*dharmin*).
(Nibandh 93)

If the first position is held, then its status as being tied to a real entity within the scope of apprehending the pervasion of both succession and non-succession, as well as causal efficiency, is not lost. Nor is there any fault possible in the second position,
because this serves as the means for proving the momentary destruction of entities.
Nor can even the final alternative be imagined,

because it has been established that the very entity which is the subject (*dharmin*) of the conceptualization of permanence is devoid of any external permanent substratum— whether characterized by succession or non-succession— just as it is devoid of any external permanent substratum for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

This is because, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is the possibility of a connection with a subject that is a real entity (*vastubhūta*) in the form of a non-momentary nature belonging to the intellect itself.
This same principle should be applied to such cases as "the speaker is not the son of a barren woman because of the absence of consciousness," and so forth.
By this, Trilocana’s position—that this [non-existence] cannot be subsumed in the same way that the absence of a tree or similar things can—is also refuted.
Nor does the absence of succession and so forth escape the three types of fallacies,

for even though it is a property of non-existence, it avoids the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). As for what was stated by him— that when the non-existence of eternal things is established through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the status of the absence of succession and so forth as a property of non-existence is thereby established— [that is not correct].
This is a difficult point to state even for a child:
for the subject (dharmin) is eternal,
while non-existence is the property to be proven (sādhya).
The reason (*hetu*) is the absence of both successive and non-successive causal efficacy.
Its nature as a non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*) is said to consist in its being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*) with its own probandum, which is characterized by non-existence.

And that [invariable concomitance] is established through the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of existence by succession and non-succession; thus, by the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*), namely existence, [there follows the absence] of succession and non-succession.

The absence of the pervader is established as being pervaded; thus, the property of non-existence is established through perception, inference, or some other single means of valid cognition prior to the proof of the pervasion between the two positive entities. Therefore, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Nor is the same consequence applicable to non-existence as it is to existence, because the underlying logic is different.
For in that case, both the probandum and the probans are real entities;
it is logical that their locus (dharmin) must also be a real entity.
Furthermore, the establishment of a real entity occurs only through perception and inference.
It is correct that in the absence of those two [the subject and the property], there is necessarily the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

However, when proving non-existence, a reason that is a property of a non-entity cannot be refuted by the fault of an unestablished locus, because the subject is established merely through conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).
Likewise, the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for a non-momentary entity through either succession or simultaneity is indeed established.
Likewise, it is established that only through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the momentary contradictory [nature] proven;
and it must also be conventionally designated that its nature is precisely what is delineated by conceptual construction and nothing else.
Otherwise, it would be illogical to negate its being devoid of succession, non-succession, and so forth, by way of restating that [conceptually constructed nature].
Because its own nature is not described and something else is described, there would follow the undesirable consequence that words such as "non-momentary" or "rabbit's horn" could not be uttered;
yet they do exist.
Therefore, just as [in the case of] that which is established by conceptual construction even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)...

(Nibandha 94) Just as the negation of beauty and so forth in the case of the son of a barren woman is appropriate, so too, what fault could there be in establishing a contradiction between a non-momentary form— which is itself presented by conceptual construction— and its opposite? If the negation of contradiction is based on the absence of experience of the non-momentary, then let there likewise be no negation of beauty and so forth in the case of the son of a barren woman simply because of the absence of experience of him.
If it is argued that, in this way, contradiction would be non-ultimate, and consequently the establishment of momentary destruction through that [contradiction] would also be non-ultimate—[we reply:

we do not accept, nor is it logically tenable, that what is called "contradiction" is some distinct entity that has its feet planted in both categories; for if that were the case, then in the absence of reality in one of the related entities, [the contradiction itself] would be non-ultimate.
It may be so;
however, according to how it is accepted, it is indeed ultimate.
The meaning of contradiction between two things considered to be contradictory is merely the mutual exclusion of their respective natures.
And that [contradiction] between existence and non-existence is indeed ultimate.

The fact that existence does not enter into the form of non-existence, nor does non-existence enter into the form of existence— this very rule of their non-confusion is what constitutes ultimate contradiction.
For permanence consists in having a single uniform nature across different times,
whereas succession and non-succession consist in having distinct natures even in two moments;
therefore, there is indeed a contradiction between permanence and the capacity to produce successive or non-successive effects, just as there is between existence and non-existence.
If it is asked: "Is there no contradiction other than the two contradictory properties of eternality and possessing succession or simultaneity; therefore, whose reality is established? We reply: No.
For we do not assert that contradiction is ultimately real merely because another property exists.
However, [this applies] when two contradictory properties exist;
otherwise, even if there were another property called "contradiction," if the two properties themselves were not contradictory, where could a real contradiction possibly occur?

If the two properties are indeed contradictory, then by that much alone the conventional usage of "real contradiction" is established—what need is there for some other entity called "contradiction" that is established merely by name?
Thus, this is the summary of the prima facie argument:

the eternal does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition; therefore, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), one's own experience is undermined, and even the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is discarded.

"Success is achieved through a pair of voids, yet non-existence is not existence; for just as contradiction with the eternal cannot be established by means of the non-existent, so it is also impossible [to establish it] by means of succession and the like."

Herein is the summary of the established doctrine: Is there, or is there not, in this world, the practical application of negation and affirmation regarding some property that is established by mind with respect to a non-entity?
If it exists somewhere, how can there not be so many objections?
If it does not exist at all, then the contradiction with one's own words is established.
Thus, the ultimate point is that a permanent entity cannot possess either successive or non-successive causal activity.

Consequently, the ultimate point is that it cannot even be endowed with existence (*sattā*). Furthermore, since there is no third category apart from the momentary and the non-momentary, this existence—which is excluded from the non-momentary—must rest solely in the momentary; thus, it is established as being pervaded by momentariness. Therefore, the proof of momentariness from existence is free from contradiction.
The very nature of all phenomena, through the awakening to which liberation is sought,
is that very momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) established here as the crusher of the non-Buddhist outsiders.
Thus ends this work of Ratnakīrti.
(Nibandha 96) 6.
// The Chapter on the Inclusion [of Other Cognitions] within the Means of Valid Cognition //

The refutation of the multitude of means of valid cognition other than the two [accepted] means of valid cognition is not being stated here as something new; rather, it is sealed here by means of formal application.
Indeed, in this regard, there is no disagreement whatsoever concerning the mere existence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

since even the Cārvāka accepts it at least in that much. Furthermore, the proponent who advocates the total abolition of valid cognition has been disregarded by our teachers, as he can be countered point-by-point regarding each of his specific objections.
If you claim that a valid means of knowledge is invalid, the occasion for inquiry is destroyed;
for by speaking thus, you must necessarily either establish something or else contradict it.
In that case, what kind of praise is there for one who speaks unreasonably in an assembly?
Is there no other reasoning superior to inference; and what is established if that [inference] is disregarded?
If there is sublation [of the Veda] by his own conviction because he has accepted it as such,
then how can there be sublation out of fear of that [sublation] when there is no such acceptance?
If it is argued that there is nothing to be proven, then the sublation [of the opponent's position] would itself be what is to be proven;
yet if that too is denied, such a statement is futile, for what fruit is there even in merely asking the question?

If the fruit [of speech] were nothing other than the cognition [it produces], then words would not be capable of conveying meaning; for it is not the case that sense-objects, smoke, and so forth are beautiful [in themselves].
If you accept pride within the conventional, then this very investigation is also conventional;
if you do not accept it even within the conventional, then let the victor speak as he may.
Conventional reality is not established by mere words alone without a means of valid cognition (māna);
if the acceptance of a means of valid cognition were difficult to prevent, it must be based on such a means of valid cognition.
The Teacher also said:
"If it is argued that [the Veda] is not desired [as authority], then indeed valid cognition is the basis for all desires;
who, without it, would be capable of establishing the distinction between existence and non-existence?"
Thus, since there is no rejection of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as such, perception (*pratyakṣa*) must first be reckoned among them,
because the establishment of other means of valid cognition is rooted in it.
Moreover, even the Cārvāka is not able to maintain his position without establishing inference,
because he performs three distinct operations. (Nibandh 97)
For in that treatise, the establishment of what is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and what is not for perception and other general categories must be effected by formulating definitions.
And regarding that definition, when the subject (*dharmin*), the object to be defined, is perception and its validity is to be recognized, the reason (*hetu*) is its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, in the case of inferring another's cognition, the activity of the body and so forth is the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
Furthermore, since the non-perception of what is perceptible must be accepted when denying the existence of another world, how can there be a repudiation of inference? As the Master [Dignāga] said:
"Because the status of both means of valid cognition and their opposites depends on the apprehension of one cognition by another..."
And because of the negation of the existence of any other means of valid cognition.
Moreover,
since there is no cognition in the absence of an object, even in the case of perception, its status as a means of valid cognition [is established];
for when that which has a restricted nature is the cause of it, both [perception and inference] are equal.

Thus, inference (anumāna) is also a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). And its validity consists in its capacity to lead one to attain an object that is certain, not grasped by another means of cognition, and which serves as the objective for purposeful activity.
If it is argued: "Let validity consist in the capacity for attainment; however, this [capacity] arises from the object itself, rather than from the perception of the object."
What is this "perception of the object"? Visibility is a property of the object;
being a perceiver is a property of the cognition.
In the first case, since visibility (*dṛśyatva*) is as common [to all subjects] as blueness (*nīlatva*), an object that is the domain of one [subject] would have to be the domain of all;
for there is no difference in objects for each individual, as that would entail the consequence of their being devoid of self-nature (*nairātmya*).
In the second case, however, while the nature of cognition is that of a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*), how could it belong to another [object] which is unrelated?
If it is argued that there must be an expectation for this object because the state of being a seer is untenable without the state of being seen— and thus implies it—
[we reply: Is this not rather the establishment of the status of seer and seen based on the power of the arising and the similarity in form between cognition and its object?
If this is not accepted, since neither the state of being a seer nor the state of being an object of sight is possible, what could be established by what?

Or, even if the relationship between seer and seen were to exist through some other mode, nevertheless, given their difference, the non-deviation [of the cognition] must have "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) alone as its cause for connection.
And since that power of apprehension (*prāpaṇa-śakti*) is no different in perception and inference, it belongs to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself.
But surely there are other means of valid cognition besides verbal testimony and comparison;

for instance, the knowledge that arises from verbal testimony in the form of an injunction regarding an unperceived object such as heaven—that too is indeed verbal knowledge and a valid means of cognition.
Furthermore, knowledge produced by the words of a trustworthy person is also a valid means of cognition.
As Kumārila said:
"And that [knowledge] arises from a sentence that has no author, or from another [source] declared by a trustworthy person.
In that context, when knowledge arising from words is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the cognition of the material cause and so forth is the result (*phala*).
But when [the word] is the means of knowledge, then the cognition having that as its object is the result.
For the Naiyāyika, however,
verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*).
Thus ends the aphorism defining verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*).
In this context, "verbal testimony" (*śabda*) is the term to be defined (*lakṣya*),
and "instruction by a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
This is its summarized meaning:

verbal testimony (*śabda*) taught by a reliable person (*āpta*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And a "reliable person" is defined as one who has directly perceived the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and who, being motivated by the desire to communicate the object exactly as it was seen, acts as a teacher.
And the determination of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its result (phala) is to be understood as before.
Likewise, for the Mīmāṃsakas, analogy (upamāna) is a means of valid cognition.
As Śabarasvāmin stated: "Analogy also produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] by means of similarity."
"Just as the sight of a gavaya [is the cause] for the recollection of a cow"—
this is its meaning;
that is, the similarity perceived in one place acts as the agent.

When one perceives an object qualified by a similarity to another perceived object, and thereby produces a cognition regarding an unperceived object in the form "that [object] is qualified by a similarity to this," that is the means of valid cognition called *upamāna* (analogy); thus, there is an ellipsis for the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*. Therefore, "remembrance" (*smaraṇa*) refers to the person who remembers.

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as the similarity perceived in a gavaya produces in a person who remembers a cow the cognition, "That cow is characterized by this similarity," this [cognition] is not to be considered mere recollection (smaraṇa),
because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the cow as qualified by similarity to the gavaya, and the similarity as qualified by the cow.

This is because the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the cow and its similarity—which is the object of the means of knowledge known as analogy—is not apprehended by any perception, whether it be the perception of a cow or the perception of a gavaya.
As Bhaṭṭa has said:
"Just as when a place is perceived and fire is being remembered..."
Since the qualified [subject] is established through other means, it possesses the status of inference as a valid means of knowledge.
When the similarity has been perceived through direct perception and the cow has been remembered,
the authority of comparison (*upamāna*) consists in the fact that the qualified [object] cannot be established by any other means.
Furthermore, there is no recollection without prior apprehension;
therefore, comparison is not recollection, and thus it is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for the Naiyāyikas and others, however, their sūtra on comparison states:
"Comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing what is to be established (*sādhya*) through a well-known similarity.
This is its meaning:

comparison is the establishment—that is, the proof—of the relationship between a name and the object named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*), which is the object to be established, such as a *gavaya*, by means of that [animal] which possesses a well-known similarity. This is the fruit of comparison.

The meaning is that analogy (upamāna) is the cause for the comprehension of the relationship between a name and its referent; this is its detailed exposition: a cognizer who knows a cow but not a gavaya [perceives it].

Having been commanded by his master, "Go to the forest and bring back a gavaya," and being ignorant of the object denoted by the word *gavaya*, he questioned a forest-dweller or someone else who knew it,
asking, "Brother, what is a gavaya like?"
And he was instructed by him [the teacher] that "as is a cow, so is a gavaya.

For one who has heard this sentence of instruction and has entered some forest, the cognition of the similarity to a cow— which is assisted by the recollection of the meaning of the sentence of instruction— produces, from the very first moment, the realization that "this object is the referent of the word *gavaya*."
The comparison being set forth is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
likewise, for the Mīmāṃsaka, that which is designated as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a means of valid cognition.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also that which, when a perceived or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for, postulates another fact;
that is presumption.
For example, when Devadatta is known to be alive, the perception of his absence from the house leads to the postulation of the fact of his being outside.
This is its meaning:

presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of an object that cannot be logically accounted for without another object which is already established by the six means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and the rest.
And since it is preceded by those six means of valid cognition, it is of exactly six types.
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called non-existence has as its intrinsic nature the absence of the five means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and inference.
Its object of cognition (prameya) is the non-existence of a jar or the like.
The result (phala) is the cognition "there is no jar here," which takes the non-existence of the jar or the like as its objective support.
As Kumārila said:
"The non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge is called the absence of a means of knowledge (pramāṇābhāva);
it is either the non-modification of the self or a cognition of another object."

Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the non-existence of that object is established by the means of valid cognition known as non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*).
Thus [it is said].

These six means of valid cognition, beginning with perception, are to be understood as having mutually non-overlapping natures because they possess their own respective, unmixed specific characteristics.
To this it is replied: First of all, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) lacks authority with respect to an external object because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which has no necessary connection with something does not possess authority regarding that thing;
for example, a donkey that has no connection to fire [lacks authority regarding fire].
And Vedic words are unconnected with external objects; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
First of all, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because in reality there is no connection between words [and their objects].
For dependence consists in having a dependent nature;
and that [nature] cannot be without a basis,
because otherwise it would follow that everything would have a dependent nature in relation to everything.
Furthermore, no basis for this [connection] other than identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*) is perceived;
for that which does not possess the nature of another and does not originate from another lacks a nature that is necessarily connected to it.
Indeed, words do not possess the nature of external objects, because they are the objects of cognitions that have distinct appearances.
Nor do words arise from external objects, because we observe the production of words even in the absence of an object, since their occurrence is bound by the desire of a person.
[Objection: But surely, by virtue of their inherent capacity (*yogyatā*), some things are perceived as having a nature that is restricted [to specific effects].
Just as the visual faculty [perceives] form—
indeed, when the eye is active, it perceives only form—
in the same way, these Vedic words, although devoid of identity or causality with their objects, [convey] a supersensuous meaning by means of mere fitness alone.

"How will they understand this? For how can there be a lack of causal necessity merely due to the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*), such that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) would be established in this way?
This is not a fault, because even the visual faculty is restricted to illuminating only form, to the exclusion of taste and so forth, precisely because it is the effect of that [form].
For form assists the eye;
the eye does not illuminate form by its mere existence, because if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving even a form that is obstructed.

Therefore, it is clearly understood that the eye, having attained the capacity to generate a cognition of that form once the form is present in a suitable location, produces the cognition of form; thus, it is its effect. Otherwise, for the eye which does not depend on such assistance from the form, the restriction that it illuminates only that form would not be possible.
For if there were no distinction in being unassisted, the eye would not be the illuminator of form alone.
The restriction [that it arises] "not from taste and so forth" does not hold.
If that is so, then from what does this very restriction arise— that the eye must perform its function through form alone, and not through taste and so forth?
If form alone benefits [the eye] by the very nature of things and not taste or other qualities,
then, alas! just as there is a restriction for the eye regarding its being benefited by form,
let there likewise be a natural restriction for words regarding their communication of external objects.
To this it is replied: There is no inherent necessity for the eye to be assisted by form, because it is impossible for any entity to possess an inherent nature.
For one who would admit that a property of an entity is inherent must be asked: what does "inherent" mean? Does it mean that it exists by itself (*svataḥ*)?
Or from another, or from no cause?
If it arises from itself, [then...]
That is inconsistent, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself;
nor is it logical that it arises without a cause.

Because it is impossible for there to be a restriction of place and so forth for that which is causeless, the specific determination of the eye’s capacity to assist form is not inherent by its own nature. What, then, is its basis? It is dependent upon its own causes.
We reply: Indeed, the eye, being produced by its own cause, is produced as such that it is precisely capable of assisting with respect to form (*rūpa*).
Form, too, is produced by its own cause as such that it possesses the nature of being an assistant to that [eye].
If it is argued that even for sounds, that very nature is dependent upon their own causes, by which they do not deviate from external objects—then [we respond as follows].
It is not possible to assert this, because the Vedic sentences are accepted as being eternal.
If, however, this objection is intended to be refuted by accepting their non-eternality, [then...]
That too is difficult to maintain,
because it entails another logical fault:
if those [cognitions] were produced by their own causes alone as possessing the capacity to indicate a restricted object, [then what need would there be for external conditions?]
In that case, even those who do not understand the convention would comprehend their own meaning;

just as the eye, having arisen from its own causes as something that illuminates form, indeed illuminates form even for one who does not know the convention, whereas there is no comprehension of a specific [meaning] from an uttered word even for one who has not previously understood the convention.
Therefore, it is certain that the restriction regarding the communication of meaning by words is not dependent upon their own causes, as is the case with the eye and other sense organs.
Now, if it is argued that this nature of theirs was bestowed by their own causes alone— such that they cause the understanding of some object only when assisted by a specific convention—
then, upon the reversal of that convention, they would not function with respect to other objects.
For if this word "agnihotra," being dependent on convention, were the conveyor of a particular sacrifice, [it could not convey anything else].
How does it convey a different object through a difference in convention?
For a seed, which has arisen from its own causes with the inherent nature of producing a sprout while depending on soil and other factors, cannot produce a donkey;
likewise, a word, being restricted to the communication of a particular object, can manifest only that very object.
Now, if it is argued that this [word] has become capable of conveying its respective meanings precisely because it depends upon those respective conventions,
that too is not useful for the present discussion;
for in this way, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is not established.

For when it is even possible that a convention might convey something that is not a human goal, then it is impossible to determine whether this [word] is an indicator of only the intended meaning or not.
In that case, there will be a relationship between word and object characterized by the signified and the signifier. And so he said:
Although the relationships between the signified and the signifier exist as real entities,
they do not serve as causes for the manifestation of meaning unless they are made manifest through conventions.
(Nibandha 101)
If this is argued, [we reply]: But has it not already been stated that if this relation were real, there would be comprehension of the object even for one who does not know the convention?
And was it not further asserted that if there were dependence on convention, it would not function toward other objects?
Therefore, this relation characterized as the signified and the signifier has already been rejected.
Therefore, the conclusion is that there is no necessary connection between words and external objects.
And therefore, the reason is not unestablished.
Nor is it contradictory, because there is no pervasion by the opposite;
and that absence [of contradiction] is demonstrated by showing its presence in the similar class (sapakṣa).
For it is not logical that a contradictory [property] should exist in a subject possessing the property of similarity (sādharmya), because the opposite of the probandum (sādhya) is absent therein;
nor is there the possibility of a pervaded (vyāpya) property existing without its pervader (vyāpaka).
Because that would entail the consequence of its falling away.
Nor is the reason inconclusive,
because there exists a subverting proof against the contrary;
for when the negation of validity is the probandum, validity itself constitutes the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
Furthermore, the reason characterized by the absence of a causal connection (pratibandha) does not exist in that [case],
because it is pervaded by a causal connection that is its own opposite.
Indeed, this term "pramāṇa," which applies only partially to cognitions, is not without a basis.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of designating all cognitions as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, no basis for such a designation is tenable other than a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own object.
Therefore, the status of being the object of the designation "valid means of knowledge" is pervaded by the necessary connection with its own object.

Therefore, since validity is observed in the subject (*dharmin*)—which is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—to be pervaded by its opposite in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the exclusion [of validity] from the counter-example is established; thus, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Nor is any other fault possible.
Consequently, that which is established by a reason free from all defects must indeed be accepted by the wise.
The venerable Paṇḍita Śrījitaripu has demonstrated this very point regarding the lack of authority of the Vedas.

Thus, when the authority of Vedic words has been refuted, the knowledge arising from them is likewise invalid. Furthermore, even though a statement composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) does not deviate from its object and the knowledge produced by it may be non-deviant, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) cannot be accepted [in the case of the Vedas].

Because the mental states of others cannot be ascertained with certainty, one’s reliability remains unknown; consequently, it is impossible to recognize that a statement was composed by such a person.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is:
whatever is not ascertained in a particular form is not treated as being such in that form.

Just as a man on the street is not recognized as being omniscient, so too the person under consideration is not recognized as being authoritative; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
This [reason] is not unestablished (asiddha),
because it is uncertain whether one regarded as authoritative is truly so.

For indeed, since the mental states of others are beyond the senses (atīndriya), they cannot be apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa) and must therefore be inferred from their physical and verbal behavior.
Furthermore, those two types of physical and verbal conduct can be performed otherwise even with prior intelligence;
therefore, since there is no certainty due to their lack of necessary connection, how can one infer a specific state of another's mind from physical and verbal conduct?
Nor is it contradictory, because its presence in the similar class (sapakṣa) is possible.
Nor is it inconclusive,

because the pervasion— between the two affirmative properties of being established as authoritative and being determined as that which is to be conventionally designated as having that nature, which stand in the relation of the pervaded and the pervader— is established through perception and non-perception by means of a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), just like the case of "treeness" and "śiṃśapā-ness."
Therefore, when a probandum is established from a means of proof that is free from the three types of defects, it is indeed inexpressible [as being produced by a person].

Thus, because the status of being a reliable authority (*āptatva*) is difficult to ascertain, and because the certainty that [a work] was composed by such an authority is lacking, the validity of the word of a reliable authority is struck down in a single blow.
Consequently, the elaborate arguments of Vācaspati and others intended to establish its validity have no occasion whatsoever.
In this way, it should be understood that even the verbal testimony (śābda) favored by the Bhaṭṭas, though arising from conditions, is refuted.
Therefore, it is established that there is no verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition regarding external objects;
rather, with respect to the form within the intellect, because it is produced as its effect, it is simply an inference of that [form].
First of all, the means of knowledge called comparison (upamāna) as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas is not a valid means of knowledge at all,
because it lacks a real object.
Here too, the formal argument is as follows:
That which lacks an object does not possess validity,
as in the case of the cognition of a mass of hair;
and since the possession of an object is not established for the cognition of analogy (*upamāna*), this constitutes the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
This reason is not unestablished,
because analogy has no object.
For it is described that the object of analogy is either an individual qualified by similarity, or similarity qualified by an individual.
Similarity cannot be established as something distinct from the similar objects, because it is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But surely, similarity is an entity that is difficult to deny; as it has been said:
Furthermore, it is impossible to deny that similarity is a real entity;
it consists in the connection of a different class of things with many common constituent parts.
Thus it is said: To this it is replied—
if similarity were a perceptible entity distinct from the similar things, then it would certainly be subsumed by the non-perception of a perceptible object.
For it is not perceived by anyone, even one who has been refined by the study of the scriptures;
and if it were to exist, the entire world would become devoid of activity and cessation, since everything would exist everywhere.
Now, if it is maintained that this similarity is imperceptible, [the following objection applies].
Nevertheless, because the characteristic mark (liṅga) well-known in that context is absent, it remains unestablished.
And by means of that [mark] being established, the possession of an object by comparison (upamāna) would be proven;

however, since the cognition of similarity is produced from its own cause even by a similar object arising in such a way, it is indeed possible [for it to occur], yet it is not capable of establishing similarity [as a distinct category].
If it is argued that the establishment of similarity occurs solely through the force of the means of valid cognition known as comparison (*upamāna*), we say no.

Since the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) pertains only to two individual objects of similarity that have already been established by other means of valid cognition, how could similarity itself be established by comparison?

Consequently, because similarity is not established [by comparison], neither the individual object qualified by similarity nor similarity qualified by the individual object can be the object of comparison.
Thus, it is established that analogy has no object; therefore, the reason is not unestablished (asiddha),
nor is it contradictory (viruddha), because it exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa).
Nor is it inconclusive;
for when the absence of validity is the probandum (*sādhya*), validity itself is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*),
and that [validity] is pervaded by having an object.
Because if it were devoid of a causal sign (*nirnimitta*), it would follow that all cognitions possess validity.

Therefore, this reason—characterized by the absence of having an object—being excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) through the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), comes to rest precisely in the absence of validity. Thus, the pervasion is established; consequently, comparison (*upamāna*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
*Nibandha* 103) This same formal argument should also be seen as intended for the refutation of the *upamāna* (analogy) postulated by the Naiyāyikas,
because that too lacks a valid object.
For it is described that the scope of that relationship of designation is the [referent],
yet that does not exist in ultimate reality.
For that relationship must be either distinct from or non-distinct from the two related entities.
If they are distinct, then how can it be said that [the relation] belongs to those two?
Nor should it be said that it arises from another relation, for if one considers how that [second relation] also relates to them, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
Nor is it appropriate to say that just as a lamp shines without another illumination, so too a relation will be related without another relation;
for when the nature of a thing is established by valid cognition, it is described as "this is its intrinsic nature," as is the case with a lamp itself.
But since the relationship is not established by any means of valid cognition,
who could know in this way that "this is its intrinsic nature," or that "this does not exist at all"?

This is the relationship between these two; however, the cognition that "these two are related" can arise even from two unrelated things through the power of its own causes, and thus it is not capable of necessitating the existence of a [real] relationship.
Therefore, a distinct relationship is not established.
If, on the other hand, it were non-distinct, then there would be only the two relata themselves, and there would be no such thing as a "relationship designated by a name."
Whatever might be the object of comparison,
is the capacity to generate a cognition of a relation distinct from or non-distinct from the related entities? If it were distinct, that itself would be the relation.
There is merely a dispute over names.
Now, if it were non-different,
then just as the nature of a related object would be common to all objects, so too would that form [be common].
If it is argued: "Since that [nature] is non-distinct and common to all things, that object would be connected with other objects just as it is with the intended object;
yet this is not the case. Therefore, one must admit that the capacity to produce the cognition of connection is distinct from the connected objects themselves."
But surely this very objection has already been refuted by the venerable Rājakula; for it was said:
"If [the self] is connected [to the body] by its own nature, then just as it is related to that which belongs to it, why is there not likewise a connection of this [self] with the entire world?"

If all this is equal even in the case of a relation with another, and if that very [relation] is the cause of restraint, why is it not the regulator? And how is that [restraint] a conjunction (yoga) in one case and not in another?

Thus, because of the absence of a relationship and, by the previously stated reasoning, the absence of similarity, the Naiyāyika’s definition of comparison (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is unestablished; it is therefore refuted by the very same non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) mentioned immediately above. The same applies to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Regarding this general definition: "Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of an object without which a given object—perceived through perception or other means of knowledge—is not logically possible," this is now examined.

If there exists a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the object whose observation leads to the postulation of another object and that postulated object itself, then presumption is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*).
We have no objection whatsoever to its being given a different name, such as "presumption."
For how can it be established that an object perceived through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not possible without something else,
unless there were some relationship between that which is being perceived and that which is being postulated?
Otherwise, no one other than a shameless person would claim that it is not possible without that [other thing].
[Nibandha 104] It is like the case of a jar and a cloth.

Furthermore, that relationship must be ascertained either through prior perception and non-perception in some cases, or—in the case of invisibility—by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary.
Otherwise, the very cognition of "inexplicability without that" would be impossible.

And this being so, when one has perceived one related thing, the conceptualization of a second related thing— without which that [first] thing situated there would not be possible— is nothing other than inference.
In that regard, when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) arises solely from an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*);
when there is a causal connection (*tadutpattipratibandha*), it arises solely from an effect-reason (*kāryaliṅga*).
As it has been said: "The property of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*) occurs in a case that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*)."
Therefore, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Consequently, when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between that which is perceived and that which is postulated, presumptive testimony is not a separate means of valid cognition.
Now, if there were no such connection between those two, [presumptive testimony would indeed be a separate means].
Therefore, it should be understood that presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because there is no connection— either direct or indirect— with its object.

One should apply the same argument previously set forth for the purpose of refuting the Veda— that "whatever lacks a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with something has no validity regarding it"— to the refutation of the validity of this [presumption] as well.

Since presumption (*arthāpatti*) has already been refuted in its general form, its specific varieties—such as that which is preceded by perception and so forth—are necessarily refuted as well; thus, no further effort is made to refute them, just as when the cow itself is refuted, the brindled cow is also refuted.
Therefore, presumption is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Likewise, the validity of the means of knowledge known as non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is also not tenable,

because it too lacks an object. Consequently, that very non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), characterized by the absence of an object, which was previously adduced for the purpose of refuting the analogy (*upamāna*) championed by the Mīmāṃsakas, must now be adduced for the purpose of refuting this [non-existence] as well.
But surely, in this case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For if the absence of a jar were not a real, cognizable entity (*prameya*), then how could the cognition "there is no jar here" arise? If this is asked:
We say it is from perception that grasps only the bare location (*pradeśa*).

Now, if this "aloneness" (*kaivalya*) is of the nature of the location itself, then since it exists even in a location containing a jar, it would follow that the cognition of it must also exist there.
Or, if it is something distinct [from the location],...
If it is argued that by this very phrasing, non-existence itself is admitted, we say no.

Terms such as "isolation," "distinctness from that," and "non-mixture" refer to a location that has not acquired the status of being a substratum for a jar, which has arisen from its own causes; this very location, being distinct from the location occupied by the jar, produces the cognition of non-existence.
What, then, would be the purpose of a separate entity called "non-existence"?

If it is argued that "the location which has not attained the status of being a substratum with respect to the jar" means "the location conjoined with the absence of the jar," then the absence of the jar itself must also have not attained the status of being a substratum with respect to the jar; does this occur through another absence or by its own nature?
In the first case, there is an infinite regress.
Now, since it consists of the absence of that [jar], the absence of the jar does not require another absence to function as its substratum with respect to the jar.

If this is so, then it is also logical that a specific location, being devoid of companions, functions as the substratum for the jar—even without an [additional] absence—by virtue of being the nature of the jar’s absence through the process of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Why, then, do you engage in such groundless boasting and false chatter, which only confuses those lacking understanding?
You are confusing the person who is the disciple.
Therefore, since non-existence as something distinct from the locus (bhūtala) is unestablished, this reason—characterized by the absence of the object's possession of a locus—is not unestablished.
Furthermore, the hope for establishing the non-existence of the object of cognition based solely on the absence of the five means of valid cognition is also untenable.
Because this [non-existence] is the object of misconception, it is impossible for the absence of the object of knowledge (*prameyābhāva*) to be established by that very [misconception];
furthermore, the fallacies of contradiction (*viruddha*) and inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) regarding the reason have already been refuted.
Therefore, it is established that what is claimed to be the means of valid cognition for non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) lacks validity.

[Nibandha 105] Or rather, let the very nature of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) be defined. But what, then, is intended by you to be the essence of the non-existence of a means of knowledge?

Does it consist in the mere non-arising of a means of valid cognition by way of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), or rather as another entity by way of relative negation (*paryudāsapratiṣedha*)?
And even if it is another entity, is it of an insentient nature or of the nature of cognition?
There are six possible alternatives: [non-existence] may be (1) of the nature of cognition, (2) mere cognition, (3) or the cognition of an object associated with that single cognition.
Among these, first of all, non-existence in the form of a cessation is not tenable;
for it, being devoid of all causal capacity, is nothing at all.
And how could that which is nothing at all delimit non-existence,
or produce a cognition having that as its object,
or even be itself cognized? Thus, everything [you have said] is merely dancing in the dark.
As they say:
"For non-existence (abhāva) is neither the apprehension of anything nor the cause of its apprehension; how, then, could there be an apprehension of that [non-existence] itself?
Nor, under the view that it is a distinct entity, is it logically consistent for non-existence to have an insentient (jaḍa) nature."
Because there is no determination of an object of cognition characterized by non-existence— since determination is a property of cognition—
nor can non-existence be said to have the nature of mere cognition.

For it would follow that even an object remote in terms of place, time, or nature would be non-existent, since— relative to that [non-existence]— it too would be nothing but cognition. If, on the other hand, you accept that its nature is the cognition of an object associated with a single act of cognition, then let your hope for the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) be set aside.

Because it is precisely a specific kind of perception that is designated by the name "non-existence," and because we ourselves have accepted that [perception] as the means of proof called the "non-perception of the perceptible" (dṛśyānupalambha),
there is no disagreement whatsoever.

Therefore, even when its essential nature as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is examined, it simply falls apart. Furthermore, as for its definition which was stated— "the non-arising of perception and the other [means of knowledge] is called the absence of a means of valid cognition"— [it is untenable].
And so forth; that too is merely borrowed ornamentation.
Therefore, this remains established:
since that which is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is included right here, it is indeed within the means of valid cognition itself.
The chapter on the inclusion [of other means of knowledge] within [the categories of] valid cognition is completed. (Nibandh 106) // 7 //
// Determination of Pervasion //
In this context, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and other such effects by fire and other causes is characterized by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*).

And that [pervasion] is established by means of specific perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*), which are directed toward the apprehension of specific positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); such is the logical principle (*nyāya*).
Regarding this, the Bhaṭṭas and others hold differing views.

For they have postulated the nature of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekitva*) based on the frequent observation of smoke in a place possessing fire, and likewise its non-observation in a place devoid of it.
If it is objected that even when observation and non-observation have occurred many times, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is found in the case of a jar or an unchaste woman, [we reply:
let there be inference in those cases as well; what does this matter?
Or let it be that the same applies even in the case of smoke and so forth.
First of all, the first position is refuted precisely because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*);
the second [position] is also refuted for the very same reason of deviation.
For when there is deviation in another [instance], it does not affect the smoke at all.

Therefore, if the non-deviation between fire and smoke is impossible, even a hundred arguments for it, or even the specific perceptions and non-perceptions that would establish it, are of no use for inference. Or, if such non-deviation were possible, what would be the point of those causal origins or the specific perceptions and non-perceptions that would serve as its proof?
For the non-deviation [of the logical mark] is established precisely through observation and non-observation;

and thus the author of the *Kāśikā* states that the necessity of smoke with respect to fire is grasped by the final cognition, aided by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by numerous previous observations.
Trilocana, however, says: "Since perception and non-perception have particulars as their objects, how can there be a comprehension of the relation between two universals by means of them?
If it is argued that the relation is indeed cognized through the exclusion of non-fire and the exclusion of non-smoke, then one must ask:
of what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is even that the object?"
First of all, it cannot be by means of direct perception,
because the latter has only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object;
nor can it be by means of inference.
Because that [conceptualization] is also preceded by that [perception],

and there is no connection whatsoever between two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Now, if it is argued that the conceptual construction arising subsequent to perception determines non-difference regarding a difference that has been perceived, [we reply:]...
That alone is the universal.
Even so, the objects of conceptual constructions do not have a real entity as their object; rather, they have the apprehended aspect as their object.
And that [cognition] is not a real entity;
since for them the real entity is entirely beyond the senses,
how could there be a grasping of the relation by means of it as well?
For us, however, by means of the mind assisted by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), the relation between [smoke] and those things belonging to that same class is grasped;

therefore, smoke does not deviate from fire. If it were to deviate from it, smoke would transcend the relation that is devoid of any limiting condition (*upādhi*). Thus, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that removes the suspicion regarding the heterogeneity of the reason (*hetu*) is that which is called non-perception (*anupalambha*), the cause for the absence of a limiting condition that meets the criteria for perceptibility.
It is indeed perceptible;
therefore, the natural relationship is established.
But according to Vācaspati, there is a proliferation [of views]:
for instance, smoke and the like have an intrinsic relation with fire and the like,
but fire and the like do not have an intrinsic relation with smoke and the like.
For those [lamps] are perceived even without smoke and the like;
whereas fire and the like, when they undergo contact with moist fuel, then become connected with smoke and the like.
Of fire and the like...
But in Nibandha 107, it is clearly stated that the connection [of smoke with fire] is produced by adventitious conditions such as wet fuel and is not inherent;
therefore, it is non-necessary.
However, the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is indeed inherent.
This is because no such limiting condition (*upādhi*) is perceived;
and since no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed anywhere, it is logically untenable to postulate a condition that is not being perceived.

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that a limiting condition—which, though unseen, is suspected due to the absence of both proving and subverting evidence because it is unfit to be seen—can obstruct the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of the relationship.
"Those who perceive no restrictive factor must necessarily entertain doubt"—

this being granted as an opening, the demoness of doubt, having transgressed worldly bounds and gained her footing, would find no place where it does not exist; consequently, this person would never engage in any activity,
because in every case there is some potential for doubt regarding some kind of harm.
Furthermore, for discerning people, the apprehension of harm is a necessary factor for desisting from action;
for even when consuming wholesome food and drink, death is observed to occur eventually.
Therefore, one who maintains the worldly course according to authoritative tradition should entertain doubts only in accordance with what is actually perceived.
Nor does it arise even with respect to what has not been seen before;
for doubt depends precisely upon the recollection of specific features and does not occur in the absence of such recollection,
and recollection cannot occur regarding that which has never been experienced.
As it has been stated by the author of the Mīmāṃsā-vārttika: "A doubt is not without a basis.

Therefore, having diligently searched for an adventitious condition (upādhi) and failing to perceive one, we understand that it does not exist and conclude that the relationship is inherent (svābhāvika).

It might be argued as follows: if an intrinsic relationship were to exist between one thing and another that is not its cause, then everything would be intrinsically related to everything else; consequently, everything would be cognizable from everything.
Now, if one thing has another as its effect, why does everything not arise from everything?
For there is no distinction in their being "other.
Consequently, that same over-extension (atiprasaṅga) remains.
If it should be argued that the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things are not to be questioned— on the grounds that,
despite the lack of distinction in their otherness, only certain things are causes and only certain things are effects—

then surely this questioning of intrinsic natures applies equally even to distinct things that are neither cause nor effect, provided there is a necessary connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) between them.
Therefore, this too is trivial.
By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), moreover, is this natural relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) apprehended?
In the case of relations involving perceptible objects, it is by perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For we consider it logical that the sense organ itself, assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation, grasps the natural connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) between smoke and fire, just as one grasps the true nature of the distinction between genuine and counterfeit gems.

Likewise, in cases where the connection is known through other means of knowledge, those very same means of knowledge—assisted by their respective repeated observations—should be inferred as the instruments for grasping the natural connection.
And if reasons (*hetu*) are naturally constrained (*pratibaddha*) to their own probandum (*sādhya*), then...

(Nibandha 108) Wherever reasons accompanied by *tarka*—which have their occurrence in the absence of the probandum eliminated and whose doubt regarding the presence of the opposite of the probandum has been dispelled—are observed, they necessarily bring about the presentation of their own probandum; for otherwise, they would exist without the probandum and would deviate from their very nature.
To this it is replied: here, indeed, in the case of difference, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is simply the relation of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*).
Nor is this—whether distinct or otherwise—established by mere repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) as an intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) connection characterized by inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
For instance, is the determination of necessity established wherever the activity of repeated observation occurs?
Or rather, the application of repeated observation occurs only where there is necessity (*niyatatva*).
In the first case, from a jar one could infer a harlot,
and from its being earthen one could establish that it is scratchable by iron.
If it is argued that this is not so because, even though repeated observation is possible, certainty is still possible [only through inference],
yet deviation is observed— then whose observation of deviation is it? That of some particular author of a treatise?
Or [is it] for the cognizer? In the first case, what has happened to the cognizer such that he would not perform inference?
Otherwise, if another person were to perceive that object through direct perception, he too would have achieved his purpose; why then would he necessarily seek out inference?
Nor is inference [valid] based on the observation of non-deviation from the word of a reliable person (*āpta*),
because— as established elsewhere— it is impossible to ascertain who a reliable person is.
Furthermore, it is unworldly to suggest that one would infer fire from smoke only after having questioned the author of the treatise regarding the observed relationship [between them].
For the cognizer, however, even if a deviation exists, it does not necessarily become an object of perception;
for it is not the case that wherever there is a deviation, it must necessarily enter into cognition at that very time or in that very place.
And there is no rule that what is not perceived simply does not exist.
Even though there is deviation [of the reason], it does not follow from that observation because the causal complex for such observation is absent;
for even after a very long interval of time, [the object] is observed, just as in the case of the deviation regarding Brahminhood and the like.
If it is argued that the cognizer himself, having already engaged with the jar, the earthen nature, and so forth,
might at that very time observe a deviation either sequentially or otherwise—
if he indeed engages in some manner, [then...]
Or, even if he proceeds, he would not perceive the non-deviation [of the cause] due to the absence of the causal totality;
or he might employ a diamond against iron.
Clearly, for him, even that has become unmeasurable—what great scholarship this is!

Therefore, if inference were based on the non-observation of deviation, then for a cognizer who has not observed deviation, it would exist even in the case of a jar's being made of clay. Thus, the absence of deviation is not established by mere non-observation,
because only the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*) has the authority to establish non-existence in all cases.
Therefore, because [the concomitance] is established through frequent co-occurrence alone, there is no room for doubt that it might be either non-invariable or not non-invariable.

If that were so, then let there be no inference from smoke either, since its deviation has not been observed. No; for such an opportunity for doubt is possible everywhere in that which lacks the production of that [effect].
Furthermore, at some point, the cognizer, having acted, may perceive a deviation.
In that case, the rule of necessity is not established wherever there is frequent observation;
how, then, can the invariable concomitance (pratibandha) be proven in the case of smoke?
Because the capacity of repeated observation to establish necessity elsewhere is impaired, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases due to its being tainted by human fallibility.
If it is argued that, since visual perception and the like are observed to be impaired in cases such as the double moon, they would likewise not present objects such as a jar, we say: no.
For perception is the effect of the sense faculty and its object;
the cognition of a double moon and the like is not such [perception], because it lacks the status of being an effect of a real object.
[Nibandha 109] Therefore, even though it possesses a different characteristic, the cognition of a jar is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, there is no difference in the characteristic of the repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*)—which grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—in the case of smoke and in the case of earthiness, such that confidence would arise in one instance [but not the other].
If it is argued that these two— being an effect of an object and not being an effect of an object— are the distinction in their definitions, we say no;

for when there is a dispute regarding whether the cognition of a jar or the like is an effect of an object, its ascertainment comes from another means of valid cognition or from the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*),
not by mere assertion.

Nor is there, in this case, a permanent concomitance of smoke with fire that has been grasped as being like the friendship between two friends—such that, when doubt arises, there would be a connection to another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of establishing that permanent concomitance, or some effect thereof would be perceived.
Furthermore, one should not say: "In that case, there will be a distinction in their definitions characterized by being sublated or not being sublated."
The first position is not tenable, because the observation of repeated concomitance—which grasps the absence of deviation—is not established as being sublated;
for a mere non-sublation (*abādha-mātram*), being a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the alternative negation (*paryudāsa*)—consisting either in the connection with another means of valid cognition or the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—is also unestablished. Thus, the first position fails.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;

for even in the absence of necessity, frequent observation is possible in cases such as "being earthen" (pārthivatva) and so forth. Thus, pervasion (vyāpti) is not something to be known through frequent observation.
Even regarding the objection raised by Trilocana, we reply as follows:

if it is stated that perception has the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as its object by means of an exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda), then this is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).
However, an exclusion of connection with another (anyayogavyavaccheda) is unestablished.

This is because all cognitions, such as perception, inference, and so forth, do not exceed a twofold nature of their objects, distinguished by way of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*).
For that which appears within a cognition is the apprehended; whereas that toward which the cognition proceeds is the determined.
In that regard, the apprehended object (*grāhya*) of perception is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); however, its determined object (*adhyavaseya*) is the universal (*sāmānya*),
which consists solely of the particular characteristic as excluded from what does not possess that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta*).

Inference, however, functions by way of exclusion (viparyaya). Consequently, with respect to conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*), just as there is an established determination of the existence of a pot— composed of a collection of color, taste, smell, and touch— through direct perception even when only a particular instance of color is apprehended, so too is there a grasp of pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the two universals of the probandum and the probans, which consist of mere entities excluded from what is not that [nature], and which serve as the objects of cognition through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
This is indeed correct;
for this very reason, it is difficult to understand that the object of conceptual constructions is strictly non-existent, whereas their actual object is entirely beyond perception.
Because all conceptual constructions have real entities as their objects insofar as they depend upon what is determined by them,
and because it is taught exactly thus in the treatises;
furthermore, it is not possible for the mind to grasp the pervasion of those things belonging to that same class.
Because the mind lacks independence with respect to external objects;
otherwise, it would follow that there could be no such things as the blind or the deaf.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that smoke, when deviating from fire, could transcend its connection [with fire] while remaining devoid of any limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Because a natural relationship imagined by one's own mind is merely a borrowed ornament.
Furthermore, as Vācaspati has argued: "When something is invariably concomitant with another by means of a limiting condition (upādhi), its relation to that [condition] is intrinsic (svābhāvika),
just as the relation of smoke to fire."
Since the visible adjunct (*upādhi*) of that [fire] is not perceived and no deviation is observed anywhere, the following is considered here:

that whose natural relationship (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is to be established through non-perception must indeed have its adjunct stated as something other than the nature of smoke itself, just as fuel is for fire.
Furthermore, some other entity is visible and some is invisible;
it is not the case that everything is necessarily visible.
