Consequently, even smoke might have an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) with respect to fire.
And since [an upādhi] is not perceived, the non-perception of a mere upādhi is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, how can it be said that there is no upādhi at all simply because it is not seen, such that the establishment of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) would follow?
[It would be so] in *Nibandha* 110.
However, if one attempts to prove the absence of a perceptible limiting adjunct (*dṛśyopādhi*), it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

As long as there is the possibility of suspecting an imperceptible limiting adjunct (*paramadṛśyopādhi*), the obstruction to [establishing] its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) remains exactly as it was.

The claim that "deviation is not observed in some cases" is entirely irrelevant; for, just as with a limiting condition (*upādhi*), the non-existence of deviation cannot be established by mere non-observation.

Even if deviation were possible at all times and in all places and were even visible, it would still be impossible to ascertain it because the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) for such ascertainment is absent at all times, in all places, and for everyone.
Just as in the case of the infidelity of a Brahmin woman and so forth, even when such an act is not witnessed directly, it is impossible to rule out its occurrence at another place or time.
If it is objected: "If an *upādhi* (limiting condition) were some other factor required by smoke, how could there be a necessary rule that fire exists simply because smoke exists?
We reply: This very point is what is being investigated—namely, whether fire necessarily occurs whenever smoke is present, or not.
Perhaps smoke might exist even without fire by depending on some other limiting condition (*upādhi*); what, then, is the fixed cause here?
Therefore, it is correct to say that since smoke is established as arising dependent upon fire, how could it admit of existence in the absence of that [fire]?
Furthermore, no deviation from fire has been observed, whether with respect to individual instances or the universal (*jāti*).
If it is asked, "How can there be doubt in that case?"—is humanity ever seen in the individual instance of a post, or in its genus, such that one would doubt whether it is a post?
If you say it was seen elsewhere in something characterized by verticality, [we reply: so be it.

Moreover, even here, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is indeed observed in other cases, such as "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) and the like which coexist with fire. However, the claim that "one requires the observation of a property only where its presence is doubted" is unworldly (*alaukika*). If deviation were observed in a particular instance of smoke, then the universal of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*) would necessarily be excluded from the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
How can there be doubt?
If it is observed in the genus (jāti), then even in that case there is a certainty of deviation (vyabhicāra);
how, then, can there be doubt?

Therefore, even when deviation or a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is not perceived in the case of smoke and so forth, it cannot be ruled out due to its unobservability; thus, doubt is difficult to ward off.

Now, this doubt regarding a limiting condition or deviation—which is essentially a doubt regarding intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*)—necessarily obstructs the certainty of intrinsic nature for the time being.
Consequently, the obstruction of the certainty of intrinsic nature is, in effect, the actual result.
Since that which indicates [the probandum] is itself ineffective without certainty,
it follows that thus, the non-perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) or the non-perception of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is inconclusive; it does not establish their absence,
because [only through such establishment] could the naturalness (*svābhāvikatva*) of the relationship be proven.
Furthermore, this non-perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is unestablished.
Just as fire is not connected with smoke without fuel, so too smoke is not connected with fire without that [fuel]; thus, fuel possesses the status of a limiting condition equally in both cases.

If, on the other hand, the establishment of the limiting condition is based on the fact that the acquisition of smoke occurs through the concomitance of fire with fuel once fire is established, [then the following applies].

If it is argued that, because smoke—which is not yet established—obtains its own nature through that [fire] as its cause, the relation is established as being essential (*svābhāvika*) due to its non-deviation;
even so, it follows that this very "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) is what constitutes the essential relation.
It is precisely that which is the essential relation.

Furthermore, it is not established by the thesis alone, consisting merely of concomitance. Moreover, because non-deviation would be due to essential nature (*svābhāvikatva*), and because essential nature would follow from non-deviation everywhere, a circular argument (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is unavoidable.

However, for one who perceives its occurrence just once as the very perception of non-deviation in all cases, this undesirable consequence does not apply. If you argue, "In that case, non-deviation is established for me too through repeated observation," we say no; because "repeatedly" does not have a fixed number of instances, by how many observations could one following the definition attain satisfaction? For us—
In the *Nibandha* (111), however, perception and non-perception are enumerated as being of only two types. As they say:
"Having previously not seen [the sequence], one who perceives it in succession knows the relationship between cause and effect;
or, having seen it, one who does not perceive it in succession [knows it]; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress."
As for the lamentation that "conception is untenable even for that which is not being perceived," that is improper even for a child;
for there is scope for conception regarding an object even when it is not being perceived.
For a pot that is currently being perceived is not called "imagined" (kalpita);
nor is it logical to say that a condition (upādhi) which is itself doubted prevents the inherent nature of a relationship,
since doubt arises as a matter of logical necessity precisely when there is an absence of both proof and disproof.
For this very reason, there is no room for the demoness of doubt everywhere.
[Objection: How then could this [person] not act?
If it is argued that doubt can be raised even regarding the object of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), we say: No.

For since the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has been accepted is certainty, the acceptance of that [cognition] is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance of certainty regarding its object, provided there is no dispute concerning its status as a valid cognition.
Nor does activity fail to occur simply because of doubt; for activity is unavoidable even when there is uncertainty regarding the object, just as in the case of consuming palatable food and drink.

Even if death is observed at some point during the employment of such means, life is seen millions of times; nor is there any impairment to the livelihood of those who follow authoritative tradition, for it is precisely by those who follow authoritative tradition that doubt is prescribed in the absence of definitive proof.
The claim that "doubt should be entertained according to what is observed" and so forth is also a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),

because it is precisely an *upādhi* (limiting condition) or a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) observed elsewhere that is being suspected. Furthermore, even in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), doubt would certainly arise from the mere presence of a proof (*sādhaka*).
Even that which has been asserted as "it might be so" is likewise devoid of substance;

for when a form is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is based on its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). However, the determination of the essential character of a thing does not occur through the mere apprehension of an intrinsic nature.

Thus, if the theory of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) is applied to a causal relationship established by the means of valid cognition—namely, perception and non-perception—which grasp the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of fixed objects, then what has come of the "intrinsic connection" (*svābhāvikasambandha*)? For in that case, having mentally discarded the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) [of production], one would have to rely on some other means for the cognition of the distinction between two co-occurring things;
and if one depends upon that complex, it is simply "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*).
What is the point of this boastful self-aggrandizement through changing the name?
Furthermore, the manner of apprehending that innate connection—such as by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) it is grasped—has already been refuted previously.
Thus, since its innate nature is unestablished, the concluding statement that "reasons are connected by their very nature" and so forth is merely a product of one's imagination.

Therefore, it is established that when another object is to be understood, there is the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*), and the proof of its existence [the pervasion] is derived from perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
Thus, the doctrine of essential nature (*svābhāvikavāda*) is to be avoided from afar, like anointing one's heart with impurity.
The *Vyāptinirṇaya* by the venerable Ratnakīrti is completed.
Nibandha 112 // 8 //
Refutation of the Proof of Stability (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇam)
Homage to Tārā!

That evil [ignorance], through connection with which the entire world is held to wander like a blind man in saṃsāra, is cast off by those who have come under the sway of compassion, once stable realization has been attained.
In this regard, others assert perception, inference, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of establishing the stability of all objects.
For instance, perception known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), arising in the form "this is that very same jar, crystal, and so forth," establishes stability.
Nor should this [scripture] be declared invalid;
for its invalidity would have to arise either from the occurrence of a cause for invalidity,
or from the absence of the characteristics of validity.
If the first position is held, what is the cause of its lack of authority: is it falsity, ignorance, or doubt?
Falsity, at least, does not apply here.
For falsity in regard to that [object] might be suspected either from a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) or from a defect arising in the cause (*hetūttha-doṣa*).
First of all, even a scent of subversion is impossible,
because it cannot occur even in other places, times, or persons.
Nor is it reasonable to suspect that sublation, even if not yet perceived, will ever occur, for a groundless suspicion is untenable; indeed,
those who perceive no restrictive factor must necessarily entertain such a suspicion.
Thus, once an opportunity has been granted, the demoness of doubt gains a foothold; thinking "it does not exist anywhere," one would not engage in anything at all.
For ultimately, since death is observed even after the consumption of wholesome food and drink, suspicion would never cease regarding everything.
Therefore, by one who maintains the worldly course of authoritative people, doubt should be entertained only regarding what is actually perceived, and not regarding what has never been seen before.
As it was stated in the *Kārikā*:
"A doubt that lacks a basis in valid cognition is not [to be entertained]."
In the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* as well,
it is said: "For he who, out of delusion, might imagine a subverting factor even where none exists, being possessed by doubt in all worldly transactions, shall come to ruin."
If it is argued that the proof of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) serves as a subverting argument against this [position], we say no;
for since inference— even indirectly— is preceded by perception, perception is primary.
And because inference is predominant, it is the sublater [of this],
but inference is not the sublater of it; rather,
another perception is the sublater.
Just as there is the perception of a rope and so forth which sublates the cognition of a snake and so forth, such [sublation] is not possible here.
Now, even if there were a sublating perception, why would there not be a lack of perceptibility for both through mutual obstruction? No.

Because there is no equality between [the two cognitions] in terms of having or not having as their object a thing capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), one of them is a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*); thus, it does not have a real entity as its object. Its falsity arises from a sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), nor from a defect in the cause (*hetūtthadoṣa*).
Because there is no contradiction regarding the object across differences of place, time, and person;
nor is ignorance a cause for invalidity here,
since the experience of recognition is possible.

Nor is there any doubt; for in the case of crystals and the like, the cognition does not arise as "Is this that very thing or not?", but rather as "This is that very crystal," with all suspicion of error dispelled.
Therefore, recognition is not invalid due to the presence of causes for invalidity, nor is it so because its definition fails.

For our established tenet is this: whatever has arisen, is free from doubt, produced by unimpaired causes, and remains unsublated across different places, times, and persons—that alone is valid cognition. As it has been said:
Therefore, let that cognition which has arisen firmly and does not undergo sublation by another cognition be recognized as valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* also states therein: "Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as recognized by the world, is that which consists of the certain cognition of an object not previously known, which is free from sublation, and which is produced by non-defective causes."
Thus [it is said]. And since this definition also applies to recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) according to the logic already stated, this too is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Now, one might object: "This [recognition] is not a single [cognition], because its causes are diverse."
Because of the difference in their objects and because of the contradiction in their intrinsic natures;
for that [consciousness] is the effect of formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
And "this" is the effect of the sense faculty.
Furthermore, there can be no non-difference in the effect despite a difference in the causes, because that would entail the consequence of the manifold variety of the universe being causeless.

This being so, even though there is no difference in the designation "crystal, crystal," [the two instances] differ by virtue of their connection with a previous place and time versus their connection with a subsequent place and time.
Because of its association with contradictory properties, the crystal must be said to differ between the earlier and later times; thus, there is a difference in the objects [of cognition]:
"that" refers to the remote, while "this" refers to direct perception.
Nor can the identity of these two, which are as opposed in nature as fire and frost, be established even by Śakra, for that would entail the absurd consequence of the three worlds being one;
nor does this [identity] possess any validity.
Because it manifests as a non-entity due to its being conceptual in nature,
and because it is no different from memory, the claim that recognition establishes the oneness of entities is merely a wishful thought.
To this it is replied: this recognition is declared to be indeed one and the same;
even though the sense organ alone is incapable, and even though there is merely the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
However, the sense faculty, when accompanied by the formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*), will produce recognition,
because the presence or absence of recognition follows the presence or absence of that [faculty].
For it is not the case that because a mere seed does not produce a sprout, it likewise fails to produce one when accompanied by soil and other factors.
Now, let there be mutual difference between the place and time, or between their respective conjunctions; however,
there is no such difference for the ruby as delimited by them,
because it is distinct from those two and from their conjunctions.
If it is asked, "In that case, if there is otherness between the two, how can they possess the property of belonging to one another? [the answer is:
"It is due to their very nature (svabhāva). This will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the *Saṃsargaparīkṣā*.
Nor is there any contradiction with their inherent nature.
For it would follow that inference, too, would be manifold;
for that [inference] is both perceptual and non-perceptual,
as well as non-conceptual and conceptual.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction between perception and other means of knowledge regarding the non-difference established by one's own experience, because there is both non-superimposition and superimposition with respect to the distinction between the essential nature and its perceived object,
we say: no, for the same logic applies here as well.

Indeed, even this cognition is not experienced or determined as being non-different from these two— that is, as a single crystal that serves as the substratum for "thatness" (*tattā*) and "thisness" (*idantā*) while being colored by them.

Furthermore, even though the object is a single entity, its status as perceptible (*pratyakṣatā*) and imperceptible (*parokṣatā*) will not be contradictory, given the distinction between "thatness" and "thisness" which color it.
Because they arise simultaneously, and because the unity of consciousness is established by valid cognition;
nor is it contradictory for a single entity to possess both the connection with a previous place and time expressed by "that," and the connection with a proximate place and time expressed by "this."

For it is logical that when the nature of a ruby (*padmarāga*) is being determined, its absence is excluded; because if that [absence] were not excluded, the nature of the ruby could not be determined, since the existence of the ruby has as its very essence the exclusion of its own non-existence, and if that [non-existence] were not excluded, its determination would be impossible.
But why are other [gems] such as emeralds excluded?
If you say it is because they are invariably absent where that [gold] is absent, then from what does that very fact [of invariable concomitance] arise?
If it is argued that this is because the identity (*tādātmya*) between topaz (*puṣparāga*) and ruby (*padmarāga*) is never perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
then in a case where their identity is indeed cognized, there can be no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between them.
And there exists this direct, manifest cognition which illuminates a single ruby as persisting through space, time, and state, such that one thinks, "This is that very ruby.
Its lack of authority is not due to its conceptual nature,
because there is no contradiction between the appearance of association with verbal expression and its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is this [knowledge] based on memory, because it possesses an excellence consisting in its conformity to place, time, and state, whereas memory pertains to that which lacks such specific place, time, and state.
If it is argued that recognition arises even when there is a difference, as in the case of hair, kuśa grass, or the trunk of a plantain tree, [we reply:
let it arise; what is the fault?
What is established by this?

Is it that recognition is inconclusive due to its commonality [with other types of cognition], or that both are invalid because of the similarity in their terminology, or is it merely intended to raise a doubt?
The first position is refuted simply by the fact that it is not accepted;
for this [inference] has not been presented as being of the nature of an inference (anumāna).
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that there is no fault in the qualification "because it is uncontradicted" even if it were an inference.
Nor is the second position tenable, because a probandum cannot be established by a mere example alone;
for if visual consciousness whose object is a mass of hair and the like were invalid, it would follow that direct perception of jars and other objects would also be invalid.
However, it has been demonstrated that mere doubt must certainly not be resorted to, as it would result in the total collapse of worldly transaction; thus, the third position is also untenable.
Furthermore, if recognition regarding hair and the like is fallacious, why is the cognition of cause and effect not also fallacious?
If you argue that whatever is fallacious cannot even be considered a cognition of cause and effect, [we reply:]...
If this is so, then that which is non-concordant is not recognition at all, because it is a mere semblance (tadābhāsa); this is the same [as the previous argument].

Furthermore, if recognition possesses validity and is not included within inference and the other means of knowledge, it must be perception itself, because it follows the presence and absence of the sense organ assisted by mental impressions (saṃskāra).
Furthermore, because this occurs when there is contact with existing objects and because the sense faculties exist,
this recognition— having as its object a single crystal or similar entity connected across multiple places, times, and states— establishes its stability.
Likewise, stability is established through inference as well.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the cognitive recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same crystal" and so forth, which is the subject of dispute, is consistent with reality (*yathārtha*), because it is an uncontradicted cognition.
Whatever cognition is uncontradicted is all found to be in accordance with reality,
just like the cognition of self-reflexive awareness;
and this [cognition] is uncontradicted.
Therefore, it is "so" (*tathā*).
And its being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*) is to be ascertained by refuting the objections raised by others against the proof of momentariness. (Nibandh 115)
Now, another formal argument: the entities under dispute possess a single nature throughout preceding and succeeding times,
because they are recognized through an uncontradicted recognition.
Whatever is recognized by an uncontradicted recognition is all non-different.
For example, the blue object is recognized as "that very same blue object which was seen by you is the one seen by me. And so it is with these entities.
Therefore, it is "so.
The distinction is that previously the condition (*pratyaya*) was the subject (*dharmin*), whereas now it is the entities (*bhāva*).
Furthermore, because destruction has a cause, stability is established.

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: those entities that are the subject of dispute do not undergo destruction prior to the presence of their respective causes of destruction, because their destruction is caused.
Whatever has a cause does not exist in the absence of that cause,
just as smoke and the like do not exist in the absence of fire and the like;
and these entities have destruction as their cause.
Therefore, it is "so" (tathā).

Furthermore, the fact that the destruction of a jar has a cause is established through perception and non-perception—just as in the case of fire and smoke—even once the causal relationship between the mallet and destruction has been proven.
Nor is it appropriate to assert that the cause of destruction is either ineffective or redundant.
For it would follow that even causes such as a sprout would possess that same nature;
indeed, one could argue that if the object is not yet coming into being, the cause of birth is ineffective, and if it is already coming into being, the cause is redundant.
Moreover, existing things are non-momentary, because they possess causes;
whatever possesses a cause is non-momentary.
Just as there is the destruction of existing things;
and these [things] possess causes;
therefore, they are non-momentary.

Since the suspicion that "having a cause" might occur in the opposite of the probandum (the non-momentary) simply removes the very idea that destruction is causeless, the non-momentariness [of things] is established by "having a cause," which possesses a well-known pervasion.
Likewise, Śaṅkara stated in the *Sthirasiddhi*:
"An entity does not perish immediately after its production,
because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatvāt*)."
Regarding the phrase "like the exclusion of the object":
because there is no existing counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the reason is indeed positive (*anvayin*).
If it is argued that the reason is of doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*) because there is no contradiction between cognizability (*prameyatva*) and momentariness, [we reply: ...
Indeed, if things were momentary, the knowability of anything would not be established,

because that which has the property of existing for only a single moment does not persist until the time of its cognition; furthermore, if what is past were knowable, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
In this very way, praising the formal argument (*prayoga*), Trilocana also said:
"All entities are non-momentary, because they are objects of cognition (*prameyatvāt*)."
Whatever is cognized is non-momentary,
just like the destruction of an entity;
and all entities are objects of cognition.
Therefore, [the reason] "because they are non-momentary" is stated.
If it is argued that the subject of the example is unestablished, we say no;
for a thing that has arisen from its own complex of causes would necessarily persist forever, unless there were both its cessation and its production.

The word "even" (*eva*)—intended here as a synonym for "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*)—is used to show that existence occurs only at that very time, neither before nor after; without the production of a continuity of being beyond that moment, this term cannot be rendered meaningful even by the gods themselves.
For a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) is the shortest duration of time in relation to the time of destruction.
Therefore, because it possesses that [moment], it must be called momentary;
otherwise, since arising and destruction would occur at the same time, they would—by virtue of having the same cause—result in being one and the same.
But if they were one, then one of the two would have to be abandoned.
In that case, if there were the abandonment of arising, it would follow as a logical consequence that entities are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
and if there were the abandonment of cessation, it would follow as an unavoidable consequence that entities belonging to those who are born are eternal.
Thus, the illustrative example is established.
(Commentary on Nibandha 116):

If it is argued that "the exclusion [of the reason] from the counter-example (vipakṣa) is doubtful because the contradiction between 'being an object of cognition' (prameyatva) and 'momentariness' (kṣaṇikatva) is not established," this is not so.
Since perception brings about some object, it brings it about by virtue of its proximity;
and this proximity is best understood as being produced from that very object,
not as identity with it.
Because the theories of cognition with form (*sākāra*) and without form (*nirākāra*) are not under discussion here,
and because they have been refuted elsewhere;

furthermore, that proximity (*pratyāsatti*), characterized by the relation of cause and effect and implied by the appearance of a determined object, is untenable for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) when they exist simultaneously.
It is like [the relationship between] the two horns of a cow.
Therefore, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), by making known the existence of an object, makes it known through its being dependent on that [existence] for its own production.
And because it is invariably concomitant with the mere state of being a cause, it must exist at a prior time.

Therefore, knowability is pervaded by existence at a prior time, and existence at a prior time is untenable if there is momentariness; thus, by the non-perception of the pervader, knowability—being excluded from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) of momentariness—is pervaded by non-momentariness. Consequently, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is beyond doubt.
Thus, in this way, it is established by the means of valid cognition known as inference that [the object] is non-momentary.
In this way, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) also serves as a proof for this [permanent self].
For instance: the apprehension of the causal relationship; the apprehension and recollection of succession and simultaneity; desire; the searching for what was buried by oneself;
the desisting from curiosity toward harmful objects; the connection between action and its fruit; determination preceded by doubt; and bondage and liberation.

The effort for liberation, engagement in actions that have auspicious results, recognition, the relationship between cause and effect, the relationship between material cause and its product, and so forth— all these, being untenable without a stable existence, establish stability. Since, if there were change at every moment, the experiencer would have perished and it would be impossible for another to grasp the causal relationship and so on, how can even the suspicion of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga) arise?
To this it is replied: This conceptual construction called recognition is indeed invalid, and its falsity is established by a subverting cognition that negates its having a real object.
Now, one might argue that a perceptual subversion of this [recognition] is impossible.
If it is argued that inference is incapable [of establishing this],
then what is the use of even a thousand perceptions for this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) if its own object is firmly established through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)?
However, if there is a lack of corroboration (*saṃvāda-śaithilya*), then even inference finds scope, just like a subverting perception (*bādhaka-pratyakṣa*).
Because it is only with respect to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself that there is the scope for establishment or sublation;

for instance, let it be granted that even in the case at hand, the recognition— such as "the magician is drawing out with his mouth the ball submerged in his head"— is indeed recognized as being sublated by an inference connected to the undesirable consequence of a hole in the head, and thus, while being sublated, it is not [considered] a valid recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Just as the appearance of a downward-turned sky is indeed sublated even when there is universal consensus, so too let the apprehension of oneness be sublated even when there is universal consensus.
Therefore, the proclamation of its status as perception here is merely a borrowed ornament and offers no protection.
How, then, can stability be established from this?

Consequently, its status as inference is also destroyed, because—by the reasoning already stated—it has been established that it possesses "sublation," which is the opposite of the qualification "non-sublated. Thus, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the failure of its qualification.
Even when no subverting argument against the proof of momentary destruction is being stated, this [inference] remains invalid nonetheless.
Because deviation is observed in cases such as a mass of hair that has been shaved and grown back again.
But was it not said that "that which is errant is not recognition," and so forth?
This is correct, provided that a difference in definition can be established, as in the case of the cognition of the relation between cause and effect.

For just as there is a difference in definition between the cognition of the relation of cause and effect— which is established through perception and non-perception inclined toward grasping positive and negative concomitance— and the cognition of what merely appears to be such,
so too, if a difference in definition were shown for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), it would be possible to demonstrate [its distinctness].
Nibandha 117) Or, if it were possible [to distinguish them] by means of their utility for error or non-error, then let there be a distinction between recognition and its semblance;
but this is not the case.
Because the recognition of ordinary persons regarding an object that is entirely similar in every respect is of a single uniform nature.
If it is argued that there is a difference in definition between being consistent and being inconsistent, we say no.

For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that lacks a logical mark (*liṅga*), what is called "consistency" is either its connection with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
In this regard, the first position is not tenable.

Even subsequently, because there is not even a trace of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) beyond the mere independent conceptual determination that "this is that very same thing," the second position is also not tenable;
for no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has been established that is tied to a single entity across prior and subsequent times.
For even if it is destroyed, there is no contradiction in its performing such purposeful action by means of another [entity] possessing an identical capacity;

for instance, just as when one jar holds water, this does not prevent another jar existing at that same time but in a different location from also holding water, so too, if a second or subsequent moment is likewise [capable of] holding water, what fault could there be?
But in the case of a dissimilar action, there is no thought [of identity] at all;
how, then, could there be the possibility of the correspondence of recognition?
Now, if it is argued: "If one instance of recognition is seen to be non-concordant, then every recognition might be suspected of being non-concordant;

in that case, since one instance of sensory cognition is observed to be non-concordant in the case of [the illusion of] a mass of hair or two moons, then all perception regarding jars and the like might also be suspected of being non-concordant, because the single defining characteristic of being produced by the senses is present everywhere," we reply: No.

For even there, a distinction in characteristics exists. To explain: when external objects exist, perceptuality consists in the direct conformity to the form of the object by virtue of being an effect of the sense faculty and the object;
and that is ascertained by perception which has attained proficiency through a specific kind of practice.
In some cases, however, because it is known through the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), its status as perception is indeed faultless.

In the case of a double moon and the like, that cognition is produced solely by an eye impaired by cataracts or similar defects, devoid of an actual object; thus, it is merely a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

Furthermore, the non-existence of objects such as a double moon is unassailable, as it is sublated by other persons in different places and times who do not perceive such an object. Therefore, even when excluding such semblances of perception, what contradiction could there be regarding those [cognitions] that are genuine perceptions?
It is not logical to claim that all this exists even in the case of recognition.

For just as an action such as cooking, which was previously established as being restricted to fire and so forth, later—when experienced—communicates the correspondence (*saṃvāda*) of the cognition of burning;
otherwise, due to the annihilation of external objects, the world would become devoid of activity;

yet no such purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), restricted by the identity between the first and last moments, is within the range of perception apart from the oneness of the prior and posterior times, such that there could be an apprehension of oneness through the impairment of engagement and so forth.
Even so, it might be consistent;

however, because it is sublated by inference and because it is tainted by the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is neither perception nor inference. Therefore, how can stability be established from this, or how can there be a refutation of inference?
Furthermore, as for what Vācaspati said— that the combined operation of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) and the sense faculty (*indriya*) alone constitutes the cause for recognition—
that is incorrect, because these two cognitions are produced by distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
For instance, when the eyes are closed, in the cognition "that," the capacity of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone, divested of the sense faculty, is perceived;
whereas in the first perception, in the cognition "this," the capacity of the sense faculty alone, devoid of the mental impression, is observed.
Therefore, [the cognition] is dependent upon two sets of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*).
[Nibandha 118] This pair of cognitions has been established.
How then is it proclaimed that, by combining both, a single act of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is produced?
As for the seed, the soil, and so forth, since their capacities are not observed to be separate, let there be only a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and thus let the sprout also be one alone.

Likewise, the claim that there is no difference in the ruby because it is distinct from its prior place and time as well as its subsequent place and time—both of which are related to it—is also untenable.
Even if two contradictory properties were distinct from the ruby itself, how could the difference in the ruby be denied due to its connection with those contradictory properties?
For otherwise, the undesirable consequence of the three worlds being a single entity would be unavoidable.

For even if the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are distinct, it is not possible for Brahminhood and Caṇḍālahood to reside in a single locus; thus, the distinction between them is insurmountable. Furthermore, there is no contradiction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavirodha*), because that would entail the consequence of inference also being manifold.
Moreover, it is also untenable to claim that perception is both perceptible and imperceptible, and that non-conceptual [perception] is both conceptual and superimposition (*samāropa*).

For inference, which in the ultimate sense consists of self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), is non-conceptual and has a nature free from superimposition; since its status as non-perceptual, conceptual, or superimposed is merely designated in dependence upon another [perspective], there is no imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddha-dharma-adhyāsa*). Thus, how could a difference between them be established? As for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same thing," the aspect of "that" involves a connection with an indistinct form.
"This" refers to the possession of a distinct form; thus, these two contradictory properties serve as the differentiators.

Nor should it be argued that, in view of "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), it is not contradictory for a single act of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) to possess both mediacy (*pārokṣya*) and immediacy (*apārokṣya*).
For this [recognition] does not exist as established in a single uniform form,
such that— like inference— it would merely be a matter of establishing mediacy and immediacy within itself.

As long as the conformity with the form of a past object and the conformity with the form of a present object are not its own intrinsic properties (svadharma), so long does it lack the very status of having those objects as its domain.
How, then, could there be a conventional distinction between being remote (pārokṣya) and being immediate (apārokṣya)?
Therefore, recognition (pratyabhijñāna) [is invalid] due to the imposition of two contradictory properties: the clear and the unclear forms.
Thus it is established that these are two conditions.

Likewise, this reason— that destruction has a cause— is also unestablished. As for what was stated here, that the fact that a jar’s destruction has a cause is established through perception and non-perception— just as with fire and smoke— due to the establishment of a causal relationship between the mallet and the jar’s destruction, that is incorrect.
Since both fire and smoke are perceptible, let the fact that smoke is an effect of fire be established through perception and non-perception; however,
no object denoted by the word "destruction" (vināśa) is perceived as a distinct entity (*idantayā*).
Indeed, it is observed that a potsherd itself is produced from both a jar and a hammer;
as the teachers have said:
"This jar was seen here, and likewise the falling hammer was seen."
A collection of potsherds has been seen, but no further destruction has been observed beyond that;
therefore, where is the basis for the verbal designation "non-existence"? What indeed is its cause here?
This is merely a row of potsherds seen lying there by itself.

Therefore, since this non-existence is sublated by the non-perception of the perceptible, how can it be determined through direct perception that [the destruction] has the hammer and so forth as its effect?
Furthermore, that web of words which claims something is seen even when it is not being seen is the science of buffoons;
one who accepts such a statement is indeed a beast. For instance, how could that which does not appear [to anyone] be established by the appearance of someone else?
"Whether this appearance belongs to it or not is not within the scope of logical reasoning.
(Nibandha 119) Now, if this is to be said, what is the use of a further destruction?
Let the potsherd itself be the destruction of the jar;
and if that were so, since the potsherd would not exist in the absence of the mallet and other such causes, the stability of the jar would remain unimpeded—
this is indeed a vain hope.

For instance, just as the word "destruction" (nāśa) refers to the potsherd, if the word "non-existence" (abhāva) were also used to refer only to the potsherd, then in a single location where one jar has been removed and another jar is placed, there would be no conventional usage of "the non-existence of the removed jar," because neither that jar's destruction nor its potsherds have arisen in that place.
Therefore, just as the conventional usage of "non-existence" applies to a placed jar with respect to the mere disappearance of a jar that has been removed, so too—

even though there is no production of either the destruction or the shards due to the absence of causes such as a hammer— the conventional usage of the jar's moment-by-moment difference is established with respect to mere disappearance alone; thus, how can stability be proven?

Therefore, even in the absence of a potsherd as a subsequent destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), our position remains unassailable, even when considering existence as consisting merely of the state of having passed away (*pracyuti*). As our teachers have said:
"Let alone the row of potsherds; the destruction of the jar is not something that existed previously."
Therefore, let stability also be established; what then is the use of a destruction that is distinct from it? To this, the reply is:
if destruction is said to be that very [state], then so too is the state of being [the jar] when another jar has appeared.
How can the statement that [the object] is non-existent during placement be maintained? Therefore, even non-existence is not established.
Thus [it is asked]: "But if destruction is not produced by its own cause,
how is there the restriction of cognition such that 'in a certain place and at a certain time, the jar is destroyed'?"
Nor can a cause for destruction other than the hammer be asserted;
for if destruction were possible even prior [to the blow], it would follow that the cognition of a "destroyed jar" could arise even then. As they say:
"If destruction does not exist as determined by its own causes, why would it occur at any particular place or time?"
The rule of the cognition "the jar is destroyed" implies that it is indeed an effect;

nor is there any other cause for it than the swift stroke of the staff. Otherwise, the destruction would have been stated [as occurring] even before [the blow], and by whom could this bold notion of a "destroyed jar"—which has not been produced [by any other cause]—be prevented?
If this is argued, then you have now begun to establish that destruction is dependent on the hammer and so forth by first establishing its existence through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

This being the case, since the fact that destruction is an effect of the hammer and such would be established through direct perception—just like smoke is an effect of fire—your boastful proclamation has been utterly snatched away.
Nor can its establishment be achieved even through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*),
because the cognition "the jar is destroyed" can be accounted for otherwise.
For even without destruction, the very experience of the potsherds produced by the mallet by one who previously saw the jar is sufficient to establish the determination that the jar is destroyed.
What further destruction needs to be produced?

For we observe that the cognition "the jar is destroyed" follows only the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the mere experience of the shards produced by the hammer, preceded by the ascertainment of the jar.
Nor does this [experience] exist prior to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

In the absence of the mallet, since the series of potsherds would likewise be absent, how could it be logical that there would be a cognition of the previously destroyed jar? As the teachers have said:
"When a cloud is seen, the series of potsherds produced by the mallet and other causes is not seen."
First, the cognition of a destroyed pot is produced through the following of convention (*saṅketa*).
In this context, within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no factor whatsoever named "destruction," nor does such a thing exist therein.
It may be that this state has never existed at any time, nor did it exist in its entirety even in the past.
Therefore, this presumption has reached its end; it is not capable of establishing destruction. Thus [it is said].
If it is argued that since there is no experience of destruction, there would only be the conceptualization of the potsherds based on the experience of the potsherds,
and not the cognition of a destroyed jar—
this is an act of extreme temerity.
For the cognition of a destroyed jar is directly experienced precisely from the sight of the circle of shards preceded by the ascertainment of the jar;
if that were denied, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that even smoke and the like could not have the certainty of being preceded by fire and so forth.
If it is argued that the cognition "the jar is destroyed" is a cognition of a qualified object (viśeṣyabuddhi),
and that it implies destruction as its qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), that is incorrect; for:
That by which a qualificand is colored through its own cognition is called a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
And that which is non-existent or imperceptible does not color anything through its own cognition.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is: that which has no manifestation of its own form cannot be the cause of a cognition colored by itself for anyone.
Just like the hair of a tortoise;
furthermore, there is no manifestation of an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) for destruction, which constitutes a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because non-existence cannot appear as "this-ness" (idantā) by its own nature,
nor is there any contradiction [with the reason], since it exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa).
Nor is there any inconclusiveness [in the reason];

for if [an entity] were the cause of a cognition colored by itself even in the absence of an appearance, then there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that even a rabbit’s horn and the like would possess such a nature. Now, if the world does not perish without destruction (dhvaṃsa), it must perish together with existence (bhāva).
Whether truth or untruth, what could be fixed in an entity? Therefore, this [distinction] follows from the nature of the entity itself.
Since it arises from that very entity, and because its cause is impossible given a different cause, its non-existence follows;
thus, even the "otherness" produced by it vanishes, so how could there be destruction at every moment?
To this it is replied: Is destruction, when arising from another cause, non-different or different [from its object]? It cannot be the first position, because it has a distinct cause.
And because that [destruction] is not accepted by them.
Now, as for the second position:
what, then, is this aversion toward existence such that it supposedly ceases when a real entity called "destruction" arises from its own cause?
Furthermore, as for this which is said— that there is no cessation of an entity other than the arising of its non-existence, but rather the very arising of non-existence is its cessation—
how can there be the cessation of one thing upon the arising of another?
In this regard, the response must be stated by means of differences in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): those things which exist through mutual exclusion arise from their own respective causes.

For it is not the case that fire is not a cause of a sprout simply because it is other than it; for if that were so, then due to the lack of distinction in "otherness," ash would also not be its cause.
However, the establishment of the causal relationship based on a difference in intrinsic nature applies equally even to the rule of existence through mutual exclusion.

Just as seeds and other factors, while not performing any specific harm toward the prior absence of a sprout— which, prior to its arising, is devoid of all causal capacity— nevertheless bring about that sprout and thereby eliminate that prior absence,
because the very arising of the sprout is of the nature of the cessation of its prior absence;
in the same way, the causes of its non-existence also do nothing at all toward an entity that already exists in a positive form (*bhāvarūpa*).
Even those [causes] that bring about its absence (abhāva) remove it,
because the production of an absence is itself the nature of the cessation of an entity.
Therefore, as before, there is no consequence of [the entity] performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
That would be appropriate if its self were established by valid cognition (pramāṇa), just as [the self] of cause and effect is;

however, it has been stated that since this [self] is swallowed up by the non-perception of the perceptible (dṛśyānupalambha), yet it is still claimed to be perceived, this is clearly a mere prattle—a "magician's trick" (bhaṇḍavidyā).
Presumption (arthāpatti) is also exhausted, and the presentation of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) as an example is merely the logic of a "magician's painting" (bhaṇḍālekhyanyāya).
Furthermore, what indeed is the contradiction here?
If, for you, contradiction is the impossibility of coexistence— just as there is no coexistence even for a moment between cold and fire— then [what of this case]?
And that destruction, by bringing about another destruction, would now become its own opposite; and that too would lead to yet another destruction—thus, in no way could there be final cessation.
Otherwise, if there were contradiction by the mere fact of established existence, it would follow that everything is contradictory with everything.
Furthermore, the [objection] that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the objective support is also refuted simply by the fact of non-perception.
Now, if [it is argued] that [contradiction] exists in the object because its very nature consists in mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), then...

Let there be the mere absence of destruction, or let it occur through the power of causes; by this, the destruction of the subject under discussion is refuted. However, its non-arising is a more powerful fact in itself; what need is there here for another [cause] in its own cessation?
As for the objection, "What could the reality be—truth or untruth?"—this must be refuted in the discussion concerning Trilocana.
For this very reason, Śaṅkara—who disregards the venerable Kīrtipāda, the sole teacher of the world—is a fool who is truly an object of pity, being a beast even among beasts.
Furthermore, as Trilocana said: "For those who do not accept cessation as something distinct from the entity itself, it is impossible to establish the cessation of its own nature."

For if that very state of his which was previously observed by you to be capable of accomplishing causal efficiency continues at a later time as well, then how can the entity be said to have ceased in its own nature? At that time,
it is called "destroyed" only if some state of his were to arise that is distinct from the nature obtained from its own causes.
At the time of its arising, that very thing becomes its own other; thus, we declare its lack of persistence (*atādavasthya*) itself to be its destruction.
If there were persistence or identity, we do not understand the true meaning of the expression "an entity has ceased in its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa nivṛtto bhāvaḥ*).
Indeed, this cessation of its own nature, if it were to occur, would necessarily be the entity itself.

Or [is it] other than the entity? If it were identical, then since the object produced from its own causes could not otherwise exist, it would follow that it is eternal because of its existence from the very moment of its arising. And if it were other, then the cessation of that [entity] would be the cessation of otherness.
This has been well-established by the beloved [teacher].
Therefore, casting aside delusion, one must accept that "destruction" is simply the occurrence of destruction. (Nibandh 122)
This is the fruit of ignorance; for indeed,
just as an entity arises from its own cause with a form delimited by another location,
why does it not likewise arise from its own cause as existing in a state of being severed and distinct in each moment?
If non-existence is the negation of a form that is a distinct entity, then another distinct entity must be observed even there;
thus, the view of the lamp-example is not acceptable, because it lacks the demonstration of its own nature.
For just as an entity produced from its own cause is excluded from other locations and excluded from non-blue and so forth, so too is it excluded from another subsequent moment.
And just as the non-abiding in one location is not contradictory with abiding in that very location,
but is indeed contradictory with abiding in another location, so too the abiding in a second moment is not contradictory with abiding in the first moment.
Furthermore, contradiction consists precisely in the state of persisting into a second moment;
it is merely designated as the mere cessation [of an entity] in another location at a second moment.
This is unavoidable even given the existence of those two categories of entities: mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
Even if one does not accept a separate non-existence (*abhāva*), if one does not accept that existence and non-existence are unmixed, it would follow that they are identical (*tādātmya*).
Therefore, there is identity between existence and non-existence.

What is intended [by this] is that just as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is in contradiction with being located in that same place, being blue, and so forth—which are distinct from it—so too is it in contradiction with not persisting into a second moment.

In ultimate reality, however, the identity of the subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*) is established, while the conventional distinction between them is produced by their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); this has been demonstrated in the *Apohasiddhi*.
Furthermore, this has been shown to be consistent with the sequence of arguments already stated.
Since the truth of the matter is thus, what can we say regarding those petty people whose souls are inflamed by the poison of hatred, who engage in mere verbal quibbling and idle chatter?

Furthermore, since the cessation of its own nature is logically possible without the occurrence of a separate cessation or production, how could the previous state of existence persist beyond a moment?
Therefore, let it be merely a conventional usage of "destroyed" with the delusion set aside;
nothing else whatsoever should be produced of it.
Because it would follow that the entity remains in its original state.

If it is asked, "How can non-existence be negated?", we say no; for it is accepted that, by means of speech and conceptual determination directed solely toward the mere non-arising of that [entity], there subsequently occurs a mere conventional usage of "non-existence," since the arising of a real thing itself has been negated.
Now, what kind of verbal artifice is this: that one accepts it as merely the conventional usage of "non-existence," yet later maintains that there is no non-existence?
If this were the case, it would result in the contradiction of the conventional usage of "non-existence" being unreliable.
And since non-existence is false, it would follow that existence itself belongs to the object of negation; furthermore,
because that non-existence occurs subsequently, its being occasional clearly implies that it possesses a cause.

And as for the claim that it is a "real entity" (*vastutva*), this is incorrect; for even if one does not accept a distinct category of entity called "non-existence," it is demonstrated that everyday linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is fully accomplished by relying merely upon the fact of disappearance.
As for the objection raised concerning the possibility that the locus, such as the ground, devoid of the object, is the actual referent:
This is not so, because the ground and such are distinct entities;
for when a distinct entity is presented or cognized, it does not follow that a thing such as a jar is thereby presented or cognized as being a real entity.
If it is argued that the objection raised against the view that "destruction is simply another entity" would thereby be refuted by that very [view] itself,
that too is irrelevant;
for since its object is merely the bare ground, how could there not be a cognition of the non-existence of the jar and so forth?
For that very state of isolation of a location which exists in relation to a jar or the like is itself the absence of the jar;
likewise, when an isolated location is communicated even by means of speech and so forth, how could this not be a communication of the absence of the jar or other things under discussion?
Moreover, isolation is indeed non-different from the location that is devoid of accompaniment.
Nor does the cognition "there is no jar here" entail [the presence of a jar] even in a location where a jar exists,
because that location containing a jar, having arisen from its own causes in such a way, is distinct from a bare location.
Furthermore, there is no identity between the location with a jar and the location without a jar based on recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
This is because it has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, if one asserts that the cause of destruction is both incapable and useless, then it would be appropriate to assert the same for the causes of sprouts and so forth;
for when an effect is unestablished, the recourse to a cause is meaningless.
This reflection is relevant only if [the destruction] is already established;
for if the object produced by the cause is either permanent or impermanent, what would be the use of a cause of destruction, since the causal process proceeds solely by means of the primary cause?
And it is not possible to assert this in the case of an unestablished effect such as a sprout.
Because its own nature does not appear, any inquiry as to whether it possesses those properties or does not possess them is devoid of an object.
But have you not also stated the distinction between the characteristics of existence and non-existence?
How then can all things be one?
It is precisely because of the difference in their characteristics that the distinction between them is established.

If it is argued that even from this [distinction] there is no establishment of difference, and thus no establishment of difference for anything from anything at all—which would entail the consequence of non-duality (advaita)—we say: no.
For that which has a perishable nature is itself destruction.

Because of the rule of *bahulam* (diversity), the suffix *ghañ* is established here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), so we maintain that this "destruction" (*nāśa*) is the very nature of the entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*). However, if one were to take "destruction" as "the act of perishing" (*naśanam nāśaḥ*), it would have to be analyzed in two ways as having an inherent nature of negation (*prasajyātmā*).

In reality, because it lacks the nature of a functional entity (*vastu*), this phenomenon is not a "thing" at all—being devoid of both identity and difference; thus, there occurs merely the negation of its existence, like a donkey’s horn.

However, on the conventional level (*saṃvṛti*), just as it appears to be occasional when conceptualized through temporal distinctions, so too does it appear as if distinct from other entities by virtue of its nature as the absence of all designations. Thus, there is no contradiction in describing the distinction that characterizes its lack of substantiality.
And this being so, since the distinction between existence and non-existence is accepted as a difference of characteristics on the conventional level.
And since, in reality, the identity of a thing's characteristics is absent, its unity with them is denied; how, then, can the objection regarding the consequence of non-duality (advaita) be leveled?
It might be argued: "And without the cognition of the distinction (*viveka*), there can be no apprehension of that which is distinguished from it;
furthermore, this distinction is not the very nature of the ground and so forth, because it functions as a qualifier.
This [argument] is outside the bounds of logic.

For the relationship between qualifier and qualified pertains to forms mounted upon conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), since there would otherwise follow the absurdity of the uselessness of words, concepts, and other signs regarding contact with external objects; this has been established at length in the treatises. And that conceptual construction perceives an entity, though non-different, as if it were different—just as in the expression, "the body of a stone statue."
In the case of "the senses and so forth in the body" or "Devadatta with long ears," and so on,
the relationship between qualifier and qualified is therefore dependent upon conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Even though an entity is non-different, how can a conventional usage of difference—which depends on the intention to express difference—extend its own nature, which is restricted to difference?
If it is argued that this designation— "the head of Rāhu," and so forth— is a case of faltering speech, then if this were true,

this designation would likewise be a case of faltering speech; for, just as there is no Rāhu distinct from his head, there is no discernment (viveka) distinct from the surface of the earth and other such things, since its existence is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible.
Nevertheless, "it is not so"—the drinking from the vessel is the proof.

Therefore, this other region [of space] arising from its own causes, distinct from the jar, arises from that same location as a separate region devoid of the jar; it is not, however, merely characterized by its distinction from the jar.
Because for that which has arisen from its own cause and is distinct, there would be an absence of distinction in the absence of [the thing] itself; furthermore,
if difference were pervaded by the relationship of qualifier and qualified, then, since that difference would have ceased, would it not follow that the relationship itself is non-existent?
Just as there exists a distinguished region, so too does this exist: the vision of the various philosophical systems perceives whether [the object] exists or does not exist.
Therefore, there is no such thing as "non-existence" (abhāva) wherein the operation of a cause could occur.
Thus, it is established that the reason "because destruction has a cause" is unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddha).
The argument that "existent things are non-momentary because they possess causes" is likewise entirely incoherent;

for there is no contradiction between momentariness and possessing causes, since the pervasion of possessing causes by non-momentariness is unestablished due to the presence of a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*).

Nor is there any suspicion of its occurrence in the opposite case; for it is precisely the causality of destruction that is being negated, since, according to the sequence already stated, destruction itself does not exist.
Likewise, the proof of stability based on the fact of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is merely a wishful thought.
For, according to the position that the arising of cognition possesses a form (*sākāra*), even if the object persists into the second moment, it is separated [from the cognition];
thus, since manifestation would be impossible, the cognition’s apprehension of the object consists solely in the apprehension of the object’s own nature.
And thus there is conformity with the present;
for even regarding the past, its proximity [to the cognition] has not ceased.
Nor is there an over-extension of the principle.

Because it does not impart similarity to any moment other than the one immediately preceding it, and because it is therefore a cause; even if "knowability" (*prameyatva*) were indeed pervaded by existence at a prior time, nevertheless, like knowability, existence at a prior time is also not contradictory in the case of a momentary entity. Thus, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), which is intended to establish the pervasion between knowability and non-momentariness, is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For being the cause consists in imparting its form to cognition,

while being an object of knowledge (prameyatva) is the state of being cognized by one who possesses valid means of knowledge; and this is established only in the very moment immediately preceding [the present].
If it is argued that [cognition] is without an object because there is no conformity with the object in the case of the non-conventionality of the *jñānasattva*, [we reply:
even in the case of conformity, the very self-awareness of the nature of the form imparted by that [object] is what constitutes the cognition of it;
and that alone is what constitutes having an object.
And since this proximity remains undiminished even in the immediately preceding moment, it has been stated that there is no requirement for its persistence into a second moment;
therefore, because its negative concomitance is doubtful, "knowability" (prameyatva) is indeed inconclusive.

Now, if—out of hostility toward the doctrine of *sākāra* (cognition with form)—you intend "knowability" (*prameyatva*) to mean being apprehended by a cognition devoid of form (*anākārajñāna*), then this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Granted that cognition may arise from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects and so forth;
yet, since that [cognition] has a uniform essence consisting solely of experience and thus possesses a similar form in respect to every object, what could possibly be its apprehender?

If it is argued that [the sense organ perceives] that with which [the object] is connected, then there would also be the perception of the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-saṃyoga*), and so forth.
If it is argued that [only] the producer is perceived, [then...]
Nevertheless, there is the undesirable consequence that the self and so forth would also be apprehended.
Furthermore, the claim that "that which produces [cognition] is apprehended by virtue of being an object" is also incorrect,
because the status of being an object has not yet been established.

If it is argued that the object is that thing regarding which there arises the determination, "this was seen," "this was heard," or "this was known," then surely such a specific linguistic convention does indeed exist. However, we ask: what is the rule of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) in this case?
If it cannot be so described, we say that even conventional usage would not be determinate according to your view.
If you argue that it nonetheless exists, we reply: [it does].
Therefore, let the similarity to the object itself be the unique cause of proximity, since a restriction [of cognition] is impossible in the absence of a cause.
(Nibandh 125)
But surely, even similarity [to the object] cannot be determined if the object is not perceived;
and is that similarity [shared] in part or in its entirety?
In the first case, everything would be known by everyone; in the second case, however, cognition would become non-cognition.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because of similarity (*sārūpya*), when an object is known, the immediately subsequent cognition would have the same object as its own object—then [we reply]: [this is not so].
Let there be no direct perception of the object itself;

rather, because one attains the purposeful efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of the object as it has been determined through the power of a specific form (*ākāra*), the conventional usage of "similarity" (*sārūpya*)—in the sense that "the object is indeed of such a kind"—is not contradictory.
For this very reason, one need not deliberate over whether similarity resides in the gross [object] or in the atoms.
Even though the form of cognition is gross, the fulfillment of human purpose is achieved because it performs the desired action due to being a specific aggregate bound by a single causal complex;
and similarity [between the object and the cognition] exists only through a portion [of its features].
Furthermore, there is no consequence here of perceiving everything.
Because [the object] is not a producer of the cognition of all [cognitions],
and because those things that are producers are to be grasped as the objects by virtue of their imparting a unique portion [of themselves] which serves as the basis for their own designation;
nor does it follow that there would be the apprehension of another cognition having the same object.
This is because it is established by the very means of valid cognition that is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*);
because any other means of valid cognition would be redundant in that regard;
and because it is accepted as a tenet that, given its insentience (*jaḍatva*), an object is graspable only insofar as it imparts its form [to consciousness].
If the existence of external objects is accepted, this consideration is entirely faultless.

Thus, it is established that this reason— "because of being an object of cognition"— is one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful under the position of the proponents of mental aspects (*sākāravāda*), and is unestablished (*asiddha*) under the position of those who deny mental aspects (*nirākāravāda*).
Nor is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) a firm proof for a permanent self,

because the apprehension of causal relations and so forth can be accounted for otherwise. For instance, since this systematic arrangement is well-established even by relying on a continuum of mind (*cittasantati*) existing in the relation of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*), how could it bring back the self (*ātman*) to life?
In this regard, the cognition of the causal relationship is indeed untroubled.

Nevertheless, with respect to a preceding object, a determination that "when this exists, that comes to be" is produced by a subsequent cognition of an object—which is the effect (*upādeya*) of the prior determinative cognition and which contains within it the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that [prior cognition].

Likewise, with respect to a preceding object, [the same occurs] by means of a cognition that determines the bare ground, which is the effect of that [prior cognition] and contains within it the mental impression deposited by it.

With respect to a future object, the cognition that determines the bare ground produces the ascertainment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the form: "In the absence of this, that does not occur. As it has been said:
"The cognition of another [object] arising immediately after the determination of one [object] establishes the reflection upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*)."
Thus, the cognition of exclusion from others, arising from the experience of being separated from that one [object], brings about the understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For this very reason, when Devadatta perceives fire and Yajñadatta perceives smoke, there is no apprehension of the relation of cause and effect, because there is no relationship of material cause and its product (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) between those two cognitions. However, where within a single continuum there is a relationship of material cause and its product between two moments of cognition, there the apprehension of the causal relation and so forth is easily established.
Otherwise, even if an eternal self (*ātman*) existed as a synthesizer (*pratisandhātṛ*), there would be no apprehension of the relations of cause and effect and the like at all.
For instance, in relation to the self, are the cognitions to be connected with it non-different, different, or both different and non-different?
In the first case, either the self alone would be the connector, or the cognitions themselves would be the things to be connected; what, then, would be the purpose of connection?
Even on the view that [the self] is distinct [from the intellect], we do not understand what purpose there could be for a dull (jaḍa) self that is separate from the cognitions to perform unification.

If it is argued that its status as a unifier—just like its status as a seer—is due to its connection with the intellect, then let the intellect alone be the seer and the unifier; if this restriction is accepted, what is the point of this "borrowed ornament" of saying that its being so is due to its connection with that [intellect]?
If it is argued that this is because cognitions lack agency,
then, by that same logic, the conventional designation of that self as a "seer" and so forth would be untenable.
For if cognition were the seer of either the cause or the effect, then it [the self] would have to be postulated as the synthesizer of the immediate sequence and its specific determination.

It might be argued that through association with that [intellect], the status of being a seer and a reconnecting agent is attributed [to the self]; yet even when the intellect has not acquired a distinction with respect to each particular object, the connection itself is not capable of bringing about a distinction in practical discourse—
[such as] "now it is the perceiver of the cause," or "now it is the perceiver of the result."
Now, regarding the phrase "to reconnect":

if one accepts such a specific quality residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), what further need is there for another self (*ātman*), since all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is fully accomplished by that alone?
If it is argued that without a stable self, that very cognition would not exist,
by whom have you been so deceived?
Oh, the greatness of delusion, that it brings even such things as these under its power!
For indeed, that which is stated here cannot be established otherwise than by determining causal capacity through perception and non-perception— just as in the case of fire and smoke, or when,

despite the presence of a complete collection of other observed causes such as the eyes and so forth, an effect is not seen, yet is seen later, leading one to conclude in a general manner that some other factor must be required.
It is clear, first of all, that the former position does not exist.

The second [alternative] is also not possible; for when the cognition of the effect occurs immediately after the cognition of the cause, there is no previously unobserved synthesis on the part of one engaged in a definitive judgment, such as "this was seen by me immediately after that," from which one might postulate the causal capacity of something else.
Having thus cast aside this delusion, one must accept the established determination of cause and effect precisely according to the sequence already stated.
As for the position of both difference and non-difference, it deserves only contempt;
for, due to the superimposition of the contradictory properties of difference and non-difference upon that very same entity in relation to itself, its unity is logically untenable.
Consequently, that which is distinct is indeed distinct, and that which is non-distinct is indeed non-distinct; thus, for a single entity, there can be neither distinction nor non-distinction.
Nevertheless, if there were non-distinction, the entire universe would be one, which would entail the absurd consequence of its simultaneous arising, persistence, and dissolution.

In this way, through successive cognitions that apprehend successive objects and stand in the relation of material cause and effect—whether directly or indirectly—it is determined that these [objects] arise in succession.

Since those cognitions that grasp multiple objects simultaneously possess a single material cause (*ekopādānatva*), the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "these have arisen all at once" is formed; thus, the apprehension of both succession and simultaneity is also faultless.

If it is asked, "How can a single conceptual construction arise from multiple cognitions?", what is the problem? Let the cognitions be distinct; nevertheless, they produce a single conceptualization by virtue of having a common material cause.
A different number [of causes] does not subvert the relationship between cause and fruit, nor are they incapable like those arising in another continuum.
