As for what was also stated by Śaṅkara— that there are cognitions of preceding and succeeding moments, from those two arises a latent impression (vāsanā), and from that arises a conceptual construction (vikalpa) which determines the relationship of cause and effect— if this is the case:
Why now do you perform this ritual by saying, "Whatever is suspected must be spoken"?
For an alternative (vikalpa) would have to be either a recollection of what was previously grasped or a superimposition of a form that is not that [of the object].
It cannot be the first position.

For a person who has not perceived positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is impossible for there to be a specific latent impression (*vāsanā-viśeṣa*)—which is the cause of the synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*)—if the relationship between cause and effect has not been grasped;
and if there were synthesis of what has not been grasped, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
(Nibandha 127)
This has not been correctly considered;

for although the preceding and succeeding moments, which stand in the relation of cause and effect, are not experienced by a single cognition, their status as cause and effect is indeed grasped by two successive cognitions that stand in the relation of material cause (upādāna) and its product (upādeya).
It is simply that at the time of the cause, the effect is absent.
Even when the capacity of that object is apprehended, because no result is seen, the determination of it remains uninitiated and is set in motion only by the observation of the effect.

Likewise, even upon seeing the result, the fact that it is the effect of that [action] is merely being synthesized by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) as something already apprehended; thus, this conceptual thought is of the nature of synthesizing what has been apprehended. This [objection] is trivial. As the *Mahābhāṣyālaṅkāra* says:
"If indeed a single perceiver does not possess the cognition of both the preceding and the succeeding [moments],
then how can there be the cognition of the prior and the posterior when two perceivers exist?"
Likewise, there is recollection, longing,
personally seeking out what has been prepared,
and the cessation of curiosity regarding objects already seen.
The connection between action and its fruit,

as well as the determination preceded by doubt, is logically accounted for as being produced by successive experiences of objects— which serve as the material cause— acting upon the latent impressions (saṃskāras) deposited by preceding experiences which served as their efficient cause;
so what is the use of postulating an additional self?

And precisely because of the restriction of the relationship between material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*), the undesirable consequence of memory and so forth occurring in another continuum is not tenable.
If it is asked, "What is this material cause?
it is said in reply:
That whose cessation within a continuum gives rise to something else is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of that thing;
as it is elaborated in the treatises, for example, clay is the material cause of a jar arising from the cessation of the continuum of clay.
And in this case, there is no harm to the doctrine of the next world (*paraloka*).
As for what was also said— that upon the cessation of the observed basis for the duration of the mind and body for a certain period, it would follow that the mind also ceases;
for by the sensation of death, the mind becomes impaired, and consequently,
a state capable of generating another unimpaired mind is no longer possible.

Therefore, [the opponent argues] that when the suffering of death— which is opposed to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)— arises, even the mind would be annihilated, and thus the view of nihilism follows. This is incorrect,
because the suffering of death is itself merely a particular state of the mind.

Since the production of knowledge is necessarily unpreventable due to the very nature of that [mind] which has the capacity to generate a subsequent moment of mind, so too is liberation from bondage; for liberation consists in the continuity of an untainted mind arising from the continuity of a mundane, bound mind.
Furthermore, the engagement in both the virtuous and other states, as well as in liberation, is likewise unpreventable.

For, even though the Self exists, one proceeds from the moment of the grasping of the Self due to the resolve, "I alone shall become liberated and happy"; it is not, however, because one has been seized by the throat by the Self. And since that false conceptualization—which has come down through a beginningless succession of ignorance, which superimposes identity between the prior and the subsequent, and whose movement remains unimpeded even when the Self is sublated—persists, how can there be a cessation of activity? Indeed, [one might object]:...
But in the position of the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), one realizes beforehand:
"After my destruction, the fruit would not exist, or else it would belong to someone other than myself."
If it is argued that there should simply be no engagement at all, let it be so; what is the fault?
If this grasping at a self, even though devoid of an object, does not induce engagement, it cannot remain for even a single moment.
It prevails;

for just as even one who knows that death is inevitable for the born may, upon the death of a son or others, wail with beating of the breast and exert effort against death and so forth due to the intensity of grief, so too, due to the intensity of ignorance, does one act even while knowing selflessness.
"What can be done about this, that one does not rest in happiness?
For the power of ignorance to proceed cannot be warded off,
and recognition has already been destroyed."
The state of being posterior and prior is determined by the relation of cause and effect;
and this is not contradictory even in the case of momentary things.

Furthermore, the relationship between the material cause and its effect is directly perceived by two successive moments of self-awareness and subsequently ascertained by the cognition that follows them.
Even in the absence of a self (*ātman*) as a reconnecting agent, the apprehension of cause and effect and so forth are logically possible; therefore, they are not capable of establishing a self.
Consequently, the argument from presumption (*arthāpatti*) is ineffective, and like the daydreams of an unfortunate man, the proof of permanence utterly collapses.
Thus, when there is doubt regarding momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the inference based on existence (*sattva*) and other such reasons finds its opportunity.
The Refutation of the Proof of Stability is completed. (Nibandha 129) // 9 //
// The Doctrine of the Manifestation of Variegated Non-duality //
Homage to Tārā.
This work is the means for establishing all [doctrines] of oneself and other opponents;
it is the destroyer of the mass of darkness consisting of ignorance regarding the manifold non-duality doctrine.
Indeed, in this world—where the entire mass of insentient objects has been rejected and refuted; where the doctrine of formless cognition (*nirākāra-vijñānavāda*) has been countered;

where the notion of ultimate reality consisting in mere luminosity associated with false forms has been thoroughly uprooted; and where the superimposition of falsity upon cognition possessing forms has been eliminated;

and where the universe consists merely of the manifestation of forms such as the body, enjoyments, and abode, which remain uncontradicted for each individual continuum like a dream—[this is the case].

When it is established that for a given person, at a given time, whatever consciousness manifests as the appearance of a circle of forms to such an extent, then that consciousness—encircled by that very circle of forms—is a manifold non-duality (*citrādvaita*); this is the settled position.
Thus, the three terms "manifold" (*citram*), "non-dual" (*advaitam*), and "consciousness" (*vijñānam*) are presented here.
And here, "disagreement" refers to the following alternatives: [is it] in diversity, in non-duality, or in the nature of consciousness, and so on in every respect?
To begin with, this [consciousness] cannot be in conformity with the variegated nature [of the object],
because that alone is established by the experience of all cognizers;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that no room would remain for conflicting views such as "this is insentient," "this is false," or "this is consciousness," just as in the case of a hare's horn and the like.
Nor is it appropriate to dispute their status as consciousness,

since it has already been established previously— by such arguments as "because they are necessarily perceived together"— that blue and other objects are indeed consciousness possessing forms (*sākāravijñāna*).

For this very reason, doubt is entirely misplaced in every respect, because it is only upon the establishment of consciousness with forms (sākāra-vijñāna) that the doctrine of the non-duality of the variegated (citrādvaita-vāda) can be introduced.
Therefore, the notion that this variegation contradicts non-duality is a delusion; since the dispute concerns unity alone, the proof for that is stated as follows.
Whatever manifests is one, just as the blue form situated in the midst of a circle of variegated forms.

And this collection of diverse forms—such as white, the note *gāndhāra*, sweet, fragrant, soft, pleasant, and its opposite—manifests; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
First of all, its non-establishment cannot be asserted,

because the state of being manifest is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the subject (*dharmin*), which is the circle of forms such as blue consisting of consciousness, whose existence is proven by the means of direct perception. Nor is it possible for this reason (*hetu*) to be contradictory (*viruddha*).
Because the probans characterized by "being manifest" is observed in the subject of the example—the blue form situated in the midst of various forms.
But surely, if unity is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), it would be appropriate here to employ as an example another locus of unity;
yet no such unity exists for this blue form.
Since multiplicity is established through the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*),
and since the distinction of place, time, and form is indeed the superimposition of contradictory properties,
it follows that just as there is a distinction in a variegated circular form due to the difference in its forms, so too there is a distinction in the blue form due to the difference in its location.
Therefore, this example is devoid of the probandum, and the reason, being observed in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), would be contradictory (viruddha) if it were restricted to that alone.
If it is argued that even in that case there is no certainty because of the possibility [of such a distinction],
it is said in reply:

if there were a distinction in the gross blue form consisting of consciousness due to spatial difference, then, since a distinction would necessarily occur for each distinct spatial location of the atoms, the gross blue form consisting of consciousness would be nothing more than a mere accumulation of atoms.

If that were the case, then since all the atoms of blue that constitute consciousness would be submerged in their own individual natures— just like many persons submerged in deep darkness— the absence of mutual perception would logically entail the impossibility of the appearance of a single, gross, undivided patch of blue.
This is because the characteristics of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) must be refuted beforehand.

Nor should it be argued that even though atoms are submerged in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the gross [object], being a mere aggregate due to having a single material cause (*ekopādānatva*), will cognize itself as gross;

for even if there is a single material cause, precisely because they are submerged in their own essential natures, it is impossible for there to be a relationship of grasped and grasper—whether between distinct selves that establish the state of grossness or among themselves.
Furthermore, because we do not admit the cognition [of one group] through identity with [another],
the statement that "a group knows a group" is untenable.

Furthermore, unlike in the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), where the appearance of a single coarse form in cognition is established as the appearance of an accumulation of external atoms because there is no other possible way [to account for it], so it is not here; for one does not admit the existence of another yogic consciousness possessing a single coarse form that could establish an accumulation of cognitive atoms.
Or, if that [atom] were admitted, it would itself serve as the illustrative example.
Therefore, to whatever extent there is an appearance, to that same extent it is pervaded by grossness;
for an appearance in a non-gross atom, or in the mere absence of grossness, is sublated by the non-perception of the perceptible.
Just as in the well-known inference, existence (*sattva*) is pervaded by momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), and it is also pervaded by the capacity for successive or simultaneous action;

and since the absence of momentariness entails the cessation of successive and simultaneous action, [existence], when it ceases [in that case], is established as being necessarily restricted to momentariness— so too here, the property of being manifest (*prakāśamānatva*) is the probans, whether in terms of unity (*ekatva*) or even in terms of magnitude (*sthaulya*).

Furthermore, because of the absence of unity in the counter-example—the aggregate of atoms—and because of the perception of that which is contradictory to itself, namely the exclusion of unity from the nature of grossness (sthūlya) as its pervader, unity is established as necessarily absent when [grossness] is excluded. Consequently, just as in the case of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*), where—by the force of a proof that sublates the opposite in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) such as a jar—one determines that existence is necessarily concomitant with momentariness, and thereby establishes the "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of its existence; so too here.

In this case as well, by the force of the valid cognition that sublates the contrary [in] the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), which is the blue form, one understands that being manifest is necessarily concomitant with oneness;

thus, because it is manifest, oneness is established in the circle of various forms, which is the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). Therefore, the example is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnya*), nor is the reason (*hetu*) contradictory.
Nor is there any inconclusiveness.
Now, if oneness is the probandum (*sādhya*), then its exclusion and duality constitute the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
At the time of realizing the absence of the reason (*hetu-vyatireka*) from that counter-example, does the nature of the counter-example manifest or not?
In the case where it manifests, [the reason would be present] because of its manifestness (*prakāśamānatva*).
(Nibandha 131) The reason is inconclusive due to being common (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*),
because it is observed even in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Alternatively, if it does not manifest, then there is uncertainty regarding its negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*).

"How can there be exclusion (vyatireka), since the very basis of delimitation (avadhi) itself does not manifest its form? How, then, can there be any hope for the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) from this?
To this it is said: Here, the object of cognitions is twofold: the apprehended (grāhya) and the determined (adhyavaseya).
That which appears [directly] is the apprehended.
Even though it is not apprehended, that which is the object of engagement is the "ascertainable" (adhyavaseya).
In that regard, for a non-omniscient inferer, because there is no appearance of the entire counter-example (vipakṣa), the counter-example cannot be said to be an object by way of being apprehended;
for if it were, it would follow that all inference would be abolished.

Because there is an absence of the appearance of all counter-instances (vipakṣa) everywhere, their exclusion [from the subject] is not established. Furthermore, if there were an appearance—meaning a direct perception (sākṣātkāra)—of all counter-instances separated by space, time, and intrinsic nature, then the poor thing that is the probandum itself would be perceived even more clearly; thus, inference would be redundant.

Therefore, even when there is no appearance, the exclusion of smoke and the like from the counter-instance is ascertained precisely through the establishment of conceptual determination (adhyavasāya).
Why, then, is the appearance of the counter-example (vipakṣa) sought here?
If, moreover, there were no even a conceptual determination (adhyavasāya) of it, then it would be correct that the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not ascertained,
because of the absence of linguistic convention regarding specific objects.
Now, in our view, since it is possible to apprehend all opposing factors consisting of both real and unreal entities, the exclusion of the reason from them can indeed be understood.
Nor does it follow that existence consists merely in appearing,
for existence is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

If it is argued: "In your view, however, being an entity (*vastutva*) is nothing other than manifestation (*prakāśa*). Therefore, when duality appears, the exclusion of oneness from the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*)—which is the proof for the property of 'being manifest' (*prakāśamānatva*)—is common to the counter-examples; and when there is no appearance, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not doubtful. Thus, this objection is truly insurmountable."
This is inconsistent.
For instance, smoke and the like, being excluded from the counter-examples (vipakṣa) such as non-fire, are established as being invariably concomitant with fire;

yet, does the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of that entire mass of counter-example entities—whether consisting of real or unreal things—occur in non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka-jñāna) or in conceptual construction (kalpanā)? [In neither case.]
If it is [the case] in the non-conceptual state,
what is the meaning of "manifestation"? Does it mean that in a formless cognition there is a direct flashing forth of the essential nature of all factors such as the adverse elements?
Is it the manifestation of an aspect similar to the nature of the object upon which the intellect is fixed;
or is it the appearance of an external-like aspect residing within the intellect, brought about by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
or rather, is it the vivid projection of a false aspect similar to the opposite [of the object], which has become the very self of the intellect?

The first position is not tenable, because objects that are remote in terms of space, time, and nature cannot appear to ordinary persons, nor can they appear in a cognition that is devoid of form; for this point has been established in detail within the treatise itself.

Furthermore, if such appearance were possible, it would follow that even what is impossible to achieve could be manifested, thereby rendering inference useless—a fact which has already been demonstrated.
Nor is the second position tenable, because precisely due to being spatially and temporally remote, it lacks the capacity to directly impart its own form.
Nor is the third position consistent.
Even if similarity were possible, because there is no proximity with the external object— since [the cognition] arises solely by the power of the immediately preceding [moment]—
the fourth alternative is also not possible,
due to the contradiction between non-existence and manifestation.
Because it is impossible for that which is manifesting to be non-existent;
for if it is said that "the non-existent appears," does this mean that the manifestation of the non-existent— such as God (Īśvara) and so forth—
is what appears, or is it that the appearing form itself is non-existent?
What is intended [by the opponent] is that nothing at all exists.

In that case, how can a person who possesses life-force declare that a given object—which has the manifestation of its own intrinsic nature—is non-existent? This applies even to the form of a mass of floating hairs that appears vividly.

(Commentary on Verse 132: If it is argued that although [the object] is sublated in its external form, its status as an object is established by the Teacher as being of the nature of cognition— and thus, since even the formless manifestation intended as the grasper would follow as being non-existent because it too is sublated despite appearing— then what is that sublater?
[The means of cognition are] either perception or inference.

If there is no trust in perception—which, in one instance, directly realizes the intrinsic nature—how could there be [trust] in another [instance], such as a sublater, where there is simply the manifestation of a different intrinsic nature? And inference, which is preceded by that [perception], is all the more an object of distrust;
thus, not even a mention of a sublating factor is possible.
As the teachers have said:
"How could that which has the manifestation of its own nature be non-existent?
If it is because of sublation, then is that sublation not itself both perceptual and inferential?"
"If there is no confidence in perception, what recourse is there elsewhere? And how can inference, which is preceded by that [perception], be an object of trust? [Objection:
But surely even what is seen is sublated, as in the case of the appearance of two moons and the like.
There is no lack of consistency in what is perceived; even that which is known by it is not sublated.
If this is argued, we say no; because that which is sublated does not appear [in cognition], and that which appears is not subject to sublation. For it is thus:
the manifestation of the form of the cognition is the sublation of the external object.
If there is no confidence even in that which has manifested, where indeed can confidence be found? Thus it is proclaimed.
By this, the second position— that the appearing form is non-existent— is also refuted,

because its existence is established by the very fact of its appearance, leaving no room for a subverting argument. Likewise, the third conception— that something existent does not appear— is also confused.
Because existence is pervaded by manifestation;
for that which is unmanifested is swallowed up by non-existence.

Now, is it not the case that what is called "manifestation" is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of an object? And yet, the absence of a means of valid cognition does not entail the non-existence of the object;
rather, existence is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*).
If it is argued that this is not contradictory even for that which is non-luminous,
this is true;
for in the doctrine of external objects (*bahirarthavāda*), capacity is admitted even for what is non-luminous.

In the case of the appearance of a mass of hair and the like, non-existence is established precisely because the object as it is determined lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). However, if there is an absolute absence of anything external, then since cognition is never dissociated from its own manifestation, existence is established by that alone; what would be the use of causal efficiency?
If it is argued that the existence of something other [than cognition] is not established by manifestation alone, how could it be otherwise?
If even causal efficiency does not belong to everything for everyone, why is there no manifestation [of it] anywhere?
Thus: first of all, in the non-conceptual [cognition], the counter-examples and so forth do not manifest apart from the specific form established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Now, if the second alternative is accepted—that these [counter-examples] appear in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*)—then even in this position, the appearing form is unique; because it is not associated with words and has entered into identity with self-awareness, it is indeed real (*vastusan*).

If it is argued that the counter-examples (vipakṣa) and so forth are apprehended by way of being objects of conceptual determination (adhyavaseyatā), even then, does their own intrinsic nature (svarūpa) appear [in perception] or not? If it appears, they are established as being directly perceived (pratyakṣasiddha).
It is not the theory of non-existent manifestation (*asatkhyāti*); for even in the treatise it is stated: "Perceptuality consists precisely in the direct realization of the thing's own form."

It has been stated: if, as in the case of other perceptions, that [cognition] is admitted even in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then because the presence of contradictory pervasions (*viruddhavyāptopalambha*) has long since cast away both the status of being conceptual and the status of being erroneous, the quality of being perception (*pratyakṣatva*) remains intact for conceptual construction as well in your view.
Therefore, how can you claim that what is established by it is sublated by another perception or by inference?
For those two [other perception and inference] also possess the capacity to illuminate a different nature [of the object].

Furthermore, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and error (*bhrāntatva*) are both pervaded by [the absence of] direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*), their presence precludes direct perception itself from occurring in conceptual construction.

Now, when it was said that "direct perception is impossible for this," it was stated that its nature as a direct realization of its own form (*svarūpasākṣātkāritva*) is impossible. To then say, by way of speech, that "an object such as a counter-example appears in this" is to describe its nature as a direct realization of its own form; this is like the story: "My mother is barren."

And you maintain that conceptual construction possesses the direct realization of the nature of the counter-example and so forth; thus, it does not transcend the status of perception, because if it were not perception, the manifestation of the actual nature of the thing would be impossible.
Consequently, even the form appearing therein is the manifestation of something existent, not the manifestation of the non-existent.
Nor is that very form appearing in conceptual construction the true nature of non-existent things such as Īśvara and so forth,
because it would follow that their very non-existence is absent; for if something were non-existent despite its own nature appearing, one could have no confidence in anything else that manifests.
Therefore, that which was prattled in the theory of *sākāravāda*— namely,
that eternal things and so forth must indeed exist— that has fallen back upon the very self [of that proponent].
As the Teachers have said:
"Direct perception [of reality] arises from the direct realization of one's own true nature, and nothing else;
for this very reason, the state of being a ground for conceptual construction and delusion is sublated."
If it were not perceived, there would be no manifestation of its form at all; therefore, the claim that God and such appear [to consciousness] while being non-existent is incoherent.
If its form were to appear, it would have to be existent; yet you claim that what appears is non-existent, and thus for you, that which shines forth is indeed non-existent.
Now, if it is asserted that in the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*) there is no appearance of the actual nature of the object to be determined (*adhyavaseya*),
then at that time there would be no determination of anything whatsoever. How, then, could the establishment of the specific determination of particular objects be achieved from this?
Furthermore, what is this so-called "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya)?
Is it the aspect of luminosity (prakāśāṃśa) imagined through the distinction of exclusions (vyāvṛttibheda), or is it the aspect of its own form (svākārāṃśa)?
The meaning of "determination" (adhyavasāya) is the manifestation of an unreal form, whether it be an external object or a non-object;
or alternatively, it is the superimposition of the external upon one's own internal form.

The alternatives are as follows: either the superimposition of one's own form onto the external object, or the conjunction of one's own form with the external object, or the unification of these two, or the single apprehension—which is apprehension as non-different—or the non-apprehension of difference; these are the meanings of "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*).
In this regard, the first two positions do not admit of logical construction.
For in its own nature, every manifestation is non-conceptual; therefore, the occurrence of a determinative judgment (*avasāya*) is impossible.
Otherwise, it would follow that non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) does not exist at all.
False manifestation, however, has already been refuted previously.
Even if manifestation were present, this [cognition] would be non-conceptual due to its lack of clarity,
like the cognition of two moons and so forth.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is non-conceptual with respect to its own apprehended object, but conceptual with respect to the external object that is determined (*adhyavaseya*), [we reply: no.
This is not so, because there is no connection between them and because it does not appear as such;
otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), as has already been stated.

If, however, there is a manifestation of the actual nature of an external object, then this is simply a case of perception; what need is there for a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)? Furthermore, the manifestation of a non-entity has already been refuted through its threefold classification.
Moreover, the superimposition of an external object upon one's own internal form is simply impossible.
For indeed, cognition arises with some aspect, whether real or unreal.

As for the superimposition of an external object upon that aspect, it must be either produced by that [cognition] itself or produced by something else. If it were produced by that [cognition] itself, no other operation could be experienced at that very moment; so how could there be such a superimposition?
And at another time, being itself non-existent, whose activity could there be?

In the second case as well, even a subsequent cognition performs no function whatsoever toward anything else by means of any other activity, apart from an arising that is colored by the imposition of a form.

Thus, even when it takes as its object a form similar to a recent cognition, it does not touch upon any further activity of superimposing the external, except for a mere imitation of a fraction of that [external] form.

Moreover, the act of making a word manifest is not an operation distinct [from cognition], because even the form of the word is included within its very nature; thus, there is no operation of cognition other than the mental image (ākāra).
And this object being superimposed is external.
In that regard, if it manifests in its own form within cognition, then this is simply the perception of reality; what superimposition could there be?
On the other hand, if it does not manifest, even then what superimposition could there be?

Or, if it does manifest, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the appearance of the form being superimposed as something distinct from the form of the cognition itself which serves as its substratum.
If it is argued that the manifestation of its [the object's] form is itself the manifestation of the [cognition], we say no;
for that [form] is the object of superimposition.
Indeed, the manifestation of a mirage is not the same as the manifestation of water; thus, there is a superimposition of the external upon its own form.

For this very reason, there is no superimposition of one's own form onto the external, because the external object, which is the locus of superimposition, does not appear [to consciousness]. For that same reason, even the conjunction of one's own form with the external is impossible.
Because there is no appearance of two things that are distinct,
and conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) is not a unification;
for what is the meaning of this "unification"?
If causality were to consist in the attainment of oneness, then it would be impossible, because there is never any actual unification between the object superimposed and the locus of superimposition;
for instance, there can be no cause whatsoever for a rabbit's horn.
Furthermore, it is not tenable for a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) to claim that what was previously manifold attains oneness later on.
There would merely be the arising of another object; yet that [new object] is not within the range of perception, except for its own form which is the object of superimposition.
And even so, since there is nothing at all of the [original] object, how can there be a unification?
Now, if it is argued that "single cognition" means "ascertainment," even so, there is no single apprehension of two [objects], because there is an absence of experience of what is to be ascertained.
Nor is mere cognition of two things itself ascertainment, as in the case of blue and yellow.
Nor is determination (adhyavasāya) a cognition [of identity] through non-difference;
for, according to the position of exclusion (paryudāsa), it would entail a cognition of oneness, and that has already been refuted.
Because there is no apprehension of that which is to be determined (*adhyavaseya*).
Even if one merely negates cognition through differentiation, it has not been stated that there is cognition of an external object; so how could there be a determination of it?
For if an external object were manifest, it would be logical for there to be a cognition of it as either one or many, or as existent or non-existent.

If it is argued that this cognition is a "single cognition" because it occurs by way of obscuring the specific nature of those [individuals] in all their aspects, then, if their specific natures are obscured, they would not appear at all.
If it is argued that this is not so because some part [of them] does appear, we say: no.
Since a real entity is partless, it must either manifest in its entirety or not manifest at all; this is precisely what the treatise examines here in detail.
Furthermore, one should not say that the non-apprehension of difference constitutes conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
For instance, is it when the external object is being perceived or when it is not being perceived?
It cannot be the first position, because the perception of an external object has already been refuted.
For if there were apprehension [of the external object], it would follow that the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) itself is perception;
but if the external object is not being apprehended, there could be no restriction on purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*),
because since other things are also not being apprehended at that time, it would follow that activity could occur toward anything else as well.
Trilocana also refutes this determination (*adhyavasāya*). What is this determination?
Is it apprehension (*grahaṇa*), or...
Is it an instrument, or a connection, or else a superimposition?

In that case, how could a conceptual construction (vikalpa) grasp or produce an object that does not exist externally but appears as itself? For it is impossible for even one skilled in the arts to grasp or produce blue as yellow.
Nor can conceptual construction (vikalpa) associate its own form with a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) that has not been apprehended;
nor is the particular characteristic the object of conceptual apprehension. Furthermore, it does not superimpose its own form—which is non-existent—as being the actual object.
Since it is not possible to superimpose [an object] without first having grasped its own form, the grasping of that form must be sought.
In this regard, does one grasp [the object] and then superimpose it, or does one superimpose it at the very same time as one grasps its own form?
Not the first [alternative],

for a momentary conceptual consciousness cannot perform both apprehension and superimposition in succession. But in the latter case, since the object of the conceptual construction— which is not the locus of the "I-notion"— is being superimposed by the conceptualization upon the form of the conceptualization itself (which is the object of non-conceptual self-cognition and is the locus of the "I-notion"), it is impossible for that object to be [perceived as] non-different from it.
Nor can it be apprehended as having an external particular characteristic (*bāhya-svalakṣaṇa*),
because an external particular characteristic does not appear within the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*).
Vācaspati also rejects the notion of "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*).
To say that it "ascertains an object as its own appearance, though the object is not [actually] there," is an unintelligible definition.
Now, when one says "it superimposes" (*āropayati*), is this superimposition merely the experience of the conceptual construction's own nature?
Or is it another operation distinct from the experience of its own nature?

It cannot be the former alternative, because experience and superimposition, being respectively of the nature of non-conceptual and conceptual, cannot possess identity, just as liquidity and solidity cannot.
If, however, there were distinct operations, they would have to occur either sequentially or simultaneously.
First of all, it cannot be sequential,
because a momentary cognition is incapable of possessing sequential operations.
Even for those who maintain that things are non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), a successive operation of cognition and action is impossible because it is illogical for them to function after having ceased.
If it is argued that experience (*anubhava*) and superimposition (*samāropa*) are simultaneous,
let there be simultaneity alone.
The self (ātman) is to be known as abiding in its own nature (svabhāva), because if it were known through another nature (parabhāva), the knowledge of its own form would be impossible.
Thus, the aspect of the grasped and the grasper (grāhya-grāhakākāra) of cognition is experienced as the self, while the object (artha) is superimposed [upon it].
The self, when being cognized, is not something superimposed, nor is the object being superimposed directly perceivable.
Furthermore, that superimposition is simply the apprehension of either what exists or what does not exist;
and it has been established that the apprehension of anything distinct from cognition is impossible.

If it is argued that there is a non-apprehension of the difference between one’s own appearance and the external object, which constitutes a superimposition of the external, and from that arises activity toward the external—
then does this occur while the external object is being apprehended or not?
It cannot be while it is being apprehended.
For it has been stated that such apprehension is not possible;

and if there is no apprehension, then in the absence of the apprehension of difference, there would be no restriction on activity, because since other things are also unapprehended at that time, there would be the undesirable consequence of activity occurring toward those as well.

Therefore, the more this mental determination (*adhyavasāya*) is examined, the more it simply falls apart. Likewise, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), superimposition (*āropa*), conceit (*abhimāna*), grasping (*graha*), and certainty (*niścaya*)—just like determination—are each restricted to their own internal forms; appearing as they do, they do not know even a mere report of an external object. Thus, they possess the very nature of determination. Even though there are differences in the causes for the application of words (*śabdapravṛtti-nimitta*), how could one who stands outside of both reasoning and scripture claim that there is the manifestation of a non-self (*anātma-sphuraṇa*)?

Now, if conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the like are impossible, or even if they do exist, if one does not admit that they reveal what is non-self (*anātma*), then there follows the consequence of the total abolition of the worldly conventions of injunction and prohibition well-known to all people; thus, there would be contradiction with the world.

Furthermore, [terms such as] "conceptual construction," "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), "superimposition" (*āropa*), "conceit" (*abhimāna*), "grasping" (*graha*), "certainty" (*niścaya*), and so forth, have been explained at every step in the treatise;
and since external objects and the like are accepted as established by those [terms], there would be contradiction with the Teacher (*ācārya*).
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with logic (*nyāya*).
For, since the nature of things would be cognized without error through all modes of cognition, error would be absolutely non-existent.
Consequently, all sentient beings would always be perfectly enlightened Buddhas (*samyaksambuddha*).
If it is argued that conceptualized cognition is an error because it determines an object in its own manifestation despite there being no actual object,
then why is that object, as determined by it, not manifested?
If it is manifest, how could it not be manifest within that [cognition]? Or, if it is indeed manifest,
then it follows that the object must be identical with it.

And if the object were non-existent, there would be a conviction in every respect— due to the force of its reality— that "Māndhātā existed," "Śaṅkha will exist," "the self exists," and "sound is eternal."
Furthermore, [the word] "cow" would manifest through its own distinct characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
however, since a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is impossible regarding a particular characteristic, that cognition would not be conceptual at all.

Therefore, one must accept that the cognition of a cow appears through a distortion consisting of a false, verbalized universal (*gotva*) common to all individual cows; such a manifestation is what constitutes the determination of the object "cow."
For in this way these faults would not arise, because even though the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not appear [to consciousness], it is determined through error.
To this it is replied:

there is no contradiction with worldly convention or with the treatises, because even when external objects are not apprehended, activity, cessation, and so forth are established; and because the nature of determination—which cannot be bypassed by one's own or an opponent’s disputants—has been defined.
However, there is not even a scent of contradiction with logic (*nyāyavirodha*).

For what, then, is this "error" (*bhrānti*)—is it the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), or the apprehension of something as what it is not (*atasmiṃstadgraha*), such that by its absence liberation would be attained right now?
It cannot be the first position.
Because the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) has been refuted; as the Teachers have said: "If that whose own form appears [is later] sublated, then it is not real."
Even when there is a sublater, what confidence can there be in that which appears as having a different nature?
The exclusion of its own nature occurs through the introduction of another nature;
even in that case, doubt arises because of the perception of a prior sublation.
If there is no other sublation for the newborn [cognition] than this very [sublation of the prior], then let it be the former alone;
for the manifestation of its form is identical.
There is no evidence for you whatsoever that "there will be no other [cognition]";
for even when the nature [of a cognition] appears clearly, there may still be the possibility of sublation.
(Nibandh 137)

"If [it is argued that] there is no manifestation of the intrinsic nature [of the cognition], because the cause has been purified, and even when there is no manifestation of a sublation, there is still a great confusion— if this is your position, then there is indeed a great confusion."

In the treatise (*śāstra*), error (*bhrānti*) is described as the apprehension of something as what it is not, because of the determination of an object within one's own appearance despite that appearance being a non-object, due to the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized. Unable to justify this [definition], he composes and propagates a poetic work (*kāvya*) asserting that error is the independent manifestation of the unreal.

[Objection: But surely, even the apprehension of that which is not [the object] as being that is an error, and having been investigated in many ways by many, it has been rejected as something distinct from a cognition that terminates in its own form.
Therefore, how is it that even on this view there is no impairment of error, such that the consequence of liberation would not occur right now? [Response:

This is merely the frantic outcry of one whose mind is agitated by the poison of hatred for the Blessed Master Bhāṣyakāra’s doctrine; it moves only those whose intellects are overcome with compassion.

For instance, determination (*adhyavasāya*) consists in the projection of activity toward another object, even though that object is not apprehended, arising solely from the experience of one's own specific appearance produced by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
And this cannot be refuted by the webs of words mentioned previously,
because it is directly known within oneself by all living beings.
Because it has not been manifested by anyone at all, and since this very [world] is *saṃsāra* while its destruction is *mokṣa*, how could there even be talk of such a thing now? For instance,

due to various beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— arising in a certain form in dependence upon specific awakening conditions— instigates a continuous stream of recollections, desires, and so forth regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that is conducive to outward-directed activity.
Consequently, for those seeking purposeful action (*puruṣārtha-kriyā*), there arise determinations of engagement and withdrawal that correspond to external objects;
this is because the causal relationship between the moments of cognition within the mental continuum of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is necessarily fixed in such a way.
Even at the time of conceptualizing an object whose connection [to reality] is not yet ascertained, there arises the impulse toward activity, such as the determination of existence or non-existence.

In this regard, that capacity of this [cognition] to function in both ways—which has been acquired through the power of its own causes—is precisely this superimposition of being an object of engagement, which is synonymous with "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*). Just as, for instance, the very production of a determination based on seeing [the moon] is the grasping-operation of a cognition of the moon, whether it be erroneous or non-erroneous; so too, this self-cognition should be understood as having the same effect as the cognition of an object.

This follows from logic. Likewise, for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in a form such as "there is fire here," its very capacity to impel activity (*pravṛttyākṣepakatva*) is what constitutes its "determination of the external" (*bāhyāvasāna*).

And just as, in the case of non-conceptual [cognition], the appearance of two moons and so forth is itself the means of determination, so too, in the case of a conceptual determination, it is that very appearance which is the means of accomplishing an activity directed away from other objects.

If it is argued: "But even if that [external object] is thus established by that [cognition], and yet it does not appear within that cognition, then there can be no conviction even through an oath," this is irrelevant. For, prior to the introduction of a subverting proof against the external object such as a cloth, its status as a real entity remains doubtful; [this doubt cannot be removed] merely by means of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Even if there is no manifestation of non-existent things—such as momentary entities or a rabbit's horn—the obstruction to their establishment cannot be countered even by Brahmā.
For the conventional usage regarding objects is of two kinds: from manifestation and from conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

Thus, here, even though there is no appearance [of the object], the status of being an object is stated for the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) excluded from others and so forth, by virtue of mere conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*); for if it were entirely without an object, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all worldly transactions, such as engagement and withdrawal, would be abolished.
Consequently, there is indeed a logical consistency in this: that the object is established by that [cognition], yet its manifestation does not exist within the cognition itself.

Even in the absence of the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator (*prakāśya-prakāśaka-bhāva*), the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayi-bhāva*) is established through the relationship between the determined and the determiner (*adhyavasāya-adhyavasāyaka-bhāva*).

(Nibandha 138) Now, if there were no cognition of the object to be determined (*adhyavaseya*), then activity would occur even toward an ungrasped particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth; thus, it would follow that [activity] occurs everywhere without distinction.

Because there is no distinction [in the object] due to its being ungrasped everywhere, and because, consequently, even the apprehension of the intended object is not certain, inference too is corrupted.
To this we reply:
Even if everything that is determined is not apprehended, and thus the entire universe remains unapprehended, nevertheless, activity is restricted to specific objects and does not occur everywhere;
for conceptualization possesses a restricted capacity due to its having a restricted form, which arises through the power of such a homogeneous immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
For entities possess fixed capacities, their natures being established by valid cognition;
they do not admit of the objection regarding the confusion of capacities.
Just as with the arising of what was previously non-existent, even though [the capacity] is absent everywhere, it is only from a seed that a sprout arises.
In that very case, its capacity is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

likewise here too, for one who desires purposeful action such as burning or cooking, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form of fire possesses the capacity—attested by valid cognition—to engage with the object that is fire itself, provided it is accompanied by the memory [of fire]. How could this be subject to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?

Furthermore, when considering proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the state of being blazing and radiant belongs to the real fire just as much as it does to that which is delineated by the conceptual construction.
To that extent, the capacity for the conceptualization of fire to function toward that very object [fire] exists, but not toward water and so forth.

But surely, regarding the superimposition based on similarity: is it the superimposition of one's own internal form (*svākāra*) upon the external object, or the superimposition of the external object upon one's own internal form?

In either case, there is an inconsistency, because it is impossible to perceive both—the internal form and the external object—which are respectively the locus of superimposition and the object superimposed. If this is argued:
We do not say that activity occurs through superimposition (*āropa*).

Rather, that cognition, arising by the power of the maturation of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), extends itself toward an external object even while not perceiving one; thus it is indeed erroneous and constitutes the nature of saṃsāra.
As for the treatise:
It is not the case that [the cognition] arises as equal to the object in its production;

rather, it is because the capacity for the production of such a form is restricted by necessity. Therefore, its activity does not proceed by way of superimposition (āropa) as in the case of silver and the like, but rather through the restriction of the power bound to the production of such a form.
Furthermore, it is not logical for one who investigates to refrain from acting due to the certainty of not perceiving an object;
for even when there is perception, action occurs because of a desire for purposeful efficacy (*arthakriyā*),
and the attainment of purposeful efficacy is contingent upon the necessity of the object's existence.

And just as that restriction arises from perception due to a direct connection with the object, so too does it arise—even through a conceptual construction—due to an indirect connection with the object; thus, even in the absence of perception, activity is justified by way of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, inference is not unstable;
and by this [argument], it is not the case that [the object] is not cognized.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the objection— that there would be an appearance of non-difference— is impossible,
because it has been shown that even in the absence of a direct appearance, there is the taking of something as an object of activity, which results in a state grounded in non-difference and so forth.
Therefore, the error— otherwise known as superimposition (*āropa*)— is simply the apprehension of one thing as another, which is charming only so long as it is not investigated.
And it is logical that liberation is the exhaustion of that [ignorance]. As the Teachers have said:
"Therefore, when there is the projection of activity and the arising of the forms of conceptual construction..."
The superimposition of water and so forth upon that [mirage] is likewise equal in status to both the real and the unreal.
Therefore, although in reality there is no such thing as superimposition for anyone, it cannot be denied because it is established by conventional usage.
As long as there is the conception of a self in what is not-self, like water in a mirage,
so long is saṃsāra merely an error; nirvāṇa is the firm establishment in reality.
Therefore, as long as the possibility of investigation has not arisen, this is the principle that "existence is one thing and tranquility is another";
but when the mind is made playful and graceful by the sport of investigation, let it be told: what here is existence and what is tranquility?
Likewise, the venerable Ārya Maitreya also said:
"In this world, there is not the slightest difference between these two—peace and birth—in terms of their actual nature;
nevertheless, for those who perform virtuous deeds, the attainment of peace is established through the exhaustion of birth."
And the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna said:
"Both nirvāṇa and cyclic existence do not exist as a duality;
the thorough understanding of cyclic existence itself is called nirvāṇa."
Thus, since the establishment of error is possible even when the nature of reality is cognized without distortion by all means of illumination, cyclic existence exists.

As for what was also said— that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has no external object as its domain and yet involves the conjunction of this [object] with a word— it is difficult to establish even its status as a conceptual construction; since there is no conjunction of words within itself, that which is called "conceptual construction" does not exist at all, so whose concern could it be to investigate conceptual construction?
To this it is replied:

Just as the determination "fire is here" produces a bodily activity, so too does it produce a verbal one in the form "fire is perceived by me," and it also produces a mental one consisting of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of that very form.

And this being the case, just as there is the certainty that "this object has been grasped by conceptual construction," so too is there the [certainty] that "it has been grasped in conjunction with a word," because the form of the word flashes forth just like a slight trace of the form of the object.

Therefore, as long as a person possesses the conceit of grasping an object, they likewise possess the conceit of grasping it as conjoined with a verbal designation; thus, the establishment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows from the force of such determination alone, and not from reality.
As the Teachers have said:
"There is no conjunction with words, either externally or within the mind."
Again, a minute fragment of the form of an object flashes forth, interspersed with the form of the perishable [mental image].

Although both forms belong only to the intellect, the mind’s determination projects them onto the external world and onto speech; therefore, there exists the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Whether there is non-appearance or appearance, there is no superimposition of anything whatsoever;
such [a distinction] is merely a conventional designation based on the difference in dependent origination.
When there is the presence of conceptualization— which, though free from conceptualization, resembles a mere fragment—
due to the words of one who establishes conventions, [this occurs] with respect to the specific form of the cognition. (Nibandh 140)
The convention was established; thus, upon hearing such a word again, there is a determination of the denotable object based on a mental state consisting of an inclination toward activity.

Thus, [it may be] a real entity such as a pot or a cloth, or a doubtful entity that transcends both proof and refutation, or it may be determined as a non-entity such as the self, space, time, or the momentary; so it is said.
The meaning is that even though [the external object] does not appear [in consciousness], it has been made the object of engagement.

This alone is the meaning of superimposition (*āropa*), unification, determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), the apprehension of non-difference, and so forth; this must be understood everywhere in the treatise.

Therefore, since determinative cognition possesses a specific form, there is a state called "fitness for engagement" even with respect to what is not [directly] grasped. If, by means of that [fitness], the relationship of grasper and grasped between the external object and the determinative cognition is difficult to avoid conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), [then it follows].

In that case, since the relationship of subject and object is also obtained, it is logical to say that the status of being an object and a subject is stated merely by way of determination (*adhyavasāya*).
As the author of the *Alaṅkāra* said: "How is there the state of being its object? Because [the word] functions toward that."
By this, that which was stated— namely, "How is it that the object of the self, while being determined by that [cognition], is not manifested? and so forth— is refuted,
because it has been established that there is a determination of that [object] even in the absence of its manifestation.

Furthermore, it is also incorrect to claim that [cognition] would not exist if the object were non-existent; for since the self and so forth—which are the objects of determination—are excluded from appearing [in cognition], they lack identity with the cognition itself.
Nor is the fault of the undesirable consequence that all aspects [of the object] must be determined a valid one.
For "ascertainment of all aspects" (sarvākāraniścaya) is defined as having the nature of causing engagement with respect to all aspects;

and since the capacity of a conceptual cognition that delineates only a single aspect to engage with other aspects is not an object of experience, it is not logical to claim that it is independent of other means of valid cognition such as verbal testimony.
In that context, non-conceptual [cognition] is established as the apprehender because its manifestation is vivid.
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), however, becomes the locus for conventional designations such as "superimposition" because it delineates a single, distinct exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Just as there may be the establishment of error regarding something external when that external object exists, so it is everywhere in the internal system as well;
it is merely said that no error occurs with respect to the self (*ātman*) when [the error] is made in relation to an outward-directed activity.

Nor is there any occasion for the manifestation of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object, because it is only one's own mental form that appears, and because it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention regarding a specific characteristic.

To claim that it would not be conceptual at all is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) with respect to its own nature; however, with respect to the external object, that cognition is indeed conceptual, just like a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, it must be accepted that the cognition of a cow manifests through a delusion consisting of a false, verbalized [form] by means of "cowness" (*gotva*), which is common to all individual cows, and this manifestation of it as such is its determination of the cow.

Even if one were to object by means of trampling the feet [of the opponent] and so forth, this would be outside the scope of both logic and scripture; for even in the absence of such [objections], the aforementioned faults are destroyed.

Indeed, there is no logical consistency in the claim that the mere manifestation of an unreal form in conceptual cognition constitutes the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external object, because the grammatical connection with the word "of the object" (*arthasya*) would be untenable.
Since there is no succession here in the cognition, it is indeed perception; how then can there be a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*)?
We do not understand [the claim] that this occurs because of a delusive determination of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), even though it is not appearing [in consciousness].

For when there is contact with the cognition of that [object] through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), what other manifestation could there be? It is also incorrect to say that there is "conceptual determination" because of indistinctness even in the cognition of that [object],
since there is an absence of indistinctness precisely in the cognition of its form.
The mutual basis for cognitions arises from that single object;
how can there be a single form that appears with diverse aspects? (Nibandh 141)
Thus, let the Teacher be remembered;
nor can that [cognition] be an error at that time,
because it manifests the very nature of the object itself.
If it is argued that this is due to false cognitive activity (*alīkavṛtti*),
let that alone be the case;
but how can there be a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external object that is not appearing?
If it is argued that "it is indeed that very same thing," [we reply:
this is false, because for one who knows this to be so, there is no established determination of an external object,
since the external does not manifest and because [the cognition] is not restricted to it.
Even if there were an obstruction, that [non-apprehension] would still exist;
however, there is no determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it, because such determination is impossible even when its non-manifestation or manifestation occurs— so enough of this excessive persistence.

Thus, even though it does not appear [as a separate entity], the reason—consisting of the nature of manifestation and free from the three defects—is established merely through the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its exclusion from the counter-position; it indeed proves the unity of the circle of various forms, which consists of cognition, as far as the limit of manifestation extends.
As the teachers have said: "That which shines is one, just as the form of white appears in a painting;
and yet the entire painting shines forth, including yellow, cold, pleasure, and so on."
There is no lack of proof here, since manifestation is observed in the variegated subject;
nor is the absence of the property to be proven seen even in the example.
Because each [atom] is submerged in its own [isolation], there is no mutual cognition;
nor does the manifestation of a single atom exist, for it is only the gross [object] that flashes forth.
If there is a single, gross cognition appearing as external atoms,
then what will the appearance of the atoms of cognition itself be?
Therefore, the manifestation that is pervaded by grossness ceases with the cessation of that [grossness]; thus, being withdrawn from the manifold, it is restricted to unity.
Just as there is the rejection of difference from a position of the same class due to the consequence of non-appearance,
so too [is there rejection] from a position of a different class.

Therefore, let there be neither a probandum nor an example, nor even doubt regarding the opposite; thus, by means of a faultless reason, the system of variegated non-duality (citrādvaita) is established.

And there is a summary verse: Just as the light that is accepted as being possessed of unity is pervaded by grossness, so too it is not pervaded atom-by-atom; for this [light] never appears even in a dream.
Therefore, because that which pervades it has ceased through the dissolution of each atom, it is encompassed as a unity; and thus this collection of forms appears.
Thus it is said.

Therefore, since the identity of the example and the subject of the illustration is established by both perception and inference, the identity of the self is likewise established by inference.
