As for this perception that is brought forward as proving difference,
is it non-self-natured (*anātmabhūta*) or self-natured (*ātmabhūta*) with respect to blue and the other [objects]? In the first case,
Let this establishment of difference through that [means] be set aside for now; even mere existence would not be established.
For that object, such as blue and so forth, must be admitted to be either insentient, or of the nature of another consciousness, or of a false essence.

In all three positions, the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator is absent. To explain: what is this so-called "illuminating nature" of cognition? Is it its mere existence, or is it the engagement in an activity? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence that everyone would be an omniscient seer of everything.
Because the existence of the knowledge of all persons is equally non-distinct with respect to everything,
there would follow the undesirable consequence that cognition would also apprehend blue and other objects,
since it is possible for them too to possess the character of being present and thus capable of being grasped.

Now, if it is argued that the definition [of consciousness] is qualified by being "existence while possessing the nature of cognition," then why must the venerable one resort to the ordeal of drinking from a bowl (*kośapāna*) regarding blue and so forth, which are not cognition? For, when consciousness and blue—

which both flash forth simultaneously with mere existence— are present, you establish for one of them (blue) such properties as insentience, unreality, sublation, and non-luminosity based on nothing more than a mere assertion.
Now, as for the second [alternative], what would that operation be? Would it be the self of perception itself, another cognition, or something other than the object of the object?
In the first alternative, there is a contradiction regarding the activity [of an entity] upon itself.
In the second case, if another cognition has a different object, it would have nothing to do with the [intended] object;
moreover, its having that as its object is not yet established, since it is precisely the nature of its proximity to that object which is currently under consideration.
Furthermore, in the third hypothesis, blue and so forth would merely be produced,
not manifested, just as a lamp is [produced] by means of oil, a wick, and so on.
But illumination is itself [the nature of consciousness].
And thus, because it would be a different cognition, there would follow the undesirable consequence of its non-appearance, just as in the case of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*).
However, in the fourth alternative, when something other than the object is postulated, blue and so forth remain exactly as they were.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to accept that cognition possesses the capacity to manifest a non-self, for manifestation, like any other operation, must be rejected in the same manner.

Nor should one assert that there is an intrinsic relationship of apprehended and apprehender between cognition and the object of cognition, as one might find in the causal relationship between fire and smoke.

Since the essential natures of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject remain as yet impossible to define— just like the relationship between cause and effect established by valid cognition— where even a mention of "blue" and so forth exists, such that the hope for establishing their distinction could be fulfilled through perception?

Now, if the second position is that it is directly perceived as being identical with the self (*ātman*), then self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself must be accepted as the proof for their difference.

And if that [self-awareness] were distinct for each individual form, then, because all [forms] would be submerged within their own respective natures, it would follow that the manifestation of the variegated whole (*citraprakāśa*) would be destroyed; this has already been stated.
Now, if— out of fear of this defect— it is maintained that the very unity of all these forms constitutes their inherent nature and is self-cognized,
then this is precisely what is called "cognitive monism" (*citradvaitavijñāna*);

namely, that which is known as the perception of an indivisible self-cognition that is the inherent nature of the various forms such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, which are intended to be manifold yet perceived simultaneously.
As the teachers have said:
"Delusions and non-delusions, conceptualizations and non-conceptualizations,
pleasure, pain, and so forth— all these arise from the totality of the sense faculties."
Cognitions are non-different because they are perceived together;
however, their status as preceding or succeeding is simply not cognizable. (Nibandh 143)

Thus, in both the case of the example and the subject of the illustration, the identity established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) is proven through inference when there is disagreement due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*).
For this very reason, since identity is established through both self-awareness and inference, no other form of direct perception is required;
nor does the opportunity arise for an inference characterized by the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) to prove difference.
Because perception that apprehends difference is invalid according to the sequence already stated, and because the thesis is sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition;
yet, one might indeed say something [in reply].
If it is argued that nevertheless there is indeed a distinction because of the difference in appearance— for nothing that is perceived can be called "impossible"—
then, alas! what is intended by the word "appearance"?
Is it the aspect (*ākāra*) or the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) that constitutes the wheel?
In that regard, if the first position is held,
then the mental aspect (*buddhyākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the external object to be cognized.
Thus, a distinction between forms must indeed be maintained;
otherwise, the distinction between external objects would not be established.

Furthermore, when the circle of forms itself is the object of cognition (*prameya*) and self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how could one who is not negligent speak of a distinction among blue and other colors, which have been unified by that very [awareness] through their own indivisible nature?
In the second alternative, however, it is stated that "vibration" (sphuraṇa) is simply the indivisible self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) which is its very nature.

Even so, how can there be a distinction [between the two]? Just as, in the case of vertical perception by the senses, although a difference between moments is perceived, there is a conceptual determination of oneness due to the power of ignorance;

likewise, in the case of horizontal self-awareness through direct perception, although a non-difference in form is apprehended, there is a determination of difference solely due to the power of ignorance.

If it is argued that, because of the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), even that which is all-pervasive would not be differentiated—just like the circle of forms within consciousness—we say:
no. This is because the plurality (*anekatva*) to be proven in the case of an external substratum (*dharmin*) is not sublated by perception or other means of valid cognition.

However, regarding the collection of mental forms (*buddhyākārakadambaka*), since their unity is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and so forth according to the sequence already stated, plurality is rejected; thus, there is simply no occasion for a sublation to arise.
Therefore, the qualification "while being cognition" must be applied to the reason, so that the distinction belongs to the external object alone.
Now, if this single wheel of various forms consists of consciousness alone, then the yellow and other forms would enter into the blue form itself. Likewise,

if there were no difference between the wheel of forms and the wheel of luminosity, as in the case of an individual and its universal, then either luminosity alone would exist, or the wheel of forms alone would exist— so it may be asked.
This is incorrect;
for there is indeed a distinction between these two, namely the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*),
and that distinction is applicable only within the framework of the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*).

In that regard, since sense-perception (*indriyapratyakṣa*) which apprehends difference is accepted [by the opponent], and because in the Vijñānavāda there is no manifestation of anything other than itself, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, since even the proof of difference—which is the opposite [of non-duality]—is established through that very [self-cognition], the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is also irrelevant; thus, non-duality (*advaita*) alone remains.
Furthermore, if it were so, even a gross form such as blue would dissolve into mere atoms, and the world would consequently become non-manifest;
yet manifestation does exist.
Therefore, unity is simply the fact that forms, exactly as they appear, have as their very nature an indivisible self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
Neither difference nor restriction should be accepted, because that would entail the consequence of non-appearance.

Likewise, one must state the further consequence that if there were no difference between "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and [properties such as] "impermanence" (*anityatva*), "substantiality" (*vastutva*), and so forth, then either producedness alone or impermanence alone would exist;
for, like the universal and the individual, those two are in reality non-different due to having an undivided nature (*akhaṇḍātmatva*).

If it is argued that the distinction [between them] is merely a matter of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), then if this is the case, the same sequence applies to the manifestation and the blue object as well; thus, the consequence of their being reduced to one is nothing but the prattle of a child. Therefore, as follows:
(Nibandh 144)

The external object does not perish even through division into atoms, because it possesses existence, performs causal efficiency, and avoids the faults of non-distinction and confusion despite its internal differentiation. Consciousness, however, perishes through mere division; since it consists of pure cognition, it is variegated even while being one, and thus does not undergo division. What can we do about this?
But surely, the attainment of spatial extension does not belong to that which is devoid of another self;
and it can also be argued that when spatial extension is lost, there is no appearance.
If this is argued, we say no: another self cannot be a part of one's own self; that [other] is logically possible only as something external.
For consciousness, which culminates in its own self-awareness, what recourse is there for that which is other than itself?
If it is argued: "Well then, even so, how can that [cognition] be one and the same as blue and so forth?"—
then how does that [blue] appear coherently as both a part and a single whole?
If that [atom] is also not desired [as a real entity], then where would there be the appearance of a division within an atom?
Furthermore, since an atom is incapable of withstanding critical examination, how could there be any division of it at that time?
If it be argued that [the unity of the appearance] does not exist because it is a non-entity, then that [non-entity] too would be destroyed by the refutation of unity;
for when the unity of the manifestation is established, the reality of self-awareness is thereby secured.
Neither dependent origination nor non-origination contradicts this,
because it exists as mere appearance even when devoid of being one or many.
Furthermore, since the cognition of a prior and a posterior does not exist in the case of non-duality,
dependent origination is therefore neither established nor is it a proof [of that non-duality].
Even non-arising is not a single certainty, for it possesses the nature of neither cause nor effect;
even when cause and fruit have ceased, where could that manifest form go?

If the pervasion of entities by unity and plurality were established anywhere, then that reason would, at the time of the [proposition of] universal emptiness, bring about the subversion of what is intended.
Furthermore, even regarding what is well-known in the world, the determination of a real entity does not rely on what is merely imagined by all the world; rather,
it relies on that which is consistent with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, nothing has ever been observed by either perception or inference that lacks parts,
such that it could possess a manifold aggregate, nor is there any entity whatsoever that is not so.
Let him be defeated whose existence is pervaded by either of the two [alternatives];
however, the proponent of existence who relies on mere non-erroneous cognition is the victor.
Thus ends this treatise on the Illumination of Variegated Non-duality.
There is no grasping of that [object] by it, nor is it empty even of being graspable by another cognition;
nevertheless, the manifestation consisting of cognition has appeared as the position of direct perception for you.
Nibandha 145 // 10 //
// Refutation of Other Mental Continuums //

Now, here, once the mass of insentient objects has been discarded by the force of proofs such as the "simultaneous apprehension with illumination" (*sahopalambha*), and it is established that the entire collection of objects— blue, yellow, and so forth— is non-dual in nature,

being of the essence of the manifestations of one's own mind like a dream or an illusion, this [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of determining the existence or non-existence of other mental continua (*santānāntara*).
For some have said as follows:
There indeed exists another continuum, established through inference; for,

since one observes the appearance of speech and conventional usage immediately following a mind of desire, and does not observe them in its absence, one determines— within one's own continuum— the causal relationship between the appearance of speech and so forth and the mind of desire by means of the body of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), which is established through perception and non-perception, at a time when that mind of desire is not being experienced.

Since one observes appearances such as interrupted speech and so forth, the volitional mind (*icchā-citta*) which is their cause is inferred; thus, it is established as being precisely another mental continuum (*santānāntara*).
Regarding this, the following is considered:

Is that volitional mind, which is established as the cause of the appearance of speech and so forth, something capable of being perceived by the inferrer, or is it merely volition (*icchā-mātra*) independent of the qualification of being visible or invisible?

If the first alternative is taken, then since the mind of desire is capable of being perceived by the inferrer, its non-perception at the time of inference indicates its very absence; thus, because it is sublated by the perception known as "non-apprehension" (anupalambha), what room is there for that inference? If, on the other hand, the mind of desire were experienced even at the time of inference, [then the objection would not hold].
In that case, what is the use of inference? Or,
if after establishing the production of fire from smoke in this manner, one were to perceive smoke in a mountain thicket but not infer fire there as well—
because the presence of fire would be sublated by its non-perception there— then [inference would be useless].
Furthermore, perception [of fire] would render inference useless.
This is not so; for at the time of inference, because fire situated at a remote location is unfit for observation, there is an absence of "non-perception of the perceptible" (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*);
and since the non-perception of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalambha*) is incompatible with proving non-existence.
However, for a mind that is the object of one's desire, there is no spatial remoteness;

for a desired mind is indeed perceptible to the inferrer as long as it is connected to oneself, and thus the claim that such a mind is remote in terms of space and so forth is contrary to common experience.
Now, as for the second alternative:

for instance, the mind of intention alone—without depending on the distinction between visible and invisible objects common to one's own and others' mental continua—is determined to be the cause of the appearance of speech and so forth.
By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that determination made?
For, having perceived that the appearance of speech and so forth does not exist in the absence of mere intention (*icchāmātra*), one seeks to establish its production [from that intention].
Yet, the non-existence of mere intention—which is common to both one's own and another's mental continuum—cannot be apprehended either by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) or by any other means.

For instance, even in the case of fire alone, which is separated by space and time, if it were present at the place and time of the smoke's production, it would certainly be perceived by the sensory perception of the person inferring it, provided it were possible [for it to be so perceived].

(Nibandha 146) Since the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of smoke is ascertained at the time of its production, it implies the establishment of that [fire]’s production; thus, even for fire situated in a remote space and time, there is an ascertainment of its causality toward smoke alone.

However, in the case of that which is remote by nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*)—such as that which exists in the stomach and so forth, which can never be perceived as absent by the inferring person—it is simply excluded from the scope of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Likewise here as well, although the mind of desire is common to the mental continua of others, if it were possible to conceive that "as long as it belongs to someone, it would certainly be perceived by me," then, by means of establishing its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it would be determined to be a cause. However, this discussion ceases when the mere mind is beyond perception due to its remote nature (*svabhāva-viprakṛṣṭa*).
Nor is another's mind temporally remote, because it is present;
for only the past and the future are conventionally designated as "temporally remote.
Nor is it spatially remote.

For indeed, in the very same location as a white conch shell or the like where one's own mind, appearing in a white form, is experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), a mind existing in another continuum (*parasantāna*) that appears in a yellow form located in that same place is not experienced. How then can there be such a spatial distance?
Now, with respect to its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the mind of desire (*icchācitta*) is not spatially remote from itself.
For even fire, though it is one, is not seen by the very same sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*) by which another [fire] is seen.

In that regard, just as fire alone is established as being visible with respect to the visual consciousness alone, so too here, with respect to self-awareness alone, the mind of desire alone is [established], even though it is common to both one's own and another's continuum.
"It is only the visible.

To this it is replied: What is intended here by the word "mere" (*mātra*)? Is it the sensory cognition of any person whatsoever—unqualified by its relation or non-relation to the cognizing subject—which, while taking an object as its domain, is accepted as being uncaused even though the visibility of that object is possible?
If this were the case, even a *piśāca* or similar being would be perceptible.

For such a being is indeed the object of sensory cognition for some person—such as one who possesses the requisite capacity—or for another *piśāca* of its own kind; thus, there would be nothing at all that is "ontologically remote" (*svabhāva-viprakṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, without discarding the connection with the person who is the cognizer, it is more appropriate that the word "only" (*mātra*) is intended solely to exclude distinctions such as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition.
Anticipating this very objection, Dharmottara stated:
"And this definition of perception is from the perspective of a single cognizer," and so forth.
By this, the possibility of being perceived is as follows: if a jar or the like were present here in this place or at this time, it would necessarily be apprehended.
It would become an object for my own visual consciousness alone;
however, it is not possible for another's mind to be so.
For if another's mind were present here, it would necessarily be [an object of] my own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
The object of cognition would become the subject.
If the mind of desire were merely that [desire] itself, it would have to be conceived as being perceptible at the time of its arising;
then, at the time of inference as well, having conceived it as being perceptible, how could this inference be undertaken to establish its non-existence through its non-perception?
For the thesis would be sublated by perception itself.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is a distinction between proximity and remoteness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) based on a difference in time; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Therefore, since it is impossible to conceive of a mere mind of desire—which is common to one's own and others' mental continua—as being perceptible, the non-existence of that [mind] is established even if it is not perceived prior to the production of verbal behavior and so forth; yet, the absence of verbal behavior and so forth is not necessarily caused by the absence of that [mind].

How can the status of being a cause be established such that it could be inferred by means of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)? For a specific state of volition (*icchācitta*) occurring within one's own continuum is certainly not visible to the inferrer.

Rather, since there is no perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) for him, how can there be an inference regarding a subject (*dharmin*) whose specific nature is sought after and which has been sublated? This has already been stated.
*Nibandha* 147):
Thus, when the probandum is a specific instance of a volitional mind (*icchācitta*) occurring within one's own continuum, there is a contradiction with perception regarding the subject (*pakṣa*).

Even when the probandum is merely a volitional mind in general, common to both one’s own and others’ continua, if its absence is perceived at the time of establishing the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—by means of mere non-perception (*anupalambha*) alone, without depending on the qualification of being "perceptible" (*dṛśya*)—[then the subject is contradicted].
In that case, when the subject (*dharmin*) is made the locus of the argument, the same fault remains.

If, on the other hand, it is not so perceived, then it is established that the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), such as speech and so forth, has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*).

Thus, some maintain: "Since there is no proof for the existence of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*), and because we do not observe any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) either, let there be mere doubt in that regard."
Let this refutation being stated by them be considered:
for if another continuum were possible, then one's own continuum would necessarily exist as distinct from it;
otherwise, there could be no distinction between that which is intended to be another's continuum and one's own continuum as it appears.

Furthermore, since there is no non-difference between those two, it follows that another continuum—which cannot be sublated by way of being either different or non-different from one's own continuum—is simply non-existent, like a universal or a rabbit’s horn; so how can there be any doubt?
Therefore, in relation to another continuum, difference from one's own continuum must necessarily exist.
And that difference, being the very nature of the continuum, would necessarily appear when one's own continuum appears.

Otherwise, how could the distinction of one's own continuum from the continuum of another—despite the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by eloquence and its absence—attain the status of being an essential nature?
Moreover, this distinction does not appear [in consciousness].
For if the appearance of a distinction were admitted, the appearance of the mental continuum of another—which serves as the limit of that distinction—would likewise be impossible to deny.
If it is argued that "this is distinct from that" is the very nature of one's own mind, [then...]
The manifestation of this [object] would either have a limit or it would not; therefore, it cannot be apprehended in its own nature.
In the case of difference, it does not possess even a trace of anything else; how, then, could it be distinct?
One should recall here the entirety of such statements from the *Pravacanapradīpa*, the *Śrīsākārasaṃgraha*, and other works.

For just as when only one's own continuum appears, no distinction is perceived from a rabbit’s horn—which does not appear—likewise, no distinction at all appears from another continuum that is likewise devoid of appearance.
Indeed, no trace of distinction whatsoever manifests in one's own continuum (svasantāna) in relation to another's continuum (parasantāna), which does not exist even in relation to a rabbit’s horn.

Furthermore, when the manifestation of one's own continuum is identical whether in relation to a rabbit’s horn or another's continuum, neither difference nor non-difference appears in relation to the rabbit’s horn.
However, it cannot be established that difference alone appears in relation to another's continuum.

For just as difference is established by avoiding the absence of both difference and non-difference, so too the appearance of difference ought to be distinct from the appearance of the absence of both difference and non-difference;
yet it is not experienced in that way.
Nevertheless, the statement "difference appears" is merely a verbal construction.
The reasoning of the *Bhāṣyakāra* regarding the refutation of the appearance of difference should also be understood in detail here. Furthermore,

if this appearance of difference were to occur even in the absence of the appearance of a limit [of perception], [it would have to be] through compassion for the minds of others (*paracittānukampayā*).
[Objection: In that case, how can the non-existence of external objects also be established?
For it is possible to introduce doubt even regarding that.

If it is argued that no external object appears to anyone, whereas the mental continuum of another certainly does appear to that other person, and therefore doubt arises only regarding this [latter case] and not regarding an external object;
All of this, moreover, is entirely doubtful;
for the mental continuum of another does not necessarily appear to oneself,
since one could just as well say that at times such a continuum does not exist at all and does not appear.

Furthermore, even if one were not to assert the existence of external objects for anyone at all, the point intended here is merely this: how can the non-existence of such objects be established for one who maintains the doctrine that the appearance of difference is accepted?
And there is no fault in this.
Therefore, how could it be acceptable even to the proponents of *vijñapti* (consciousness-only) that there exists another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) common to an external object?
Furthermore, even the causal relationship between two cognitions cannot be subverted by one who maintains that there is an appearance of difference;
for a preceding cognition, even when the appearance of a limit has ceased, necessarily grasps its own difference and its own priority in relation to a subsequent cognition.
Even a consciousness that arises later attains its own distinction and otherness in relation to a preceding consciousness,

just as in the case of a different mental continuum; thus, when the causal relationship— characterized by a fixed sequence of prior and posterior— is manifest and determined, how [could it be otherwise], given that it possesses variegated forms such as blue and so forth?
The view here is established by the statement of the Blessed One, the author of the *Vārttika*: "Conventionally, let it be as it may.

Furthermore, regarding the reason—namely, "the state of being manifest"—which was adduced for the purpose of proving non-duality in the subject (dharmin) consisting of the circle of variegated forms, [the opponent] points out that its object has been snatched away by perception (*pratyakṣa*) which apprehends difference.
Since you admit that the opponent perceives a distinction [between selves], how could you have answered without the doubt regarding another mental continuum?
But even so, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the non-existence of other continua established?
It cannot be by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that has affirmation as its object and lacks the capacity to establish a negation.

Nor can it be established by inference, because inference— which is restricted to proving the absence of perceptible objects— does not apply to proving the absence of another's mind, which is beyond the reach of the senses. To this we reply:
If another continuum were possible, then there would be a necessary existence [of that object], and from that follows the distinction of one's own mind.
If there were no distinction from one's own continuum, it would simply be another's continuum.

Furthermore, whatever is being perceived, if it does not appear in a certain form, it is not fit for conventional usage as existing in that form; just as blue is not [fit for conventional usage] in the form of yellow.

And one's own mind, when it is perceived, is not perceived as having a form distinct from the mental continuum of another; thus, this is a non-apprehension of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) that does not depend on the employment of a qualification of the perceptible (*dṛśyaviśeṣaṇa*), since it negates the identity of difference with one's own mind.
Nor is there a lack of proof [for the distinction],
because when a distinction appears, its limit (avadhi) must also appear.

However, if the limit does not appear, the absence of the appearance of distinction is established just as in the case of the non-appearance of the distinction between a hare's horn and something else.

Thus, by this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when the difference of another continuum (*santānāntara*) relative to one’s own mind has been refuted, and since non-difference is itself impossible, its inexpressibility in terms of either difference or non-difference is established.

Since its status as a real entity (*vastutā*) is lost—just like [the categories of] universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth—how can it be said that there is doubt regarding another continuum due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*)? (Nibandh 149)
And this has been written down merely as a reminder of the objects of knowledge established by the treatises;
however, the further implications here must be investigated by oneself.
Moreover, you yourselves admit that for those with limited vision, doubt arises regarding other mental continua.
But what state could be established for the Blessed One? If he were established as being in a state of doubt, how could there be omniscience?
Even though another mental continuum currently existing might at some time not be perceived by the Blessed One, how can it still be said that he is omniscient?
Furthermore, the inference concerning the objects of another's mental continuum has already been examined.
Even if [the omniscient one] were to perceive through inference, omniscience would not be possible.

If the mind of another were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the relationship of grasped object and grasping subject (*grāhya-grāhakabhāva*) between the other's mind and the Blessed One’s mind would also follow; thus, the doctrine of external objects (*bahirarthavāda*) would simply have been accepted under a different guise.
How does this argument deceive?

According to our own view, however, the mind of another does not exist at all; therefore, there is no fault of impairment to the Blessed One’s omniscience resulting from such a definitive determination.

Furthermore, as long as conventional reality consists of the conceit of grasping at distinctions, speech and so forth are employed to communicate with others due to the presence of doubt regarding their mental continuums; thus, there is no contradiction with one's own words either.
Indeed, it is not our intention to claim that doubt regarding another continuum does not exist in every respect;
rather, this is a demonstration of the ultimate reality.

For this proof of the non-existence of another continuum is common to the proof of non-duality (advaya); thus, contradiction with one's own words and the like is not restricted to a single case, nor is its resolution restricted to a single way.
Moreover, the dispelling of the darkness of the Vedānta has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya through the mere arising of various forms [of cognition].
Thus says the Bhāṣya on the Vārttika commentary: "That Self is his own experience, and that belongs to no one else," and so forth.

If it is argued that the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*) would then follow as a consequence, [we reply]: no, because of the cognition of diverse forms (*citrākārasaṃvedana*), and so forth. Indeed, the entire Vedānta position is merely a husk defiled by hatred; failing to perceive this, they do not even raise the objections found in those texts. For, in relation to other mental continua, everything included within conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) indeed passes away.
Thus, everything is entirely without confusion.
The Refutation of Other Continuums is completed.
